Tables with long-text columns do not get a raw task, because an IDMC STRING write would re-cut the text. Their raw object is a view with the same SELECT, recreated by DDL each cycle, after deleting any TABLE standing in its place.
evidence: raw-layer text byte-identical to the previous engine's; long-text parity checks passed

title: Guards around a cycle: long-text capacity before, truncation suspects after
text: - **Before landing:** query the source for the longest value of each long-text column, and abort if any exceeds the landing capacity (32,000 characters for JSON-typed BigQuery columns). - **After the full cycle:** compute `max(length(col))` for STRING columns and `max(length(JSON_VALUE(col)))` for JSON columns of every IDMC-written table. Exactly 255 or exactly 32,000 means probable truncation, so fail the cycle. - **When the guard trips on a column that grew:** move it to the JSON landing path, make the next layer a view, and delete the redundant copy task.
evidence: the guard found a 354-character column, which moved to the JSON path; a forced full run verified 49 rows longer than 255 intact

title: Truncate the targets of 0-row successes yourself, stage by stage
text: With the BigQuery V2 target in Bulk mode and "Write truncate", a task whose source returns 0 rows does not touch the target, so a table that drops from N rows to 0 keeps its stale rows. After each stage, run `TRUNCATE TABLE` on the target of every task that SUCCEEDED writing 0 rows. Go stage by stage (landing, then raw) so an emptied upstream cascades.
evidence: a table whose source dropped to 0 rows kept its stale rows; the guard's log showed the zero-row truncates

title: Reverse-ETL into PostgreSQL is a template task with an upsert target
text: Clone the template task. `$Source$` = the warehouse connection with `customQuery 'SELECT ... QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY <key> ORDER BY <built_at> DESC, <id>) = 1'`. `$Target$`: `targetConnectionId=<pgConnId>`, `targetObject = objectName = '<schema>/TABLE/<table>'`, labels `'<table>'`, pop `newObjectName`, `newObject=false`, empty `tgtObjectAttributes`/`runtimeAttrs`/`oprRuntimeAttrs`, `operationType='Upsert'`, `targetUpdateColumns=[<key>]`, `truncateTarget=false`. Write into a new schema beside the operational tables, and schedule it after the forward cycle.
evidence: first run SUCCESS (about 31,000 golden records); the reverse-ETL ran in every customer and full lane; the older in-app fan-out retired

title: SaaS upsert task: columns aliased to API names, Upsert on an external id
text: `$Source$`: the warehouse connection plus a `customQuery` whose column aliases are the SaaS API field names. `$Target$`: `targetConnectionId=<sfConnId>`, `targetObject = objectName =` labels `= '<SObject>'`, pop `newObjectName`, `newObject=false`, `operationType='Upsert'`, `targetUpdateColumns=['<ExtId__c>']`, `truncateTarget=false`. If the self-hosted agent's connector does not work, set the task-level `runtimeEnvironmentId` to a hosted runtime and drop `agentId`. Order the tasks parent before child.
evidence: the SaaS block ran last in every full lane; linked children verified by count

title: Guard every CRM upsert: count gate, test-identity exclusion, retention window
text: Append to every CRM/SaaS upsert query: - **a count gate:** push nothing unless this cycle's count of valid golden records is at least 80% of what the target already holds, so a broken upstream load never overwrites good CRM data; - **a test-identity exclusion** that matches the BI layer's test filter; - **a retention window** for child objects when the target's storage is small. Filter test identities at the source query: deleting them in the target is pointless while scheduled upserts re-create them.
evidence: the batch sync stopped adding test rows; the target stayed within storage until real-time test traffic filled it

title: Incremental append: insert only new ids with an anti-join and a dedupe
text: For append-only feeds: `operationType='Insert'`, `oprRuntimeAttrs.writeDisposition='Write append'`, `newObject=false`, and a `customQuery` that LEFT JOINs the target over a lookback window and keeps only ids not already present, deduplicated with `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY <id> ORDER BY <ts>) = 1`. Re-runs and overlapping schedules never duplicate rows.
evidence: idempotent loads verified on a 5-minute feed and on hourly snapshot tasks

title: Make full reloads incremental with a watermark MERGE
text: Replace truncate-and-reload SQL with a watermark store: read the watermark, MERGE rows whose change timestamp is later than watermark − lookback, then write back `MAX(change timestamp)`. The first run backfills and later runs process only the delta. It works for SQL run by a task's `customQuery` as well as for warehouse-native jobs.
evidence: proven on a development table (first run backfilled 266,643 rows, later runs processed the delta)

title: Evidence tasks: append-only snapshots, a once-per-day guard, and a run log written by load jobs
text: - **Daily snapshot:** a Write-append task whose SQL ends in `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM <target> d WHERE d.snapshot_date = CURRENT_DATE())`. An hourly schedule then writes once per UTC day. - **Run log:** after each lane, append one row per task run (`run_id, task, kind, target, rows_written, status, error, started_at, ended_at`) with a **load job**, not streaming, so rows are queryable and correctable at once. A failed log write must never mask the pipeline result. - **Keep append snapshots out of event-driven consolidated mappings:** an append-mode snapshot target folded into a multi-target mapping inherits that mapping's cadence, so in a per-event lane every event appends another snapshot row. Leave append snapshots in their own task on their own schedule (with the once-per-day guard), consolidate only truncate-loaded targets into event-driven mappings, check every target's write disposition in the swap spec, and run the new mapping twice in a row: the second run must not change row counts.
evidence: hourly snapshot runs wrote once per UTC day; run-log history queried by consoles and rehydrated after restarts; a readiness snapshot kept on its own task during a consolidation swap, with the double-run idempotency check part of the parity method (2026-09-29)

title: Flat-file ingest task: srcFFAttrs, file name in the object, header read at run time
text: Clone a proven flat-file landing task. Set `$Source$.srcFFAttrs = {"@type":"flatFileAttrs","delimiter":",","textQualifier":"\"","escapeChar":"","headerLineNo":1,"firstDataRow":2,"consecutiveDelimiterAsOne":false}`, put the file name in `extendedObject.object`/`objects[].name` and `label`, and set `fetchMode:"RUNTIME"` on `$Source$` and `$Target$` so the columns come from the file header at run time.
evidence: the file lane landed every rehearsed file

title: The plan file is the contract with the orchestrator; keep one per org
text: The generator writes `{"mode","landing":[{name,id,target,pg_table,chunked,chunk_capacity}],"raw":[...],"raw_views":[{target,sql}],"medallion":[{name,id,target,kind,reads}],"views":[{name,target,ddl}]}`. Ids are v2 task ids. A partial build (`--only`) must not overwrite it. Keep one plan per org, and treat copies baked into images or copied to other hosts as generated from it.
evidence: three copies drifted; one held the previous org's ids after a migration

title: Hard-coded ids and hosts in builders go stale after an org move
text: Resolve per-org ids (template task, connections, runtime environment, project and folder) by name inside the target org at start-up. Derive hosts from the login answer: the pod base comes from `serverUrl`/`baseApiUrl`, and the CAI host is `https://<pod>-cai.<rest of the pod host>`. A string replace of one pod literal silently stops working when the org moves pods.
evidence: builders still held the previous org's template, connection and runtime ids; one controller image had 72 ids baked in

title: Land a second schema into its own dataset; run large cross-cloud full reloads daily
text: When adding tables from a second schema whose names collide with tables already landed, land them into their own dataset (or with a prefix) using `<schema>/TABLE/<table>`. Full reloads of large tables across clouds cost egress on every run, so give them a daily schedule rather than an hourly lane unless a consumer needs fresher data.
evidence: first run SUCCESS (127,694 / 75,071 / 36,836 rows); about 240k rows per full reload

title: dbt-to-IDMC staged method and the one-technique mart migration
text: 1. Rebuild every mart from the old tool's **compiled** SQL into a scratch schema with zero changes, and require a byte-identical match of the existing DQ gate. That proves the tool was only an orchestrator, and makes the per-mart SQL the spec. 2. Migrate each mart the same way: a Query source with the mart's SELECT verbatim, executed by the warehouse; the same table name in a scratch schema as target; Insert with a manual TRUNCATE per run; poll by `runId`; exact parity plus `SHOW CREATE`. 3. Keep the legacy pipeline live until IDMC produces the tables.
evidence: a DQ gate 21/21 byte-identical; 16/16 marts at parity 0/0 with identical `SHOW CREATE`

title: Normalize drifting source schemas once, in a schema-adaptive landing view
text: When two producers write the same table under different column names (e.g. during concurrent redeploys of two app versions), make the landing view schema-adaptive. Introspect the physical columns, and re-create the view adding `<physical> AS <canonical>` for each missing canonical name. Downstream mappings keep referencing canonical names.
evidence: 21 tasks successful after the change; an old-schema test row aliased correctly, then removed

title: Recover lost transform SQL from the warehouse job history
text: If the SQL that built some marts is lost, search the warehouse's query/job history (e.g. BigQuery `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` jobs) for jobs whose destination table matches each mart. Recover the statement and validate it against the current table. That becomes the spec for new tasks or mappings.
evidence: 14 build statements recovered read-only; 12/14 exact parity (2 were stale one-off snapshots)

title: External runner: dependency waves, single-writer lock, guards and one lineage row per run
text: Before linear taskflows owned execution, a runner executed each cycle's tasks from outside IDMC: - dependency waves (landing, then raw, then medallion), in parallel within a wave; - a single-writer lock so overlapping cron runs never interleave; - a long-text capacity guard and a 255-character truncation guard; - one lineage row per run in a runs table. Every task still ran in IDMC through `POST /api/v2/job`. Measured: 46 tasks and about 1.5M rows in 12–13 min per cycle. Newer evidence: L-CDI-294.
evidence: the first live cycle 46/46 SUCCESS in 13 min; about 1.48M rows per cycle

title: Informatica expression idioms are not SQL
text: - Conditionals: `IIF(ISNULL(x), 'INSERT', x)`. `IIF` is the ternary and `DECODE` the switch. An empty string is not NULL. - Current time: `SYSTIMESTAMP()`. - Concatenation: `||`. A NULL operand makes the result NULL. - Date math: `DATEADD(DAY, -1, $$LOAD_DATE)`. Date key: `TO_NUMBER(TO_CHAR(d,'YYYYMMDD'))`. - `$$NAME` is a runtime parameter from a parameter set; `$NAME` is a system variable. Never hardcode dates, paths or connection names.
evidence: Documented, not live-proven: a third-party reference implementation; not live-probed; function availability across licence tiers unverified

title: Proven Expression cleanse formulas for name, email, phone, codes and a validity flag
text: - Name: plain `INITCAP(LTRIM(RTRIM(REG_REPLACE(full_name,' +',' '))))` lower-cases deliberate internal capitals (McDonald -> Mcdonald, MacArthur -> Macarthur) and capitalises lower-case particles (de la Cruz -> De La Cruz), so it fights any other writer that keeps them. A per-word rule works with VARIABLE ports evaluated in order before the output port: collapse whitespace with `REG_REPLACE`, count words, extract word i with `REG_EXTRACT(v_nm, '^(\S+ ){i-1}(\S+).*$', 2)`, keep the typed word when it matches `^\p{Lu}\p{Ll}+(\p{Lu}\p{Ll}{2,}){1,2}$` (Unicode classes are accepted), keep a typed lower-case particle when it is neither the first nor the last word, otherwise `INITCAP` the word; join with `||` and fall back to `INITCAP` for names longer than the number of word ports (8). Anchor `REG_MATCH` alternations and put the longest alternatives first: an unanchored `(de|der|...)` took the first branch for 'der' and failed the whole-string match, so 'van der' came out 'van Der'; write `^(della|del|der|das|dos|den|da|de|di|do|du|la|le|van|von|ter|ten|bin|ibn|al|el)$`. Use the same rule in every writer of the name (L-CAI-086), and prove it with a scratch probe mapping that writes only a parity table, fed by a SQL source that UNIONs fixed test names with every live value, before swapping the live mapping (same GUID, OVERWRITE import). - Email: `LOWER(LTRIM(RTRIM(email)))`. - Phone to E.164: nested `IIF` over `REG_REPLACE(phone,'[^0-9]','')`. 10 digits → `'+1'||d`; 11 digits starting with 1 → `'+'||d`; else `''`. Emit this canonical form on the first run: a format dimension can read green over non-canonical stored values (L-DQ-105). - Canonical code: `DECODE(LOWER(TRIM(tier)),'gold','Gold','silver','Silver','bronze','Bronze','Unknown')`. - Flag: `IIF(REG_MATCH(email_clean,'^[a-z0-9._%+-]+@[a-z0-9.-]+[.][a-z][a-z]+$'),'1','0')`. Newer evidence: L-DQ-161.
evidence: 52 rows transformed; changed-value counts per column verified; the validity flag exactly on the 4 malformed emails; the particle defect reproduced on a first probe run and disappeared with anchored, longest-first alternatives (2026-10-03)

title: Expression OUTPUT ports cannot reference other OUTPUT ports
text: In an Expression transformation, an OUTPUT port's expression cannot use another OUTPUT port: put intermediate values in VARIABLE ports. To put an apostrophe inside a string literal, concatenate `CHR(39)` (`'...' || CHR(39) || '...'`).
evidence: consolidated-mapping build notes

title: One source feeding both sides of a Joiner hangs with no error
text: Never let one source feed a Joiner's master and also (directly or downstream) its detail: the session hangs forever with no error. When two branches of the same pipeline must meet in a Joiner, set "Sorted Input" on the Joiner and put Sorters on both branches. Without that, the import itself fails ("Choose sorted input for <JNR> to join data from the same source").
evidence: a hung parity run had to be stopped; the rebuilt mapping passed

title: SCD Type 2 in seven steps, with a fixed-order change hash
text: 1. Read the increment by run id, not by date. 2. Look up the dimension `WHERE IS_CURRENT = TRUE` (surrogate key, stored hash, start date). 3. `NEW_HASH = MD5(<attributes in a fixed order>)`, never including a load timestamp, and never reordering the fields. 4. Filter `ISNULL(LKP_SK) OR NEW_HASH != LKP_RECORD_HASH`. 5. Route NEW vs CHANGED. 6. Update the old version (`EFF_END_DATE = DATEADD(DAY,-1,$$LOAD_DATE)`, `IS_CURRENT = FALSE`). 7. Insert the new version (`EFF_START_DATE = $$LOAD_DATE`, `IS_CURRENT = TRUE`, `RECORD_HASH`, the run id). Make expire-then-insert atomic.
evidence: Documented, not live-proven: a third-party reference implementation; not live-probed

title: Never drop a row silently: a structured reject sink and a reject-rate breaker
text: - **Reject sink:** every failed row goes to an ERROR table with the run id, source entity, business key, a reason of the form `<rule id> | <code> | <field>='<value>'`, and the full raw record, so it can be reprocessed. - **Breaker:** fail the quality step and abort the flow when the reject rate exceeds a threshold (e.g. 10%). - **Fail vs flag:** choose per rule. - **Dedup:** deduplicate facts with a Lookup on the natural key, so re-runs never double rows. - **Domains:** keep them in reference tables, not hard-coded lists.
evidence: Documented, not live-proven: a third-party reference implementation; not live-probed

title: Layering: RAW append-only, CURATED, ERROR, stamped in the ingest mapping
text: RAW is append-only (an immutable audit of every ingest, which lets you reprocess without re-fetching the source), CURATED is modelled and mutable, and ERROR holds rejects. Stamp every RAW row with the run id, source file name and load timestamp inside the ingest mapping itself, not afterwards.
evidence: Documented, not live-proven: a third-party reference implementation; not live-probed

title: Taskflow shape, an explicit error policy, and one parameterized definition
text: - **Shape:** a master flow runs INGEST → QUALITY → CURATED, with CURATED sequential (dimensions before facts) and parallelism only inside a stage. - **Error policy, stated up front:** ingest failure aborts all; a quality breach aborts; a curated failure aborts; per-row rejects within threshold route and continue. - **Parameterization:** use one definition plus a parameter set (the scheduler passes `$$LOAD_DATE`), not clones per date or environment. No endpoint, file format or upload mechanism for CDI parameter sets was captured.
evidence: Documented, not live-proven: a third-party reference implementation; not live-probed; no parameter-set endpoint captured

title: Transformation and object naming convention
text: - Transformations: `EXP_` expression, `LKP_` lookup (it also marks a round-trip hotspot), `FIL_` filter (pair each with a reject path), `RTR_` router (prefer it over two filters), `JNR_`, `AGG_`, `SRT_`, `SRC_`, `TGT_`. - Objects: `m_` mapping, `mt_` mapping task, `wf_`/`tf_` taskflow, kept 1:1 and same-named. With a generator, the spec file is the reviewable artifact, and an export's IMF is the read-back.
evidence: Documented, not live-proven: reference convention; used consistently by a generator on 2026-09-29

title: Decide where logic lives; SQL in a copy-data task is CDI SQL, not CDQ
text: Putting all logic in IDMC makes rules reusable, visible in lineage and editable by non-SQL users, at a pushdown cost. Keeping logic as warehouse SQL fits a headless build. Neither is an Informatica requirement: choose deliberately and write it down. When cleanse, dedup or DQ logic is warehouse SQL inside mapping tasks, describe it as CDI SQL, not as Cloud Data Quality, and say which steps are genuine CDQ assets.
evidence: an architecture review corrected labels; the copy-data design ran all cleanse and DQ as warehouse SQL

title: Define each shared metric once and point every task at it
text: When the same metric (e.g. lifetime value) is computed separately by a CRM sync, a real-time process payload and an app API, the numbers drift apart. Define it once as a warehouse view with an explicit formula, and make every mapping task and consumer read it.
evidence: two sample records went from three different values to one value everywhere

title: As few mappings as possible: never one task per table per stage
text: Group same-shaped loads into one parameterized object: a Dynamic Mapping Task with one job per table, or one mapping with several pipelines. Read each source table once and write every consumer from the same pipeline. Use a dependency map (reads, writes, dependencies per task) to pick merge groups: stages with no internal dependency merge first, and ordered chains (e.g. a parent-child SaaS chain) stay intact.
evidence: 159 tasks on one template, each with ~20 s fixed cost; an 11-mapping build replaced 40 of them

title: Copy-data template tasks are not real mappings; audit for the sprawl patterns
text: Tasks on `dsst__copy_data_new_tgt` keep all their logic in `customQuery` strings. An org can hold hundreds of tasks and zero designer mappings: empty two-box canvases, logic invisible to lineage and CLAIRE. Audit for: - land and raw as two tasks per table; - two pipelines reading the same source; - subset lanes that duplicate the full lane; - unscheduled shadow copies; - read-back chains before child upserts. Newer evidence: L-MIG-094.
evidence: a read-only audit parsed every task JSON in an export: 159/159 on the template, 0 real mappings

title: Anti-pattern: a second task per table that only casts to STRING
text: A raw-layer task that only CASTs every column to STRING doubles the task count, and with it the fixed cost and the jobs. Do the STRING projection in an Expression inside the ingest pipeline (one read, two writes), or as a view.
evidence: 10 tables × 2 tasks in an audited design

title: Anti-pattern: two task families reading the same source tables on separate schedules
text: When one pipeline lands a source table into the warehouse and a second one lands the same table into another store, each on its own schedule, the source is read twice and the copies drift in time. One mapping can read once and write both targets.
evidence: a warehouse landing family and a second-warehouse landing family (12–17 tasks) read the same tables

title: Anti-pattern: reading SaaS record Ids back before child upserts builds a long serial chain
text: Upserting parents, reading their record Ids back into the warehouse (SObject → `sf_ids_<object>`, Write truncate) and joining them into child upserts makes a chain that must run strictly in order. It set the floor of the whole lane. Upsert children with external-ID relationship fields (`<Parent>__r.<Parent_Ext_Id__c>`) instead, which removes the read-back tasks.
evidence: a DAG model put a 62-task lane in 15 stages with an 11-task SaaS chain as the floor

title: Consolidation: 11 mappings replaced 40 tasks; lanes of 16, 19 and 62 tasks became 7, 11 and 23 jobs
text: Each consolidated mapping ran in 28–87 s, while each task it replaced ran in 8–60 s, about 20 s of it fixed. For example, one ingest mapping (85 s) replaced 6 raw tasks of 34–38 s each. Fewer tasks also meant fewer jobs against the monthly cap and a shorter critical path. In production, after the live lanes moved to consolidated mappings (one ingest per source group, one golden-record mapping with many targets, key-sync or insert/update writers) and the 1 s BigQuery writer poll interval was added to every generated target (L-CDI-200): the per-record lane went from 16 tasks (98-108 s) to 7 jobs (84-96 s average, 82 s fastest), the activity lane from 19 tasks to 11 (about 145-159 s), and the full refresh from 62 tasks (about 20 min) to 23 jobs (258-358 s; 6.7 min before the poll-interval fix). Jobs per full-lane run fell from 63 to 24 against the monthly cap. A 59-transformation golden-record mapping with 11 targets ran a median 65 s (55-79 s, 27 of 27 successful); ingest mappings that read a source once and write several targets ran a median 24-41 s; single-target marts 8-27 s. Without the poll-interval setting the consolidated mappings were slower than expected, because each BigQuery target paid up to about 9 s of polling. Each step was accepted only with parity 0/0 against the old outputs (L-CDI-141) plus an independent check, and the replaced tasks were deleted only after 24 h green (L-CDI-142). The same mappings also ran 1.6-3x faster after the agent host went from 4 to 8 vCPU, but the poll-interval fix landed the same day, so the two effects are not separable.
evidence: measured runs per mapping and per replaced task; lane wall-clock before the swap, after it and after the poll-interval re-import (2026-09-30); 711 job runs over 24 h with 2 failures and per-mapping medians from the activity log (2026-10-01)

title: The consolidation plan shape: about 160 tasks to about 11 mappings, 10 taskflows to 3
text: The target design: - a parameterized ingest (a Dynamic Mapping Task, or a few multi-pipeline mappings) that reads each source once and writes typed landing, a STRING layer via an Expression, and a second store; - a golden-record mapping (cleanse → lookup/dedupe → golden → reverse-ETL targets); - a DQ mapping (rule checks → Router → Aggregator scorecard); - facts and marts mappings with Joiners and Aggregators; - a SaaS sync mapping with targets in load order and external-ID relationships; - a file-ingest mapping (validation Expression → Router: valid → ready and post, invalid → quarantine). Three taskflows: batch, a second application, files. Keep the work in the warehouse with full pushdown where possible.
evidence: an audit plan; the first 11 mappings built and parity-green; the remaining folds were planned

title: Every mapping task pays about 20 s of fixed time
text: Each task pays roughly 14 s of DTM startup plus about 5 s of cloud dispatch before it moves any data. A linear taskflow's duration is therefore about tasks × 20 s. The fixes are fewer tasks (consolidation) or concurrency, not larger machines.
evidence: a 62-task linear lane took 21.6–24.5 min for about 53k rows; the uniform 20 s/task model matched the session timings

title: Measured linear-taskflow durations on one agent
text: One Secure Agent, one task at a time: 50 tasks in 15 min; 62 tasks in about 19–24 min; a 16-task lane at a median of 4.6 min (max 5.5); a 19-task lane in about 6 min (max about 10). For sub-minute freshness use CDC (about 20 s median source to warehouse, p95 26 s).
evidence: medians and maxima from the activity log and the run log

title: Model a lane as a read/write dependency DAG
text: - **Reads:** its source object, or every `dataset.table` in its SQL with warehouse views expanded to base tables through `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS`. - **Writes:** its target. - **Dependencies:** for tasks *i < j* in lane order, *j* depends on *i* on read-after-write, write-after-read or write-after-write of one object. - **Special cases:** SaaS parent-child chains stay ordered; a task writing outside the warehouse waits for every earlier internal task; an unresolvable task is a barrier. Stage = longest-path level, and lane order is a valid topological order.
evidence: 0 unresolved tasks; 0 dependency violations against the executor

title: DAG staging at concurrency 4 cut a 62-task lane from about 21 to about 5.5 min
text: A 62-task lane had 15 stages: 20.7 min sequential, 5.3 min at concurrency 4, and 5.0 min at concurrency 8. The floor was an 11-task sequential SaaS chain, so shorten that chain before adding concurrency. A 16-task lane went from about 5.5 to 2.2 min, and a 19-task lane from about 7.4 to 2.3 min (estimates). Lanes that write the same targets must stay mutually exclusive.
evidence: a model at 20 s/task and a replay with measured durations (22m25s sequential vs 5m41s at concurrency 4)

title: Staged fan-out: start each task when its dependencies finish, at most N at once
text: The orchestrator starts every task itself (still `POST /api/v2/job`, so everything runs in IDMC) as soon as its dependencies are done, at most N at once, waiting on the first completion. A WARNING does not stop the lane, an error stops new starts, and tasks never started are NOT_RUN: the same verdict as the linear taskflow. Put it behind a flag whose off position restores the linear taskflow without a rebuild, and never switch mid-lane.
evidence: a 7-check lane smoke passed with the flag on; 0 dependency violations

title: Measured staged lanes at concurrency 4 on a shared 4-vCPU host
text: With at most 4 concurrent task jobs on a 4-vCPU host shared by two agents: a 16-task lane went from 462 s to 215–279 s, a 19-task lane from 357 s to 240–267 s, and a new record reached the golden table in 93 s instead of about 5 min. Cap concurrency near the host's vCPU count when agents share a host.
evidence: staged runs 16/16 and 19/19 SUCCESS

title: Before staging a full lane, add missing reads and keep it exclusive with subset lanes
text: A full lane that shares targets with smaller event lanes must never run at the same time as them. Its declared reads were incomplete (reads through raw views were missing), which would let a task start before its input landed. Fix the declared reads, or add barriers, before staging. If an IDMC schedule starts the full lane, unbind it and let the orchestrator start it inside the slot window.
evidence: 4 undeclared landing reads through raw views found before the switch

title: Event-driven lanes: coalesce, round-robin, guests beside a long lane with per-table conflict locks, priority, quiet window
text: - **Coalesce:** events increment a pending counter per lane instead of starting a run each, and the next run takes all pending events. - **Gap:** a minimum gap per lane limits starts (0 = start as soon as something is pending). - **Fairness:** alternate between event lanes. - **Guests, not one global lock:** a single run lock made a new record wait behind a 20-minute full refresh (1,027 s to its golden record in one case). Admit the critical event lane (new records) as a guest beside a running lane, one guest per lane, and block only real conflicts per table: the same mapping task, two writes of one table, or a read of a table another run is writing. Lower-value event lanes wait for a running full lane, which refreshes the same targets anyway. - **Priority:** new-record lane > file lane > activity lane > full lane. A lower-priority run starts no task that a waiting higher-priority task conflicts with (bounded wait, for example 600 s), keeps at most concurrency minus 2 tasks while a higher-priority run is active (1 while a new-record run is), and a global cap limits tasks across all runs. - **Critical path first:** in the new-record lane, tasks that are not on the path to the golden table start only after it lands. - **Soft-fail side tasks:** a failed DQ side task is reported (the run ends FAILED and alerts) but does not stop activation, reverse-ETL or SaaS tasks; one DQ task's heap OOM had stopped the whole downstream tail. - **One retry** per task for transient failures only, never for the job-cap error (L-CDI-205). - **Quiet window:** hold event lanes before a scheduled full run, and block full refreshes in a blackout window (plus 30 min before it). - **Drain:** while a drain file exists no run starts, so the orchestrator can be recreated between runs; every switch (plan, lanes, guests, blackout) drains, waits for idle, recreates the orchestrator and then runs one catch-up for the events queued meanwhile. Because IDMC refuses a second taskflow that runs the same tasks (REPO_17314), the orchestrator, not IDMC schedules, owns every start. - **Latency:** a 5 s scheduler tick keeps pickup latency low.
evidence: Before round-robin one event lane starved the other (2026-09-26); record to golden 76-88 s both solo and beside a full refresh (was up to 1,027 s); later lanes 38/38 and 23/23 tasks ok with guests and retries; a 93-check sandbox suite (side-by-side runs, per-table overlap, caps, soft-fail, drain, blackout) passed before every deploy (2026-09-29/30)

title: At most about 5 BigQuery readers per mapping on a small shared agent
text: Each BigQuery source (reader) takes Java heap in the DTM, and the heap is agent-wide, not settable per task. With 7–8 readers in one mapping the DTM died with heap / GC-overhead errors; 6 worked once, and at most 5 (the splitter targets 4) was reliable. Select only the columns a pipeline needs, give STRING reader fields a small precision (256; 4000 made the reader allocate huge row buffers), and split big specs into connected components.
evidence: OOMs with 7–8 readers; the splits then ran clean

title: Transient GCS-staging 5001 errors on parallel BigQuery runs
text: Launching many BigQuery-staged tasks in parallel produced transient GCS-staging errors (`5001` with 409/404) that cleared on a serial retry. Sometimes the data still landed. Check the target row count before treating a 5001 as a real failure.
evidence: rows present despite the error; serial retries cleared it

title: The monthly job cap: every task and taskflow run is one job
text: An org hit a cap of 10,000 jobs per month. The cap is invisible headless (license limits read `-1`, and neither the cap nor its lift appeared in the audit log), and CDC and CAI kept running. A linear taskflow of N tasks costs N + 1 jobs. An event lane of 16–20 tasks costs 17–21 jobs per event, and a 5-minute feed of 4 tasks costs 1,440 jobs per day. Levers: coalescing, fewer full runs, slower feeds, consolidation, and CDC/CAI for per-event freshness.
evidence: every lane failed within ~5 s with "You have exceeded your monthly limit of 10,000 jobs"; the license API showed all limits as -1

title: Quota breaker: pause lanes on the job-cap error, one probe, one alert per day
text: After each run, look for "monthly limit" in the run or task errors. If found: - pause the automatic lanes for a backoff (60 min), recording SKIPPED entries instead of failures; - after the backoff, let exactly one lane through as a probe: the same error pauses again, a success clears the pause; - send one alert per 24 h; - expose the blocked-until time on the health endpoint; - leave manual starts and relays that are not IDMC jobs ungated; - re-derive the pause from the run log after a restart.
evidence: the breaker un-paused by itself when the cap was lifted; 0 new alert mails across later events

title: CDI consumption is metered on compute hours per run, not data volume
text: Data Integration consumption is driven by runs × compute time, not by the volume of data moved. Fewer, better-packed mappings reduce metered time as well as job counts. For rates and licensing see the IPU domain.
evidence: a metering analysis (hedged: rates and tiers not re-verified here)

title: Cap concurrency near the host's vCPU count and select only the agent services you need
text: On a small host shared by two agents, 4 concurrent task jobs was the working point, and more mostly added contention. The agents contended for CPU, not memory. Give each agent its own OS user and systemd unit with memory limits and CPU/IO weights, add swap for idle JVM pages, and enable only the services and connectors the lanes need. Turn heavy catalog metadata services on only for scans (3.7 GB freed after deselecting them).
evidence: selecting all services pulled 18 GB of packages in 8 minutes, load 189 on 4 vCPU, swap exhausted; concurrency 8 gained little over 4

title: Change a task's SQL safely: back up, anchored replace, diff, then switch
text: 1. Save the `GET /api/v2/mttask/<id>` JSON, the current `customQuery` as a `.sql` file, and a v3 export of the task (lookup by path → export → zip). 2. GET the task, pop `orgId/createTime/updateTime/createdBy/updatedBy/agentId` and each parameter `id`, and replace the snippet in `$Source$.customQuery` only after asserting it occurs exactly once. Save the new SQL, then POST it back. 3. Diff the old and new SQL results in the warehouse before the live run. 4. Run the task once standalone, then patch the generator. Undo = POST the saved JSON.
evidence: display-text and name-rule changes applied this way, each with a backup; a standalone run with 663 rows succeeded and 0 failed

title: Shadow mode: build the whole chain against shadow datasets first
text: A generator's shadow mode writes every layer to shadow datasets (typed landing, raw, staging, gold) from shadow source views, as unscheduled `_shadow` tasks. Keep the shadow source views in their **own** schema, or a shadow build can silently redefine the views the live tasks read. Run it, compare it with the live outputs or a reference build, cut over only when clean, and delete the shadow objects afterwards.
evidence: a shadow cycle ran 46/46 without touching live views; the cutover followed shadow parity

title: Parity SQL: counts plus two-way EXCEPT DISTINCT on JSON-serialized rows
text: For each table pair: - compare `count(*)` on both sides; - compare `count(*) FROM (SELECT to_json_string(struct(<common cols>)) FROM a EXCEPT DISTINCT SELECT ... FROM b)` in both directions; - for duplicates, compare multisets: `GROUP BY` the JSON string with `count(*)`; - exclude run-time columns (`run_at, ingested_at, run_id, loaded_at, computed_at, refreshed_at, ...`); - for a mismatch, diff per column on the join key, with two sample rows for the first differing column.
evidence: "all identical" or per-table diff counts drove every cutover decision

title: Logic parity and frozen parity give both engines the same input
text: - **Logic parity:** point the shadow raw views at the live raw tables, so the new engine reads exactly what the old one read. - **Frozen parity:** snapshot the raw tables into a dataset, build a reference with the same SQL (`CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE AS`, in topological order), run the new engine on the snapshot, and compare as multisets. Frozen parity separates logic differences from data arriving mid-run. Keep text formats byte-identical where consumers parse them (e.g. `%.2f` numerics, ISO timestamps).
evidence: 23/23 outputs row-for-row identical before a cutover

title: Parity for marts that stamp now(): exclude the stamp, check freshness
text: Marts that set `run_at`/`ingested_at` with `now()` can never reach full-row parity with a live copy. Assert parity on all other columns (0 rows only in A, 0 only in B) and check separately that the timestamp is fresh. For heavy queries over federated or remote views, compute parity in one execution, e.g. `SELECT countIf(cnt != 2) FROM (SELECT ..., count() cnt FROM (<A> UNION ALL <B>) GROUP BY ...)`.
evidence: parity 0/0 excluding the stamp; the stamp fresh on every row

title: Cross-engine parity fingerprints: normalize, then counts and a keyset hash
text: Compute on both engines `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(DISTINCT key)` and an order-independent keyset hash: `BIT_XOR(FARM_FINGERPRINT(ARRAY_TO_STRING([...], '|')))` on BigQuery, `CHECKSUM_AGG(CONVERT(bigint, HASHBYTES('SHA2_256', CONCAT_WS('|', ...))))` on T-SQL. The engines hash and render NULL, decimals and dates differently, so normalize first: NULL → '', money to NUMERIC(18,2), dates as ISO UTC, the same TRIM, column order and delimiter.
evidence: dual-dialect fingerprint SQL used between two warehouses

title: Consolidation parity: parity-only dataset, original SQL at the same moment, idempotency double run
text: Build the new mappings in a separate folder, writing only to a parity dataset, and check at run time that no task target points at a live dataset. Compare each new target with the **original** task SQL run at the same moment (upstream references repointed), using two-way `EXCEPT DISTINCT`. Then run everything twice in stage order and compare run 1 with run 2, run-time columns excluded. Exclude parity datasets and `_v2` names from freshness and health checks meanwhile. Count a parity verdict only from runs that ended in state 1 AND rewrote the compared table: check that each table's `last_modified_time` is at or after the start of the run that should have produced it, record run id, state, start time and the table's last-modified time next to each diff, and treat a missing or older last-modified as 'not tested', never as 'no difference'. A mapping that failed with Java heap OOM on both test runs was reported idempotent and 0-diff because the compare read the tables of an earlier good run; it then failed 3 of 3 live runs.
evidence: 11 mappings: two-way EXCEPT DISTINCT = 0, and run 1 = run 2; a false 0-diff read from stale tables caught (2026-09-29)

title: The swap gate: story suite green, swap in place, plan v2, re-gate, then delete
text: 1. The application's end-to-end story suite at 100% on the current stack. 2. Retarget the new mappings to live targets (swap packages, same GUID). 3. Update the taskflows in place. 4. Switch the orchestrator to the new plan. 5. Run the story suite again. 6. Only then delete the old tasks, with an export backup. Each step has its own rollback: the saved workflow bodies, the old plan file, and the saved mapping packages.
evidence: a staged swap process with rollback for every step (applied up to the swap packages)

title: Swap tasks inside existing taskflows in place, keeping ids and schedules
text: For each workflow: 1. `GET /api/v2/workflow/<wfId>` and back up the whole body to a timestamped file. 2. Build the new task list. Every replaced task becomes its successor, once, at its first occurrence (`{"@type":"workflowTask","taskId":"<new>","type":"MTT","name":"<new>","stopOnError":..,"stopOnWarning":..}`); keep the others. 3. Re-sort by a stage function (landing, raw, staging, DQ, reverse-ETL, SaaS). 4. POST without the audit fields, then GET and check the task count and `scheduleId`. Rollback = POST each backed-up body.
evidence: plan/apply/rollback tooling with a backup per workflow (staged)

title: Generate the orchestrator's new plan with a generator that proves coverage and order
text: Before switching an orchestrator to consolidated mappings, generate its plan from the old plan plus the swap spec. Make the generator exit non-zero unless: - every replaced task's target is written by a new task; - every lane's new order is a valid topological order (reads after writers; raw views count as reads of their landing tables); - every replaced task in a lane has its successor in that lane. Run it with no network, inside the orchestrator's own image, and ship the plan as a separate file selected by an environment variable.
evidence: the generator ran sandboxed and emitted a plan, workflows and a report (staged)

title: Build the swap-ready package from the parity spec under the same mapping GUID
text: To point a parity-proven generated mapping at live tables, rebuild its package from the same spec: - set each target object to its live table; - rewrite parity-dataset references inside query sources to the live datasets; - keep the mapping GUID; - assert that no parity reference is left. Import it with OVERWRITE and re-read the task. POSTing new targets to the task instead is a silent no-op (L-CDI-050).
evidence: 11 swap packages imported SUCCESSFUL; tasks then showed the live targets

title: Before calling a task an orphan, check task-level schedules, app readers and orchestrator id lists
text: "Not in any taskflow" is not enough to call a task unused. Check its detail GET for a task-level `scheduleId` (the list hides it). Check whether any app endpoint or view reads its output table. Check whether an orchestrator or host script starts it by id: grep the baked plan, workflow files and host id files.
evidence: an "orphan" had its own hourly schedule and fed an app API; REPO_52013 on its delete

title: A task in no taskflow may be obsolete, not a bug: check whether its target became a view
text: An audit flagged a raw task in no taskflow as leaving a mart on a stale snapshot. Its raw object had become a live view over the landing table when that table's long text moved to the JSON path, so the mart read live data and the task was simply obsolete. Delete it; do not add it back to a taskflow, because it would overwrite the view with a table.
evidence: the audit's stale-data bug retracted the same day; a coverage map marked the task for deletion

title: Delete shadow and parity copies right after the proof
text: Unscheduled shadow tasks, duplicate tasks writing an unused dataset, and stray samples stay in the org long after the parity test. They inflate the design, confuse audits and the catalog, and make cleanup risky later. Delete them right after the comparison, with an export backup first.
evidence: 46 unscheduled shadow tasks, duplicate landing tasks and a stray sample pruned (160 → 94 tasks, export backup first)

title: One writer per org; read back after every write, including rejected tool calls
text: One lead session is the only one that logs in to each IDMC org and the only importer or publisher. Other sessions work read-only or host-side, coordinating with lease comments, heartbeats and DONE posts with evidence. Announce before any import. Read back after every write: a tool call rejected mid-run can already have executed server-side.
evidence: a migration and cutover run by one lead session; 68 repository deletes had landed from a tool call the user rejected mid-run

title: When CAI real time and a CDI batch write the same fields, both apply the same rule
text: If a real-time CAI process and a scheduled CDI task both write the same fields in a target system, the batch SQL must implement the same transformation rule. Otherwise the batch run minutes later silently undoes the real-time cleansing. When changing the rule, update both, prove the batch change with a full diff against the old SQL plus synthetic cases, and keep an undo of the previous task definition.
evidence: a full diff 701/701 rows with 0 changed columns, 12/12 synthetic cases, and 126/127 runs OK after the change

title: Retire or retarget load tasks before turning their target tables into views
text: If you replace a warehouse table with a same-name view (e.g. to switch consumers to a streaming source), every IDMC task still loading that table fails on each run. Stop or retarget the lane first (schedule end, taskflow removal), and keep the old table as a renamed history table for the view to union.
evidence: a 5-minute lane failed on every run until its schedule was really stopped

title: The BigQuery V2 writer cuts every STRING port to 255 characters
text: Tasks built over parameterized templates typed strings as `string(255)`, and the BigQuery V2 writer silently cut longer values, whatever the target schema. Tested without success: a `varchar(4000)` source view, `allowMaxFieldLength=true`, `retainFieldMetadata=true`, a pre-created `STRING(4000)` column, and Streaming instead of Bulk. Land long text into JSON-typed columns (L-CDI-153).
evidence: 585-character values intact in a CSV target and cut in BigQuery; `overriddenFields` 400; every variant tested stayed at 255

title: A pre-created JSON target column carries the full text up to 32,000 characters
text: When the pre-created BigQuery target column is typed JSON, IDMC writes the full text as a JSON string scalar up to 32,000 characters; longer values are cut to exactly 32,000. BYTES targets fail with `CMN_1081`, and "Write truncate" keeps the JSON schema across reruns. Read the text with `JSON_VALUE()` in views, fail a cycle on values of exactly 32,000, and serve the next layer as a view, since a STRING write would cut it again.
evidence: byte-exact live checks 176,175/176,175 and 26,067/26,067 rows; shadow and live cycles 46/46

title: Bulk + Write truncate needs GCS staging; Streaming mode cannot truncate
text: With the BigQuery V2 target in Streaming mode, truncate is not honoured and a second run appends. For full reloads use `writeMode` Bulk with `writeDisposition` "Write truncate". That needs a GCS staging path on the BigQuery connection, and the connection's service account needs `roles/storage.objectAdmin` on the bucket. A short bucket lifecycle rule (about 2 days) keeps staging files from accumulating.
evidence: a second Streaming run doubled a table (33,106 → 66,230); Bulk + truncate cycles were stable afterwards

title: truncateTarget=true was ignored on some BigQuery targets; use the write disposition
text: With BigQuery V2 as the target, `truncateTarget=true` on the task was ignored for some mappings and rows doubled on every run. Set `writeDisposition` "Write truncate" in `oprRuntimeAttrs`, or truncate each target yourself right before its run. If rows double on an Insert-mode mapping, also check the mapping model's `TruncateTable` property: with NO it appends.
evidence: gold tables doubled on every run (19 → 38 → 57) while other tasks with the same flag truncated

title: Never flip the BigQuery connection to Hybrid mode (4005)
text: Switching a BigQuery V2 connection from Simple to Hybrid mode broke all mappings on it. Keep Simple mode. For JSON columns, declare the fields as STRING instead (L-CDI-039).
evidence: the flip returned 200 and then every mapping failed with 4005 "Direct Read + Hybrid unsupported"

title: Booleans land as 'true'/'false' strings through the copy template
text: Through `dsst__copy_data_new_tgt`, PostgreSQL booleans land in BigQuery as STRING values `'true'`/`'false'`. Cast them in the next layer. A synthesized mapping reading PostgreSQL through JDBC rendered booleans as `'t'`/`'f'` and needed an Expression to match.
evidence: observed in landed tables; a JDBC read in a synthesized mapping rendered 't'/'f' (2026-09-29)

title: Streamed rows sit in the buffer and cannot be changed at once; write ledgers with load jobs
text: Rows written by BigQuery streaming inserts (e.g. per-run lineage rows) sit in the streaming buffer and cannot be updated or deleted by DML right away. Write such ledgers with load jobs (`load_table_from_json`, `WRITE_APPEND`), or schedule corrections later.
evidence: first-run row counts needed a delayed backfill; load-job rows were editable immediately

title: Type fidelity through generated BigQuery mappings: DATE in and out, the decimal(28,9) ceiling, and the lint rules worth enforcing
text: Writing a BigQuery DATE column from a synthesized mapping: the native DATE type showed as "unknown", and a `'YYYY-MM-DD'` string failed the Timestamp cast; send a STRING in the form `'YYYY-MM-DD 00:00:00'`. Reading one: a DATE column declared as DATE in a source query that feeds a Salesforce date field failed with 'Unknown native type for field ... Type: DATE'; `CAST(col AS TIMESTAMP)` (midnight) loads the same date. These survived exactly: unicode text, 255+ character strings, empty string versus NULL, embedded newlines, NUMERIC with scale 9, integers above 2^53 and microsecond timestamps. A 29-digit NUMERIC overflows the platform's decimal(28,9) and fails with TE_7007: cap or cast wide numerics in the source query. Encode the known runtime traps as a lint that blocks a build: Expression OUTPUT ports that reference other OUTPUT ports; one source feeding both sides of a Joiner without sorted input; more than about 5 warehouse readers per mapping; DATE and JSON declared types; dangling or duplicate links; non-ASCII characters and '--' comments in custom SQL.
evidence: Consolidated-mapping build notes (2026-09-29); a type diagnostic 8/8 rows exact with one TE_7007 overflow; a DATE failure on a draft build fixed with CAST AS TIMESTAMP; the lint (106 rules) found 3 real issues in existing specs (2026-10-03)

title: BigQuery query-source temp views: concurrent runs collide on the Temp_View<epoch-ms> name, and failed or stopped runs leave them behind
text: When a mapping with a BigQuery V2 query (custom SQL) source fails or is stopped, the connector's temporary view (`Temp_View<epoch-ms>`, created in the connection's dataset) stays behind. The name comes from a millisecond timestamp, so two DTMs that reach that step in the same millisecond collide: one fails with 409 'Already Exists', and the other's cleanup DELETE gets 404 although it has already written its rows, which stops a staged lane on a run that mostly succeeded. It is rare (1 in about 1,717 task runs at concurrency 4) but appears exactly when you raise concurrency: treat `temp_view[0-9]+` with 409 or 404 as transient and re-run the task once after about 20 s (L-CDI-205; it gets a new timestamp, and a truncate-load is idempotent), optionally with a 1-2 s start jitter between the tasks of one stage; never retry a quota error. List and drop leftover `Temp_View*` views after aborted runs and before catalog rescans: they otherwise pile up, get cataloged and appear in CLAIRE lineage answers (L-CDGC-149).
evidence: An orphan view dropped after a hung run (2026-09-29); one collision in about 1,717 staged runs at concurrency 4 with 409 and 404 in the two session logs; a catch-up ran 16 of 16 tasks in 113 s and the lanes stayed green after the one-shot retry (2026-09-29/30)

title: BigQuery time travel reaches back about 7 days: start snapshot tasks early
text: To backfill a daily snapshot table from history, `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF` reaches back only about 168 hours, and tables recreated in between cannot be read at older times. Start daily snapshot tasks early, in append mode.
evidence: a partial backfill; days older than the window could not be rebuilt

title: PostgreSQL source objects need the <schema>/TABLE/<table> path; a cold catalog is not a blocker
text: For the native PostgreSQL connector as `$Source$`, the object path is `<schema>/TABLE/<table>` or `<schema>/VIEW/<view>`. `public/<table>` fails with `SDK_APP_COM_20000` "Incorrect list of path is populated with size: 1". Bare names, `public.<table>`, quoted identifiers and `db.schema.table` give "Object(s) [X] not found": a cache-only lookup. With the right path, the adapter resolves the object at run time with no prior UI browse. The connection has no schema parameter.
evidence: 33,106 rows landed with 0 errors once the path was right; PG statement logging had shown no query reaching the database before

title: The PostgreSQL connector truncates text and cannot land jsonb: land from ::text views
text: The native PostgreSQL connector types text as `string(255)` and cannot land `jsonb` or `json`. Create a view in a dedicated source schema that selects every column, with `jsonb::text` for the JSON ones, and land from `<schema>/VIEW/<table>` into JSON-typed warehouse columns. Tables without such columns land from `public/TABLE/<table>`. The views are additive and reversible.
evidence: long-text parity checks passed after the switch

title: Native PostgreSQL connector type limits (enum, json, arrays) need cast views
text: The native PostgreSQL connector raised "native type system does not support the data type [<ENUM>]" and "could not identify an equality operator for type json", and skipped array columns. Cast such columns to text in a source view before landing or profiling them.
evidence: recorded connector errors

title: Target-port NOT NULL flags are baked into a cloned mapping
text: A mapping cloned from one target type carries `notNull` on its target ports regardless of the live target's nullability, and making the target column nullable does not help. Fix it at the source: a view that coalesces nullable text columns (keep keys and timestamps native), with the mapping source repointed to `<schema>/VIEW/<view>`.
evidence: a run failed "Cannot set null to non-nullable column #N"; after a view repoint it ran SUCCESS 52/52

title: Create-new-at-runtime targets in Insert mode append duplicates on re-runs
text: A mapping whose target is created at run time, in Insert mode, creates the table on the first run and appends the full row set on every later run. Truncate first, or use an upsert. If a table with an older schema already exists, the run does not rebuild it and hits column mismatches: drop it first. In cloned template packages the mapping's target session property `TruncateTable` (some entries spell it `Truncate Table`) can be NO, which makes every run append its full row set (a re-fired task doubled its target from 10 to 20 rows): patch both spellings to YES in the mapping model and recompute the package checksums before importing; the engine then truncates before load with no external pre-step (L-CDI-155).
evidence: source 52 = target 52 after one run; duplicates on re-runs; write failures cleared after dropping the old tables; re-runs doubled a target 10 -> 20 before the TruncateTable patch, and it stayed at 10 across repeated re-fires and 18 scheduler-fired runs after it (2026-07-09)

title: An upsert writes every mapped column; protect non-empty values at the target
text: An IDMC upsert writes all mapped columns, so an empty source value can blank a populated target field. Where the contract is "only overwrite with non-empty values", enforce it at the target with a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger that keeps the old value when the new one is empty, or leave those columns out of the source SQL.
evidence: reverse-ETL moved to IDMC with the "non-empty only" contract kept

title: Truncate-then-reload flaps to 0 rows for readers mid-run
text: A mapping that truncates its target and then reloads it non-transactionally leaves a window where readers see 0 rows. For tables read continuously, load a staging table and swap or rename, or reload inside a transaction, and resample during runs to catch it.
evidence: live resampling caught a dimension at 0 rows mid-reload

title: A post-only-valid task with truncateTarget=true on a system-of-record table is a wipe risk
text: A task that posts validated rows into a system-of-record table (e.g. accounts receivable) with `truncateTarget=true` may empty that table on the next run, including a run over an almost-empty file. Use Insert or Upsert without truncate, and make postings idempotent in the database: a `BEFORE INSERT` trigger that skips a row whose business key already exists.
evidence: a flagged configuration on an accounting table (an open risk, not an observed wipe)

title: Salesforce targets: API v64+, hosted runtime if needed, parents first, external-ID relationships
text: - Use a Salesforce connection on API version 64 or newer. If the Secure Agent's Salesforce connector misbehaves, run those tasks on a hosted runtime. - Upsert on external ids, with the source columns aliased to API field names. Checkbox fields need 1/0, and the connector dropped SOAP long fields. - Order parents before children, and map merged duplicates to the golden survivor's key. - Prefer child upserts through external-ID relationship fields over Id read-back tasks (L-CDI-118). - Gate every upsert on DQ volume (L-CDI-091). - For live counts when both a batch read-back and a real-time path write the CRM, count the read-back plus the real-time upserts newer than the last read-back (the read-back alone missed 19 recent records; L-CAI-113). - **One mapping can replace the whole chain:** eleven serial Salesforce copy tasks (accounts, account-id read-back, contacts, contact-id read-back, child objects, activities, invoices, a DQ scorecard object) were folded headless into one mapping with eleven flows in the old parent-before-child order, each an Upsert on an external id with nulls not sent, non-bulk, fields mapped by name and the source SQL copied verbatim; edit it by exporting, changing the source customQuery and re-importing OVERWRITE. The Salesforce step took 85-92 s for about 3,100 rows to 11 targets and made about 30-40 counted Salesforce API calls per run (one login per flow, upserts in batches of 200); jobs per lane run fell from 11 (full) or 5 (event lane) to 1, about 175 fewer a day. Parity before the swap: the SQL columns equal the mapping's source ports, target ports and Salesforce fields for every flow; an updates-only test run (created-since = 0 on every object); after the live run Salesforce equals the SQL output for every source key. Keep the old tasks as the rollback path for a week.
evidence: an 11-task SaaS block ran in every full cycle; 642 contacts plus related objects written; 7 lane runs after the one-mapping swap all SUCCESS, Salesforce = SQL for 8 objects (15 to 748 rows each) with 0 missing and 0 mismatches, 0 records created by the test run (2026-10-03)

title: JDBC V2 targets ignore truncateTarget: use runtimeAttrs "Pre SQL" (with the space)
text: A task writing through JDBC V2 does not honour `truncateTarget`. For a full reload, set the target's `runtimeAttrs` to `{"Pre SQL": "TRUNCATE TABLE <t>"}`; the key needs the space, and `preSQL`/`PreSQL` are silently ignored. The MySQL JDBC jar goes in the agent's `ext/connectors/thirdparty/informatica.jdbc_v2/common`. The Pre SQL runs before the source is read, so a failed read leaves the target empty: see L-CDI-208 before relying on it for objects that downstream readers refresh from.
evidence: a landing lane into a MySQL-protocol warehouse ran full reloads this way; a failed source login left a lane's targets empty after the truncate (2026-09-26)

title: ClickHouse through JDBC V2: truncate, string precision and UInt64 quirks
text: - `truncateTarget:true` can report SUCCESS and leave 0 rows. Set it false and run an explicit `TRUNCATE TABLE` before each Insert-mode run. - ClickHouse `String` reports JDBC precision 0 ("Length/Precision must be > 0"). Cast outputs with `toFixedString(col,N)` in the source query; JDBC V2 strips the padding on write. - `UInt64` reads as NULL, so cast it with `toInt64`. - Use the `-shaded` driver jar, with `http_connection_provider=HTTP_URL_CONNECTION` in the URL.
evidence: SUCCESS with 0 rows when truncateTarget was true; clean loads after the casts

title: Flat-file connections: CSVFile type, placeholders for empty fields, agent-readable directory
text: - Create flat-file connections with type `CSVFile`; the native `FLATFILE` type gave `APP_10519`. - The directory must be readable by the agent's OS user. - That reader rejected empty fields (`FR_3085` null character). Write a placeholder such as `(blank)` for empty cells and turn it back into NULL in the cleanse step. - Write files to a temp name and rename them into place atomically.
evidence: the file lane landed every rehearsed file; the cleanse step showed the restored NULLs

title: CDI mapping authoring is UI-only; one mapping must be authored in the UI first
text: The belief was that new mappings need the designer canvas ("build once in the designer, run over REST"), and that headless work needs one UI-authored seed. Tasks over the parameterized bundle templates (2026-09-23) and synthesized IMF mappings (2026-09-29) removed both claims. `POST /api/v2/mapping` is still not a create route (L-CDI-020). Was believed 2026-06-27 to 2026-09-22; overturned by L-CDI-003, L-CDI-021, L-CDI-033.
evidence: Was believed 2026-06-27 to 2026-09-22; overturned by L-CDI-003, L-CDI-021, L-CDI-033

title: v2-created mapping tasks do not surface in a v3 type=='MTT' scan
text: A scan saw 0 MTTs while the tasks ran hourly. Later reads listed all of them; the earlier result was probably a filter or paging artifact. Was believed 2026-09-23; overturned by L-CDI-012.
evidence: Was believed 2026-09-23; overturned by L-CDI-012

title: The v2 task resources exist on every pod
text: `/api/v2/dss`, `dtemplate`, `dmask`, `dreplicate`, `plan` and `fileListener` were assumed universal. They mount per pod and per licensed engine. Was believed July 2026; overturned by L-CDI-015.
evidence: Was believed July 2026; overturned by L-CDI-015

title: Moving an asset to another project is a UI Explore action
text: FRS `MoveEntities` moves objects headless, and runs key off immutable ids, so moves are harmless to running pipelines. Was believed 2026-08-19; overturned by L-CDI-016.
evidence: Was believed 2026-08-19; overturned by L-CDI-016

title: Headless CDI data movement is walled (a cold PostgreSQL source cannot resolve)
text: The verdict: template sources browse at run time, a task carries no field array, and a never-browsed PostgreSQL source cannot resolve, so a UI browse or catalog seeding would be needed. The object path `<schema>/TABLE/<table>` and cloned template tasks moved data headless the same day. Was believed 2026-09-22 to 2026-09-23; overturned by L-CDI-021, L-CDI-162.
evidence: Was believed 2026-09-22 to 2026-09-23; overturned by L-CDI-021, L-CDI-162

title: Mapping tasks, taskflows and schedules for a redesign are UI-only
text: Tasks were cloned headless (`mtTask.json` + the `iics` CLI) and schedules were created and bound over v2. Was believed early July 2026; overturned by L-CDI-025, L-CDI-075.
evidence: Was believed early July 2026; overturned by L-CDI-025, L-CDI-075

title: A mapping's connection and SQL are compiled into a binary bin/@3.bin that cannot be edited
text: The IMF file is JSON text. It was edited and later synthesized from scratch. The part that still stands: package edits did not change a mapping's connector **type** (L-CDI-031). Was believed 2026-07-05 to 2026-09-22; overturned by L-CDI-027.
evidence: Was believed 2026-07-05 to 2026-09-22; overturned by L-CDI-027

title: Hand-built import packages are always rejected with MigrationSvc_030
text: Packages built from scratch import SUCCESSFUL when `exportMetadata.v2.json`, the project and folder entries and the checksums are right. `MigrationSvc_030` is an empty or invalid multipart. Was believed 2026-06-28 to 2026-09-28; overturned by L-CDI-032.
evidence: Was believed 2026-06-28 to 2026-09-28; overturned by L-CDI-032

title: There is no REST read-back or diff of a mapping's internals
text: Exporting a mapping returns its IMF JSON, which can be read, diffed and regenerated. A written spec is still the best review artifact. Was believed 2026-07-26; overturned by L-CDI-027.
evidence: Was believed 2026-07-26; overturned by L-CDI-027

title: Scheduling and monitoring mapping tasks requires the Administrator UI
text: `POST /api/v2/schedule` returns 200 and creates a real schedule, `scheduleId` binds it, and the activity log monitors every run. Was believed early July 2026; overturned by L-CDI-073, L-CDI-075.
evidence: Was believed early July 2026; overturned by L-CDI-073, L-CDI-075

title: Taskflow creation is UI-only
text: Linear taskflows are created and updated with `POST /api/v2/workflow` and need no publish. Advanced-taskflow publish is still walled (L-CDI-070). Was believed July 2026 (`/public/core/v3/taskflow` 404); overturned by L-CDI-069.
evidence: Was believed July 2026 (`/public/core/v3/taskflow` 404); overturned by L-CDI-069

title: Binding a schedule over v2 is untested; plan a UI fallback
text: Bind and unbind by POSTing `scheduleId` (or null) worked with read-back in two orgs. Was believed 2026-09-28 (a draft runbook); overturned by L-CDI-075.
evidence: Was believed 2026-09-28 (a draft runbook); overturned by L-CDI-075

title: Long text can only be kept by chunking into 250-character columns or by a Fields-tab edit
text: The interim design landed long text as 16 × 250-character chunk columns re-joined in a view. JSON-typed target columns replaced it the same afternoon. Was believed 2026-09-23 to 2026-09-24; overturned by L-CDI-153.
evidence: Was believed 2026-09-23 to 2026-09-24; overturned by L-CDI-153

title: Reverse-ETL into the app database needs a UI-authored mapping
text: A template task with a warehouse query source and a PostgreSQL upsert target delivered reverse-ETL headless. Was believed 2026-09-24; overturned by L-CDI-089.
evidence: Was believed 2026-09-24; overturned by L-CDI-089

title: A raw task in no taskflow means the downstream mart reads stale data
text: The raw object had become a live view over the landing table, so the task was obsolete, not a bug. Was believed 2026-09-29 (morning audit); overturned by L-CDI-147.
evidence: Was believed 2026-09-29 (morning audit); overturned by L-CDI-147

title: REST-started agent jobs start on a ~3-minute job-poll cadence
text: On the agents used from 2026-09-23, dispatch took about 5 s and a task's fixed cost was about 20 s. Treat minutes-long dispatch as an agent problem to investigate. Was believed 2026-08-20 (one agent; 15 serial tasks ≈ 45 min); overturned by L-CDI-121.
evidence: Was believed 2026-08-20 (one agent; 15 serial tasks ≈ 45 min); overturned by L-CDI-121

title: Swapping a mapping's target connection to another warehouse later is a quick change
text: Cross-connector retargets of tasks silently reverted, and target changes on tasks over real mappings are no-ops. Retargeting means changing the mapping. Was believed 2026-06-27 (a plan); overturned by L-CDI-050, L-CDI-031.
evidence: Was believed 2026-06-27 (a plan); overturned by L-CDI-050, L-CDI-031

title: The first mapping for a new connector pair must be authored in the UI
text: A generator built mappings with PostgreSQL sources and BigQuery targets from harvested exemplars, with no UI seed for that pair. Adapters never tried (Salesforce and PostgreSQL targets, flat-file sources) remain unproven. Was believed 2026-07-07; overturned by L-CDI-033.
evidence: Was believed 2026-07-07; overturned by L-CDI-033

title: A mapping task can be run through POST /public/core/v3/jobs with taskFederatedId
text: One July record says `POST /public/core/v3/jobs {"taskFederatedId":"<id>","taskType":"MTT"}` returned a runId, polled at `GET /public/core/v3/jobs/<runId>`. No other source reproduces it. Use `POST /api/v2/job` with the v2 `taskId` (L-CDI-056).
evidence: a single report of 22 runs; the same tasks are recorded elsewhere as run through `POST /api/v2/job`

title: Whether an advanced taskflow can be published over REST
text: No route is known that publishes an advanced taskflow created by API. Whether a body swapped into a designer-created shell publishes was not settled. Build on linear taskflows or controller staging (L-CDI-069, L-CDI-125).
evidence: July: every publish route 404; one July report of `publicationStatus=published` read back over REST, with no endpoint named; September: `asset/v1/publish` faulted `AvrEntryNotFoundFault` for API-made taskflows

title: Whether truncateTarget=true on a PostgreSQL target truncates or is ignored
text: Do not rely on either reading. Never set `truncateTarget=true` on a system-of-record table, and make postings idempotent in the database (L-CDI-169).
evidence: one source states the PostgreSQL target ignores truncateTarget; another flags a task with it as a wipe risk; no observed wipe

title: Prove which org you are in with a live read before any delete
text: Before a delete batch, read the org live: `GET /api/v2/org` (id and orgUUID) and the session-service user endpoint `/session-service/api/v1/session/User` (name and orgId; its exact host was not recorded), and make destructive scripts assert the expected org id before their first call. When two orgs are in play, pin the org explicitly in every script instead of relying on a default.
evidence: the owner stopped a cleanup to ask which org it targeted (2026-09-28)

title: Clean an org in five steps: prove it, agree a keep list, back up, delete in order, read back
text: (1) Prove the org. (2) Agree explicit KEEP and DELETE lists by id, and move into KEEP anything a KEEP object uses. (3) Back up everything on the DELETE list. (4) Delete in dependency order, matching by id (frsGuid), never by name. (5) Log each write with its read-back, tell the migration lead before each batch, and never delete while an import runs. Undo = re-import the backup package with REUSE, then republish CAI; agents and runtime environments must be re-registered.
evidence: one pass removed 81 of 83 CAI objects, 18 mapping tasks, 18 mappings, 25 DQ assets, 9 connections, agents, runtime environments, schedules and 29 users with 0 KEEP objects touched (2026-09-28)

title: FRS DeleteEntities: batch delete with a result code per item
text: `POST https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/frs/v1/DeleteEntities` with header `IDS-SESSION-ID: <v2 icSessionId>` and body `{"artifactIds":["<frsGuid>", ...]}` returns a code per item: `FRS_200` deleted, `FRS_082` still published or out of date (unpublish first), `FRS_087` project not empty (delete its contents first); a later read gives `FRS_070` not found. With `INFA-SESSION-ID` instead, FRS answers with the login page. An older body, `{"deleteSpec":{"sourceSpecArr":[{"sourceEntityId":"<id>"}]}}` on `/frs/api/v1/DeleteEntities`, was tried once and its outcome was not recorded. Supersedes L-CLEAN-031.
evidence: per-item codes and FRS_070 read-backs; 80 of 83 legacy CAI objects in one pass (2026-09-28)

title: Check what uses an object before deleting it
text: FRS `POST .../frs/v1/GetInboundDocRefs` (who references this document) and `POST .../frs/v1/GetAllDependencies` (what it depends on) give exact used-by checks, and `GET /public/core/v3/objects/<id>/references?refType=usedBy` is a second source. Move any candidate that a KEEP object uses back into KEEP; an address-verification entity stayed because a kept mapping used it. FRS `$metadata` needs `Accept: */*`; the request bodies of the two FRS actions were not recorded.
evidence: used-by checks kept a dependency out of the delete list (2026-09-28)

title: Delete a single repository object with FRS `BaseEntities`, not `Documents`
text: `DELETE https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/frs/api/v1/BaseEntities('<frsGuid>')` with `IDS-SESSION-ID` (the call the Explore UI makes) deletes DBMI tasks (undeploy first), CAI processes (unpublish first), taskflows and profiles, answering 204. `DELETE .../frs/api/v1/Documents('<id>')` gives 403. Supersedes L-CLEAN-030, L-CLEAN-033.
evidence: 204 on DBMI tasks, CAI processes and profiles (2026-09-26 to 2026-09-29)

title: v2 DELETE routes and how to read them back
text: With `icSessionId` on the v2 `serverUrl`, `DELETE /api/v2/{mttask|mapping|connection|agent|runtimeEnvironment|schedule|workflow}/<id>` returns 200. A read-back 403 means gone; a deleted schedule's GET returns an empty 200 shell, so check the `GET /api/v2/schedule` list instead. Resolve a task's v2 id from its v3 id through `frsGuid` and a mapping's through `assetFrsGuid`; a mapping deletes only when its `tasks[]` is empty. `/api/v2/dtemplate/<id>` is a wrong path (404 HTML), and `DELETE /public/core/v3/objects/<id>` returned 404. Supersedes L-CLEAN-028.
evidence: 200 per delete with counts falling (mappings 123 to 61, 2026-08-20); read-backs across a full org cleanup (2026-09-28)

title: A connection delete is blocked first by mappings (REPO_10242), then by catalog sources
text: `DELETE /api/v2/connection/<id>` returns 403 `REPO_10242` while any mapping still references the connection; delete those mappings first. If the error then becomes a generic 'The asset is used by another asset', a CDGC catalog source holds the connection: remove the source (the definition delete is a UI step) and retry.
evidence: error progression observed on two connections (2026-08-20)

title: REPO_52013: the mapping task still has its own schedule
text: A v2 DELETE of a mapping task that has a task-level schedule fails with `REPO_52013`. Treat it as a sign the task is live: find the binding in the task detail (`scheduleId`), check who reads its output, and unbind deliberately only if the task really must go.
evidence: REPO_52013 on a delete attempt (2026-09-29)

title: Delete users with `DELETE /public/core/v3/users/<id>` (204)
text: `DELETE https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/saas/public/core/v3/users/<userId>` (header `INFA-SESSION-ID`) returns 204. Back up `GET /public/core/v3/users` to JSON first, and keep the `CAI_Anonymous_<orgIdV3>` system user (anonymous `/active-bpel/public/rt` calls need it) and any service user a live process or catalog scanner signs in as (grep the hosts and configs first). In-place edit (PUT or PATCH) remains unproven, so an edit is delete plus re-create. Supersedes L-CLEAN-029.
evidence: 29 users deleted and read back (2026-09-28)

title: Re-create a user with `name` and `groups`, and test one seat before a batch
text: `POST /public/core/v3/users` with `{"name":"<login>","firstName":"<first>","lastName":"<last>","email":"<email>","groups":["<groupId>"]}`: the identity key is `name` (`userName` gives 400), `groups` is a list of plain id strings, and at least one role or group is required. Snapshot before any batch delete-and-recreate and test the recreate on one seat first, because a wrong body once left 27 seats deleted.
evidence: 400 on the wrong key; one batch that lost 27 seats (2026-07-09)

title: Unpublish CAI assets before deleting them, in dependency order
text: `POST https://<pod>-cai.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/active-bpel/asset/v1/unpublish` with `Content-Type` and `Accept` both `application/vnd.api+json` and body `{"data":{"type":"unpublish","attributes":{"assetPaths":["Explore/<project>/<folder>/<name>.<TYPE>.xml"]}}}` returns `data.id`; poll `/active-bpel/asset/v1/unpublish/<id>/Status` and read each item. Unpublish processes first, then app connections, then connectors (up to 199 paths per call). A published asset refuses the FRS delete with FRS_082.
evidence: 59 legacy assets unpublished, then deleted (2026-09-28); the same order in a second org (2026-09-29)

title: CAI assets stuck with duplicate runtime rows or no runtime entry cannot be deleted
text: If the CAI runtime holds two catalog rows for one asset, publish and unpublish both fault with 'singleton sequence ... 2 items'; an asset with no runtime entry faults with `AvrEntryNotFoundFault`. Both stay flagged published, so FRS refuses the delete (FRS_082) and their projects cannot be emptied (FRS_087). This needs Informatica support or a UI attempt.
evidence: 2 of 83 legacy CAI objects left behind (2026-09-28)

title: Delete in dependency order
text: CAI unpublish (processes, then app connections, then connectors), CAI assets, taskflows (after unbinding their schedules), mapping tasks, mappings, DBMI tasks (stop, undeploy, then FRS delete), DQ assets and profiles, connections (after a used-by check), agents, runtime environments, schedules, empty folders, empty projects, users. For CDGC, delete glossary items and purge the catalog sources over REST, then delete the source definitions in the UI.
evidence: the order held across a full org cleanup and a one-app removal in two orgs (2026-09-28/29)

title: Back up everything a cleanup touches, and log each write
text: Take v3 export packages of the connections, design content, CAI and MDM configuration you will delete (stored privately, because packages can hold secrets); MDM business records as JSON; CDGC glossary and catalog content as JSON; and the user list. The MDM search returns at most 10,000 records per query (`POST https://<pod>-mdm.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/search/public/api/v1/search` with `{"search":"*","entityType":"<be>","recordOffset":0,"recordsToReturn":1000}`, Bearer JWT plus `IDS-SESSION-ID` and `X-INFA-ORG-ID`), so export larger entities as a union of term and prefix-wildcard queries and check the union count against the entity count. Append every delete and its read-back to a log file.
evidence: four backup packages, about 27,000 MDM records and the CDGC content saved before the deletes (2026-09-28)

title: A REST delete of a CDGC catalog source only purges it; the definition stays
text: `DELETE https://cdgc-api.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/ccgf-catalog-source-management/api/v1/datasources/<id>` purges the harvested metadata (a bulk purge job) and leaves the definition listed; delete the definition in Metadata Command Center, and back up the source JSON first. A delete while a scan is stuck returns 400 'Job is in progress ... cancel current job', with no cancel API, and de-registration can lag many minutes. Supersedes L-CLEAN-032.
evidence: purges confirmed with the definitions still listed (2026-09-29); 400 on a stuck scan (2026-06-29)

title: Never delete platform content
text: Keep Add-On Bundles (FRS reports `delete:false` even for an admin, and tasks built on a bundle template break without it), the Default project and the system API policy, the CDGC home dashboard and widgets, the system classifications, policies and roles, the `CAI_Anonymous_<orgIdV3>` user, stock samples and utilities (`dsst__*`, `B2B_Gateway_*`, `infacore_*` DQ utilities that kept DQ mappings may reference), and the Reference360, Business360 and MultidomainMDM system content.
evidence: keep list of a full org cleanup (2026-09-28); utility dependency risk (2026-08-20)

title: A rejected or interrupted tool call may already have run: read back and report
text: When a user rejects or interrupts a call mid-run, the server-side work may still have happened (68 FRS deletes had landed). Read back the real state and report exactly what happened before continuing.
evidence: 68 deletes found after the rejection (2026-09-28)

title: 'Objects Listing Failed: null' (500) while another session writes: retry
text: `GET /public/core/v3/objects` returned a one-off 500 'Objects Listing Failed: null' while a peer session was importing into the same org, and a retry worked. Retry list calls once or twice before treating the error as real, and do not run large deletes during another session's import or cutover.
