title: An FRS PATCH of a document's `customAttributes` returns 204 and changes nothing
text: Read back every write; a 204 from FRS is not proof that anything changed.
evidence: read-back after the 204 (2026-09-28)

title: Select what to delete by owning agent or runtime, never by name
text: Names mislead: a task named like one program can belong to another. Build the delete list from the runtime environment or agent each task runs on, keep an explicit denylist of what to keep, re-check each object's binding immediately before deleting it (other sessions may be creating assets meanwhile), and verify that the kept program still works after each wave.
evidence: kept program verified intact after each delete wave while a peer added objects (2026-08-19/20)

title: In an org you do not own, change only what you created, and prove the rest is untouched
text: Relocate or modify only the assets your sessions created, and compare a location count of everything else before and after. Projects and folders cannot be tagged, so the ownership marker is a dedicated project or folder plus an asset tag; organization-level objects (connections, schedules, runtime environments) carry a name or description marker. Get the owner's OK before writes and log each write with its undo.
evidence: non-owned location counts identical before and after a move of 95 assets (2026-09-24)

title: Remove one application's whole footprint in dependency order
text: Export with dependencies first; unbind its schedule; delete its taskflow; remove its tasks from any shared taskflow (GET the workflow, filter `tasks[]`, POST it back); delete its mapping tasks by v2 id; unpublish, then FRS-delete, its CAI processes; stop and undeploy, then FRS-delete, its DBMI tasks; delete its profiles, glossary domain and terms, and catalog source (purge now, definition later in the UI); delete its connections last, after a used-by check. Off-platform, comment out its IDMC cron jobs (with an undo file), switch its app-side calls off and label it honestly, then verify at the next scheduled slots that no run of it happened on any agent.
evidence: zero runs of the removed app on either agent at the next scheduled slots (2026-09-29)

title: Delete superseded tasks only after a chunked export backup and a name-to-id map
text: Export the tasks with v3 export in chunks (for example 20 per package) and save a name to frsGuid map; the undo is a re-import of those packages. Keep live-plan tasks and templates, delete only superseded ones (shadow copies, spikes, failed probes), and leave cheap, harmless evidence in place.
evidence: 50 tasks deleted with the live pipeline unaffected (2026-09-24)

title: Never delete on an inventory verdict alone: refute orphanhood, then stage the removal
text: Try to refute every 'orphan' label (code and pipeline SQL, dashboards, IDMC tasks, freshness metadata); in one audit 37 of 90 orphans were refuted. Then stage the removal: quarantine (rename and revoke writes), soak (for example 7 days, confirming no writer repopulates it), archive, and drop, each drop approved separately; exclude anything that serves an app. 100%-NULL columns on connected tables are unpopulated, not dead.
evidence: 37 false positives caught before any delete (2026-07-05)

title: 'In no taskflow' is not 'unused'
text: A task outside every taskflow can still run on its own schedule, feed an application endpoint, or be started by an external orchestrator by id. Check its detail GET for `scheduleId`, search the application code and views for its output, and grep orchestrator plans and id files before deleting it. Also check whether its target is still a table: one flagged task wrote a table that had become a live view, so it was obsolete rather than a data bug.
evidence: one 'orphan' had its own hourly schedule and fed an app API; another was obsolete (2026-09-29)

title: For a project that mixes keepers and junk, move the keepers out first
text: Move the assets to keep into a new project (FRS MoveEntities preserves ids), then delete the old project wholesale; this avoids item-by-item picking inside mixed projects.
evidence: cleanup plan for two mixed projects (2026-08-20)

title: Post-cutover host cleanup must never drop the live replication slot
text: When a new CDC task took over an old slot, that slot is the live one: host cleanup scripts must be check-only by default and refuse to drop a slot unless its consumer is known to be undeployed for good.
evidence: a staged host-cleanup script was rewritten to check-only (2026-09-29)

title: The headless delete surface is five DELETE endpoints; design objects have no headless delete
text: The July corpus listed only connection, users, userGroups and catalog-source DELETEs as proven ('that is all') and left DELETE on mttask, mapping, runtimeEnvironment and schedule untested. v2 DELETE works on seven resources and FRS deletes design objects. Was believed July 2026 to 2026-08-20; overturned by L-CLEAN-006.
evidence: CAN/CANNOT section 2.3 (2026-07-25)

title: DELETE /public/core/v3/users/{id} returns 405; delete through the collection and recreate
text: An endpoint table recorded GET, PUT, PATCH and DELETE on `/public/core/v3/users/{id}` as 405, although another section of the same corpus listed DELETE as supported. DELETE answers 204. Was believed 2026-07-25 to 2026-09-28; overturned by L-CLEAN-009.
evidence: endpoint table (2026-07-25)

title: An FRS delete is DELETE /frs/api/v1/Documents('<id>')
text: A runbook note recorded `Documents('<id>')` as the repository delete. That call gives 403; `BaseEntities('<id>')`, the call the Explore UI makes, deletes. Was believed 2026-09-25 to 2026-09-26; overturned by L-CLEAN-005.
evidence: runbook note (2026-09-25)

title: Agents, runtime environments, projects, MDM content and catalog sources have no headless delete
text: An August cleanup did these in the UI and kept an exact-id checklist. Agents and runtime environments delete with v2 DELETE, and empty folders and projects with FRS DeleteEntities; catalog-source definitions still need the UI (L-CLEAN-015). Was believed 2026-08-20 to 2026-09-28; overturned by L-CLEAN-003.
evidence: August cleanup checklist (2026-08-20)

title: The catalog-source management prefix is not routed on some orgs, so catalog-source delete is UI-only
text: In August the catalog-source DELETE returned an empty-body 404 on every host of one org while search worked with the same token. On the same org the prefix answered 200 later, and a REST DELETE purges a source (only the definition delete stays in the UI). Was believed 2026-08-20 to 2026-09-28; overturned by L-CLEAN-015.
evidence: empty 404 with an identical bogus twin (2026-08-20)

title: DBMI tasks have no delete API; delete them in the Explore UI
text: A dead DBMI task was first removed through the Explore UI by browser automation because no delete API was known. The Explore UI itself calls FRS `BaseEntities('<id>')` DELETE, which works headless. Was believed 2026-09-25 to 2026-09-26; overturned by L-CLEAN-005.
evidence: UI delete of a dead task (2026-09-25/26)

title: Create connections with type TOOLKIT_CCI and the connector name in instanceName
text: `POST <serverUrl>/api/v2/connection`, headers `icSessionId` and `Content-Type: application/json`, body `{"@type":"connection","name":"<name>","type":"TOOLKIT_CCI","instanceName":"<connector name exactly as Administrator shows it>","runtimeEnvironmentId":"<reId>","connParams":{...}}` (some proven bodies also carry the connector GUID, `agentId`, `agentGroupId` and `orgId`). The `type` is never the connector name: `"PostgreSQL"`, `"ClickHouse"` or a shortName such as `"PostgreSQLadapter"` return 403 APP_10519 'The connection type is not valid', which is easily misread as a licensing problem. A short type string alone fails; the full body works. Read the object back after the create. Exception: a SharePoint Online connection needs type TOOLKIT (L-CONN-128).
evidence: 200 on three orgs and several connectors (2026-06-27, 2026-07-26, 2026-09-12); APP_10519 for flat bodies

title: The create validator names one missing field per call: iterate until 200
text: POST what you have and read the answer: 403 APP_105054 (or a 400/422) names one missing or misnamed `connParams` attribute per response, so add it and repeat; 405 means stop (no such verb); 403 APP_10519 means the `type` is wrong, go back to `TOOLKIT_CCI`. If one type string yields a different error from the rest (ODBC gave `UI_13427 Code page is not valid` while others gave APP_10519), your request reaches real validation and the others fail at the type gate, not at licensing. This loop found keys (`dbName`, `jdbcdriverclassname`, `connectionstring`) that appear in no local vendor PDF.
evidence: Iterative 105054 responses ending in 200 (2026-06-27, 2026-07-26)

title: Read a connector's field names from the agent-side manifest instead of guessing
text: Every CCI connector ships its attribute list on the agent: `grep -o '"attributeName":"[a-zA-Z_]*"' <agent_home>/downloads/package-<CONNECTOR>.<ver>/CCIManifest.txt`, or the plugin XML under `<agent_home>/downloads/package-<CONNECTOR>*/package/rdtm/plugins/*.xml`, which also states whether the type can carry credentials (`HASUSERNAME`/`HASUSERPASSWORD`). The other reliable sources are one UI-created connection of the same type, or a working connection read with `GET /api/v2/connection/<connId>`: copy its key set and change only what you need.
evidence: Settled the JDBC V2 and native PostgreSQL key sets (2026-06-27, 2026-07-26); BigQuery V2 from a working GET (2026-09-16)

title: Clone a working connection over v2, and build mirrors from the running stack
text: GET a working connection, change its name and database (and host if needed), POST it to `/api/v2/connection` without an id, then test it; this gave a clean second source without touching the live one. For environment mirrors, read the dev database credentials from the running containers (`docker inspect` env) instead of waiting for production passwords, name mirrors predictably (base name plus a suffix), bind them to the mirror's runtime environment and make the script idempotent. Creating, testing and deleting connection objects costs 0 IPU and needs no licence change.
evidence: Clone tested green (2026-09-03); 4 mirror connections created (2026-07-04/08)

title: A new add-on connector type is registered in the org by one UI-created connection
text: The connector package can be on the agent while the cloud-side connector type is not yet registered for the org; then `POST /api/v2/connection` fails with 403 'no connector with type=<shortName>' (for example `GoogleBigQueryV2`) or APP_10519 'connection type not valid', for every body shape (full CCI with GUID and instanceName, type=shortName, no instanceName, instanceName=GUID). Creating ONE connection of that type in Administrator > Connections registers it; afterwards the same REST body creates and manages connections of that type. Proven in July 2026 for BigQuery V2 and native PostgreSQL; not re-tested since connector selection became headless (L-AGENT-039), which may or may not register the type.
evidence: 403 on four body shapes, then 200 after one UI-created connection (2026-06-28 to 2026-07-08)

title: Update a connection by POSTing the full body to /api/v2/connection/<connId>
text: `GET /api/v2/connection/<connId>`, change the fields, strip `createTime`, `updateTime`, `createdBy` and `updatedBy`, and POST the whole body back to `/api/v2/connection/<connId>` (there is no PUT on this resource). `POST /api/v2/connection` without the id is create-only and fails with REPO_10200 (name already exists) for an existing connection. Read the connection back after the update: a 200 whose value reverts is a silent rejection.
evidence: REPO_10200 without the id, 200 with it (2026-08-20); 8 connections updated and tested (2026-09-28)

title: GET returns secrets masked, so every update must re-supply them
text: `GET /api/v2/connection/<connId>` returns the password or private key masked. POSTing the body back to change one attribute (for example `useLegacySQLForCustomQuery`) blanks the secret and breaks the connection unless the secret field is re-supplied. Rule: never POST a connection update without the secret, and re-test after every update.
evidence: Private key blanked by an update, test green after re-supplying it (2026-09-23)

title: Set connection secrets headless on the host that holds them
text: GET the full body; set `connParams.password` (or `connParams.privateKey`; for Salesforce the top-level `username`, `password` and `securityToken`); POST it back to `/api/v2/connection/<connId>`; then `GET /api/v2/connection/test/<connId>`. Read each secret from a 0600 file at run time inside the script, on the host that holds it, so it never reaches a transcript or command line. Connections that arrive by migration import carry no passwords: bind them to the target runtime environment, set every secret this way and test each one on the target agent before any run.
evidence: 8 of 8 imported connections tested 200 on the target agent (2026-09-28); 3 connections fixed after a password rotation (2026-09-16)

title: Repoint connections after a database move without changing their ids
text: After moving source databases, update each connection in place with `POST /api/v2/connection/<connId>` and the full body (new host and port, secret re-supplied), so mapping tasks and catalog sources that reference the connection id stay bound. Test before relying on it. Catalog scans that failed after the move recover on their next run.
evidence: 4 of 4 connection tests SUCCESS with ids preserved (2026-07-12)

title: Renaming a shared connection is risky
text: A rename is an update that re-sends the whole object: for key-based connections (BigQuery V2) a rewrite without the secret blanks the key, and other tools and sessions may reference the connection by name. Rename only in a coordinated window, re-supply the secret, and re-test.
evidence: Decision note after a key was blanked (2026-09-24)

title: Before renaming or retiring a database user, find every IDMC connection that logs in as it
text: A shared database role is often used by several IDMC connections, plus CDC tasks, BI tools and backups. When it is renamed or retired, every connection still logging in as the old user fails at run time, and every dependent task and taskflow fails each cycle ('password authentication failed for user <old>'). List all connections whose `userName` is the old role (not only the one named after the app), update them in the same window with the password re-supplied, and run a health watcher that alerts on state changes.
evidence: One connection missed for 6 hours; lanes green again after the update (2026-09-26)

title: Give IDMC its own database user, with least privilege
text: When other services share a database's default user, create a dedicated user for IDMC connections instead of changing the default user's password, which would break the other services. Connections created during a proof of concept often reuse the containers' own credentials; replace them with least-privilege, read-only users before the integration is more than a POC. Newer evidence: L-CONN-135.
evidence: Connections tested 200 with a dedicated user (2026-08-20); open item recorded (2026-07-26)

title: Take database credentials from the running application, and do not trust a green JDBC V2 test
text: A JDBC V2 connection test reported success while the stored password was wrong (JDBC V2 may not pass the password at all, L-CONN-048); a native-connector test exposed the real authentication failure. Take credentials from the running application's own configuration (for example `docker exec <app> printenv DATABASE_URL`) rather than guessing.
evidence: Native test failed with the assumed password and passed with the runtime one (2026-06-27)

title: Test a connection with GET /api/v2/connection/test/<connId>: a free metadata handshake
text: `GET <serverUrl>/api/v2/connection/test/<connId>` (header `icSessionId`; some native CCI tests append `?type=TOOLKIT_CCI`, and one July record got 400 without it) returns 200 'test successful' or an error such as 403 APP_105060. It is a read-only metadata handshake: no data run, 0 IPU, so it is the tool for reachability matrices across runtime environments. `POST /api/v2/connection/test` returned 500 (APP_21000 seen) and `/api/v2/connection/<connId>/test` 404. The managed MCP `connectionmanagement.test_connection_by_id` is a reliable alternative. `GET /api/v2/connection/<connId>` carries a cached `status` of the last test (success, failed, or absent).
evidence: 200 'test successful' on dozens of connections (2026-06-27 to 2026-09-28); POST variants 500/404

title: A passing test is not the proof; a run that lands rows is
text: A connection test only proves the handshake. It can pass with a wrong password (JDBC V2), and it can fail while the path works for jobs. The definitive proof of a connection is a mapping run that lands rows in the target, checked by count.
evidence: Test and run results diverged on JDBC V2 connections (2026-08-18/19)

title: Connection and connector reads
text: `GET /api/v2/connection` lists connections (with the cached test `status`); `GET /api/v2/connection/<connId>` reads one; `GET /api/v2/connection/source/<connId>?type=table` browses source objects (200 or 403 per connection, and it can surface target-side errors such as a throttled warehouse), but it can also return 200 with an empty list for a working connection (two native PostgreSQL connections whose databases held tables, a known-good BigQuery connection), so an empty browse proves nothing: confirm objects through a consumer (profile source fields, a mapping preview, a catalog Metadata Extraction); `GET /api/v2/connector` returns the connector type catalog; `GET /api/v2/connector/metadata?connectorName=<name>` returns a connector's schema, and `200 []` means the connector is not activated. The v3 `/public/core/v3/connections` path is 404: connections are v2 only. To prove that a connection test really reached the database and was not a cached status, diff the database's own counters around `GET /api/v2/connection/test/<connId>`: on PostgreSQL the test opened one session and committed about 8 transactions (`pg_stat_database.sessions` +1, `xact_commit` +8) in 1.4 s.
evidence: 200 live (2026-07-04 to 2026-07-25); browse 200 [] with and without ?type=table on two working PostgreSQL connections, the test 200 in 1.4 s with sessions 10 -> 11 and xact_commit +8 (2026-10-03)

title: Delete a connection with DELETE /api/v2/connection/<connId>, after a used-by check
text: `DELETE <serverUrl>/api/v2/connection/<connId>` returns 200 and leaves no orphan (an Amazon S3 v2 create-then-delete round trip proved it); a read-back 403 or 404 means gone. Check users first: REPO_10242 means mappings still reference the connection, and 'used by another asset' means a catalog source holds it. In a cleanup, delete connections late, after the tasks, mappings and catalog sources that use them.
evidence: Create/delete round trip (2026-07-04/09); connection deletes in a headless org cleanup (2026-09-28)

title: 403 APP_105060 is a family: read the message to know which gate failed
text: The same code carries different causes, and the connection definition is usually fine. 'Unable to resolve channel service. No running service found of type <Engine> <ver>.* service for AgentGroup: <reId>' means that engine is not selected, still deploying or down on that runtime environment (L-AGENT-076). 'Unable to fetch Connector attributes, Ensure adapter ID is valid and the service is enabled [com.informatica.adapter.<x>]' means the connector adapter is not enabled or not deployed on that agent (L-CONN-019). 'No running service found of type Connector_Service' usually means the connection is bound to another runtime environment (L-CONN-023). Check `agentEngines[]` and the runtime-environment selections before touching the connection.
evidence: Each message seen on live tests (2026-07-26 to 2026-09-22)

title: 'Unable to fetch Connector attributes [com.informatica.adapter.<x>]' means the adapter is not on the agent
text: The create validates in the cloud, so the connection saves fine, but Test and runs fail with this message until the connector's runtime package is enabled and deployed on the agent that serves the connection. Enabling engines does not enable connectors. Check the agent's registry under `<agent_home>/apps/Connector_Service/<ver>/connectors/cci/plugins/` (the ADAPTER_HOME its log prints) and `<agent_home>/ext/connectors/thirdparty/`. Fix: select the connector on the runtime environment (L-AGENT-039); in June 2026, creating one connection of that type in the UI also triggered the package download.
evidence: Adapter registry listed on-host without the connector (2026-07-26); 200 after the connector was re-added (2026-09-22)

title: Copying adapter jars into the agent does not enable a connector
text: Connector enablement is a control-plane push: once the connector is selected for the runtime environment, the control plane registers its attributes (which clears APP_105060) and pushes a new DIS appspec, and the agent downloads the package and deploys the jars itself. Adapter jars copied by hand into plugin folders are not registered and are reconciled away on restart, and `consoleAgentManager` has no install verb. This differs from third-party JDBC driver jars for a connector that is already enabled, which are staged by hand (L-CONN-049).
evidence: Jar-copy attempts failed (2026-09-20/22); package auto-downloaded after enablement (2026-09-14)

title: GET /api/v2/connector is a type catalog, not what the agent can run
text: `GET /api/v2/connector` returned 153 types on one org, 342 on another and 352 on a third; the Product Availability Matrix lists about 301. It is not what the agent installed: a connection POSTs 200 against any listed type whose adapter was never deployed and fails only at test time, and a package can sit in `downloads/` with no adapter extracted (downloaded, extracted and registered are three states). Sources disagree on whether the list is org-specific (June) or Informatica's sellable catalog (July); either way the per-agent truth is the runtime environment's `connectors.selections[]` with `enabled` flags (L-AGENT-039) plus the agent's adapter registry. Check the list for gaps before designing (seen missing on one org: Stripe, so use REST V2; Fabric connectors; OpenAI, so use the generic LLM connector).
evidence: Counts 153/342/352 across orgs (2026-06-27 to 2026-09-23); adapter registry inspected (2026-07-26)

title: Connectors are per agent: every connector a mapping uses must be on the agent that runs it
text: Connector availability is per Secure Agent / runtime environment. A mapping task whose source connector is on one agent and target connector on another failed within about 2 s (state 3, 0 rows) with 'DTM process terminated unexpectedly'. A task that aborts during session setup at 'Importing Connection: <conn>' (for example `trepcnx.cpp:296`) means its runtime cannot use that connection: the connection is bound to another runtime environment, or the agent lacks that connector. Use connections bound to the task's own runtime environment and co-locate source and target connectors (pushdown needs them on one agent too).
evidence: state=3 in 2 s with connectors on separate agents (2026-07-04); agent package inventory plus binding check (2026-07-06/08)

title: 'No running service found of type Connector_Service' usually means the connection is bound elsewhere
text: A test failing with 'No running service found of type Connector_Service' usually means the connection is bound to another runtime environment (for example a hosted or regional agent) rather than your Secure Agent. Use or create a connection bound to your own runtime environment.
evidence: Connection bound to a managed agent in another region failed; a locally bound one passed (2026-09-16)

title: The reserved 'Informatica Cloud Hosted Agent' runtime cannot be created in an org that lacks it
text: Tasks and connections bound to the hosted runtime environment fail to import into an org that does not have one, and the name is reserved (REPO_38210), so you cannot create it. Remap those objects to your own runtime environment inside the package (the inner files, the `exportMetadata.v2.json` entry and every `objectRefs` list) or at import. The remapped Salesforce tasks then ran on the self-hosted agent.
evidence: Import SUCCESSFUL after the remap (2026-09-28)

title: A containerized agent must use Docker service names, not 127.0.0.1, in connection hosts
text: When the agent runs in a container on a Docker network, `127.0.0.1` or `localhost` in a connection points at the agent container itself. Use the Docker network aliases of the database containers (for example `postgres:5432`). Prove reachability from inside the agent container (for example a `/dev/tcp/<host>/<port>` probe) before debugging the connection.
evidence: Tests green after switching to the aliases (2026-08-18)

title: Containerized databases often bind a private interface, not localhost
text: Databases in containers commonly publish on a private IP, so every localhost port is closed and a connection sheet saying `localhost` fails. Find the real bind address and credentials with `ss -ltnp`, `docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Ports}}'` and `docker inspect -f '{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}' <container>`. A host's login banner can show a different private address from the provider's API; trust `ss`.
evidence: Verified on-host (2026-07-26)

title: Native PostgreSQL connection body (and its drifting key names)
text: `type:"TOOLKIT_CCI"`, `instanceName:"PostgreSQL"`, connector GUID `com.informatica.adapter.postgres`. The parameter set on a September 2026 connection was `hostName`, `port`, `database`, `userName`, `password`, `authenticationType`, `encryptionMethod`, plus `agentId`, `agentGroupId` and `orgId`; there is no schema parameter (do not send `schemaName`). Earlier proven bodies also sent `encryptionMethod:"noEncryption"`, `tlsv1_2:false`, `sslv3:false`, `validateServerCertificate:false`. The accepted `authenticationType` value and user key drifted between connector builds and pods: `Database` ('Basic' rejected as 'not a valid choice', June), `UserIdPassword` with `userName` (a DataDirect driver rename; `user` gave an NPE 'error [null]', July), and `Standard` with `user` and both `databaseName` and `database` (another pod, July). Copy the key set from a UI-created or working connection of the same type (L-CONN-003).
evidence: Native PostgreSQL connections tested 200 on four orgs (2026-06-27, 2026-07-07, 2026-07-26, 2026-09-23)

title: PostgreSQL object paths are <schema>/TABLE/<table> or <schema>/VIEW/<view>
text: As `$Source$` (or target) object of a task, the native PostgreSQL connector wants `<schema>/TABLE/<table>` or `<schema>/VIEW/<view>`. `public/<table>` fails with SDK_APP_COM_20000 'Incorrect list of path is populated with size: 1' (parsed as a live browse path), and bare names, `schema.table`, quoted identifiers or `db.schema.table` give 'Object(s) [X] not found' (a cache-only lookup; database statement logging showed no query arrived). With the right path the adapter resolves the object at run time, even on a connection created over REST and never browsed in the UI.
evidence: Task ran with the path form; database logs showed no query for the failing forms (2026-09-22/23)

title: The PostgreSQL connector types text as string(255) and cannot land jsonb
text: In template mapping tasks the native PostgreSQL connector typed every string as string(255) and truncated longer values silently, and it cannot land `jsonb`/`json`; field-precision overrides through v2 `overriddenFields` returned 400. For such tables create a PostgreSQL view in a source schema that selects every column with `jsonb::text` and land from `<schema>/VIEW/<table>`; on a BigQuery target also use a JSON-typed column (L-CONN-044). Views are additive and reversible (`DROP SCHEMA <schema> CASCADE`).
evidence: 585-char values survived only to a flat-file diagnostic target; views plus JSON columns kept full text (2026-09-23 to 2026-09-26)

title: Use the native PostgreSQL connector, not JDBC V2, for ingestion, CDC and cataloging
text: Per the Product Availability Matrix (v39.1) JDBC V2 supports Data Integration and Data Quality but not Database Ingestion and Replication. The native PostgreSQL connector supports DBMI/CDC and gives richer catalog metadata; JDBC-based catalog scans of PostgreSQL ended COMPLETED WITH ERRORS because the JDBC scanner cannot read the system catalogs (and dropped sequences, constraints and foreign keys).
evidence: PAM lookup (2026-06-27); JDBC scans completed with errors (2026-07-08)

title: Connection test and catalog scans read JDBC drivers from different folders
text: On a minimal agent without the PostgreSQL jar, place the driver (for example `postgresql-42.7.4.jar`) in the JDBC V2 folder used by Test (`<agent_home>/ext/connectors/thirdparty/informatica.jdbc_v2/common/`) and in the scanner folders: `Metadata_Foundation_Agent/.../data/browse/drivers/` (plus a `postgresql` subfolder), `Metadata_Platform_Service/.../lib/drivers/` and `Database_Ingestion/.../dbmi_libs/libs/`. If a scanner still cannot find the driver, drop the jar into the `drivers/` directory of every engine.
evidence: Test and scan both succeeded after placement (2026-06-27)

title: truncateTarget is not a reliable reload switch on any connector seen
text: BigQuery V2 targets appended on some tasks despite `truncateTarget=true` (July; the later BigQuery path uses `$Target$.oprRuntimeAttrs` `writeDisposition: "Write truncate"`); a ClickHouse JDBC V2 target reported SUCCESS with 0 rows when it was true; JDBC V2 targets ignore it (use the `Pre SQL` runtime attribute, L-CONN-056); on a PostgreSQL target it was observed ignored (a rerun of the same file posted 0 new rows), yet a posting task built with `truncateTarget=true` was flagged as able to wipe its system-of-record table. Do not rely on it either way: truncate explicitly (pre-SQL or a TRUNCATE step) for full reloads, keep postings idempotent in the database (for example a BEFORE INSERT trigger that skips existing business keys), and verify row counts.
evidence: Doubled gold tables (2026-07-04); 0-row SUCCESS (2026-08-19); PG rerun posted 0 rows (2026-09-24); risk flag in a code review (2026-09-28)

title: Rule out source-database blockers with one read-only diagnostic as the connection role
text: Before blaming the source database for failed scans or runs, run a read-only diagnostic as the exact IDMC connection role: role privileges and SELECT gaps, schema USAGE, row-level security policies, `statement_timeout`, lock and idle-in-transaction timeouts, `temp_file_limit`, plus live checks for blocked queries and long idle transactions during a scan.
evidence: 0 blocked queries and 0 idle-in-transaction sessions during scans on 4 databases (2026-06-28)

title: BigQuery V2 connection identifiers, parameters and service-account roles
text: Connector GUID `com.infa.adapter.bigqueryv2`, shortName `GoogleBigQueryV2`, sdkType CCI, display name Google BigQuery V2 (connector name 'Google Big Query V2'). `connParams`: `connectorType:"Simple"`, `clientEmail`, `privateKey`, `projectId`, `storagePath` (a `gs://` staging bucket), `datasetNameForCustomQuery`, plus a large `CCM_CONN_PRESENTATION` blob; the easiest path is to GET a working connection and change only these fields. The service account needs at least `roles/bigquery.dataEditor` and `roles/bigquery.jobUser`, plus access to the staging bucket (Bulk writes with truncate needed `roles/storage.objectAdmin`). Keep the key file out of git. Newer evidence: L-ENV-133.
evidence: Connections created and tested (2026-06-27 to 2026-09-16)

title: The BigQuery private-key format differs by engine and pod: test each consumer, split connections
text: Never send real newlines in `privateKey` (the v2 API strips them and the key fails as 'Invalid PKCS#8 data'). Beyond that, the accepted form varies: on one dmp-us pod CDI accepted the stripped base64 body, but the Data Gateway behind CLAIRE GPT data queries required the full PEM with literal `\n` escapes exactly as in the service-account JSON; on another dm-us pod the CDI BigQuery V2 connector accepted only the PEM body without the BEGIN/END header lines and rejected the escaped-PEM form, while Database Ingestion's Simba JDBC driver rejected the header-less form and accepted the PEM form (the reports call it 'escaped PEM'; the script's replace was a byte-for-byte no-op, so probably the unmodified PEM). Test each candidate per engine (CDI test, DBMI deploy, a gateway query) and keep one BigQuery connection per consumer when they disagree.
evidence: 'Invalid PKCS#8 data' on the wrong form per engine; 5 formats tested against CDI and DBMI (2026-09-22 to 2026-09-28)

title: Find a working key format with a probe loop, and restore the last good value if none passes
text: Cycle the candidate encodings (stripped base64, full PEM, PEM without header, one-line PEM, PEM with literal `\n`) through GET / modify / POST `/api/v2/connection/<connId>`. After each, run `GET /api/v2/connection/test/<connId>` and, for DBMI, `POST https://<pod>-ing.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/dbmi/public/api/v2/task/deploy/<taskId>` and poll the job. Keep the first format that passes every consumer; if none does, restore the last known-good value and split the connection.
evidence: No single format passed both CDI and DBMI on one pod, so two connections were created (2026-09-28)

title: Pasting a service-account key into the UI fails on wrapped lines
text: Pasting `private_key` into the BigQuery V2 connection form failed with `BaseEncoding DecodingException: Unrecognized character: 0x20` (a space from line wrapping) or a truncated start (missing `-----BEGIN`). Use the key-file upload option, or write the exact `private_key` value to a text file and copy it whole.
evidence: Connection test 200 after a clean copy (2026-06-29)

title: An org policy can block service-account key creation
text: If `gcloud iam service-accounts keys create` produces a 0-byte file or fails, the Google org probably enforces `constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`. Grant the BigQuery roles to the service account attached to the agent VM (with the cloud-platform scope) and plan the IDMC connection around that identity; the VM authenticated to BigQuery through the metadata server, but an IDMC connection using it was not proven in these sources.
evidence: VM authenticated to BigQuery with a metadata token and no key (2026-06-27)

title: Service-account keys used by connections never expire by default: rotate and prove the old key is dead
text: User-managed GCP service-account keys never expire unless given a TTL, so old keys accumulate. List them with `gcloud iam service-accounts keys list --iam-account=<sa>@<project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, check that a key is not shared by other hosts before deleting a VM, and rotate before a repo goes public or a stack moves. A key committed to git must be rotated at once: the fix is `gcloud iam service-accounts keys delete`, not a history rewrite (purge history as hygiene). Update every consumer, including the IDMC connection's `privateKey`, and confirm in Cloud Logging (principal filter, grouped by `callerIp` and `private_key_id`) that the old key shows no activity.
evidence: Key rotated; zero activity on the old key id afterwards (2026-09-08)

title: Key files mounted from absolute host paths break silently when a stack moves
text: A docker-compose bind mount of a service-account key from a cloud-specific absolute path (for example a default user's home on one cloud) creates an empty directory when the path does not exist on the new host; the container starts, and jobs fail later with authentication errors or '[Errno 21] Is a directory'. Use project-relative paths, Docker secrets or a secret manager. A fixed file reaches a running container only after `docker compose up -d --force-recreate <service>`.
evidence: Broken mount found after a cross-cloud move (2026-09-08)

title: BigQuery custom-query sources need useLegacySQLForCustomQuery=false
text: For a BigQuery V2 connection used as a custom SQL query source, set the connection attribute `useLegacySQLForCustomQuery=false` so queries run as standard SQL, and re-supply the private key in the same update (L-CONN-007).
evidence: A custom-query task then succeeded with 33,138 rows (2026-09-23)

title: Never flip a BigQuery V2 connection from Simple to Hybrid mode
text: Updating a BigQuery V2 connection to `connectorType=Hybrid` through `POST /api/v2/connection/<connId>` returns 200 but breaks every mapping that uses Full pushdown / direct read: '4005 - Direct Read Mode with Hybrid connection mode is not supported'. Keep Simple mode and fix type issues in the schema instead.
evidence: All 22 mappings failed with 4005 until reverted (2026-07-04)

title: BigQuery V2 Simple mode rejected JSON columns in July; JSON targets worked in September
text: In July 2026, mappings reading a JSON column, or writing a JSON-typed target column from a STRING source, failed in Simple mode with 'table contains [JSON] data type incompatible with [Simple] connection mode'; the fix was a STRING cast in the source query or a STRING target column. In September 2026, on another org and pod, template mapping tasks (Bulk write) wrote full text into pre-created JSON target columns (L-CONN-044). The difference may be the connector build or the mapping path; test on your pod before choosing.
evidence: Task failures fixed by STRING casts (2026-07-04/06); JSON targets written (2026-09-24)

title: The BigQuery V2 writer cuts STRING ports to 255 characters; a JSON-typed target column keeps the full text
text: Mapping tasks writing through BigQuery V2 truncated every STRING port to 255 characters whatever the target schema (tested: a varchar(4000) source view, `allowMaxFieldLength=true`, `retainFieldMetadata=true`, a pre-created STRING(4000) column, Streaming instead of Bulk: all 255). When the pre-created target column is typed JSON, IDMC writes the full text as a JSON string scalar up to 32,000 characters (longer values are cut to exactly 32,000); BYTES targets fail with CMN_1081. Write truncate keeps the JSON schema across reruns. Read it with `JSON_VALUE()` in views, and guard: fail before landing if a source value exceeds 32,000, and flag any IDMC-written STRING column whose maximum length is exactly 255 (or JSON exactly 32,000) as probable truncation.
evidence: All variants cut at 255; JSON columns kept full values (2026-09-24); a newly long column moved to JSON (2026-09-27)

title: Database Ingestion to BigQuery needs the Simba JDBC jars on the agent, then a restart
text: A DBMI task with a BigQuery target fails to deploy with 'Failed to load driver class com.simba.googlebigquery.jdbc.Driver' on an agent without the Simba BigQuery JDBC set. Copy the set (about 73 jars) into `<agent_home>/apps/Database_Ingestion/ext/connectors/thirdparty` and `GoogleBigQueryJDBC42.jar` into `<agent_home>/apps/Database_Ingestion/<ver>/dbmi_libs/libs`, then restart the agent, because the classloader caches at start. The DBMI connection then needs its own key format (L-CONN-035).
evidence: The CDC task deployed and ran after the copy and restart (2026-09-28)

title: JDBC V2 connection body: instanceName JDBCV2 with lowercase driver and URL keys
text: Use `type:"TOOLKIT_CCI"`, `instanceName:"JDBCV2"` (connector GUID `com.informatica.adapter.jdbc_v2`); `"JDBC_V2"` and `"JDBC V2"` return 403 'There is no connector with type='. `connParams` take all-lowercase `jdbcdriverclassname` (for example `com.clickhouse.jdbc.ClickHouseDriver`) and `connectionstring` (the JDBC URL). The object stores `connectionstring` and `jdbcUrl`; host, port and database read back empty, which is correct and not a half-written record. The driver jar must be on the agent before the connection can open.

title: JDBC V2 credential attributes are username and password, from its manifest
text: The JDBC V2 attribute names are `username`, `password` and `additionalsecurityproperties` (lowercase), not `user`, and credentials do not belong in the JDBC URL. Read them from `CCIManifest.txt` or the plugin XML (L-CONN-003) instead of copying field names from other connectors; `user` silently does nothing.
evidence: Manifest read (2026-07-26)

title: Whether JDBC V2 passes a password to the database is unresolved
text: The JDBC V2 plugin XML declares `HASUSERNAME="NO" HASUSERPASSWORD="NO"`. In July 2026, credentials placed in `connParams`, in the URL, in userinfo form or in additional security properties were stripped or ignored: the database's own log showed no password, the driver authenticated as the default account, and the same URL forms worked from a plain `java -cp` test on the host. In August 2026 another setup used the manifest fields `username`/`password` against a database that rejects empty passwords, and tests passed only after a password was set. Diagnose from both ends (the database's auth log) and prefer server-side auth configuration until this is settled.
evidence: Both-ends proof of no password (2026-07-26); password-dependent success on another setup (2026-08-16/18)

title: Stage third-party JDBC drivers in ext/connectors/thirdparty/informatica.jdbc_v2/common, then restart
text: The canonical directory for JDBC V2 third-party drivers is `<agent_home>/ext/connectors/thirdparty/informatica.jdbc_v2/common/` (Informatica drops its own DB2, MSSQL and Oracle drivers there, which confirms it). It exists only after the engine deploys, so stage the jar afterwards, owned by the agent user with mode 644, and restart Connector_Service or the agent, because the connector caches its classpath. `ext/jdbc/` and `apps/Data_Integration_Server/ext/drivers/` were ignored. The CAI process-engine reads JDBC jars from `<agent_home>/apps/process-engine/ext` when 'JDBC Jar Directory' is blank.
evidence: Driver invisible until Connector_Service restarted (2026-07-26); MySQL jar staged, 8/8 connections green (2026-09-28)

title: A DIS auto-upgrade drops hand-placed jars: also stage them in ext/deploy_to_main
text: When Data_Integration_Server auto-upgrades (for example 77.0.2 to 77.0.3), jars placed by hand in the old version's directories (`<ver>/connectors/thirdparty/informatica.jdbc_v2/`) are not carried forward, and tests fail with a generic 'JDBC driver is available at the correct location' error. Copy the jar into the active version's directory and also into `<agent_home>/ext/deploy_to_main/bin/rdtm-extra/jdbc_v2/` and `<agent_home>/ext/deploy_to_main/bin/rdtm/javalib/` (redeployed into the active version on restart, so it survives future upgrades), fix ownership, and restart the agent. The active DIS version appears in the tomcat log file name.
evidence: Connection test 200 after the copy and restart (2026-08-20)

title: Third-party JDBC drivers load from a file copy plus a restart; the upload-JAR UI is not required
text: In July and August 2026, 'Unable to load driver' survived copies of a known-good jar (Java 8 bytecode, a `META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver` entry) into several agent folders plus restarts, and one case was fixed only by the Administrator upload-JAR flow, so a UI step was budgeted. Later evidence: the driver loaded with no UI upload once the DTM native-library gaps were fixed (L-AGENT-060) and the jar sat in the canonical directory (2026-08-19), and on 2026-09-28 a MySQL driver copied into `common/` plus the Simba set for DBMI worked after a restart. The July failures were most likely other gates (native libraries, staging before the engine deployed, no restart). Order: adapter enabled, jar in `common/` (and `deploy_to_main`), restart, test, then a run that lands rows.
evidence: Tests SUCCESSFUL and a run wrote 52/52 rows with no UI upload (2026-08-19); 8/8 connections green and lanes ran 12/12 (2026-09-28)

title: Diagnose JDBC failures with a probe on the agent's own JDK and the tomcat log
text: To separate driver, URL and credential problems from IDMC problems, compile a tiny JDBC probe with the agent's bundled JDK (for example `<agent_home>/jdk8/bin/javac`, or `java -cp <driver.jar>`) and run it against the same URL on the agent host. Then read the real error in `<agent_home>/apps/Data_Integration_Server/logs/tomcat/tomcat_<ver>.log` (look for `op:testConnection` and `adpId:com.informatica.adapter.jdbc_v2`), and the database's own auth log.
evidence: Probe OK while the IDMC test failed; the log showed the real cause (2026-08-20)

title: Verify a downloaded JDBC jar before staging it
text: The `-all` classifier is not necessarily shaded: clickhouse-jdbc 0.6.5 `-all` omits `com.clickhouse.client.*` and throws `NoClassDefFoundError ClickHouseClient`; the `-shaded` build is right. Check with `unzip -l <jar> | grep -c client/`, and check size and type: one failed download was a 554-byte HTML 404 page saved with a `.jar` name.
evidence: 554-byte jar found; class-count check (2026-07-26)

title: ClickHouse has no native connector: use JDBC V2 with the shaded driver and an explicit HTTP provider
text: Use `instanceName:"JDBCV2"`, the `clickhouse-jdbc-<ver>-shaded.jar`, driver class `com.clickhouse.jdbc.ClickHouseDriver` and `jdbc:clickhouse://<host>:8123/<db>?http_connection_provider=HTTP_URL_CONNECTION`; a bare URL picks the Apache HTTP client, which needs slf4j and fails on the agent. No Java install is needed on the host; the agent's bundled JRE runs the driver. ClickHouse 24.x rejects the `default` user with an empty password over HTTP, so give IDMC a dedicated user (L-CONN-012).
evidence: Live JDBC test against ClickHouse 24.8, connection tests SUCCESSFUL and mapping runs landed rows (2026-08-18 to 2026-08-20)

title: ClickHouse type quirks through JDBC V2
text: A ClickHouse `String` reports JDBC precision 0, so the mapping designer refuses to save ('Length/Precision must be greater than 0') and a target selected while precision was 0 fails at run time; Edit Metadata changes do not persist. Fix at the source with `toFixedString(col, N)` in the query (the JDBC V2 writer strips the NUL padding, so a plain String target lands clean values), or on the target by recreating the empty table with FixedString(N) columns, selecting the target, then recreating it as String and running without re-selecting (or use a create-new-at-runtime target). `UInt64` reads as NULL: cast with `toInt64`. `DateTime` and `DateTime64(6)` pass through. ClickHouse forbids `ALTER ... MODIFY COLUMN` on an ORDER BY key column (error 524), so use DROP and CREATE and confirm `SHOW CREATE TABLE` matches afterwards.
evidence: Full-row 0-diff on every mart; no NUL padding (2026-08-19/20)

title: JDBC V2 targets ignore truncateTarget: use the 'Pre SQL' runtime attribute, with the space
text: For a full reload through JDBC V2 set the target's `runtimeAttrs` to `{"Pre SQL": "TRUNCATE TABLE <t>"}`. The key must be exactly `Pre SQL` with the space; `preSQL` and `PreSQL` are silently ignored. The Pre SQL runs before the source is read, so a failed read leaves the target empty: for reloads that downstream objects refresh from, prefer a stage-and-swap or a key-sync mirror (L-CDI-208).
evidence: Reloads truncate as expected (2026-09-24/26); a failed source login after the truncate left a lane's targets empty (2026-09-26)

title: MySQL-protocol warehouses (for example Apache Doris) through JDBC V2
text: Write through a JDBC V2 connection with the MySQL JDBC driver (`mysql-connector-j`) staged in `<agent_home>/ext/connectors/thirdparty/informatica.jdbc_v2/common` (agent user, mode 644, checksum-identical when copied between agents), and truncate with `Pre SQL` for reloads. Without the jar on the DTM path runs fail with an 'invalid format' error. Rows written to UNIQUE KEY tables of such a warehouse are upserted by key and the writer does not truncate, so rows deleted at the source stay in the target: keep the `Pre SQL` truncate for full reloads (mind its failure mode, L-CDI-208), and for mirror tables in a consolidated mapping add a key-sync delete branch (a Joiner with the source keys as master, outer, against the target keys, a Filter `ISNULL(<source_key>)`, then a target instance with operation Delete); never on append-history targets (L-CDI-199). Because a JDBC V2 target writes into the database bound on its connection (L-CDI-040), prove the branch through a scratch connection bound to a scratch database seeded with a few fake keys that must disappear.
evidence: Target connections green and the lane validated 12/12 and 17/17 (2026-09-17 to 2026-09-28); two fake keys seeded into three scratch tables were removed and counts matched the source on 12 tables (2026-09-29)

title: Salesforce connection for CDI: user, password and token as top-level fields, API v64 or newer
text: The v2 Salesforce connection keeps `username`, `password` and `securityToken` as top-level fields (not in `connParams`); from an IP range the Salesforce org trusts, an empty `securityToken` worked. Use a connection on Salesforce API version 64 or newer. When the Secure Agent's Salesforce connector misbehaved (cause not recorded), the Salesforce tasks ran on the Informatica Cloud Hosted Agent; after a migration the same tasks ran on a self-hosted agent. The integration user needs field-level security on every field it writes. For a low-risk demo target: a Developer Edition org, a standard object, plain Insert (no external id), an API user plus security token, Salesforce as target only, and deleting test records between rehearsals.
evidence: Connection tested 200 without a token from a trusted host (2026-09-28); tasks ran on the hosted agent (2026-09-25)

title: Salesforce checkbox fields need integer 1/0
text: When writing a Salesforce checkbox (boolean) field through the IDMC Salesforce connector, send an integer 1 or 0; string or boolean-looking values did not set the field.
evidence: 645 of 646 records correct after the fix (2026-09-26)

title: The Salesforce connector drops SOAP 'long' fields on read
text: Reading Salesforce objects through the IDMC Salesforce connector dropped fields of SOAP type long, so count fields came back empty. Fetch those fields with the Salesforce REST API in a helper and join them in the warehouse.
evidence: Counts populated only through REST (2026-09-26)

title: A Salesforce duplicate rule can silently block IDMC and CAI upserts
text: An active standard Contact duplicate rule blocked new Contacts from both a CAI real-time path and a batch CDI sync. Decide where deduplication lives (for example in the IDMC match step) and deactivate or adjust the Salesforce rule, then re-test both paths.
evidence: Records reached Salesforce after the rule was deactivated (2026-09-26)

title: Salesforce fields that look empty may be hidden by field-level security
text: When fields written by IDMC look empty to a Salesforce user, check field-level security on that user's permission set before debugging the pipeline; the data may be there. The integration user also needs FLS on the fields it writes (for example lookup fields such as AccountId).
evidence: Data present once FLS was checked (2026-09-26)

title: Real-time Salesforce writes: OAuth client credentials through a CAI REST connector, now on an External Client App
text: The built-in CAI Salesforce connector needs the ModifyMetadata permission, which breaks least privilege for an integration user. For real-time writes, build your own CAI REST service connector that obtains a token with OAuth client credentials from a Connected App (token parameters sent as a form-encoded body, not in the URL) and upserts idempotently with `PATCH /services/data/v<nn>/sobjects/<Object>/<ExternalIdField>/<value>`, linking parents through external-id relationship fields. CDI connections in these sources used user, password and token (L-CONN-058); OAuth on a CDI Salesforce connection was not tested. A newly created Salesforce Connected App could no longer be given a client-credentials Run As user (Setup > Edit Policies answered 'Invalid User' for every user, and the Metadata API silently dropped `oauthClientCredentialUser`); older apps keep the Run As they got at creation. Create an External Client App with the client-credentials flow running as the integration user instead, read its secret once (it is shown once), point the CAI REST connection at it by re-importing the connection with OVERWRITE and republishing (L-CAI-061), prove one real call, then block the old app (its token call then returns `app_blocked`). Rotating the integration user's password: the REST `/password` resource returned NOT_FOUND while SOAP `setPassword` worked; delete the user's AuthSession records to revoke live sessions (cached sessions then get 401 INVALID_SESSION_ID); update the IDMC Salesforce connection in the same minute (the security token can stay empty when the agent's IP is trusted), and rerun any task that logged in during the swap.
evidence: Service connector, app connection and processes published and served (2026-09-25); all CAI logins moved to an External Client App within minutes, the old app blocked, a new record created its CRM contact in real time, and 87 integration logins after the password rotation had 0 failures (2026-10-03)

title: Export packages can carry connection secrets in plaintext
text: Connection passwords are masked in v3 exports, but CAI app connections authored with `encrypted="false"` store values such as an OAuth client secret in clear, and every package that contains them does too. Keep packages in a private 0600 location (never a shared desktop, drive, ticket or repo), never print their contents, and rotate the affected secrets after the migration.
evidence: A Salesforce OAuth client secret found in plaintext in export packages (2026-09-28)

title: Flat-file connections work headless with type CSVFile
text: A native FLATFILE connection returns APP_10519 and a CCI 'Flat File' type returns 'no connector with type', which looked like a missing flat-file connector. A connection of type `CSVFile` created with `POST <serverUrl>/api/v2/connection`, bound to the agent's runtime environment, with the directory on the agent host in the top-level `database` field, tests green and works as a mapping-task source and target. FileIO, Sequential File and CSVFile appear among an org's licensed connector types.
evidence: Connection test green; a real run wrote 50 rows from PostgreSQL to CSV (2026-09-24)

title: A CSV source fails with FR_3085 'null character' on empty fields
text: A flat-file source can fail with FR_3085 'null character' when fields are empty. Have the file writer put a placeholder such as `(blank)` in empty cells and convert it back with NULLIF in the staging SQL.
evidence: The lane then ran 189 rows per file (2026-09-24)

title: The flat-file directory must be readable by the OS user of the agent that runs the task
text: A flat-file connection's directory must be readable (and, for targets, writable) by the OS user of the agent that runs the task. A second agent under its own user could not read the first agent's home (mode 750). Create a shared directory owned by `<agentuser>:<appgroup>` with mode 2775, copy the files there, and point the connection's directory at it (and any file shipper or mount that writes there).
evidence: The file lane ran 5/5 in the new org from the shared directory (2026-09-28/29)

title: Flat-file source attributes on a task, and reading the header at run time
text: On a cloned flat-file landing task set `$Source$.srcFFAttrs = {"@type":"flatFileAttrs","delimiter":",","textQualifier":"\"","escapeChar":"","headerLineNo":1,"firstDataRow":2,"consecutiveDelimiterAsOne":false}`, put the file name in `extendedObject.object` / `objects[].name` and label, and set `fetchMode: "RUNTIME"` on `$Source$` and `$Target$` so the columns come from the file header at run time.
evidence: Runs of the file lanes (2026-09-24 to 2026-09-27)

title: Amazon S3 v2 connection body quirks
text: `instanceName` must be the display string `Amazon S3 v2` (not a GUID), `connParams.FolderPath` is the bucket name and the top-level `folderPath` is `/`. With that body `POST /api/v2/connection` returned 200 and DELETE removed it cleanly.
evidence: 200 create and clean delete (2026-07-04/09)

title: MongoDB connection body needs dbName
text: `instanceName:"MongoDB"`; `connParams` need `hostName`, `port` and `dbName` (not `databaseName` or `database`); one reference spells the host field `hostname`.

title: Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse and Lakehouse connections
text: Fabric DW (connector `com.informatica.adapter.fabricdw`) writes over JDBC to `<workspace>.datawarehouse.fabric.microsoft.com:1433` with a service principal (`clientId`, `clientSecret`, `tenantId`), `WorkspaceName` and `Database`. Mapping runs fail with 'Staging Lakehouse Name is not set' until `StagingLakehouseName` names an existing lakehouse (set it with an update POST). IDMC tasks do write Fabric natively: a PostgreSQL source with a create-new-at-runtime Fabric target landed rows (prove it by truncating outside IDMC and running only the task). Pushdown into Fabric needs the source and Fabric connectors on the same agent and an ADLS Gen2 staging container; one source says plain DW inserts needed no ADLS staging. Always verify target row counts: a drop test once reported SUCCESS with 0 rows. The Lakehouse connector needs a workspace and lakehouse, an Entra app (client id, tenant id, secret) with Contributor, and the `<server>.lakehouse.pbidedicated.windows.net` SQL endpoint (documented).
evidence: 0 -> 10 rows written by the IDMC task alone (2026-07-09); staging lakehouse error cleared by an update (2026-07-07)

title: A preview connector build can crash pmdtm before any write
text: With a preview (SNAPSHOT) FabricDW connector build, every Fabric mapping task aborted during session prepare: pmdtm exit 134 (SIGABRT) at `trepcnx.cpp:296` (`TRepConnection::setAttributes`), even for a probe task with correct runtime binding. It was not a library, ODBC, datatype or capacity problem, and a bigger capacity would not help because the crash comes before any write. Check the connector package version on the agent; a preview build needs a vendor fix or a GA build.
evidence: Crash reproduced on a correctly bound probe task (2026-07-07)

title: Fabric capacity errors: 24801 throttled, 24800 paused, APP_13400 on browse
text: Error 24801 'capacity exceeded' (or the connection-test text 'Fabric compute capacity has exceeded its limits') is a capacity throttle; it can be self-inflicted by failing jobs that keep hammering the capacity. Free fix before any resize: pause every job that hits it, kill orphan loaders holding port 1433 connections, then suspend and resume the capacity (`az fabric capacity suspend|resume -g <rg> --capacity-name <name>`). Error 24800 means the capacity is paused. `GET /api/v2/connection/source/<connId>?type=table` on a Fabric connection returned 403 APP_13400 'compute capacity exceeded' while the credentials were fine. An F2 handled light reads but locked for minutes after one mapping job; sustained loads needed F4. Capacity metrics live in the Fabric Capacity Metrics app, and the admin API is the source of truth for the SKU.
evidence: 24801 cleared by pausing jobs plus suspend/resume (2026-07-07); 24800 on every run while paused (2026-07-12)

title: Fabric warehouse SQL quirks that affect IDMC pre/post SQL and verification
text: Fabric DW DDL is eventually consistent: reuse after DROP/CREATE fails with 2714 or lags, so TRUNCATE and reuse tables and drop stale dependent views before reloads. Load with multi-row `INSERT ... VALUES` (pyodbc `executemany` is unusably slow; statements have a 2,100 bind-parameter limit) and count with `SELECT COUNT(*)` (`sys.partitions` can be stale). Replace per-table COUNT monitoring with one batched metadata query to keep a small capacity out of throttling. `FABRICDW_10000 Invalid operation field name <column>` points at a specific column of the Fabric source. SQL that runs on a Fabric warehouse (pre/post SQL, target DDL, verification and contract queries) must stay inside Fabric DW's T-SQL subset: declare timestamps as DATETIME2(6) (the legacy DATETIME type and precision above 6 were refused), replace QUALIFY with ROW_NUMBER() in a CTE or subquery filtered outside, and replace REGEXP_* with LIKE/PATINDEX or move the regex upstream into the source customQuery, which runs in the source engine's dialect (L-CDI-023). Validate each statement by materializing it once on Fabric before it goes into a task or a dashboard.
evidence: Direct loader and monitor rewrites (2026-07-04 to 2026-07-09); an 18-statement contract cleaned of DATETIME, QUALIFY and REGEXP and validated 18/18 by materializing each statement (2026-07-09)

title: Keep Salesforce and other SaaS targets inside their API and storage limits
text: A small SaaS target (for example a Developer Edition org with a few MB of storage) fills quickly: count the API calls per lane (about 10 per activity-lane run and 18 per customer-lane run were seen, about 2,000 a day) and cap child-object retention in the source query (a 60-day window still refilled a 5 MB org, while 7 days plus a daily retention job held, L-CONN-088), or writes start failing with storage errors that look like pipeline bugs.
evidence: Storage at 4 of 5 MB and ~2k API calls/day measured (2026-09-25/26); a 60-day window refilled the org and a 7-day window held (2026-10-01)

title: Creating a CCI connection (or any new source connection) requires the Administrator UI
text: An early REST probe listed TOOLKIT_CCI connection creation as UI-only because short type strings failed, and early July planning assumed new source connections needed the UI. Posting the full body works; only one first connection per add-on connector type needed the UI (L-CONN-005). Was believed 2026-06-27 to 2026-07-04; overturned by L-CONN-001.
evidence: Full-body creates 200 (2026-06-27 onward)

title: 'Unable to load driver' on JDBC V2 needs the Administrator upload-JAR flow; a file copy is never enough
text: After copies into several folders and restarts failed, the working hypothesis was that upload-JAR writes org-side metadata a copy cannot. File copies into the canonical directory plus a restart loaded drivers on 2026-08-19 and 2026-09-28. Was believed 2026-07-26 to 2026-08-18; overturned by L-CONN-051.
evidence: Driver loaded with no UI upload (2026-08-19, 2026-09-28)

title: JDBC V2 takes credentials in connParams.user like other connectors
text: JDBC V2 credentials were sent as `connParams.user` / `password`, copied from other connectors. The manifest names them `username` and `password`, and `user` does nothing. Was believed until 2026-07-26; overturned by L-CONN-047.
evidence: Manifest read (2026-07-26)

title: If a connector appears in GET /api/v2/connector, the org can use it
text: The connector list (hundreds of types) was read as the org's usable set. It is a type catalog; the agent's selections and adapter registry decide what runs. Was believed until 2026-07-26; overturned by L-CONN-021.
evidence: Adapter registry inspected (2026-07-26)

title: Fix a BigQuery JSON-column failure by flipping the connection from Simple to Hybrid
text: Planned as a one-dropdown fix. Hybrid broke every full-pushdown mapping (4005); recasting the column to STRING was the fix. Was believed 2026-07-04 (plan); overturned by L-CONN-042.
evidence: Plan cancelled after 4005 failures (2026-07-04)

title: Flat-file connections need the flat-file connector enabled in the UI
text: APP_10519 on a FLATFILE connection and 'no connector with type' on a CCI 'Flat File' type were read as a missing flat-file connector that only Administrator could enable, and a demo moved its source to PostgreSQL. A `CSVFile` connection worked headless. Was believed 2026-09-20 to 2026-09-23; overturned by L-CONN-065.
evidence: CSVFile test green and a run wrote rows (2026-09-24)

title: The BigQuery privateKey can be sent as the stripped base64 body everywhere
text: Stripped base64 (no BEGIN/END lines) passed CDI on one pod, so it was taken as sufficient. The Data Gateway rejected it there with 'Invalid PKCS#8 data'. Was believed 2026-09-22 to 2026-09-23; overturned by L-CONN-035.
evidence: Gateway failures until 2026-09-25

title: The full PEM with literal \n escapes works for CDI and every other consumer
text: After it fixed CDI plus the Data Gateway on one pod, the escaped-PEM form was prescribed for every org. On another pod the CDI connector rejected it while DBMI needed the PEM form. Was believed 2026-09-24 to 2026-09-28; overturned by L-CONN-035.
evidence: 'Invalid PKCS#8 data' from CDI on the second pod (2026-09-28)

title: A never-browsed PostgreSQL connection cannot resolve source objects over REST
text: Tasks over a REST-created PostgreSQL connection failed to find objects, so a UI browse, catalog seeding or a flat-file source was thought necessary. The object path format was the cause. Was believed 2026-09-22; overturned by L-CONN-028.
evidence: Tasks resolved with `<schema>/TABLE/<table>` (2026-09-23)

title: IDMC native writes into Fabric land nothing
text: A Fabric-target task reported SUCCESS with 0 rows in a drop test, attributed to an unset OneLake staging setting, so rows were landed by a direct loader instead. A later task with a create-new-at-runtime target landed rows through the IDMC engine. Was believed early July 2026; overturned by L-CONN-071.
evidence: 0 -> 10 rows by the IDMC task alone (2026-07-09)

title: Chunking long text into 250-character columns is the only in-IDMC way past the 255 cut
text: After the 255-character spikes, long text was split into 16 x 250-character columns (or landed via flat files). A JSON-typed BigQuery target column superseded it the same day. Was believed 2026-09-23 to 2026-09-24; overturned by L-CONN-044.
evidence: JSON columns kept full values (2026-09-24)

title: An older ClickHouse -all jar plus slf4j needed a UI connection test
text: A JDBC V2 connection using `clickhouse-jdbc-0.4.6-all.jar` plus slf4j failed its headless test on an slf4j classloading problem and was left for a UI test. The shaded 0.6.5 jar with `http_connection_provider=HTTP_URL_CONNECTION` works headless. Was believed 2026-07-13; overturned by L-CONN-054.
evidence: Later connections SUCCESSFUL (2026-08-19/20)

title: DBMI is served on its own `<pod>-ing` host, not the pod `/saas` host
text: Database Ingestion (DBMI) REST lives on `https://<pod>-ing.<domain>.informaticacloud.com`: design and job control under `/dbmi/public/api/v2/*`, job status under `/dbmi/api/v1/task/<taskId>/job`. A second prefix, `/mi/public/api/v2/*`, answers with typed DBMI errors and is unmapped. The same path gives a bare 404 on the pod host and a typed DBMI error on `-ing`, and `<pod>-ing` resolves in DNS while a bogus sibling does not. Take `<pod>` and `<domain>` from the login's `serverUrl` or `baseApiUrl`, and sweep the host family before believing any DBMI 404. Supersedes L-DBMI-045.
evidence: DNS plus same-path A/B test with a bogus-twin control (2026-07-26); full task lifecycle on two pods (2026-09-22 to 2026-09-29)

title: Read the `-ing` host's answers: a typed error is a live handler, `No static resource` is an absent route
text: `GET https://<pod>-ing.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/dbmi/public/api/v2/task/details` with a bogus id returns `{errorCode:404, errorMessage:'DBMI_TASK_WAS_NOT_FOUND'}`: a live handler that missed the id. `No static resource <path>` means the route is absent on that host. `GET .../task/create` returns 405 (the POST exists), and an empty `POST` returns 500 `Cannot invoke "Object.getClass()" because "o" is null` (the handler parsed and ran). `GET .../dbmi/public/api/v2/job/status` returned 415 `Content-Type is not supported` with and without parameters; read status from `GET /dbmi/api/v1/task/<taskId>/job` instead.
evidence: live probes 2026-07-26; one 2026-09-22 run reports job/status answering a GET that carried a JSON body {"jobId":<n>} (not re-verified)

title: The DBMI task lifecycle is fully headless: create, deploy, start, stop, resume, undeploy
text: On `https://<pod>-ing.<domain>.informaticacloud.com` with `IDS-SESSION-ID: <v2 icSessionId>`: `POST /dbmi/public/api/v2/task/create` (plain task JSON) returns 200/201 `{taskId, frsId}`; `POST /dbmi/public/api/v2/task/deploy/<taskId>` with `{}` returns 202 `data.jobId`; `POST /dbmi/public/api/v2/job/start|stop|resume|undeploy` takes `{"jobId":<n>}`; poll `GET /dbmi/api/v1/task/<taskId>/job` for `status` (`processing_deploy`, `deployed`, `running`, `stopped`, `failed`, `undeployed`, and `completed` for an initial load) and `runId` (the job id). The working helpers also sent `INFA-SESSION-ID` and `icSessionId` with the same value, and one early run used `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` plus `IDS-SESSION-ID`, so the minimum header set was not isolated. Runs also show in `GET /api/v2/activity/activityLog`. Supersedes L-DBMI-047, L-DBMI-048.
evidence: initial load of 24 tables / 682,385 rows (2026-09-22); CDC tasks created, deployed and started 2026-09-26, 2026-09-28 and 2026-09-29, jobs running with 0 errors

title: The task JSON that `task/create` accepts (PostgreSQL to BigQuery CDC)
text: `{"taskType":"dbmi","general":{"name":"<task>","location":"<project>","runtimeEnvironment":"<RE name>","type":"combined"},"source":{"connection":"<pg conn name>","schema":"public","replicationSlotName":"<slot>","replicationPlugin":"pgoutput","publication":"<pub>","restartPointForIncrementalLoad":"LATEST","selectionRules":[{"include":"<table>"}],"customProperties":{"loadType":"CDC_COMBINED","selectionMode":"RULE_BASED","lobsEnabled":"true","pwx.cdcreader.postgresql.connection.repl.slotname":"<slot>","pwx.cdcreader.postgresql.connection.repl.publication":"<pub>","pwx.cdcreader.postgresql.connection.repl.plugin":"pgoutput"}},"target":{"connection":"<bq conn name>","schema":"<dataset>","bucket":"<gcs bucket>","directory":"<dir>","dataTypeRules":[],"customProperties":{"auditColumnsPrefix":"INFA_","targetBucket":"<gcs bucket>","targetDirectory":"<dir>"}},"runtimeOptions":{"applyCycleIntervalSecs":"10","customProperties":{"FlushPeriod":"5","rat.cdcfile.cycle.interval.secs":"10"}}}`. The slot and publication appear twice (top level and in `customProperties`); keep them equal. The quickest complete body is an existing task's: `GET /dbmi/public/api/v2/task/details?taskId=<n>` returns it as `documents[].dbmiTask`.
evidence: the body that created three CDC tasks on 2026-09-28/29

title: `general.location` must be a project; connections and the runtime environment are referenced by name
text: task/create accepts only a project name in `general.location` (a folder path is rejected): create the task in `<project>`, then move it with FRS `MoveEntities` by its `frsId` and tag it. `general.runtimeEnvironment`, `source.connection` and `target.connection` take names, not ids, and a runtime-environment name copied from another org's template resolves to nothing. `task/details` reports `location` as the full path, so reset it before re-creating a task from a details body.
evidence: code comment 'create API only accepts the project' (2026-09-26); a copied runtime-environment name failed until the real name was used (2026-09-22)

title: The `-ing` plane uses numeric task and job ids; the 22-character `frsId` is the FRS / v3 id
text: DBMI task and job routes take integer ids; calling them with a design-time GUID returns a routing 404 that looks like a missing route. The 22-character `frsId` returned by task/create (also `extraData.taskId` in the job status) is the task's v3 object id: use it for FRS move and delete, `TagObjects` and v3 export. Every deploy creates a new job id.
evidence: GUID GET gave a routing 404 (2026-09-23); FRS moves and deletes by frsId worked (2026-09-26 to 2026-09-29)

title: There is no DBMI update verb: re-import an edited export, or create a new task and delete the old one
text: Option A: stop and undeploy the job (an import is refused while the task is deployed), v3-export the task, edit `<name>.DBMI_TASK.dat` (for example `common.runtimeSettings.runtimePropsMap` or `datatypeChangeRules`), replace that file's SHA-256 line in `exportPackage.chksum`, import with OVERWRITE, then deploy and start again (a new job id). Option B: read the task with `task/details`, edit `documents[].dbmiTask`, `POST task/create` a new task, deploy it, and delete the old one with `DELETE https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/frs/api/v1/BaseEntities('<frsId>')` (header `IDS-SESSION-ID`). Option B is also the quickest way to clone a working task.
evidence: a FlushPeriod change took effect through option A (2026-09-26); an imported task that would not deploy was replaced through option B (2026-09-28)

title: `job/resume` on a deployed job that never started returns 409 `WRONG_ACTION_FOR_DEPLOYED_JOB`
text: Start a freshly deployed job with `job/start`; `job/resume` answers 409 `WRONG_ACTION_FOR_DEPLOYED_JOB`. `job/resume` is for a job that was stopped or failed, and it served as the rollback and auto-recovery verb later.
evidence: single run 2026-09-22; resume of stopped and failed jobs 2026-09-26 and 2026-09-28

title: A redeploy creates a new job id and briefly gaps the target
text: After an import of changed settings, a deploy yields a new job id and a CDC_COMBINED task re-baselines; views over the target gapped for about 3 minutes. For a clean initial load, stop and undeploy, drop the target tables and the source-side `public.infa_persistent_<task>_<jobId>` table, then deploy and start.
evidence: job id changed on each redeploy; about 3 minutes of view gap (2026-09-26)

title: DBMI tasks are not v2 tasks: `/api/v2/job` gives UI_13404 and `/api/v2/mttask` gives REPO_19035
text: `POST /saas/api/v2/job` with a DBMI task id returns 403 `UI_13404 'Object identifier is not valid or missing'` for every taskType tried (MI_TASK, DMI, DBMI, DRS, MTT), and so does the agent's runAJob utility. `GET /saas/api/v2/mttask/<id>` on a DBMI id returns 403 `REPO_19035`. No managed MCP tool deploys a DBMI task. Use the `-ing` plane.
evidence: five taskType variants all 403 UI_13404 and 403 REPO_19035 (2026-09-22); full managed MCP registry enumeration (2026-09-23)

title: PostgreSQL CDC prerequisites: logical WAL, a replication role, a dedicated publication, a capped slot
text: Set `wal_level=logical` (`ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_level='logical'`, then restart; logical is a superset of replica, so a physical streaming replica keeps streaming: check `pg_stat_replication`). Leave free `max_replication_slots` and `max_wal_senders`. Create a `LOGIN REPLICATION` role with CONNECT, SELECT on the captured tables and USAGE + CREATE on the schema where DBMI writes its persistence table, plus a `pg_hba.conf` line `host replication <cdc_user> <agent-cidr> scram-sha-256`. `CREATE PUBLICATION <pub> FOR TABLE ...`, set each captured table `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`, cap retention with `max_slot_wal_keep_size` (for example 8GB), and create the slot last. On a container, check that the compose command does not pin `wal_level`, snapshot the disk first, and verify `SHOW wal_level` after the restart.
evidence: flip proven on a preprod container with the streaming replica unaffected (2026-07-09); all prerequisites applied and CDC live (2026-09-26)

title: Four source rules that each failed a DBMI CDC job until fixed
text: (1) DBMI creates `public.infa_persistent_<task>_<job>` itself, so the CDC role needs CREATE on schema `public`. (2) That table must not be in any publication, so no `FOR ALL TABLES` publication may exist: drop it and list the tables explicitly. (3) Every captured table must be `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` (deletes on tables without a primary key need it too). (4) Create the slot (`pg_create_logical_replication_slot('<slot>','pgoutput')`) after the publication, because pgoutput decodes with the historic catalog.
evidence: each rule failed the job until fixed; the task deployed after the changes (2026-09-24 to 2026-09-26)

title: The CDC role needs replication and read, not DML on the application tables
text: A Database Ingestion CDC source role needs REPLICATION, CONNECT and SELECT on the captured tables, plus CREATE on the one schema where DBMI writes its persistence table. A governance review found a CDC role holding full DML on 27 application tables; scope it down.
evidence: access-map finding (2026-09-28)

title: An unconsumed slot pins WAL: create it at the switch, cap retention, watch the lag
text: A logical slot that no job consumes keeps WAL until `max_slot_wal_keep_size` is reached, and then the slot is invalidated. Create a migration's new slot only right before the switch (a slot created days early can fill a nearly full disk), and expect a stopped job's slot to start retaining WAL. Check with `SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), confirmed_flush_lsn)) FROM pg_replication_slots;`. Newer evidence: L-DBMI-064.
evidence: disk about 95% full during planning; retention capped at 8 GB (2026-09-26 to 2026-09-28)

title: One DBMI job per replication slot; never run two CDC jobs into the same target
text: Only one job may consume a logical slot, and an old-org and a new-org job writing the same warehouse tables would double-write. Create or import the new task early and deploy it, but do not start it; at the switch, stop the old job first, then start the new one.
evidence: one consumer, 0 errors, confirmed_flush lag 0 after the switch (2026-09-28)

title: A slot used by a polling DBMI job shows `active=f` between cycles; never drop a live slot
text: DBMI polls its slot, so `pg_replication_slots.active` is false between cycles while `confirmed_flush_lsn` keeps advancing and retained WAL stays small. Judge a slot by its lag and by end-to-end freshness, never by the active flag. Cleanup scripts must refuse to drop a slot unless its job is known to be undeployed for good; after a cutover that reused a slot, that slot is the live one.
evidence: 10-second slot samples showed lag 0 bytes at nearly every sample while active=f (2026-09-28); the host cleanup script was made check-only (2026-09-29)

title: CDC_COMBINED task settings for PostgreSQL log-based capture
text: Use load type CDC_COMBINED (initial load, then incremental), plugin `pgoutput`, the publication and slot, restart point LATEST, a continuous job, and a BigQuery target typed and merged on the primary key. The target holds current state (MERGE), not a change log, so build views over it. When CDC takes over a table, retire any truncate-and-reload batch job writing the same target, because a full reload fights the stream.

title: `FlushPeriod` sets the latency floor: 60 s by default; 5 s cut about 85 s to about 25 s
text: The BigQuery writer's `FlushPeriod` defaults to 60 s. A task at the default measured about 85 s from source write to BigQuery; redeployed with `FlushPeriod=5` and `applyCycleIntervalSecs=10` it measured 24.9 s to the CDC table and 21.9 s to a view over it. Set `runtimeOptions.applyCycleIntervalSecs` and, in `runtimeOptions.customProperties`, `FlushPeriod` and `rat.cdcfile.cycle.interval.secs`.
evidence: end-to-end timer runs before and after the redeploy (2026-09-26)

title: Tables apply one after another in each cycle; split hot and cold tables into two tasks
text: Within a cycle DBMI applies tables sequentially: with 13 tables the first landed in about 15 s and the last in 30-35 s.
