title: A 403 on GET entity/<be>/<id> means the entity exists and you only lack rights
text: The identical 403 fires for a fabricated entity name, because the access check runs before the metadata lookup. Was believed to 2026-07-26; overturned by L-MDM-009.
evidence: 403 read as existence (to 2026-07-26)

title: MDM model deploy must have a REST verb somewhere: keep hunting
text: Absence was treated as "not yet found". Eighteen shapes returning a uniform 404 with no 405 meet the stopping rule: the route does not exist; plan the Modeler step. Was believed to 2026-07-26; overturned by L-MDM-005.
evidence: open-ended route hunting (to 2026-07-26)

title: The <pod>-mdm host is not mounted on this org
text: Declared after `/business-360/*` returned 404. Another prefix on the same host answered with a role-gap 403 while its bogus sibling returned 404. Was believed 2026-07-26; overturned by L-MDM-010.
evidence: 404 on one prefix (2026-07-26)

title: Reference 360 is unavailable because referenceDataSets returns 404
text: One 404 on one path was generalised to the service. The search sibling returns a validator 400, so Reference 360 lookup is headless. Was believed 2026-07-26; overturned by L-MDM-026.

title: MDM / Customer 360 is not licensed on the org
text: Inferred from the login `products[]` list, which showed only Integration Cloud. Privileges, roles, the console apps and dozens of MDM design objects showed full entitlement. Was believed 2026-07-04 to 2026-07-06; overturned by L-MDM-011.
evidence: products[] read as entitlement (2026-07-04 to 2026-07-06)

title: The Product 360 documentation describes the MDM you have
text: A P360 doc URL was assumed to cover the licensed MDM, so its automation notes were applied. P360 Cloud Edition is a different, AWS-hosted product with no REST API. Was believed to 2026-07-26; overturned by L-MDM-055.
evidence: doc assumed to match the license (to 2026-07-26)

title: The migration clone route is closed on this pod (import/package 404 MigrationSvc_025)
text: The probe had sent `application/json`. With `multipart/form-data` the import route accepts uploads; what the org lacked was a template to clone. Was believed 2026-07-26; overturned by L-MDM-014.
evidence: 404 MigrationSvc_025 under application/json (2026-07-26)

title: There is no public REST search, list or count of MDM records, so master-record counts cannot be read headless
text: Held while the probed routes were `.../entity/<be>/search` (404/405) and job routes. `POST /search/public/api/v1/search` pages and exports master records, up to 10,000 per query. Was believed 2026-07-08 to 2026-09-27; overturned by L-MDM-025.
evidence: 405/404 on the business-entity search route (2026-07-08 to 2026-07-26)

title: Credentials come from environment variables or a 0600 file outside any repo, never literals
text: Read IDMC credentials at run time from environment variables (for example `IDMC_USER` / `IDMC_PASS`) or from a mode-0600 file that lives outside every repository and shared folder, one file per org. Never put a credential literal in a script, a committed config, a command line, a tracker comment or chat. Session caches, OAuth env files and service-account key files are credentials too: gitignore them and keep them 0600. A path to a secret is fine to share; its contents are not.
evidence: Standing rule of the reference skill and of the September host tooling; secret-scan gates on committed tooling came back clean

title: Put every IDMC call behind one org-aware session module
text: Give every script on a host one small module that exposes `sess()`, `get()`, `post()`, `call(method, path, body, v3=False)` and `v3_login()`, plus the constants `ORG` and `HOST`. The org comes from an env var (for example `IDMC_ORG`), else the first word of a switch file, else a safe default; each org has its own creds file, session cache and login host. Moving a whole host to another org is then one write to the switch file plus remapped id files; a single cron job can stay pinned to the old org by setting the env var on its line, and scripts that must only ever touch one org assert `ORG` at import time.
evidence: A host was flipped between orgs with one switch-file write; post-flip verification returned the new org id and pod base

title: Cache the session for at most 25 minutes and log in again exactly once on a 401
text: The v2 `icSessionId` (and any JWT minted from it) dies about 30 minutes after it is granted, whatever the activity. Cache `{sid, serverUrl, orgId, t}` in a 0600 file and log in again when the cache is older than 1500 s (one helper refreshes at 24 min); keep a separate cache for the v3 `sessionId` used by catalog, profiling and MCP-management calls. On an API 401, delete the cache and log in exactly once more, then return the error. A long-running service does the same in memory.
evidence: Stable across the host tooling and a full org-to-org migration; the absolute 30-minute death was observed repeatedly

title: Lockout guard: serialize logins and block on a rejected login until the creds change
text: Take an exclusive `fcntl.flock` on a lock file before logging in, then re-check the session cache (another process may just have logged in). If the server rejects the login (HTTP 4xx other than 429), write a block file holding the SHA-256 fingerprint of the creds file; while the fingerprint still matches, every process refuses to log in ("fix the creds or delete the block file"). 5xx and 429 do not block. A long-running service whose scheduler ticks every few seconds pauses logins for hours after an auth rejection (for example 21,600 s) and for about 60 s after a transient failure, and shows the block on its health endpoint. A password-rotation script writes the new value in place, deletes the block file and the caches, and verifies with exactly one login.
evidence: Mocked-network tests 11/11 for the host helper and 14/14 for the service: a rejected login followed by 10-20 attempts made 0 network calls; a 503 did not block

title: Test login guards and patched services offline before deploying them
text: Before deploying a login or lockout change, unit-test the helper against a fake `urlopen` (success, 401, 503, rejected logins) in a temporary HOME with fake creds files, and count the network calls. Run a patched service in a throwaway container built from the live image with `--network none` and a fake login server. Deploy only when every case passes.
evidence: 11/11 cases for the org-aware helper and 14/14 for the staged service

title: The helper returns (status, body) and does not raise: check the status
text: A `call()` that returns `(HTTP status, parsed JSON or text)` for 2xx and error answers alike lets an error payload be read as data when the caller treats the return value as the body or ignores the status. Unpack the tuple and require the expected status before using the body; a small `body()` helper that raises on non-2xx removes the trap.
evidence: Recorded as the known trip in a shared operations helper

title: Derive every host from the login answer; never string-replace a pod literal
text: Take the pod base from the v2 `serverUrl` or the v3 `products[].baseApiUrl` and derive service hosts from it, for example the CAI host by splitting the base host at the first dot (`<pod>-cai.<rest-of-host>`). Builders that computed the CAI host by replacing a pod literal (`"<pod1>.<dom1>"` to `"<pod1>-cai.<dom1>"`) silently stopped working when the org moved to another pod, and hard-coded hosts and ids in builders kept pointing at the old org after a migration. The login host is the domain host `https://<domain>.informaticacloud.com`, never the pod host.
evidence: Stale builders after an org move still held the old pod's host literals and ids

title: Establish the org first, and make destructive scripts prove it from a live read
text: At the start of every session derive the org name, both org-id shapes (6-character v2, 22-character v3), the pod, the domain label and the base URL from `POST https://<domain>.informaticacloud.com/saas/public/core/v3/login` (`products[].baseApiUrl`), `GET /api/v2/org` and `GET /api/v2/agent`; a proven row from one org or pod is not evidence for another. Before any delete or bulk write, assert the org from a live read (`GET /api/v2/org` must return the expected `id`), not from a variable, because the same script may run under the other org's switch file.
evidence: An owner asked which org a cleanup was deleting from; the live read answered it

title: Address IDMC objects by id, never by name
text: Task, taskflow and connection names repeat across folders, projects and orgs, so resolve every object to its id and act on the id: v2 ids for `/api/v2/*`, the 22-character `frsGuid` for v3 and FRS calls. Resolve by path with `POST /public/core/v3/lookup {"objects":[{"path":"<project>/<folder>/<name>","type":"MTT"}]}` and require exactly one match; a v2 mapping task's v3 id is its `frsGuid`, which only the detail GET returns. In migrations and cleanups remap by id and block any file that would keep an unmapped id.
evidence: Same-named tasks existed in unrelated older folders; a migration flip tool cross-checked 138 name/id pairs with 0 mismatches

title: How a session changes a mapping task headless, end to end
text: Back up first: the v2 task JSON, the old SQL as a file and a v3 export of the task. `GET /api/v2/mttask/<id>`, drop the read-only fields (`orgId`, `createTime`, `updateTime`, `createdBy`, `updatedBy`, `agentId` when retargeting, and each parameter `id`), change only the field you mean (for SQL, replace an anchor inside `$Source$.customQuery` after asserting it occurs exactly once), `POST /api/v2/mttask/<id>` and read the task back. Diff old and new SQL against current data in the warehouse before the live task runs it, then run with `POST /api/v2/job {"@type":"job","taskId":"<taskId>","taskType":"MTT"}` and poll `GET /api/v2/activity/activityLog?taskId=<taskId>&rowLimit=1` until the `runId` matches. Bigger changes go side by side (new folder, parity-only target, parity plus an idempotency double run) before any swap.
evidence: The pattern behind every SQL change and the consolidation swap; parity diffs of 0 rows before switching

title: Where MCP fits: enumerate the real registry, then choose REST or MCP per call
text: MCP is a calling convention, not a network position: it never replaces a Secure Agent, never reaches a private database the agent cannot, and its backing calls still bill IPUs. Before calling anything MCP-walled, list the org's managed servers (`GET https://hdm.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/a2e-mcp-asset-mgmt-svc/api/v1/mcp-servers?type=MANAGED`; one org exposed 19 servers and about 140 tools) instead of reasoning from the servers wired into your session. Prefer REST for writes and for anything REST already does; use MCP where it adds something (lineage reads, fuzzy identity match, the hosted DQ agent on uploaded files, address verification) or as one uniform tool surface through a local gateway that holds a single OAuth client. Check which org and host a locally configured MCP server logs in to before trusting an empty answer: one local server was pointed at a different org and showed nothing.
evidence: An early 'most capabilities walled' verdict came from the two servers wired into a session; the full registry falsified several walls

title: Keep a GET-only probe harness and a dry-run ops script instead of one-off probes
text: Wrap preflight and probing in a script you keep: it logs in on every plane, is GET-only by default, gates writes behind an explicit flag (for example `--allow-write` for a create-and-delete round trip), offers `--dry-run` that prints a body without sending it, and encodes the traps once (bogus-twin fake-200 filter, empty-POST verb probe, per-agent health read instead of the runtime-environment list, the verified connection body). Re-run it and stamp `last_verified` before relying on a live row. Fresh one-off probes re-learn every trap.
evidence: The July endpoint corpus was built with such a harness; walked-back conclusions came from ad-hoc probes

title: Write-capable tooling: dry run by default, --execute to act, backup plus UNDO log plus manifest
text: Scripts that change live systems run as a dry run unless `--execute` is given and print exactly what they would do. With `--execute` they first back each file or object up into a timestamped directory (preserving mode, so 0600 stays 0600), append one line per change to an UNDO log (`restore <backup> -> <path>` or `delete <path> (created)`), write a manifest, and offer `rollback --backup <ts>`. Cron changes are made by commenting lines out with a tag, so the undo is mechanical. For IDMC objects the backup is a v3 export package (undo = re-import with REUSE).
evidence: The backup sets were used for a real flip-back and for several rollbacks

title: Patches are anchored and idempotent; prove a patch chain by re-running it on its own output
text: Change live code and generated artifacts only by edits on exact anchors: skip when the new text is already present; otherwise require the anchor to occur exactly N times and fail with "file changed since the plan; re-read it" if it does not. When several patches rewrite one artifact, keep ONE canonical chain in a fixed order, add "also accept the later rewrite" markers, normalize encodings (CRLF, encoded newlines) before comparing, rename superseded scripts so nobody runs them, and prove the chain on a fresh download of the published artifact: every step must SKIP and the bytes must be identical. Fold the chain into the generator when you can.
evidence: A 15-step chain was a byte-identical no-op on the live artifact after the fixes

title: After editing a safety switch, assert it actually changed
text: A purge script's "validate" mode once ran as "apply" because a string replacement silently failed to match. After any edit to a dry-run/apply flag, a feature flag or a guard, read the new value back (or print it) and assert it before running the script.
evidence: Validate ran as apply

title: Deploys export the current version, apply, verify and roll back in the same run
text: A deploy script exports the current version first (the undo), applies the change, runs the verification calls and restores the export automatically if any check fails, all in one run, so a failed deploy never waits for a human to notice. For IDMC design objects this is export, swap, import OVERWRITE, publish, verify or roll back.
evidence: Name-rule redeploys of CAI processes ran this way

title: Risky runtime behaviour goes behind env flags with an instant rollback
text: New execution modes (staged instead of linear lanes, a new plan file, a coalescing knob) default to off in code and are switched by env vars. A small flag script edits the env file in place, waits until the service is idle, recreates only that container and prints the running value; `off` is the rollback and needs no rebuild. Never switch runtime flags in the middle of a run.
evidence: Staged execution switched on with a flag script; the rollback path was documented in the cutover report

title: Rebuild a controller that starts its own jobs without a race
text: Build the new image while the old container keeps serving; poll its current-run endpoint until it reports idle (give up after about 15 minutes); then recreate at once, so no run can start between the idle check and the swap.
evidence: The flip waited for idle (0 s) and came up healthy

title: Single-writer locks for cron-driven runners, with real liveness checks
text: A runner that cron may start while an earlier run is still going takes a non-blocking exclusive lock (`fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB)`) on a per-mode lock file and exits 0 with "another run holds the lock; skipping"; wrap long cron jobs in `flock -n` and `timeout` as well. A single-flight marker such as `state == RUNNING` jams forever when a run is killed, so record the pid and a heartbeat and treat a dead pid as free; `kill -0` also succeeds for a zombie (`<defunct>`), so check that `ps -o stat= -p <pid>` does not start with Z, and keep a manual finalize script as a fallback.
evidence: A recurring 409 on a dead run stopped after the liveness check

title: Keep one source of truth for builders, plans, id files and generated documents
text: When the same generator lives in two or three directories, a fix lands in one copy and the others keep the bug (a deleted template reference, a missing lane, retired behaviour); plan files baked into an image and copied elsewhere drifted, and one copy still held the old org's ids after a migration. Keep one source per org and generate or symlink the rest, or at least diff the copies after every change. The same holds for generated documents and skills: edit the source, not the rendered copy, or the next build silently reverts the edit.
evidence: A diff of three builder copies showed divergent fixes; a hand edit to a generated skill was lost on rebuild

title: A tool call the user rejected may already have run: read back before reporting
text: When a user interrupts or rejects a tool call, the request may already have reached the server. Before saying that nothing happened, read the affected objects back and report what actually changed.
evidence: 68 FRS deletes had already landed when a call was rejected mid-run

title: Log every IDMC write in one central tracker with its id and exact undo
text: Keep one tracker project as the single log of all IDMC activity and freeze older projects as read-only archives with cross-reference comments. Log each write with the object id and its exact undo, each wall with its exact call and date, and each probe with its cleanup. The actionable queue is open issues with no `blocked:*` label, and every blocked label names the human or gate it waits on. For writers that may re-run, embed a unique idempotency marker inside the comment body (the HTML), because some trackers regenerate the plain-text field on save.
evidence: One central log served every session through a week of parallel work

title: Four evidence states are never merged: WORKS, DOC, REJECTED, UNTESTED
text: WORKS = a live status code observed on a stated org and date ("proven as of <date>"). DOC = a named Informatica guide states it but nobody exercised it ("documented, unproven"; never report it as working). REJECTED = refused with a code (`405` = read-only at any permission level). UNTESTED = absent from all evidence: unknown, not unsupported. A blank or `--` cell means untested, not absent; `405` means absent. List every verified verb per endpoint and keep `untested: PUT, PATCH` apart from `rejected: PUT 405`. Never upgrade DOC to WORKS without a live response.
evidence: 569 of 830 endpoint-verb combinations were untested in the July corpus; earlier wrong calls traced to merging untested with rejected

title: Bogus-twin every input you control, including error codes and 503s
text: Probe a nonsense sibling next to the real input: the path (`/.../bogusZZZ`), the object name (`entity/ZZFAKEENTITY`), the host (an unroutable IP) and the error-producing route (`/api/v2/agent/bogusZZZ`). If the twin answers identically (the same zero-byte 200, 403, 500 or nginx 503), the response is an artifact and says nothing about the real input. Recorded artifacts: 403/500 router answers under `/api/v2/agent/*`; an MDM 403 that fires before the metadata lookup; nginx 503 on the `-apim` / `-apigw` hosts for every path; `error [error [null]]` from a connection test aimed at an unroutable host.
evidence: Four artifact classes proven with twins

title: A 200 can be fake: never report a zero-byte 200 or a 200 that carries login HTML
text: A `200` with `Content-Length: 0` and no `Content-Type` means a gateway routed the prefix and nothing is serving: `GET /data360/search/api/v99/bogusZZZ` also returned 200 with 0 bytes, while the control `GET /api/v2/bogusZZZnope` returned `404 "Resource not found"` (that plane is real). A `200` carrying the identity-service login page means the wrong plane or header, or a stale session. Assert on the body shape, not the status.
evidence: Bogus-twin A/B on a real org; a record read reported as 200 was login HTML and fooled a slide and a first check

title: Read what kind of 404 it is before concluding anything
text: `404` with a JSON or text body usually means a wrong path or host: keep hunting (the most common false negative). `404` with an empty body, or `No static resource <path>`, means the route is absent. A typed product error inside a 404 (for example `DBMI_TASK_WAS_NOT_FOUND`) is a live handler answering a lookup. `403` and `405` point at a role gap or a read-only resource, never at entitlement. The MDM host returns `404 CMN00005` for bogus siblings too, so treat it as "no such route" unless a bogus twin differs.
evidence: Status decoder plus ingestion-host and MDM-host probes

title: There is no HEAD or OPTIONS: probe a write verb with an empty POST
text: IDMC offers no preflight discovery. POST an empty body: `400` / `415` / `422` means the verb exists and the body is wrong; a `500` naming a null field (for example `Cannot invoke Object.getClass() because o is null`) means the handler parsed and ran; `405` means the verb does not exist. An empty body cannot create anything, so the probe is safe.
evidence: How an ingestion task create, a reference-data search and a runtime-environment create were shown to exist

title: Vary the Content-Type before declaring an upload route absent
text: A write route has two axes. On `POST /public/core/v3/import/package` one org answered `application/json` with `404 MigrationSvc_025`, `application/zip` and `application/octet-stream` with `415`, and `multipart/form-data` with `400 MigrationSvc_030` (handler reached). Try `application/json`, `multipart/form-data`, `application/zip` and `application/octet-stream`; only `405` on every encoding is a verdict. The JSON 404 is the dangerous cell because it reads as "wrong path".
evidence: A four-encoding matrix on one org; a false 'the clone path is closed' conclusion had come from the JSON 404

title: Sweep the host family first; uniform 404 with no 405 means the route is absent
text: IDMC fans services onto per-product hosts (`<pod>.<domain>` with `/saas`, `idmc-api.<domain>`, `cdgc-api.<domain>`, `hdm.<domain>`, `<pod>-cai`, `<pod>-mdm`, `<pod>-ing`, `<pod>-dqprofile`, `<pod>-dqcloud-api`), so resolve candidate hosts by DNS (free, no auth; a bogus suffix must not resolve) before believing any service-level 404. Then use 404 versus 405 as the stopping rule: any `405` means the route exists with the wrong verb (keep going); uniform `404` across many plausible shapes, each matching its bogus twin, means the route is absent (stop and design the click in).
evidence: A DNS sweep found the ingestion service live on the -ing host after it had been recorded as UI-only; six MDM deploy shapes and twelve model-authoring shapes all gave 404 with no 405

title: Read back after every write; a 200 whose value reverts is a silent rejection
text: After every write, read the object back and compare the field you changed: a v2 `POST .../{id}` is checked with a `GET` of the same id (for example `scheduleId` after a bind); a v2 `DELETE` returns 200 and a read-back 403 means gone; a deleted schedule's GET returns an empty 200 shell, so check the list instead; FRS deletes report per item (`FRS_200` ok, `FRS_082` still published, `FRS_087` project not empty) and a read-back gives `FRS_070`; an FRS PATCH of `customAttributes` returned 204 and changed nothing. A `200` whose value reverts on read-back (a mapping-task connection retarget across connector types did this) is a silent rejection.
evidence: Read-backs caught reverted retargets, a 204 no-op PATCH and an empty-shell schedule GET

title: POST to start, GET to poll, and read per-item status inside a 200 envelope
text: Scans, CAI publish, migration export and import, metering export and MDM jobs work the same way: a `201` / `202` with a job id is success of the submission, not of the work. Poll the job (a `GET` on the starter path returns 405 by design). Items can fail inside a `200` envelope (CAI publish `itemDetail[].itemState`, catalog `207 Multi-Status`, import per-object states), so read every item before reporting.
evidence: The pattern behind every headless win in the corpus

title: A verb census is a dated snapshot: PUT is proven on runtime-environment selections
text: `PUT /runtime/api/v2/runtimeEnvironment/<reId>/selections/ui` on the pod host with `IDS-SESSION-ID` (the v2 session) works, so "no PUT anywhere in IDMC" is false. The practical idiom still holds for most resources: on the v2 plane `POST /api/v2/<resource>/{id}` with the full GET body is the update; elsewhere DELETE and re-POST; any documented PUT or PATCH stays unproven until a live call succeeds. Treat every verb census as dated: DELETEs on six v2 resources, FRS deletes and v3 user deletes were also proven after the July count.
evidence: Service and connector selections changed and read back over PUT; July census had counted PUT 0 proven / 14 documented / 12 rejected / 140 untested

title: Entitlement comes from deployed engines, privileges and selections, never from products[] or a 404
text: Never conclude a capability is unlicensed from a REST probe or from the login `products[]` list, which is a launcher label (orgs that listed only "Integration Cloud" held catalog, CAI and ingestion capabilities). Read the engines on each agent (`GET /api/v2/agent/details/<agentId>`: `agentEngines[].appname` and `agentEngineStatus.status`), the privileges from the identity-service login, the runtime-environment service selections, and whether a real create call validates. With no agent installed, entitlement is unresolved, not disproven.
evidence: About 90 issues had been falsely escalated as buy-a-licence in one program; in another, 'no catalog entitlement' fell when catalog sources, scans and a glossary were created headless

title: Search the existing evidence before calling anything a wall
text: Before concluding "not possible" or "not entitled", grep the KB's evidence, section content and endpoint-verb matrix for the endpoint and for the exact error string. The canonical failure: a session got `403 APP_10519` creating a PostgreSQL connection with `type: "PostgreSQL"`, swept 13 spellings and recommended a licensing ticket, while the verified body (`type: "TOOLKIT_CCI"`, connector name in `instanceName`) was already on disk and the org held hundreds of licences.
evidence: Incident reconstructed from session history

title: Date every wall and re-test it when anything changes
text: IDMC verdicts flipped repeatedly within days (authoring UI-only, connector enablement UI-only, catalog unentitled, CDC deploy UI-only, CAI publish needs a designer Save); in one July corpus live verdicts flipped on a 3-5 day cadence. Record each wall with the exact verb, host, path, headers, body shape, error code, org and date, and re-probe when the agent build, pod, header, path, content type or available tools change. Do not re-grind a wall without a new angle, and prefer "let me verify on your org" over quoting a dated row to a customer.
evidence: At least six verdicts overturned between 2026-09-20 and 2026-09-28

title: Say the right kind of no: six headless verdicts and four kinds of cannot
text: Use HEADLESS (a live status proved it), HEADLESS-DOC (documented, unexercised), NEEDS SHELL (no browser, but a host shell: agent install, driver staging), UI-ONLY (licensed and working; a human clicks), UNTESTED (unknown) and WRONG-HOST RISK (recorded absent, host family never swept). Classify every "cannot" as a hard wall (empty-body 404 or 405 on every verb: design a click in), a read-only resource (405 on this verb: use the update idiom), not on this host (404 with a body: try the other host) or nobody checked (never quote it as a limit). Commercially, UI-ONLY (one click in something the customer already owns) and GAP (not there) must never be confused.
evidence: Decision guide of the reference corpus

title: The wall is usually a UI-only final step or a gate, rarely licensing
text: When a capability looks blocked, assume first that reads and runs work and the missing piece is a UI-only final action (a publish, a deploy, an accept), a spend gate or a production-cutover gate. Prepare everything headless up to that step (specs, worklists, clones), hand over one precise UI step, and later re-test the step's headless route by capturing the UI's own API call. Keep purchase conversations for engines genuinely absent from every agent.
evidence: Of 44 catalogued walls in one program almost none were licensing; many September 'UI-only' steps later proved headless

title: Suspect your own input first: walls that were operator errors
text: Several written "walls" were inputs. `IDS_085` came from a truncated username or the wrong login domain, not a lockout. A v3 scan found "0 objects" because the type filter was wrong (`type=='DBMI'` returns 0 while the type is `DBMI_TASK`) and the objects sat in another user's project. A CAI publish `BAD_REQUEST "Invalid asset path"` came from the path format (`Explore/<project>/<folder>/<name>.PROCESS.xml` works). A 404 came from the wrong Content-Type. Before escalating, re-check host, full username, exact type names, path format and encoding, and remember that the v3 `q` type filter is not validated.
evidence: Each reached a written verdict before being walked back

title: Report stage by stage: authored, deployed, running, integrated; never round up
text: Say exactly which stage is proven. Authored (a design object exists) is not deployed (published or deployed to a runtime), deployed is not running (a run completed with rows), and running is not integrated (the live application reads IDMC-produced data, reacts to a CAI decision or shows DQ results). Keep a dual gate per step (works in the app, visible in the IDMC UI), track each capability-by-app pair as its own gate, never simulate IDMC behaviour and present it as real, and label in-house analogs as such until the genuine runtime produces the outputs.
evidence: An acceptance bar of 'CAI, CDI and DQ actually integrated into each application' was met only when the apps consumed IDMC outputs

title: A schedule is not proven until an unattended run fires green
text: Setting a schedule (in the API and in persisted config) proves only configuration. Treat it as "set, not yet proven to auto-fire" until a run started by the scheduler itself, not a manual trigger, completes successfully at its window. The same holds for IDMC task and taskflow schedules and for host crons (prove a cron fix by waiting for one autonomous fire).
evidence: Manual runs green while the first unattended run was still pending

title: False greens: never score from a status, a container state or an issue state
text: Each acceptance box needs a positive observation of correct behaviour: the right content (not just a 200), rows present in the target (not just a connection success), a completed authenticated journey (not just a login page), data flowing end to end (not just containers Up). Recorded false greens: a hostname returning 200 while routed to the wrong application; containers Up (healthy) over a pipeline that had processed nothing for 38 hours; health checks green while every route returned 500; items marked Done whose code was not on disk; tests green while the app could not parse a request body; a swallowed 404 read as a count of 0. Quote the command and its output as evidence. Newer evidence: L-METHOD-147.
evidence: Seven false greens in one night, all of the same shape

title: Monitors emit an explicit unavailable or UNKNOWN with a reason, never a green zero
text: A collector whose source is absent or not yet deployed should detect that (for example a 404 from the native runtime) and emit `available=0` or `is_materialized=false` with a reason label, using the schema of the future native feed so it switches over automatically. An audit that cannot reach a system (missing client library, auth failure, network) records UNKNOWN, not NO: one missing library painted a whole column red. Never let a panel fall back to hard-coded green values when its source disappears, treat no-data as alerting, and confirm an "empty" reading with an independent query through a different client, because the monitor itself can be broken.
evidence: A dropped scorecard table regressed a panel to a hard-coded 18/18 green (live value 9/15); a column went 0/6 to 5/6 once the audit ran under the right interpreter

title: Prove what actually wrote the data before crediting IDMC
text: Keep an explicit evidence layer per capability (IDMC-native output versus an equivalent built in warehouse SQL or scripts). Check the warehouse's query history for the writer (service identity, program name, statement shape): Python or ODBC clients with no Informatica engine signature mean the data was written outside IDMC. Confirm which schema the running tasks actually write (a hand-loaded look-alike can hold stale rows), audit wrapper scripts for side-channel DDL (TRUNCATE or DROP over ODBC around each run), and classify claims as REAL, FACADE (defined, never ran), NOT IDMC (SQL or scripts) or DISCONNECTED. A task reporting SUCCESS with `successTargetRows == 0` is a failure (treat a missing count as unknown, not zero). Newer evidence: L-CDI-295. Newer evidence: L-MDM-087, L-METHOD-159.
evidence: One audit found about 15% of 697 org assets load-bearing and a task reporting success with 0 rows in its target

title: Prove a mapping transformed data, and build its spec from the real producer
text: To show the engine applied logic rather than copying, join target to source on the business key, count rows where each cleansed column differs from the raw column, list before/after examples, and show that any DQ flag discriminates exactly the known-bad rows; pair it with the job's own read-back (success rows, rejected rows, "completed with [0] row transformation errors"). Before declaring a transform hard to reproduce, find the SQL that actually produces the live table (the running pipeline's code) and diff it against the staged spec, because staged copies go stale.
evidence: Per-column change counts plus 4 flagged malformed emails matched exactly; a feared mismatch vanished with the real producer SQL (0/0 diff)

title: Verify claimed completion independently; the doer never validates
text: Agents sign work off as done when it is only scaffolded. Before accepting Done, confirm the cited files exist and are committed, re-run the claimed tests or queries yourself, and probe live endpoints expecting 401/405 (route mounted) rather than 404 (route absent). Add a Validated state after Done, set only by a different agent that reproduces the evidence; match the doer by persona family (a name-suffix sub-agent must not validate its parent's work), and bounce the item if an artifact is missing or the result does not reproduce.
evidence: A '32/32 pass' claim re-ran as 2 pass / 3 fail / 27 skip; disk checks disproved 3 Done claims

title: Use adversarial, refute-only verification for figures and blocker lists
text: For numbers someone will act on, run an independent read-only recompute that re-parses the raw sources without importing the build script, plus reviewers told only to refute the result from raw documents; for large fact tables run two passes (adjudicate every cell, then a skeptic defends the current value) and change a cell only when both agree. For boards that claim many items are blocked, assign one verifier per cluster to refute each block with a live probe. When two audits disagree, investigate and report the stricter one, especially the one the stakeholder sees. Before executing an IDMC plan, do the same against the live captures, not just the plan text: discovery lanes write FACTS, GAPS and RISKS tagged with provenance (live, kb or inferred) and the evidence path, several independent critics tag their findings blocker, major or minor with evidence and a fix, and an authoritative decisions list overrides the plan wherever they differ. In one plan 4 critics found 5 blockers and 46 majors, including a job-budget guard that could not see profile runs or catalog jobs (L-IPU-055), a catalog source to be cloned with DQ automation on (L-CDGC-152) and a host-protection step ordered after the run it was meant to protect. Newer evidence: L-METHOD-131.
evidence: Refute-only reviewers caught a 1x-versus-2x modelling error; of 145 claimed blocks about 44 were false; two scanners read 8/8 and 4/6 until reconciled; 4 critic passes over a plan built from 8 read-only discovery lanes found 5 blockers and 46 majors, each traced to a raw capture (2026-10-03)

title: Prove every verifier can fail, and read the summary instead of the exit code
text: Inject a known fault for each check and confirm it goes red: a parity checker that greps for FAIL while the tool prints DRIFT or MISSING never fails, and one that treats "did not run" as a skip hides outages. Do not trust a driver that exits 0 regardless: read its summary line (for example `99/114; residue=0`) and trace every non-green to harness causes or real defects. Reconcile the discovered inventory (files, specs, lanes) against what actually executed, so a green aggregate cannot silently skip a suite.
evidence: Fault injection: all-missing gave ok:false f=4, partial drift gave f=2

title: Measurement over inference before any delete
text: Every delete decision rests on an enumeration, not an inference: "no VMs, so the project is empty" (it held live warehouse datasets), "same size, so identical" (different checksums), "unmounted, so stale" (it held the fuller copy) and "the job reported success" (0-byte objects) were all false. Confirm dormant or orphan objects with a live read-only count; try to refute orphanhood by grepping every producer and consumer (other services, pipeline SQL, IDMC tasks, governance builders) and by checking task-level schedules, which only the task detail GET shows, and app endpoints that read the output. Inability to enumerate (a 403) means not deletable.
evidence: Four false delete verdicts overturned by measurement; 37 of 90 flagged tables refuted; one 'orphan' task had its own hourly schedule and fed an app API

title: Every number from a query, every timing measured
text: Back every dashboard or runbook claim ("answered in 4 s", "updates within about 30 s") with a query or a measurement and its window. Hard-coded SQL unions and typed text boxes go stale and undermine every true claim: replace them with live queries or label them. Do not show percentiles on tiny samples (p50 only with at least about 5 timed calls, p95 with at least about 20; a p95 over 13 samples is just the slowest call), compute latency from the same calls you count, and never publish a coverage percentage that was estimated rather than counted (state proven verbs out of total routes and the untested share). Publish latencies only from a read-only collector, never typed in: compute each hop from timestamps the platform already records (source commit proxy -> CDC landing; event -> first successful CAI upsert in your decision log; event -> end of the first fully successful lane run that started after it; event -> first verification row) over a rolling window as n, average, fastest, last and last_at. Rules: success only (a call with ok=true; IDMC runs SUCCESS or WARNING; a lane only when every task succeeded); a sample belongs to the window in which it completed; drop samples overlapping a deploy and negative values; match an outcome to its event only within N minutes and count the event's own first check, so a later re-check is not reported as event latency; keep every hop independent, so one failing query marks only its hop unavailable; write the output atomically and refuse to publish when fewer than 3 hops were measured; hide hops with no samples instead of printing a placeholder; split lane statistics by pipeline mode; show batch schedules as cadence plus last run, never as a latency. Make collectors read-only by construction (a READ ONLY transaction with a statement_timeout; SELECT-only warehouse access with a maximum-bytes-billed cap and job labels), mark every assumed name or meaning with '# ASSUMPTION:' and its evidence, and check that each hop keys on names the callers actually log (hops keyed on process names nobody writes stay at 0 samples forever). Traps found in one audit of 37 published figures: averages over all calls including failures (809 ms at 51.8% success); a client that stores latency only for the final attempt; wall-clock time versus the IDMC task span; a 'real-time view' hop that is only a view over the CDC table; cadences copied from an old schedule; a re-check that overwrites its own first timestamp; a re-applied DDL file that silently drops a measure; and browser timings that depend on a cold CDN cache (17-26 s cold against 8-9 s warm): time pages cold and warm.
evidence: A tie-out of a 40-zone executive page found hard-coded rows and unmeasured timing claims; a 37-row inventory of user-visible figures found 15 inconsistencies, after which the success-only collector fed the pages every 5 min and an independent run matched it (CAI to SaaS avg 2.0 s; CDC row avg 26.0 s, n=295; event lane avg 106 s, n=21) (2026-09-30 to 2026-10-02)

title: Check which environment and which checkout a piece of evidence came from
text: A monitoring or test result from a dev overlay does not prove production: before closing an item, confirm the host, datasource and config the evidence came from, and report UNKNOWN when evidence for an environment is missing. Verify code against the working tree and branch actually deployed (a local clone can be far behind), diff the deployed copy against your local copy before overwriting in either direction, and re-check your on-host edits after agent or container restarts, which can revert patched files.
evidence: A 'done' monitoring item reflected the dev overlay; a stale local push reverted a server-side fix

title: Prove a server-side fault with a same-session asymmetry test, and diagnose from both ends
text: To show a failure is the platform's and not your automation's, make the identical call with the same session and endpoint on a case that should work and one that fails (for example a re-publish versus a first publish); a deterministic split, plus the vendor UI failing the same way, is strong evidence for a support ticket. When an API error is ambiguous, reproduce the operation outside IDMC (run the JDBC driver on the agent host with the same URL, read the target database's own auth log) to separate "the platform will not do it" from "my body is wrong".
evidence: A CAI first-publish 500 versus re-publish 200 reproduced; a connector's no-password behaviour proven from both ends

title: Quiesce before measuring: one gate at a time on a shared backend
text: Concurrent gates, agent fleets or background crons hitting the same backend manufacture timeouts (login fixtures taking 66 s instead of 4 s) and fake failures. Stop other runs and crons, run exactly one gate or benchmark, restore paused crons afterwards, and only then trust the numbers. Keep write-heavy test agents to two or fewer at a time on a shared database host, which otherwise saturated and made SSH unresponsive.
evidence: Uncontended runs near 99% versus contended runs with dozens of false failures; an estate-wide hang cleared when agents stopped

title: Parity checks: the same watermark, both directions, never a wider tolerance
text: A source-versus-target parity check run before the latest sync completes fails on timing, not data: force the sync and wait, or compare both sides at the same watermark. Compare row counts both ways plus `EXCEPT DISTINCT` on `to_json_string(struct(<common cols>))` in both directions (or a multiset `GROUP BY` on that JSON) with run-time columns excluded; pin snapshot-table reads to the latest snapshot timestamp; read the drift direction (extras with nothing missing means the manifest is stale, not a gap); run a full delete-aware reload after purges, because incremental appends never propagate deletes; never widen tolerances or set test floors equal to today's actuals. Newer evidence: L-DQ-147.
evidence: Flaky parity failures eliminated; a migration's landing parity was 14/14 exact

title: Fix at the source: scheduled rebuilds wipe manual fixes
text: When a pipeline rebuilds its outputs on a schedule, a manual fix to an output table is gone at the next run and can regress silently. Put the durable fix in the pipeline SQL, configuration or seed data (for IDMC, in the task's `customQuery` or in the mapping), then verify that it survives a rebuild.
evidence: A 15-minute rebuild cycle erased ad-hoc overrides

title: Report the true ceiling: free is not finishable, and some residue needs a human
text: Once the headless-doable surface is exhausted, report the ceiling and the residue grouped by owner and blocker (spend, entitlement, credential, UI-only, production approval, product decision) instead of re-dispatching agents at blocked work or marking it done. "Costs nothing" is not "finishable in one pass": check that the deliverable exists and can be completed now before labelling an item doable.
evidence: Of 13 'free-doable' items only 1 was one-pass finishable; a 456-issue board plateaued at 71% with the residue genuinely gated

title: Red flags: about to say X, check Y first
text: About to say "not entitled": read `agentEngines[]`, privileges and runtime-environment selections, not a 404 or `products[]`. "Not possible": grep the evidence and verb matrix, sweep the hosts, empty-POST the verb, vary the Content-Type, capture the UI's own call. "Locked out": check the login domain and the full username. "It works": bogus-twin the 200 and read the body. "Done": name the stage and the environment of the evidence. "It vanished": check the exact type name and other users' projects. Quoting a limitation: confirm the cell is not UNTESTED. Reusing an endpoint across orgs: re-derive org, pod and domain. Reaching for MCP to write: read the server's tool list. Concluding from `count: 0`: the type filter is not validated.
evidence: Distilled from every walked-back conclusion in the July corpus and the September log

title: A read-only IDMC health suite and smoke gate
text: Useful read-only verifier lanes: catalog and classification coverage, catalog-config parity across environments, access review, CAI process inventory, Secure Agent health scoped to one runtime environment, endpoint reachability, IPU metering, observability parity, lineage and profiling freshness. Chain them into one read-only gate (no runs, scans or IPU) that classifies tracked, expected non-greens as AMBER and exits non-zero only on unexpected RED; in an application release gate keep lanes that depend on IDMC schedules advisory so platform cadence cannot flap the core gate. Exclude verifiers whose dependencies are unreachable from the test host instead of letting them skip silently. After any agent, selection or pipeline change, run one read-only sweep scoped to 'since <change time T>': agents (`GET /api/v2/agent`, then per agent `GET /api/v2/agent/<id>`, skipping `active: false` agents whose engine lists are stale, and `GET /api/v2/agent/details/<id>` listing every engine not RUNNING); runs (`GET /api/v2/activity/activityLog?rowLimit=1000`, count runs since T by state and print each failed or warning run with its error, and check that the oldest returned row is older than T or page with `offset`); `GET /api/v2/activity/activityMonitor?details=true`; `GET /api/v2/schedule`; each CDC job; the minutes since the last write of each landed table (`__TABLES__`) and the real-time leg's failures and p50 from its decision table; host free memory. Run it in every org that shares the host, then time one real end-to-end story hop by hop; a green sweep is evidence only for the window it covered (L-METHOD-041).
evidence: A clean fast run 1757/0; a release gate 3034/0 with the IDMC lanes advisory; used after a 17-service selection change: it surfaced the non-RUNNING engines per agent in both orgs, the failed runs since the change, CDC state and warehouse freshness in one pass (2026-09-30)

title: Build IDMC observability collectors that cannot lie
text: A read-only exporter pulls v2/v3 platform data and catalog search counts on a schedule into snapshot tables (features, connectors, catalog sources, scan jobs, KPIs) with a snapshot timestamp. Iterate every runtime environment from `GET /api/v2/runtimeEnvironment` (no break after the first) and stamp an environment column on every row; append to time-series tables (job runs, agent health) and replace only status snapshots; run exactly one scheduled writer (a stale second writer re-polluted snapshots); name probe assets with markers (`zz_`, `_probe`, `deleteme`) and filter them out of KPIs; label proxy estimates `estimate=true, billed=false` next to billed metering rows.
evidence: Multi-environment rows appeared only after all-environment iteration; a stale second writer was found and removed

title: Check that no IDMC run is active before re-arming a cron or restarting an orchestrator
text: Before uncommenting a cron that was paused "for an IDMC run", confirm with `GET /api/v2/activity/activityMonitor` (0 running jobs) and on the agent host (no DTM process) that the run finished, then run it once. Restarting the service that tails and finalizes runs orphans any active run (the worker finishes, the orchestrator never records the terminal state): check for active runs first and give the orchestrator a reconcile step for orphans.
evidence: A pause outlived its run; a restart froze a run at RUNNING 42%

title: One lead plus lanes, and exactly one IDMC writer per org
text: When several sessions work one program, name one lead and split the rest into lanes by component. During migrations and cutovers only the lead logs in to each IDMC org, and only one session imports or publishes at a time; the other lanes take host work (agent, systemd, drivers, ports), caller-repoint preparation (read-only until GO), documentation and checklists, or cleanup lists. One session drives each shared login and each serialized channel (such as a per-VM run-command). Stage risky host scripts as dry runs whose every step prints its undo, and run them only on the lead's GO. Newer evidence: L-METHOD-135.
evidence: A cutover finished with no lockout and no duplicate import after a morning in which three sessions had tried the same login

title: When the same prompt reaches several sessions, find the others and split first
text: Several sessions often receive the same instruction or bug list. Before starting, search other sessions' recent transcripts or tracker comments for the same prompt, agree over SendMessage on one lead and a split by component (one session per system), and post leases on the board. A bug list sent to three sessions split cleanly into CAI steps, a database trigger and the app; a migration prompt resent to several sessions converged on one lead. Before messaging a peer, check its permission mode: a session in a prompting mode holds every incoming cross-session message for the user's approval (each one costs the user a click, many expire undelivered, and about 15 in one clean-up interrupted the user), so message only peers that receive directly, post one tracker comment on the issue the others read, and never resend a denied or expired message. Settle on one coordinator before anyone writes (two crossed splits caused most of the traffic), send the lane rules to every session that joins later, and before coding a fix assigned to you read the tracker comments and the deploy undo list: a peer may already have shipped an interim version, so rebase on the live file (L-METHOD-071).
evidence: The lockout and the duplicate-import risk happened before the split, not after it; messages held, denied and expired in one day; two interim fixes found before a duplicate deploy; an md5 guard stopped one overwrite of a live fix (2026-10-01)

title: Claim, lease, heartbeat, complete on the tracker
text: Pick the highest-priority unclaimed, unblocked item and claim it atomically (assignee = your session, state = In Progress, comment `LEASE owner=<session> since=<ISO> expires=<ISO+30m>`); heartbeat at least every 15 minutes on long work; complete with `DONE by <session> <ISO>: <evidence>` and release explicitly. Never edit an item under another session's live lease; comments are append-only; post findings as comments, not only in chat, so the next session inherits them; open an issue for newly discovered work instead of doing it silently; move blocked work to a blocked state with the reason and pick something else. Newer evidence: L-METHOD-142.
evidence: In use from 2026-09-07 across 115 issues and 12 parallel agents, and again through a migration

title: A CLAIM names the items owned and the actions peers must not take; fence live files
text: When taking a lane, post a CLAIM with timestamp and session identity that lists the items now owned and the actions peers must not take (for example: do not create or run these tasks, do not restart the Secure Agent, do not stop the legacy service), and post "CLAIM RELEASED - free for any session" when done. Runbooks carry an explicit FENCE listing paths and services another session owns; if another session appears to be editing live files (recent modification times), stay off them, switch to verification or read-only work, and log that you did.
evidence: Claim and release comments; fenced files were not touched by peers

title: One canonical lease format, and a reaper that understands exactly that format
text: Mixing claim schemes (a `wip:` label, a `claimed:` label, and a LEASE label with a JSON comment where a later `released:true` block supersedes it) caused double claims, and a reaper written for one format left crashed leases stale forever and once reaped a live one. Pick one canonical tool and format; reap by the tracker's own `updated_at` (heartbeat labels get clobbered by concurrent label PATCHes); sweep orphans (a lease label with no active lease comment) separately; re-assert terminal states after a reaper race; and ship the reaper and validate-sweep crons with the deploy script so they cannot drift to retired scripts.
evidence: Stale leases reaped correctly after the fix; a reaper pointing at a retired script had been reaping nothing

title: Gated actions wait for a human: spend, shared deletes, DNS, production data, privilege
text: Stop for explicit human approval before: spending money or paid credits (two approvals, a request stating what and why and then a separate confirm; write the free carve-outs down first, for example ordinary IDMC usage on an existing licence); destructive deletes of shared data; DNS and other outward-facing changes; production data changes; any write in an org you do not own; and privilege escalation (if an integration user is correctly not allowed to delete, back the records up, list their ids and wait rather than switching to a higher-privilege login). Label such items blocked with the name of the human they wait on, and keep working on everything else.
evidence: Standing rule since July; applied to record deletes in an external system and to writes in a shared org in September

title: Under a 'no questions' directive, take the reversible default and write down the undo
text: When the owner says to finish without asking, find the answer yourself, act, verify and report; pick the documented default that is reversible and cheap, record the decision and its undo on the tracker, and leave the item easy to reopen. The hard gates still hold (spend, destructive deletes of shared data, external writes in someone else's org, secret exposure): work around them rather than asking, and flag them. Put every task on one path: (1) Claude does it; (2) Claude does it through a named workaround (an API or CLI instead of a console, a scripted browser, a self-managed runtime, a test identity, a free alternative to a paid service, a wildcard DNS name instead of a DNS change); or (3) the human, only when it needs their identity, money, legal standing, people or an owner-only business decision (or an account Claude has no credential for), no workaround exists and the attempts are listed, their step is reduced to exact clicks or words with minutes, and it appears in one place only. One-line approvals (a production deploy, a destructive delete, spend) stay on Claude's task, batched into one list (L-METHOD-121), never turned into a human task; group the remaining human steps by sitting. A strict workaround hunt cut one human task list from 86 items (about 100 h) to 16 (about 3 h).
evidence: Decision comments with undo on several items; a task board re-planned with the three paths: 86 human tasks to 16 (2026-10-02/03)

title: At a secret boundary, build everything else and hand over one named secret and one command
text: Headless work cannot fabricate a credential. Build every part that does not need the secret, pre-wire the consumer, and document exactly which secret goes where and the single command that consumes it, so the human's step is one paste into the secret store or env file (never into the repository or chat).
evidence: Escalation pattern for credentials only the owner held

title: Guard run harnesses with explicit approval flags
text: A harness that can trigger IPU-consuming or deploy-dependent runs refuses to run unless explicit approval flags are present (for example `RUN_APPROVED=1` plus a flag asserting that the prerequisite UI step was done). Build and commit the harness, but do not run it until the gate is satisfied.
evidence: A harness was built and committed, then held until the gate cleared

title: Probe a production or shared login with one serial session and reversible probes
text: When exploring an org through a production or shared login, use one serial session (no parallel logins), make only reversible probes (create then delete, verify zero residue), spend nothing, move as little data as possible, and log each probe with its cleanup. A shared login and a serialized host channel are effectively single-tenant: concurrent sessions collide.
evidence: Probe tasks created and deleted with zero residue

title: Lockout avoidance across a fleet: one designated session, one attempt, one shared cache
text: Failed IDMC logins from every session and tool count against the same account; about six failures locked one, and each further attempt restarted the lock (`IDS_086` "User account is locked. Contact your organization administrator."). Stop all automated logins at the first rejection, let the owner reset (a reset also unlocks), confirm the password in a browser, then let ONE designated session make ONE attempt and share its cached session with every script and browser run. Login volume alone once tripped a lock (every probe opened fresh sessions), and cron pollers holding a stale password re-lock an account right after each unlock. Prefer a dedicated native automation user over a personal or SSO account; the Secure Agent keeps running scheduled work during a user lock.
evidence: A lock after 6 failures from 3 sessions; one successful login after the reset; no lockout across dozens of sessions with a shared cache

title: Do not move or overwrite files a peer is using
text: With many sessions running, skip anything whose files changed in the last 20 minutes or so (moving a child also refreshes the folder mtime), protect files that recent scripts reference, and leave files that are open in Office where they are. Before writing a shared file, record its hash (or mtime and size) at read time and refuse to overwrite if it changed; for co-editing use compare-and-swap (re-stat just before an atomic replace, reload and retry on drift, guard on the full expected content, skip targets the peer already changed); edit shared deployed files from the live copy, three-way merge peers' live edits, and ship only the files you changed.
evidence: Content-hash gates prevented clobbering; 19 concurrent sessions during one cleanup with no collisions

title: Do not double-drive; commit an unclaimed live change before fixing on top of it
text: Concurrent sessions re-authoring the same IDMC tasks or editing the same scripts corrupt each other: before live execution, check for recent edits by others (for example files modified in the last few minutes) and, if a sibling is active, defer to it and mirror the honest state. When a file that is live in production has uncommitted changes from an unknown or absent session, first commit the live content as-is (so production has a source of record), then commit your fix on top; never overwrite another session's in-flight edit. Newer evidence: L-METHOD-132.
evidence: The live page was verified after the two-commit sequence

title: Never purge another session's data; delete only the ids you created
text: Test cleanup deletes the exact ids the test created; a time-window sweep deleted another session's synthetic rows. Use a unique namespace for your own test data (for example a distinct email domain), wait for a concurrent writer to stop before sweeping its namespace, never delete append-only audit rows other writers share, and before deleting resources that look unused check whether another session's scripts own and recreate them (keep an inspect or dump of what you remove).
evidence: About 27 rows belonging to other sessions over-deleted by a time-window sweep, then corrected

title: One live publisher for a shared artifact, with a lock file and a version guard
text: For an artifact several sessions change (a BI workbook, a pipeline plan), name ONE live publisher at a time with a LEASE; take a lock file before publishing; announce each publish with the exact version it replaces and make the replace conditional on that version still being live (an updatedAt guard; a concurrent-update rejection is the guard working); post DONE and release. A guardian cron downloads the live artifact, runs the canonical patch chain and republishes only if fixes were reverted, after a quiet period, with no publisher running and no fresh lock file; if any patch fails it never publishes and alerts instead.
evidence: Twelve publish rounds without lost edits; guardian runs logged IN SYNC

title: Live-stack changes in a demo week: windows, rollback tags, freeze, rehearsal
text: When several sessions share a live stack, announce each rebuild window on the tracker, tag the previous image as a rollback tag and roll back automatically if the new container is unhealthy, and propose a change freeze (no rebuilds, restarts, proxy or gateway edits) from two hours before a demo until it ends. Before the demo run one rehearsal command that exercises every hop and cleans up after itself, a real-browser smoke of each public surface (0 console errors, 0 failed requests) and a monitor that alerts on DOWN and RECOVERED. For headless IDMC demos, stage the slow parts (a new agent's engines can take more than 30 minutes) and run only the headless moments live. Zero preparation for the person presenting: Claude runs and undoes every switch (freezes, rebuilds, forced lanes, fast modes), and a pre-demo checklist for them is a defect; raise only a real external wall that only they can clear (for example a BI login that expires on a known policy), with its exact time and the one-time permanent fix. After any change of instructions or wording, grep every copy (runbook, UI strings, status lines, tracker pages): one rewording missed three places. Never trade live behaviour for cost without saying so (a longer lane gap silently broke the live record-to-governed moment), and keep internal items out of their summary.
evidence: Services rebuilt with 10-30 s restarts and no regressions; rehearsal 28/28 and smoke 16/16; three stale copies found after a rewording, and a broken live moment traced to a cost-saving gap and reverted (2026-09-30)

title: Two rate limits bind an agent fleet: the model API and the tracker API
text: The model API limit is account-wide across all subagents and the main loop (about 50 requests per minute in July 2026): hold concurrency to about 6-7 agents and fill slots as they finish, never run two fleets of the same specialists on one key, and resume a 429-killed agent with SendMessage (its context is intact) instead of respawning it. Do mechanical tracker work (scans, label and state edits, reaping) from the main loop over plain HTTP, which does not consume the model budget. The tracker has its own throttle (HTTP 429, or `error_code 5900 RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` on one self-hosted tracker): pace reads about 0.4-1.4 s apart, sleep 15-20 s on the limit error and retry, and never let a client silently truncate a paginated read.
evidence: Agents died on 429 with two fleets running and were stable at seven or fewer; a first board read missed about 15 issues until backoff

title: Self-hosted tracker API quirks that break fleet tooling
text: List endpoints dropped items non-deterministically under load (never trust one full-board snapshot: retry and union; single per-issue calls are fine); labels came back as UUIDs (resolve them through the project label map); state PATCH was eventually consistent (re-read after sign-out and re-PATCH); project names rejected `&` and parentheses; there was no issue-relation REST endpoint (dependencies were inserted in the database). Through the tracker's ORM shell: the label through-table needs project and workspace ids; removing a label is a soft delete that still shows through the raw accessor; comments regenerate their plain-text field from the HTML on save, so put idempotency markers inside the HTML; issue create takes HTML description fields; `QuerySet.delete()` did not return the usual tuple (re-count to verify).
evidence: Phantom labels and duplicated comments before the fixes

title: Board hygiene: the queue, the labels, the terminal state and the measure
text: The actionable queue is open issues without a `blocked:*` label; each blocked label (or `needs:<person>-decision`) names the human or gate (ui-only, entitlement, decision, app-deploy, spend) and must not be re-ground. Set native priority as the do-order and mirror it in tier labels; end every issue in exactly one terminal state (Done, or a Blocked state that exists in every project) with a structured escalation comment (why blocked, what was done, plan after unblock); tag built-but-undeployed work as awaiting deploy rather than Done. Measure dispositioned issues (Done plus blocked-with-reason) over total, not the open count. When agents grow the board faster than they drain it, broadcast a convergence directive (finish or release before creating), and merge duplicate epics into one parent with pointer comments.
evidence: 391 of 391 issues dispositioned in one fleet run; board-map comments explained the conventions

title: Fleet shape: domain specialists, gap-fillers only, a tracker reconciled against reality
text: Give each specialist agent a domain label and a generated worklist of the issues carrying it, plus the runbook and hard rules; contention drops to near zero. Do not start a second competing fleet on a board a live fleet is draining: add gap-fillers only on projects with no live lease, with distinct doer ids, told to skip leased issues. Agents over-claim UI blockers, so require proof that no API or CLI path exists before accepting UI-only. Periodically audit the board cluster by cluster against live reality, applying only high-confidence corrections with an evidence comment; fix misclassification in the classifier itself (with tests) rather than by hand-editing labels, and look items up by name because other actors may renumber them. Newer evidence: L-METHOD-137.
evidence: A board went from 11 to 241 Done jointly with no collisions; 50 audited corrections applied with comments

title: Serialize browser work; parallelize backend and IDMC REST work
text: Five or six agents doing backend, warehouse or IDMC REST work in parallel ran cleanly, but several agents writing browser tests or driving the IDMC UI against one shared working tree and one backend clobbered each other's untracked files, collided on shared browser-state files and triggered identity-provider brute-force lockouts. Give browser and UI-authoring work one serialized owner.
evidence: Clobbered files and temporarily disabled test users observed

title: Wait on the exact agent label, not a substring
text: When polling for a subagent, lane or reviewer to finish, match its exact label or id. A substring match fired early and a deploy went out before its review had finished.
evidence: An API was redeployed after the early trigger

title: Subagent traps: inherited effort, missing definitions, big joins, barriers
text: Subagents inherit the parent's reasoning effort, so one deep generation can exceed an agent's time window and return empty: pass a low effort level for bulk review and chunk inputs (for example 24 claims or fewer per agent). `Agent type '<name>' not found` means the agent definition files are missing or the host was not restarted after adding them. Build large deterministic joins and matrices in code from agents' structured partial results; one agent asked to emit the whole matrix thrashed. A workflow barrier over parallel agents stalls on its slowest agent under a shared rate limit; a pipeline shape avoids that.
evidence: Stalls stopped after low effort plus chunking; a stalled matrix agent was replaced by a deterministic script

title: Ask on the board before acting on a sudden data drop, and keep the pre-drop backup
text: If a nightly dump or a table count collapses unexpectedly, do not change alert thresholds or "repair" data first: post the evidence (row counts, delete counters, earliest timestamps, backup location) as a question to the owning session, keep the last good dump, and act only after the cause is confirmed; it may be an intended reset.
evidence: A 220 MB to 19 MB drop was an intended reset; the owner confirmed before any change

title: One canonical KB plus a per-agent standing file; one source file per section
text: Per-agent knowledge folders with no workflow hook stay empty stubs. One shared canonical knowledge base that every agent reads (nobody forks it), plus a living per-agent STANDING file that each agent's verify step updates on every task, keeps knowledge current; flag organization-wide changes to one owner. For a reference that many agents improve in parallel, keep the source as one file per section (two agents never edit the same file; a binary document silently loses one writer's changes), a deterministic builder that is the only writer of the rendered document, a validator gate, and a contract file; never hand-edit generated outputs. Keeping a shared IDMC knowledge base current and shareable: reference skills built from an earlier snapshot do not contain later lessons, so start each skill with a pointer to read the canonical KB first; when several sessions add lessons the same day, allocate each id at write time from the maximum over the markdown headings and the machine-readable file, write both in one pass and check for duplicate ids (ids moved by five within minutes once); a share gate that reads only text files passes leaks inside .docx, .pptx, .xlsx and PDFs and in file names (a package that passed a text-only gate failed the full gate with about 250 hits), so scan every format and every name, refuse to build the share archive unless the gate is clean, and never weaken the gate to pass (L-METHOD-090); keep private provenance outside the shared folder, with no link into it.
evidence: 70 empty stub folders found; two agents editing one binary document had silently lost work; two skills found to be older snapshots (2026-09-30); a share package failed the full gate after passing a text-only one (2026-10-02/03)

title: Idempotent seeders and a file-locked task board for a large backlog
text: Write every backlog seeder as append-only with dedup by name: re-running all seeders and getting `added=0` from each is a cheap proof that every known item is on the board. A simple file-locked board also works for a fleet: a `tasks.json` backlog, a CLI whose `next` atomically claims one task under a file lock (only the claimer can finish it), stale claims reaped after 30 minutes, an append-only ledger and one artifact per task. When a large fan-out partly fails on rate limits, resume only the failed groups from the per-agent results already in the journal.
evidence: 354 tasks drained from 32% to 100% in one session with waves of 14 workers and zero overlap

title: Keep a shared org tidy: builders place assets at creation and an hourly guard sweeps
text: Make every builder place new assets into the owned project and folder at creation (FRS `MoveEntities`) and tag them (`POST /public/core/v3/TagObjects`, at most 50 per call), through one shared place-and-tag helper; run an hourly guard that moves owned-name assets found outside the folder, tags untagged ones and warns on unclassifiable new assets. The guard relies on a strict name-prefix convention per service. Check that its v3 type filter is exact: `type=='DBMI'` returns 0 rather than an error, so assets of type `DBMI_TASK` sat outside the folder unnoticed.
evidence: 0 strays after the audit; 23 misplaced ingestion tasks found once the type name was corrected

title: Keep secrets out of transcripts: use them where they live and print only key names
text: Never print credential files: use them on the host or inside the container that holds them (for example psql with the password taken from the container's own environment, or a script that reads the env file itself). Print only key names. Inspect credential files of unknown format only with size and metadata commands (`wc -c`, `stat`), never `cat`, `head` or `grep`, because name=value redaction filters miss files that are plain lines (user on one line, password on the next). `docker inspect` prints DSN passwords from the environment. Treat anything printed into a transcript, and any session cookie pasted into one, as exposed and due for rotation.
evidence: Credential files printed into session transcripts on three different days; each was logged for rotation

title: Never paste tokens, cookies or browser Network-tab requests into chat
text: A Network-tab dump carries `Cookie:` and `Authorization:` headers, and session cookies are full account credentials that bypass the password and MFA. Share the error text, not the request. Credentials come from environment variables read at run time or from a file path, never from file contents or literals in scripts. If a secret is exposed anyway: say so, tell the user to rotate it and log out, and do not use or store it. Org ids, pod names, agent ids and host addresses are configuration, not secrets.
evidence: Environment-trap rules of the reference skill

title: Secrets in automation: 0600 files read at run time, never on a command line
text: Keep each secret in a mode-0600 file on the host that uses it and read it at apply time inside the script that needs it; never pass it on a command line, echo it, or write it into boards or chat. When a secret is shown only once (an OAuth client secret), write it straight to its file with `os.open(path, O_CREAT|O_TRUNC|O_WRONLY, 0o600)`; if any part of it reaches a log, delete the client and recreate it. Mask the password in any echoed error (`.replace(pw, '***')`). Keep other OS users (for example a second agent's user) out of the apps' secret files, and report secret files by name only.
evidence: No secret values appeared in any receipt; the second agent's user was verified denied

title: Sanitize with identifier and prose rules, prove the gate both ways, then read the output
text: Word-boundary regexes miss names embedded in identifiers (`<name>_iam`, `wh_<name>`): use substring rules for identifiers and two replacements per name (an identifier form and a prose form). Prove the gate fails on the private build and passes on the clean one. A leak gate proves nothing leaked, not that the result still works: blanket replacements produced unrunnable commands in code fences, collapsed distinct table rows into identical targets and left dangling tool references, so handle each context separately and read the generated output. Filter non-domain content (workspace rules, deck branding, personal task boards) out of a portable skill rather than paraphrasing it.
evidence: The gate failed the private skill on 233 leaks and passed the public one; three defects were found only by reading the output

title: Build an evidenced data-access map of every identity that can reach each store
text: For governance reviews, list every identity (AI agents and MCP servers, pipeline service accounts, CDC roles, BI connections, CRM apps) against every store (app databases, warehouse datasets, CRM, CDP) with its access level, the evidence (IAM roles, dataset ACLs, database grants, MCP configuration) and the gaps. Typical findings: BI connections running as a project owner, CDC roles holding DML rights, apps with project-wide read.
evidence: A 10-identity map with its gaps shown on a governance dashboard

title: When egress is constrained, keep data on the agent host and meter the control plane
text: Keep loads, transforms and DQ local to the agent host (loopback database connections) so only control-plane calls leave the network, avoid heavy browser sessions (an admin UI session pulls megabytes of SaaS JavaScript), and keep an egress ledger (bytes per action, retries included). Uploading a file to a hosted DQ agent is egress too: use small synthetic or sampled data with no real PII, one dataset at a time.
evidence: Zero data egress for a database-to-database demo spine; about 1.6-1.9 MB of samples logged

title: The boundary-pushers that move the most IDMC work out of the UI
text: Create connections as `TOOLKIT_CCI` over v2 REST; clone instead of author (v3 export and import of existing assets, parameterized bundle templates wrapped in mapping tasks); publish CAI processes over REST on the `<pod>-cai` host; run and read everything over REST with session re-auth; capture the UI's own XHR when a step still looks UI-only. By late September the same approach also covered ingestion-task deploy, runtime-environment service selection, MCP OAuth clients, glossary writes, deletes and new multi-transformation mappings built as IMF JSON packages. What stayed a click is listed in the UI automation doc.
evidence: Design note in August; each route proven in its domain's lessons through 2026-09-29

title: Test a reference skill against a no-skill control; the failure mode is retrieval cost
text: Run the control (skill withheld) first, and withhold every copy (source, generated and installed folders) or the baseline is contaminated. In the July tests (7 to 9 subagent runs over four adversarial scenarios) every run refused the wrong answer, including the controls; the measured failure was retrieval cost (20-50 tool calls, up to 34 files). A single generated answers page (hosts, caps, corrections) cut a cold-start run from 21 to 9 tool calls. Treat subagent "top gaps" reports as leads and grep the skill yourself: 2 of 5 reported gaps were already covered. Newer evidence: L-METHOD-156.
evidence: Tool calls fell from 21 to 9 after the answers page

title: Reference-building traps: clipped cells, frontmatter names, web research, missing guides
text: Never clip a table cell whose text is the deliverable: caveats ("bills IPUs", "UI-only") sit at the end of the sentence.
