text: Catalog answers take 29-114 s (median about 54 s); single 'Query the data' answers 53-195 s (typically 70-105 s), plus about 35 s when CLAIRE asks 'table or view?'; rule generation 3-7 minutes; file cleansing 6-9 minutes. Some runs hang on 'Mapping identified concepts...' or 'Generating queries...' until about 405 s or a CLAIRE timeout message: stop waiting at about 6 minutes and re-ask in a new conversation. The managed MCP routes answer the same prompts in 28-80 s (L-MCP-111).
evidence: Timed runs: catalog median about 54 s; data 53-195 s; four hangs ended at about 405 s

title: The managed agent MCP routes answer CLAIRE GPT's questions headless, with the same answers as the UI
text: `datamanagementorchestrator.orchestrate` returned the same DQ score breakdown, unscored-table lists and diagnosis as the CLAIRE GPT UI; `orchestrate_master_data_analysis` returned MDM entities and match rules; `dataexplorationagent.data_explore` (with `name` and `external_id`) answered natural-language data questions with a chart and an SQL citation. They are faster (28-80 s vs 50-130 s in the UI) and leave no conversation in the shared UI list. Plans come back as a plan to approve, not executed, and a mapping request stops at 'Table or View?'. On an unprofiled table, `orchestrate` runs its own read-only profiling SQL through the gateway (no catalog job). Mechanics: L-MCP-112. This overturns 'NL-to-SQL has no headless invocation route' in L-MCP-053; the CLAIRE GPT chat itself still has no public API (L-MCP-051).
evidence: 13 calls on orchestrate, orchestrate_master_data_analysis, data_explore and the DQ agent: 11 PASS, 2 plan-only; answers compared with the UI for the same prompts

title: Driving the managed agent routes: nested envelope, cursor polling from '0', TOKEN fragments, probe_message, upload retries
text: Every agent tool argument goes inside a nested inner JSON-RPC envelope, and results are nested the same way (unwrap as in L-MCP-030). After the submit, poll `get_skill_execution_updates` with `cursor` starting at "0" and feed back `pagination.cursor` (L-MCP-044). The answer streams as TOKEN items whose `content` fragments you concatenate, plus ARTIFACT items carrying GridView data; a HUMAN_PROBE arrives with its question in `probe_message`, and you answer it in the same conversation ('Yes, proceed with the plan.'). For a file, `request_upload_url` returns a single-use PUT URL: the PUT can still answer 409 (the preflight race, L-DQ-072), so request a fresh URL and retry; two retries were enough.
evidence: Full transcripts of 13 agent calls, including a probe answered and an upload that needed retries

title: CLAIRE GPT answers MDM and Data Marketplace questions in the same chat
text: 'Show all business entities in Customer 360.' lists the entities; 'What are the match and survivorship rules of the Person business entity?' returns the fuzzy and exact match combinations, auto-merge vs manual review, and survivorship by source rank. 'What data collections have never been requested in Data Marketplace?' and 'Show an overview of the data collection <collection>.' return real collections with category, contained tables, delivery target and lifecycle. Use bare names: the vendor samples use '@', which a harness cannot send (L-MCP-055). Ordering stays in Data Marketplace or the order-management MCP server.
evidence: MDM and marketplace prompts 7 of 7 in the UI; MDM match rules 2 of 2 over MCP

title: 'Query the data' sources, preview cap and prerequisites (documented)
text: Documented sources for data exploration: Amazon Redshift (v2), Databricks (PAT), Google BigQuery V2 (service account), Azure Synapse SQL, Azure SQL Server, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle and Snowflake. PostgreSQL is not on the list, which matches the live refusal ('this data source is currently not supported', L-MCP-061). A preview shows at most 100 rows x 100 columns, and the cap is in the generated SQL itself: every 'Query the data' statement in Show Code ends in `LIMIT 100`, even single-row aggregates, so a list question returns at most the first 100 qualifying rows with no truncation warning (the downloadable card holds the same capped result). Ask for aggregates, counts or an explicit top-N of 100 or fewer; for full extracts take the SQL from Show Code, remove the LIMIT and run it in the warehouse or a mapping. Prerequisites: connections enabled on the Secure Agent group, the Data Gateway Service, PK/FK constraints for inferred joins (for BigQuery and Synapse through a custom catalog source in Metadata Command Center), and profiling for value-level accuracy. Documented caveats: names with special characters, or columns containing ': \ ~ .', are not previewable; Oracle and SQL Server exploration can fail until the gateway service is restarted after the Data Integration service is up.
evidence: Vendor data-exploration prerequisites page (June 2026); the PostgreSQL refusal and the table-or-view question observed live; 8 of 8 Show Code captures (group-bys, CASE buckets, window functions, single-row counts) ended in LIMIT 100

title: Data Gateway tuning properties for 'Query the data' (documented)
text: In Administrator > Runtime Environments, the Data Gateway Service takes APP_CFG properties `idmc_dgs_connectionPoolMaxSize` (default 100, range 10-1000), `idmc_dgs_connectionPoolCacheExpiryDuration` (30 minutes, 10-120) and `idmc_dgs_queryExecutionTimeout` (default 60 s, minimum 1). A slow warehouse view can fail in CLAIRE before it fails anywhere else: raise the timeout on the agent before blaming the prompt. Python for generated cleansing code takes `python_enabled=true` (optional `idmc_dgs_pythonHome`) with Pandas and PyArrow installed (L-MCP-109).
evidence: Vendor data-exploration prerequisites page (June 2026); the 60 s timeout was not hit by a window query over about 1,800 rows

title: CLAIRE GPT metering: 50 IPU per 1,000 queries, and design-time use is free until 2027-01-31 (documented)
text: A query is any natural-language request in the CLAIRE GPT UI, metered at 50 IPU per 1,000 queries and reported in the Administrator Metering console. A vendor promotion through 2027-01-31 lets eligible customers (a paid IDMC subscription on a pod with CLAIRE GPT) use any number of IPUs at no extra cost to try CLAIRE GPT and to use CLAIRE copilots, agents and headless features at design time; MDM SaaS users get the same for MDM. Runtime work that CLAIRE triggers (profiling runs, DQ runs, generated mappings when run) still bills its own service meters.
evidence: Measurement Guide and Cloud Product Description Schedule v39.1 (effective 2026-06-05); vendor CLAIRE promotion page read 2026-09-30

title: CLAIRE GPT models, regional stacks and retention (documented)
text: CLAIRE uses third-party LLMs deployed privately per region: Azure OpenAI in the vendor's Azure account and Anthropic Claude through Amazon Bedrock in the vendor's AWS account (a GCP-hosted catalog may use Google's agent platform). US and EU have a full regional stack (models, metadata, conversation store); some regions keep only metadata and conversations locally. Prompts and responses are stored encrypted per customer, customer data in responses is not stored, and sample data shown in a conversation is gone after a refresh. Conversations go inactive after 180 days and are deleted after 13 months (2 months if CLAIRE is disabled); the UI archives conversations older than 6 months.
evidence: Vendor CLAIRE security, privacy and compliance white paper; CLAIRE GPT conversations documentation (July 2026)

title: Which CLAIRE agents ship and which are roadmap (documented status board)
text: Generally available: the Discovery agent (catalog, Data Integration, Data Marketplace and MDM discovery, metadata and data exploration), the Data Quality agent (assessment, diagnosis, recommendation, cleanse, rule generation; GA spring 2026), the Data Integration (ELT) agent, the Product Help agent, and headless CLAIRE over MCP. Preview: the Product Experience agent in Product 360. Announced or planned, not to be promised as shipping: Data Lineage, Data Ingestion and Modernization agents (announced May 2025, absent from the September 2026 agent docs), the Metadata Enrichment agent, agentic multidomain MDM and data-steward agents, CLAIRE in chat tools and agent-to-agent (A2A) access, targeted for Q4 or fall 2026. CLAIRE GPT itself is agentic: a supervisor routes to these agents, shows its reasoning, and needs approval before executing a plan.
evidence: Vendor agent documentation, What's New guides and release announcements, October 2025 to September 2026

title: The managed MCP catalog: 20 servers, and the documented argument schemas of the agent tools
text: The September 2026 guide documents 20 shared servers (protocol 2025-06-18, streamable HTTP), and one org's registry listed 20, including an order-management server with the full order lifecycle (create, get, list, approve, reject, cancel, fulfill, delete). Agent tool schemas: `data_explore` requires `prompt`, `name` and `external_id`, and takes `conversation_id` or `history`, `deferred`, `events`, `reasoning` and `artifacts`; `request_upload_url` returns a single-use PUT URL valid for 5 minutes; `data_profiling` profiles catalog assets only (files go through `data_quality_cleansing`); `get_skill_execution_updates` streams REASONING_TRACE, EXECUTION_INSIGHT, TOKEN, HUMAN_PROBE, PLAN and ARTIFACT frames (GridView, PropertiesView, GraphView, DataExploreResult). An OAuth 2.1 server for human-in-the-loop clients was rolled out in September 2026; OAuth 2.0 client credentials remain for machine-to-machine. Composite servers (the only kind a newer org can create, L-MCP-081) have documented prerequisites for the CAI process behind them: active and published as an API, deployed with Basic Authentication (anonymous access cannot be used), REST/SOAP binding, running on the Cloud Server (not a Secure Agent), and not restricted to accept requests only from the API Gateway; documented limits are 1,000 requests a minute and a 1 MB payload. Creating the server selects the process and the operations to expose as tools; deploying it creates an instance agents can call (one server can be deployed several times), and after the process changes you update the server and refresh each deployed instance. The IDMC Troubleshooting managed server is a preview since the July 2026 release (evaluation only), and the Audit Management server is read-only telemetry (audit trail plus security and identity events). Newer evidence: L-MCP-131.
evidence: Vendor MCP getting-started guide (September 2026); one org's managed registry listed 20 servers (proven 2026-10-01); composite-server, troubleshooting-server and audit-server pages of the vendor MCP guide read 2026-09-29, composite creation not exercised

title: CLAIRE GPT role privileges and file limits (documented)
text: The predefined CLAIRE GPT User role grants: access to the CLAIRE GPT application, create transformation pipelines, data download, data exploration, data preview, run data profiling, run data quality, and read on connections; add Designer to open, save and run generated mappings. File profiling accepts CSV or XLSX up to 25 MB and 10,000 rows x 50 columns, with row and column filters (honoured in tests). Scores cover the default dimensions only. Treat the chat as English-first: no language list is documented.
evidence: Vendor CLAIRE GPT administration and DQ agent documentation (July-August 2026)

title: A CLAIRE GPT harness needs a publish guard: stop at Publish/Accept prompts, and audit the org afterwards
text: Give the harness an explicit allow-list of buttons (for example only 'Yes, proceed with the plan' and 'Proceed without testing') and a deny-list it never clicks (Publish Rules, Accept, save, delete). Before sending any scripted follow-up, check the newest reply: if 'Publish Rules / Don't Publish Rules', an 'Accept rule' chip or a save offer is visible, stop the scenario or click 'Don't Publish Rules' plus Enter, because free text at that prompt can be taken as consent (L-MCP-096). Auto-answer only harmless clarifications ('The Table'). After each batch, list `GET /public/core/v3/objects` for rule specifications, dictionaries, mappings, tasks and mapplets updated since the batch began, and record what was created.
evidence: A run without the guard published one rule specification; about 150 guarded runs created nothing beyond one dictionary (L-MCP-097), checked with v3 objects by update time

title: Profile runs are not in the v2 activity log: count profiling and catalog jobs where they run
text: Paging `GET /api/v2/activity/activityLog` over a window in which Data Profiling runs completed returned only MTT, WORKFLOW and MAPPING rows: no PROFILE-type row appeared. Catalog scans and catalog Data Quality capability jobs are listed by the catalog's own jobs API, not there. Rule-specification previews do appear (`PreviewMapping_RULE_SPECIFICATION`). A budget or job-cap guard that reads only the activity log therefore under-counts a profiling-heavy workload: count profile runs from the profiling service's run history for the profiles you own, catalog jobs from the catalog jobs API filtered by your catalog-source id, and previews and mapping tasks from the activity log by name. Whether profile runs and their subtasks count toward the hidden monthly job cap (L-IPU-041) is not known; until it is measured, weight one profile run as 1 + 3 + ceil((columns + rules) / 50) jobs (L-DQ-098).
evidence: One org's activity log read in full (about 3,700 rows over 4 days) while two profiles ran to COMPLETED inside the same window

title: Choose a CLAIRE GPT sample's store by what the Data Gateway reads: BigQuery yes, PostgreSQL and ClickHouse no
text: 'Query the data' executes through the Data Gateway on a Secure Agent (L-AGENT-051). Its documented sources (L-MCP-114) include BigQuery V2 but not PostgreSQL (refused live, L-MCP-061) and not ClickHouse, which has no native connector (L-CONN-054); a JDBC V2 connection is not a gateway source. Catalog, glossary, profiling, rule generation and recommendation, data quality scores and score, trust, glossary and lineage questions all work on a PostgreSQL-hosted sample: only the data-query scene needs a supported warehouse. Decide this before building the sample. If the data may not be copied into a supported warehouse (a data-residency or architecture decision), plan the CLAIRE GPT scene without 'Query the data' instead of staging a warehouse copy that breaks that decision.
evidence: Vendor data-exploration source list (June 2026); PostgreSQL refusal seen live twice; ClickHouse absent from the list (no live test)

title: JDBC V2 cannot import ClickHouse object metadata (JDBC_V2_ERROR_205) although the driver's own metadata is clean
text: With a ClickHouse JDBC V2 connection that tests OK (L-CONN-054), every object or field fetch for a profile failed with `JDBC_V2_ERROR_205 'entry [<database>] already exists in the collection [null]'`: with the URL's default database set, with `databaseTerm=schema`, and without a schema name. The driver's DatabaseMetaData for the same table was clean, so the fault sits in the connector's catalog builder, not in the driver or the grants. Do not plan direct profiling or cataloging of ClickHouse through JDBC V2: stage a sample in a natively supported database (for example PostgreSQL) and profile that (a catalog source needs a native scanner anyway). Untested fixes: `databaseTerm=catalog` in the URL, or a profile created over REST with hand-built fields.
evidence: Three URL variants, each failing on every object fetch; the driver's metadata read on the same table returned one table row and every column [disputed 2026-11-03 by L-DQ-128: profiles on a JDBC V2 ClickHouse connection imported their objects and completed, so the metadata wall does not hold for profiling]

title: Size the agent before profiling: the subtask math, and two DTMs per profile thrash a 4 GB agent cgroup
text: A profile run is 3 fixed subtasks (row count, generate mappings, load to the metric store) plus one per 50 columns and rules at or below 100M rows, or one per column above 100M rows (vendor profiling guide): a 181-column table above 100M rows means about 184 subtasks per run, while a 100k-row sample needs about 7. The Data Integration service runs up to `maxDTMProcesses` DTMs at once (documented default 2). One profile of a 181-column staging table on an agent confined to a 4 GB, 1-vCPU systemd slice started two profiling DTM sessions of 33-36 threads each (consistent with the default; the agent's own value was not read): the slice sat at its MemoryMax and thrashed, the host (a 4-vCPU database server) reached load 63, and several agent services stayed in ERROR until a restart. Before profiling on a small or shared host: profile a sample table (at most 100k rows), set `maxDTMProcesses=1` through the cloud-side custom configuration (L-AGENT-088), keep the DTM heap at or below 1 GB, run one profile at a time off-peak, and never profile from an agent that shares a production database host. Newer evidence: L-DQ-158.
evidence: Process, cgroup and load readings during one profile run on a database host; subtask rules from the vendor profiling guide

title: A SHA-256 pseudo-random number is the portable sample key across ClickHouse, BigQuery and PostgreSQL (untested in the engines)
text: To profile a sample in IDMC and check the same rows in other engines, select by `prn32` = the first 4 bytes of SHA-256('<tag>:' + key) read big-endian, in the sample when `prn32 < threshold(stratum)`. Engine-specific hashes do not port (`cityHash64` exists only in ClickHouse, and BigQuery's `FARM_FINGERPRINT` is a different function), while SHA-256 is built in everywhere: ClickHouse `reinterpretAsUInt32(reverse(substring(SHA256(concat(tag, key)), 1, 4)))` (reverse, because reinterpretAsUInt32 reads little-endian); BigQuery `CAST(CONCAT('0x', SUBSTR(TO_HEX(SHA256(CONCAT(tag, key))), 1, 8)) AS INT64)`; PostgreSQL 11+ `('x' || lpad(substr(encode(sha256(convert_to(tag || key, 'UTF8')), 'hex'), 1, 8), 16, '0'))::bit(64)::bigint`. A key stays in or out at every refresh, which run-over-run profiling insights need, and a new tag gives a new independent sample. Keep a test-vector file (empty, padded, non-ASCII and very long keys) and make every engine reproduce it before first use.
evidence: Engine function docs; the three SQL forms emulated against a Python reference on 10 test vectors; not yet run in the engines

title: Prove a rules translation with per-rule counts from one CDI task: profile rule results are not readable over REST (untested)
text: When IDMC rules are re-implemented in another engine (for example as dbt tests), parity means the same checked and failed counts per rule on the same rows. Per-rule profile pass rates have no REST read (L-DQ-031) and the catalog's data quality results are per dimension, so a profile cannot be the IDMC side of that comparison. First try one rule: read the metric store's value frequencies for the rule's output column on a profiled table; if they give exact valid and invalid counts, use them. Otherwise run the exported rule specifications as Rule Specification transformations in ONE CDI mapping task over the same sample and write per-rule checked and failed counts to a table (the scorecard pattern, L-DQ-054): one job per cycle, readable by SQL. Until one route works, send every translated rule to a reviewer instead of auto-accepting it, and mark anything the translator cannot map as needs-review, never as translated.
evidence: Builds on L-DQ-031 (no REST read, observed) and L-DQ-054 (CDI scorecard task, proven); the parity comparison itself is untested

title: Full SQL ELT (pushdown) is switched on headless on the v2 mapping task: three fields, proved only by OPT_63367 in the session log
text: `GET <serverUrl>/api/v2/mttask/<taskId>` (header `icSessionId`), drop the read-only fields, set `"sessionProperties": {"Pushdown Optimization": "Full", "Allow Temporary View for Pushdown": "Yes"}` and the top-level `"enableCrossSchemaPushdown": true` (needed when sources and targets sit in different datasets of one warehouse), then `POST /api/v2/mttask/<taskId>` with the full body (L-CDI-084) and read it back. The mapping's BigQuery targets must carry no write disposition, because BigQuery rejects one on DML jobs. `Pushdown Optimization: Full` on its own persists on read-back but the run stays in agent mode, which is why pushdown once looked walled; which added key is decisive was not isolated, so set all three. The only proof is the run's session log (`GET /api/v2/activity/activityLog/<entryId>/sessionLog`, L-CDI-211): `TM_6721 Started [SQL ELT optimization]`, `OPT_63321 [Full SQL ELT optimization is supported between the source and the target system.]`, `OPT_63367 Full SQL ELT optimization was successfully enabled.`, `TM_6722 Finished [SQL ELT optimization]` (about 3 s), then for every target a `BIGQUERYV2_10000 ... final query ... in full SQL ELT mode: [INSERT INTO ...]` line between its pre-SQL and post-SQL lines; `OPT_63375` names the fallback mode, and 'Partial SQL ELT' means part of the mapping ran on the agent. No OPT_63367 and no INSERT lines means no pushdown, whatever the task JSON says. Mappings that also read or write another system cannot push down fully (L-CDI-043). To find the REST name of any task setting without a UI capture, diff the v2 JSON of a task the UI switched against an identical task that was not switched. Prove it on an unscheduled scratch copy that writes parity targets, then gate on speed (L-CDI-203); the rollback is `sessionProperties {}` and `enableCrossSchemaPushdown: false`.
evidence: A scratch copy configured over v2 ran 11 times (10 SUCCESS); every session log showed OPT_63367 and one BigQuery INSERT INTO per target (5 targets, each INSERT 0-1 s); a field-by-field diff against the agent-mode task showed only these three keys as functional differences; an earlier attempt with only 'Pushdown Optimization: Full' read back but logged no SQL ELT lines

title: Full pushdown writes a mapping's targets one after another: on small data a multi-target mapping gets slower, not faster
text: In full SQL ELT the agent writes a mapping's targets serially, each as two pre-SQL statements, the INSERT and a post-SQL statement, at about 5.4 s per target even when the warehouse INSERT itself takes 0-1 s, after an optimization step of about 3 s; agent mode writes all targets of the mapping in parallel. A 5-target BigQuery-to-BigQuery mapping took a median 43 s with pushdown (n=6, 38-49 s) against 27-29 s in agent mode (n=30-32). Rule of thumb: pushdown costs about 3 s + 5.4 s x targets on top of the ~20 s fixed task cost (L-CDI-121), so a 1-target mapping at 12 s cannot gain much and an 11-target golden-record mapping gets slower. Pushdown does not change the job count (each run is still one job), but it is metered per million rows processed instead of per compute hour (L-IPU-003), so it can still pay for cost at high volume. Keep pushdown on a mapping only if a parity run matches exactly (two-way EXCEPT DISTINCT = 0 on every target) and the median of at least 3 timed runs is at least 20% or 10 s faster; otherwise revert. At thousands to tens of thousands of rows per run the bigger lever was removing jobs from the critical path, for example reading the CDC copies already in the warehouse instead of re-reading the source database in every lane. Where pushdown should pay (large volumes, few targets) was not measured here.
evidence: Session-log timestamps of the pushdown run: the 5 targets finished about 6.4, 11.1, 16.2, 21.9 and 27.2 s after the optimization step; medians from 24 h of activity-log rows for both tasks; the pilot was closed as 'measured slower'

title: Transformations proven headless with a spec-to-IMF generator, and where their IMF shapes come from
text: A generator (spec JSON -> IMF JSON -> DTEMPLATE package -> v3 import -> mapping task -> run) built and ran real multi-transformation mappings with Source, Target, Filter, Expression (variable ports), Sorter, Joiner (normal, master outer, full outer, chained, sorted same-source self-join), Router, Aggregator (stacked), Union, Rank (top-N), Sequence Generator, connected and unconnected Lookup, Data Masking, Rule Specification, Cleanse, Deduplicate, Normalizer, mapplets, in-out parameters for incremental loads, and Update, Upsert, Delete and Data Driven writes on BigQuery and PostgreSQL targets. The class model lives in the Mapping Designer's JavaScript bundle (`cmd-all-<build>.min.js` and `cmd-webpack-<build>.min.js` under the designer's static path): search it for `infaw.template.T<Name>Generator` (`initTx`, `createDefaultGroups`). `GET https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/da/w3.imf/iclass/?infaToken=<icSessionId>` returns the class-header catalogue (HTTP 400 status but a real body, no property lists), and the masking techniques come from `infaw.saas.SaaSService.instance().getMaskRulesAsJSON()` evaluated inside a logged-in designer page (27 techniques). Shapes that ran: Union = plain groups Input1..n plus OutputGroup, with `inputGroups` = TmplUnionGroup {name, fieldMapping: {fields: [TxFieldMapping name=<incoming field>, txField=<ref to the output field>]}} (TmplUnionGroup is not a group: putting it in `groups` fails with a cast error); Rank = a DefaultGroup with `isTop`, `rankField`, `numOfRows` and `groupByFieldsList` (it adds RANKINDEX); Sequence = TmplGenerator with `midstream=true` and a GeneratorState `state` (it adds NEXTVAL; the start value was ignored and numbering began at 1); unconnected Lookup = no groups, `inputPortNames`, `lookupConditions`, `returnPortName`, `unconnected=true` and a warehouse adapter like a source's, called as `:LKP.<NAME>(arg)` in an Expression; Data Masking (TmplDmo) = `maskingType` with the human label ('Email address', 'Phone', 'SSN', 'Credit card', 'Key') and that rule's parameters, outputs `out_<field>`, format-preserving, and pass-through fields do not flow through it (link them around it); Rule Specification = the package must carry the asset (a mappingTemplate `references` entry of refType `frsDocument`, an `exportedObjects` RULE_SPECIFICATION entry and the objectRefs). A failed import leaves a broken shell that a later REUSE import picks up (REPO_36004): re-import under a new name. Copy the DQ assets a mapping references (cleanse, dedupe) in from another org by package import first, and harvest real IMF exemplars of each class by export (L-CDI-035). For the Deduplicate match-field trap see L-DQ-101. Still unproven headless: the Data Quality transformation and Update Strategy.
evidence: Every node type above ran in real jobs from scratch mappings (2026-09-30); three showcase mappings (21, 28 and 11 transformations, 16 types) tied to the reporting layer exactly; a suite of 9 complex scenarios passed exact two-way keyed diffs on a real Secure Agent (3 chained outer joiners 22,895 rows in 42 s; full-outer 2-key reconciliation 18,491 rows; sorted self-join 9,289 rows in 284 s; SCD2 with MD5; local-day lookups across a DST change) (2026-10-03)

title: Retry a FAILED IDMC task once on transient error signatures only, never on the job-cap error, and classify SaaS-target WARNINGs separately
text: When an external orchestrator or watcher starts mapping tasks or taskflows (`POST /api/v2/job`, watched through the activity log), classify a FAILED task's error text and start it once more (after about 20 s, or at once for a lane's critical-path task) only if it matches a transient pattern: 'Retrying may solve the problem' (a BigQuery 503 backend error), HTTP 500/502/503/504 in the message, 'backend error', 'service unavailable', 'rate limit', 'connection reset', a staging-file upload error, "Table [<table>] does not exist" for a table that does exist, and `Temp_View<digits>` with 409 or 404 (concurrent BigQuery query-source collisions, L-CDI-160). Never retry 'monthly limit' (the job-cap error, L-IPU-041): hand it to the quota breaker (L-CDI-132). Report every other failure (heap OOM, validation, authentication, data errors) without retrying, and do not auto-retry SaaS writes that failed on target-side limits such as a full CRM (they only repeat, L-CAI-080). Retry only once: record the first error and a RETRYING state so the retry shows in run history, keep a state file of runs already re-run so a second failure is never retried, and count each retry as one more job against the monthly cap. A persistent 'Internal error ... DTM process terminated unexpectedly' is a host problem (L-AGENT-063); after a staging 5001 check the target row count first (L-CDI-130). Keep the watcher's own network errors (DNS, timeouts) from triggering any IDMC call, and stop it at once on a rejected login instead of looping (L-AUTH-042). Without a retry an event-driven lane leaves the triggering record waiting for the next event: one transient 'does not exist' failure on the golden-record mapping cost a record 28 minutes. Treat WARNING per task, not per lane: a WARNING with rejected rows on a SaaS target (storage full, duplicates, locks) is a target problem to alert on, not a pipeline failure, while a WARNING that wrote 0 rows is a failure (L-CDI-060); an orchestrator that failed whole lanes on any WARNING marked lanes FAILED although the golden records and marts had landed.
evidence: 24 h census of one org (711 top-level entries: 612 SUCCESS, 97 WARNING, 2 FAILED): both failures were transient cloud errors (a BigQuery 503 and a staging-file upload error) and the next run of each succeeded; all 97 WARNINGs were SaaS upserts rejected with STORAGE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED; a golden-record mapping failed 1 in 52 runs with 'Table [...] does not exist' on an existing table (2026-10-01); a scheduled taskflow's single re-run after a BigQuery 503 succeeded (2026-09-29); the overall recovery rate of the retry was not recorded

title: Measure record-to-golden latency per hop with CDC APPENDS() plus warehouse time travel at each publish, never the truncate-load stamp
text: A golden-record mapping that truncate-loads its target restamps one load time on every row, so that stamp cannot time a single record. Measure instead: (1) list new source rows and their first `_CHANGE_TIMESTAMP` from the CDC replica's `APPENDS(TABLE <cdc_dataset>.<table>, <t0>, NULL)` history (L-DBMI-029; it also keeps rows later purged at the source), or take the source `created_at`; (2) list every successful publish of the golden table (task end) from your run ledger or the activity log (page at `rowLimit=1000` and flatten taskflow entries; a stand-alone task's sub-entry has an empty objectName); (3) for each publish query the golden table `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF TIMESTAMP_ADD(<task end>, INTERVAL 2 SECOND)` for the new keys: the first snapshot that holds a key gives its latency. BigQuery traps: only one `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF` value per table per query, so snapshots cannot be UNIONed (one small query per publish, run in parallel); `AT` is reserved and cannot be an alias; time travel reaches back about 7 days (L-CDI-161). Decompose each sample into wait-to-start (run start minus event: it can be negative, because the mapping reads the source after its fixed start-up cost, so a row committed up to about 35 s after the start still made that run) and the mapping's runtime, and confirm the orchestrator is idle before timing. Report n, average, fastest, last and median over a rolling 24 h, success-only (L-METHOD-049), and say whether a number is the orchestrator's wall time or the IDMC task span (they differed by about 74 s on a full lane). Measured on one 8-vCPU agent host (source row -> CDC copy -> one consolidated golden mapping with 11 targets; 60 s minimum gap between lane starts): created to golden average 76 s, median 67 s, p90 116 s, fastest 33 s (n=58); the golden mapping ran a median 65 s (about 8,900 rows) and was the bottleneck, and the median wait to start was 1.5 s; the 7 of 58 records that missed a run (the lane gap or another lane's lock) formed the whole 104-156 s tail. In the same window CDC to the warehouse averaged about 21 s and the real-time CAI decision about 0.1 s; lane wall times were about 96 s (7 tasks), 145-159 s (11 tasks) and 258-358 s (a 23-task full rebuild). Conclusions: seconds end to end through batch CDI lanes are not reachable (each lane takes 85-150 s), so CDC and CAI must carry the per-event story; optimize the dominant step on the path, not the trigger. Newer evidence: L-METHOD-158.
evidence: 61 inserts over 24.6 h (58 new records, 3 merged into existing survivors) read against 42 golden-table publishes by time travel (about 1 GB billed for all snapshot queries); per-hop numbers from the activity log and the CDC change history; 0 records seen before their source event

title: PostgreSQL targets in generated mappings: an Upsert that applied nothing, keep-when-null, uuid reads, and mirror versus history deletes
text: In an IMF-generated mapping that fans out to several PostgreSQL reverse-ETL targets, the targets set to operation Upsert behaved as update-only: on a scratch copy where every key was new the session requested 736 rows and applied 0, with no error, because the generator had not written the writer attributes the UI sets for that operation (the exact attribute was not isolated). Two fixes worked: (a) a Joiner against the target's keys (outer, so unmatched source rows survive), then a Router into an Update target instance (key found) and an Insert target instance (key not found); (b) a later generator that writes those attributes, with which Upsert, Update, Delete and Data Driven all ran on PostgreSQL and BigQuery targets. The template-task Upsert with `targetUpdateColumns` (L-CDI-089) was not affected; test new-key inserts on every Upsert target of a generated mapping before it goes live. Other rules from the same swaps: an old per-column update never overwrote a stored value with NULL, so the consolidated mapping needs a keep-when-null Expression (take the stored value when the incoming one is NULL) or stored values get blanked; read PostgreSQL uuid columns as `::text` in the source query; for mirror targets (a database or a JDBC warehouse) do upsert plus a key-sync delete (a master-outer Joiner of target keys to source keys, a Filter where the source key is null, then Delete), never a TRUNCATE (L-CDI-208); for append-history targets use insert + update only (L-CDI-199).
evidence: 736 requested / 0 applied on the first build; the Joiner + Router build wrote 753 updates + 5 inserts, 780 + 5 and 780 + 5 on three targets with 0 mismatched keys; a mirror with a delete group did Insert 7 / Update 764 / Delete 2; keep-when-null verified on 51 rows; a mirror equal to the source on 12 of 12 tables (2026-09-29/30)

title: A 'Pre SQL' TRUNCATE runs before the source is read: a failed read leaves the target empty
text: The full-reload switch for JDBC V2 targets, the runtime attribute `Pre SQL` = `TRUNCATE TABLE <t>` (L-CDI-171, L-CONN-056), executes when the session starts, before the reader has fetched a row. If the source login or object then fails (a renamed or retired database role, a dropped table, a network drop), the task ends in error with the target already empty, and whatever refreshes from it next (materialized views, BI extracts, dashboards) publishes empty results until a good run. A failed read should leave the last good data in place: (1) load a stage table and swap or rename it in only after a successful run (post-SQL did not run when the read failed; verify this on your connector); or (2) use a key-sync mirror (upsert every source row, then delete target keys missing from the source) whose deletes run only after a successful read, guarded by a count gate that skips the deletes when the source returns 0 rows or far fewer than the target holds (L-CDI-091). Never use key-sync deletes on append-history targets (L-CDI-199). Prove the design by pointing a scratch copy at a source object that does not exist: the task must fail and the target must keep its rows. Before retiring or renaming a database role, list every connection that logs in as it (L-CONN-011).
evidence: A source-login failure made every landing task of one mirror lane fail after its Pre SQL truncate had already run; the next hourly downstream refresh published empty marts and 5 dashboard charts showed no results for about 4.5 h (2026-09-26). After the redesign as key-sync mappings (parity 0/0), a scratch task aimed at a missing table ended state 3 'Object [...] not found' and the target kept its 822 rows (2026-09-30)

title: A reverse-ETL guard trigger that never blanks a governed field must still allow an explicit clear
text: A database trigger on reverse-ETL targets that reverts any NULL written over a non-NULL value protects governed fields from a broken upstream load, but it also reverts legitimate business clears (for example a cancellation that empties a plan or status field), so the CRM and downstream syncs keep the old value. Let the application opt in per transaction: it runs `SET LOCAL <namespace>.allow_clear = 'on'` only for an explicit clear, and the trigger returns NEW unchanged when `current_setting('<namespace>.allow_clear', true) = 'on'`. IDMC writes never set it, so they stay guarded. Test it in a rolled-back transaction: without the flag a NULL is reverted, with it the NULL lands, and the flag is gone after commit.
evidence: Stale-value drift 68 -> 0 after a backfill; CRM versus source mismatches 3 -> 0 of 721 linked records; guard behaviour tested in a rolled-back transaction

title: A DTM heap OOM shows up as 'Unexpected error refreshing access token' on the other BigQuery reader partitions
text: When a DTM runs out of heap, the first error is `PLUGIN_1762 [ERROR] java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` in one reader thread (stack in `CCIRuntimeDataClientImpl.readData`). Seconds later the other BigQuery V2 reader partitions fail with `BIGQUERYV2_10000 ... [5001 - Unexpected error refreshing access token]` and the targets log `WRT_8044 No data loaded for this target`. The token errors are a cascade of the dying JVM, not a credential problem: read the first `[ERROR]` in the session log. Generated multi-transformation mappings with many Joiners, Sorters and Aggregators are the usual victims: an unsorted Joiner runs as `TT_11098 The Joiner transformation [...] is configured with the join algorithm: Nested-Loop` and caches its master side, a Sorter reserved about 150 MB per partition, and Aggregators grow their caches at start (`TE_7212 Increasing [Data Cache] size`). Such a mapping can pass alone and fail beside other lanes, because the heap is per DTM and several DTMs run at once (L-AGENT-099). Fix in this order: take the mapping out of the live taskflows (restore the tasks it replaced), raise the DTM heap cloud-side (L-AGENT-056), then split the mapping or give its Joiners sorted input before putting it back.
evidence: A 17-transformation data-quality mapping failed 3 of 3 live runs with this sequence (PLUGIN_1762 OOM first, then BIGQUERYV2_10000 5001 token errors on four reader partitions, WRT_8044) after passing a solo run; with a 2 GB DTM heap it ran solo OK (859 rows, parity 0/0)

title: Download a task run's session log over REST: GET /api/v2/activity/activityLog/<entryId>/sessionLog
text: `GET <serverUrl>/api/v2/activity/activityLog/<entryId>/sessionLog` with header `icSessionId: <v2 session>` and `Accept: */*` returns the run's session log as plain text (about 75 KB for a 5-target mapping), so run evidence can be read without a shell on the agent host (the on-disk logs of L-CDI-064). `<entryId>` is the `id` of the run's activity-log entry, not its `runId`. Grep the text for what you must prove: `TM_6721`/`TM_6722` (optimization start and finish with its duration), `OPT_63367` (full SQL ELT enabled, L-CDI-202), `OPT_63375` (the fallback mode), the connector's `INSERT INTO` lines and per-step execution times, or the first `[ERROR]` of a failed run (L-CDI-210). Save the text with the run id as evidence: it is the only proof of what the engine actually did.
evidence: HTTP 200 for two runs (76,677 and 76,524 characters, one pushdown and one agent-mode run of the same mapping); used to prove pushdown

title: The Data Integration Server runs only 2 DTMs at once by default: measure the queue, then raise maxDTMProcesses cloud-side
text: Every mapping-task session waits for a slot in the Data Integration Server (DIS) DTM pool. Its size is the Tomcat property `maxDTMProcesses`; with no such line in `tomcat.cfg` the documented default 2 applies, and DIS logs it at startup in `<agent_home>/apps/Data_Integration_Server/logs/tomcat/tomcat_<disVersion>.log` as `maxDTMProcesses(poolSize)=2`. Each session logs 'Submit job to thread pool queue', 'Creating DTM process' and 'DTM process started'; the gap between the first and the last is its queue wait. With the default pool an orchestrator that starts 4 tasks at once never gets more than 2 concurrent DTMs, so its speed-up is capped however many tasks it submits. CPU was not the limit: a warehouse-bound DTM spends most of its 14-20 s waiting on the warehouse load or query job and only about 2 s on JVM start. Fix: add the Custom Configuration row Data Integration Server / TOMCAT_CFG / `maxDTMProcesses` = N (the Tomcat type does not list this property, so it must be a custom row; headless through the agent.do form, L-AGENT-088), together with the DTM heap (`JVMOption1=-Xmx2048m`, type DTM, L-AGENT-056), so both survive version rolls. Size N to memory (about 0.5-1 GB per DTM plus heap headroom inside the agent's memory limit) and to the vCPUs (4 on a 4-vCPU host shared with a second agent); on hosts too small for 2 DTMs go the other way (`maxDTMProcesses=1`, L-DQ-098). Apply it in a drained window: the save restarts DIS by itself about 1.5-2 min later and may roll it to a pending build; the old JVM kept dispatching until the new one's tunnel opened (no dispatch gap was seen) and lingered 5-8 min, so verify on the running DIS and DTM command lines (`ps -o args`) and the new startup log line, not on the newest version directory. Re-measure the queue-wait histogram (aim for p90 under 10 s), sample concurrent DTM child processes, and add a soak check that alerts when the pool size or the heap drifts from the intended values.
evidence: Default pool, 472 sessions: queue wait p50 13.9 s, p90 39.7 s, p99 70.1 s, max 76.3 s; 61% waited over 10 s; at most 2 concurrent DTMs. After the cloud-side row (N=4) plus a 2 GB DTM heap: the startup log showed poolSize=4; a 15-minute burst sampled every 5 s reached 4 concurrent DTMs, minimum MemAvailable 10.1 GB, agent unit peak 7.55 GB under a 12 GB MemoryHigh; a 40-task full refresh ran 40/40 in 321 s and an event lane's record-to-golden time fell from 62-85 s to 47 s

title: Agent log signatures of a flapping Process Server and a looping service, and two monitor-parser traps
text: A flapping Process Server shows `/process-engine/status` returning 404, then agentcore logs `[LCM_10012] ... Status script return code: EXITED_NONZERO` and restarts it. Cloud Integration Hub writes the same LCM_10012 lines, so count restarts per engine name, not per message. The Data Access Management agent/proxy loop of an org without DAM (L-AGENT-091) ends each cycle with `ProcessSupervisor ... state[EXITED] ... exit code: 133` about 3.5 min after 'Application status set to running'. `agentcore.log` timestamps are 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' with a space, so a time filter built with the ISO 'T' silently matches nothing. A monitor that parses the agent's status output must skip its trailing blank line: reading the last line as the state raised false alerts.
evidence: Log reads on two agents with about 17 services selected; false alerts stopped after the parser fix

title: A BigQuery CDC target dataset holds DBMI's own _EXT twins and an INFORMATICA_CDC_RECOVERY table: exclude them, never drop them
text: Each table that a running PostgreSQL-to-BigQuery CDC task replicates gets a managed table plus a `<table>_EXT` external table (the staging twin over the GCS files the job writes), and the dataset holds an `INFORMATICA_CDC_RECOVERY` table (the job's restart bookkeeping). They change without new business rows, so exclude `_EXT` and `INFORMATICA%` tables from BI, catalog include filters, table counts and change detection (for example `WHERE table_id NOT LIKE 'INFORMATICA%' AND table_id NOT LIKE '%_EXT'` on `__TABLES__`, L-ENV-082); derive any 'tables replicated by CDC' list from the dataset metadata instead of hard-coding it; never drop or rewrite them while the job is deployed (dropping them was not tested); and expect them in every dataset inventory. On the source side the slot of a healthy job reads inactive between apply cycles: judge it by lag and freshness (L-DBMI-016).
evidence: Live check: slots idle while both CDC jobs ran with 0 bytes lag and error-free task logs; a dataset inventory showed every managed CDC table paired with an _EXT external table plus one INFORMATICA_CDC_RECOVERY table (2026-09-29/30); a dashboard that hard-coded 10 replicated tables missed 3 of the 13 (2026-09-28)

title: Erasure through a CDC pipeline: deletes reach the warehouse, but change history, IDMC-built layers, SaaS copies and logins keep the person
text: A delete in the operational database flows through CDC to the warehouse tables (L-DBMI-026), but that is not erasure. The warehouse change history (`APPENDS()` and time travel, about 7 days) still returns the deleted rows; IDMC-built layers that are not mirrors keep their copies (three minutes after an erase the old email, phone or name still sat in 4 CDC tables, 5 real-time views and 6 curated or activation tables of 36 checked, plus log and outbox tables in the source database); a CRM contact created by a real-time process or a batch upsert keeps name, email and phone; and the identity provider keeps the login. Design erasure as an explicit fan-out with a per-system check: delete or anonymize the CRM record (a minute-level job anonymized one in about 36 s), delete the login, tombstone-and-purge each warehouse layer, keep only a tombstone without personal data, exclude erased keys from every reverse-ETL, activation and SaaS upsert, and document the residual window of warehouse time travel (or shorten the dataset's time-travel window if policy requires).
evidence: An erasure test left the login working and the CRM contact intact until two fixes, after which the contact anonymization job completed in 36 s (2026-09-29); an erase inventory by key across 36 warehouse tables (2026-10-03); latency studies read purged test records back from the CDC change history (2026-10-01)

title: A live SaaS mirror for BI is the batch read-back UNION the CAI upserts newer than the read-back
text: When CAI writes records to a SaaS application in real time and a CDI task reads the SaaS objects back into the warehouse in batch, a BI reconciliation ('is this record in the SaaS app?') built only on the read-back table flags every record created since the last read-back as missing, and all new records once batch stops (for example at the job cap). Build the BI view as the read-back rows UNION the successful upserts from your own CAI decision log (CAI runs are not in the activity log, L-CAI-041) that are newer than the read-back's watermark, deduplicated on the SaaS record id or the natural key. New records then appear within the CAI round trip plus the view's own latency, and the SaaS count ties out with the real-time path.
evidence: A read-back-only check grew from 1 to 12 false 'only in the warehouse' rows although CAI had created each SaaS record 2-3 s after it was entered; the union view showed +1 per CAI-synced record within about 25 s

title: Empty fields: a CAI process omits empty outputs from its JSON response, and a Salesforce PATCH that carries an empty field blanks it
text: When a process output field evaluates to empty, the REST response of the published process leaves the key out instead of returning an empty string or null. A caller that indexes the key directly fails on exactly the records where the optional output is empty (for example normalized first and last name parts when only a full name was sent). Read every optional output with a default (`resp.get('field', '')`), and add new outputs to a process without assuming old callers will see them. In the other direction, a Salesforce upsert (`PATCH .../sobjects/<Object>/<ExternalIdField>/<value>`) that carries a field with an empty value sets that field empty: build the request body from the fields that have values and omit the rest instead of sending blanks.
evidence: Observed on a cleansing process after optional name-part outputs were added: the keys were absent for records without those parts (2026-09-28); the PATCH behaviour recorded in a review of the real-time CRM writes (2026-10-03)

title: A fuzzy Deduplicate asset matches nothing if a unique id is mapped into its 'Id' match field
text: In a stock or cloned Deduplicate (fuzzy match) asset, `Id` is one of the match fields; mapping the record's unique business key into it makes every pair differ, so no record ever matches. Leave the unique id out of the match fields (or leave the port unmapped, as the asset expects), block on a coarse key (for example the street number) and sort by the group key. Read a dedupe asset's match fields before its first run, and compare its duplicate count with an independent SQL survivorship query.
evidence: Matching worked after the id was removed from the match fields (2026-09-30); the fuzzy Deduplicate in a generated mapping then found the same 41 duplicates as the SQL survivorship (2026-10-03)

title: Profiling sampling options are fixed per connector: BigQuery V2 profiles All Rows only, so make the sample a table
text: Data Profiling offers All Rows, First N Rows or Random N Rows depending on the connection type (vendor guide, October 2025). All Rows only: Google BigQuery V2, Flat File, Amazon S3 V2, ADLS Gen2, Google Cloud Storage V2, SAP BW Reader and mapplets. All Rows and First N Rows: JDBC V2, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Salesforce, Amazon Athena, Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse and ODBC. Random N Rows: only Amazon Redshift V2, Azure Synapse SQL and Snowflake. Databricks Delta has Sample N Rows only on Data Integration Server execution. First N reads whatever rows the source returns first, so it is rarely representative. For a large source, build a deterministic, stratified sample table outside IDMC (for example at most 100k rows and at most 50 profiled columns, selected with a portable hash key, L-DQ-099), then profile that table with All Rows; the profile body carries `samplingOptions: {"samplingType": "ALL_ROWS", "rows": -1}`. A catalog source's Data Quality scope samples separately: All Rows, Limit N Rows (default 1000) or Custom Query (L-CDGC-016).
evidence: Vendor Data Profiling guide (October 2025) connector sampling table; in one org a 33,277-row, 39-column staged sample profiled to COMPLETED with ALL_ROWS on a small agent, while a 181-column full-width profile had overloaded that agent

title: Control profile fan-out per profile: runtimeOptions.profileAdvProps carries the split and memory knobs
text: The profile body's `runtimeOptions.profileAdvProps` holds the vendor's advanced options as fields (null means the default): `maxColumnsPerMapping` (Maximum Number of Columns per Mapping, default 50), `minNoOfRowsForSplitMapping` (Minimum Number of Rows for Split Process per Column, default 100,000,000), `maxMemory` and `maxPercentMemory` (Maximum Memory per Mapping, default 512 MB), `dtmBufferSize`, `defaultBufferBlockSize`, `lineSequentialBufferLength`, `maxTopN`, `maxPatterns`, `maxPatternThresholdPercent`, `maxRanks`, `detectOutliers`, `inferDateTime`, `enableClaireAnomalyDetection`, `stopOnErrors` and `tracingLevel`. Subtasks follow these knobs: below the row threshold a profile gets one subtask per `maxColumnsPerMapping` columns plus rules, above it one subtask per column (the vendor example: 10M rows x 100 columns gives 2 subtasks by default and 4 smaller ones with 25 columns per mapping, each using less memory). Tune them on the profile itself (PUT the full body, L-DQ-019) when the agent is shared with other pipelines, rather than lowering the agent-wide `maxDTMProcesses` that the other pipelines rely on (L-DQ-098); for that agent-wide value the vendor sizing rule is n = int(0.8 x cores). `runtimeOptions.runtimeEnvironmentId: null` means the profile runs on its connection's runtime environment.
evidence: Field names read from GET /profile/<id> on a live profile in one org; defaults and the worked example from the vendor Data Profiling guide (October 2025); a PUT that changes these fields not yet exercised

title: Read a rule specification's logic from a v3 export: documentBlob, then ruleModel, then the script or the statements tree
text: In a v3 export package each `<name>.RULE_SPECIFICATION.json` has the shape `{id, name, description, documentType, customAttributes.stringAttrs[], nativeData.documentBlob}`. The `stringAttrs` hold the DIMENSION (for example VALIDITY, COMPLETENESS, CONSISTENCY) and EXCEPTION. `documentBlob` is a JSON string holding `{inputFields, outputFields, ruleModel}`, and `ruleModel` is itself a JSON string (class `com.informatica.dq.rulebuilder.RuleDefinition`), so parse twice. Advanced-mode specs, the form CLAIRE writes, keep their logic in `alternateDefinition.script` as `IF <cond> THEN Output='VALID' ELSE Output='INVALID' ENDIF`, using functions such as ISNULL, LENGTH, IS_SPACES, REG_MATCH and IN(x,[...]). Basic-mode specs hold a `topRuleFamily.statements` tree of operations (SetField, Equals, NotEquals, DefaultValue, WithinList, NotWithinList, GreaterThanOrEqualTo, LessThanOrEqualTo, Valid, Expression, standardize, convertCase) plus `testData` arrays. A row passes when the output is Valid, True, 1, Yes or Ok (L-DQ-049). An advanced script translates deterministically into a SQL predicate, `upper(CASE ... END) IN ('VALID','TRUE','1','YES','OK')`, so IDMC-authored rules can run at scale in a warehouse engine; basic mode needs an operation mapper. Check three semantics against each rule's testData before trusting a translation: whether REG_MATCH is a full-string match, what IS_SPACES('') returns, and whether IN is case-sensitive; RE2-based engines also reject lookarounds and backreferences. Mark anything the translator cannot map as needs-review (L-DQ-100).
evidence: 19 rule specifications parsed from v3 export packages (7 advanced, 12 basic); a prototype translated 7 of 7 advanced specs into ClickHouse, BigQuery and PostgreSQL predicates; the three semantics points not yet verified against IDMC output

title: A format DQ dimension can read green while the stored values are not canonical: test the exact stored form
text: A golden table's phone column held '1XXXXXXXXXX' in 768 rows and 'XXXXXXXXXX' in 33 rows, with no '+', while its DQ dimension 'phone E.164' scored 0.9918; the application database and the CRM held +E.164 only because a later write-back round trip normalised them. A dimension score is not proof of the stored form: make a format rule test the stored representation literally (for E.164 `^\+[1-9]\d{7,14}$`, or `^\+1\d{10}$` for one country), look at the output pattern distribution of the column, and make the golden mapping emit the canonical form on its first run (L-CDI-104), so first-cycle records do not differ from later ones.
evidence: Counts from the warehouse golden table against the DQ scorecard row on the same day; 810 E.164 rows in the database and the CRM

title: Golden-record write-back must reach every copy the screens read, including the identity provider's login name, under strict invariants
text: A governed write-back of golden-record fields onto the system of origin should accept only a whitelist of identity, contact and address columns (never status, financial, lifecycle, keys or derived values), normalise each golden value to the source's own convention before comparing (for example phone to +E.164) so an unchanged record writes nothing, push only records the DQ rules mark valid, audit every change by record id with before and after values and no raw PII in the audit key, and arrive through the application's own API with service credentials (one writer of golden data into the app, L-CAI-088). Before calling a write-back done, list every copy the screens actually read (database rows, the identity provider's profile and token claims, the CRM, caches): web and mobile apps usually render the person's name from the login token (a name claim taken at sign-in), so a DQ-corrected name (for example an ALL CAPS sign-up) reached the database but stayed wrong in every app. Update the identity-provider user too, only when the words are equal ignoring case (a re-casing, never another person's name), keeping its own first/last split, never failing the write-back on an identity-provider error, and audited; make the web session re-read userinfo about once a minute, let mobile prefer the API profile value when the email matches, and back-fill logins that already differ. Measured: source insert to database and identity provider corrected in 1.5-2.7 min (the golden mapping plus a 120 s activation loop), and an open web session followed about 20 s later. During that gap the golden record is clean while the write-back has not landed, so a page that shows both disagrees: poll until they match (every 5-10 s, up to 3 min). For erasure, the opposite direction, see L-DBMI-051.
evidence: End-to-end browser tests on web and mobile for ALL CAPS sign-ups, 5 of 5: the name corrected in the database, the identity provider and an open session; both page cards agreed about 85 s after sign-up without a reload; 18 of 31 drifted logins back-filled, drift 0 of 30 afterwards (2026-10-02/03)

title: Two agent users on one host: catalog scans end PARTIAL_COMPLETED on a shared /tmp/poifiles directory
text: The catalog scanner (Metadata_Foundation_Agent) writes its Excel scan report through Apache POI into `/tmp/poifiles` (the JVMs use `/tmp` as `java.io.tmpdir`). The first agent user that scans creates the directory with mode 755. A second agent on the same host, running as another OS user, then gets `AccessDeniedException` on it, and Metadata Extraction ends PARTIAL_COMPLETED with 'Total objects processed count <n> is the same as objects count with errors' although the objects were read; the first agent never sees the problem because it owns the directory. Make it shared like /tmp (`chmod 1777 /tmp/poifiles`), write-test it as both agent users, and look for other /tmp directories owned by the first agent user without group or other write. On a new shared host create the directory 1777 up front or give each agent its own `java.io.tmpdir`.
evidence: AccessDeniedException on /tmp/poifiles in the second agent's scanner log on every run of a BigQuery source (328 objects, all counted with errors); after chmod 1777 both agent users passed a write test and later scans of 155 and 656 objects completed

title: BigQuery catalog sources: view SQL the lineage parser cannot read, single-backtick names, and include filters naming missing datasets
text: Metadata Extraction on a BigQuery catalog source parses each view's SQL to build lineage. Two failure forms: (1) the BigQuery SQL analyzer throws `UnsupportedOperationException` on some views (32 times for one view that combined a raw-string regex inside a CTE used as a scalar-subquery argument, IN-subquery flags in the select list and about 20 COUNTIF calls); that view gets no lineage and looks skipped; (2) `Parse error NoViableAlt` on a single backticked fully qualified name such as `` `<project>.<dataset>.<table>` ``, while `` `<project>`.<dataset>.<table> `` parses. Other views in the same source parsed fine. Separately, an include filter that names a dataset that does not exist logs 'Could not find matching schemas': remove the entry. For views whose lineage matters, quote the project on its own and keep complex logic parse-friendly (prove any rewrite with a parity check first). The v2 connection browse proves nothing about which tables a scan will see (L-CONN-016): Metadata Extraction does.
evidence: One scan log: 32 UnsupportedOperationException for one view, one NoViableAlt on a single-backtick name, 'Could not find matching schemas' for a stale include entry; 54 other views read fine; the NoViableAlt view parsed after re-quoting

title: Catalog Data Quality creates org schedules named DQ_Capability_Schedule_*; clone catalog sources with DQ automation off
text: In an org running catalog Data Quality scoring with CLAIRE rule recommendations, three schedules appeared in `GET /api/v2/schedule`: `DQ_Capability_Schedule_Daily_<epochMs>`, `..._Weekly_<epochMs>` and `..._Monthly_<epochMs>`, created within one second of each other with the description 'Auto generated schedule for existing Rule Templates' and owned by the user who ran the job. A working warehouse catalog source's `Data Quality Scope` read `Run Rule Occurrence Frequency: true`, `Data Quality Automation: true` and `Data Quality Automation Scope: Apply on all Data Elements`, so a source cloned from that body (L-CDGC-015) is set up to run accepted rule occurrences on IDMC-side schedules and to attach automation rules to every data element in scope. For a new estate set both switches to false unless you want IDMC-side scheduling, run Metadata Extraction alone first, and enable profiling, classification and DQ only once the asset list holds just the intended tables; re-read the schedules after each accept. Those runs are not in the v2 activity log: count them through the catalog jobs API (L-IPU-055). How many jobs these schedules add was not measured.
evidence: GET /api/v2/schedule listed the three auto-generated schedules (created within one second, Daily at 05:00Z) next to the user-made ones; the catalog-source definition read back with the three switches above

title: 'Query the data' wording: ask the count and its business impact in one prompt, name the platform and object type, never pin the dataset
text: For a data question whose answer must carry business meaning, put both asks in one prompt in a new conversation: 'How many <entities> in the <warehouse> table <T> have <condition>? Query the data and explain the business impact on <business process>.' That shape returned the exact warehouse numbers plus a grounded impact paragraph every time. A separate follow-up ('What is the business impact of this for <process>, and what should we fix first?') is routed to the product-help agent unless the turn itself queries data: it answered 'No relevant information was found in the product documentation', or answered from vendor product docs instead of the numbers just computed, and a statement-style prompt ('Phone numbers in <asset> are not stored in ...') went to the docs as well. Do not add 'in the <dataset> dataset' to a 'Query the data' prompt: CLAIRE can treat the dataset name as an asset to find ('the asset <dataset> is not found in the limited set of 25 results') and then answer from another asset that shares the bare name (a view instead of the table), with plausible but different numbers. Name the platform, the object type and the bare name ('the <warehouse> table <T>'), answer 'table or view?' with 'The Table' or 'The View', confirm the asset in Show Code (it shows the fully qualified name that ran), and remove or rename stale same-name copies in other datasets (L-CDGC-090): with seven same-name assets CLAIRE sometimes stopped with 'missing scope or asset details'. A mid-chain 'connection issue with the <warehouse> source system' was transient: re-ask the same turn. Saved and pinned conversations drop query results ('no longer available due to privacy guidelines'), so only catalog answers can be kept as pinned fallbacks (L-UI-029). This narrows L-MCP-054's dataset anchor to catalog and DQ-score questions.
evidence: Timed UI runs in fresh conversations on one warehouse table: one-prompt count plus impact 3 of 3 with warehouse-identical counts; count turns without a dataset name 6 of 7 and 8 of 9 (the misses were a transient source-connection error); separate impact follow-ups 2 of 4 and 2 of 5; a dataset-pinned count 1 of 2 (the miss searched for the dataset as an asset and returned the same-named view's numbers); 55-95 s per turn

title: Connect Claude to IDMC with the vendor's Informatica plugin: an OAuth 2.1 public client, two connectors, then the plugin (documented)
text: The vendor publishes an 'Informatica' plugin for Claude Enterprise (Claude Desktop, Cowork and Claude Code). It bundles a 'catalog-and-data-discovery' skill (metadata-first discovery in the catalog: terms, ownership, certification, PII tags; it treats missing metadata as a gap rather than guessing) and two connectors to vendor-hosted MCP servers: Catalog Discovery (`https://mcp.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/mcp-servers/public/cdgccatalogdiscovery`) and CLAIRE Data Exploration Agent (`.../mcp-servers/public/dataexplorationagent`). Setup order: (1) in IDMC, AI Agent Engineering > Configuration > MCP Server Authorization > Informatica OAuth 2.1 > Add OAuth 2.1 Client: name it, choose Token Endpoint Authentication Method = Public, add the Claude callback URL `https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback`, select BOTH servers, Create, and copy the Client ID (a public client has no secret); (2) in Claude Desktop as the organization admin: Organization settings > Connectors > Add > 'Informatica Catalog Discovery' and 'Informatica Data Exploration', each with the pod-specific server URL and the Client ID; (3) Settings > Plugins > add the Informatica plugin, then Connect each connector: the browser redirects to the IDMC login and 'Continue Connecting' completes the per-user OAuth grant; (4) in a new conversation the plugin and its skill appear under the plugins menu. Prerequisites: a Claude Enterprise plan, an IDMC user with catalog permissions, a runtime environment with the Data Gateway (data exploration runs through it, L-AGENT-097), and an IDMC admin to create the OAuth 2.1 client. This is the interactive, per-user counterpart of the client-credentials OAuth client used for headless machine-to-machine calls (L-MCP-119).
evidence: Documented: vendor walkthroughs published 2026-09-17 and 2026-09-28 (setup steps, URLs and prerequisites); the OAuth 2.1 server rollout is in the September 2026 MCP guide (L-MCP-119); not yet run end to end

title: Check community MCP shims for disabled TLS verification before reusing them
text: A field-distributed stdio MCP shim for the CLAIRE agent and DQ servers was found creating its HTTPS context with `ssl.CERT_NONE` and `check_hostname=False`, so it would accept any certificate for the identity and API hosts it sends the IDMC user's credentials to. Before wiring any third-party shim into an MCP client, grep it for `CERT_NONE`, `check_hostname`, `verify=False` and `_create_unverified_context`, restore default verification (or pin a CA bundle behind a corporate proxy), and check that it reads credentials from a 0600 file or the environment rather than its arguments (L-METHOD-001).
evidence: Code inspection of the shim in use; flagged before reuse elsewhere

title: Delete retired mapping tasks in gated waves: categorise, scan configuration files too, merge every keep list, export, DELETE, read back, rescan the catalog
text: Inventory every mapping task fresh and put each in exactly one category: LIVE (in a lane, linear taskflow, taskflow or schedule), REFERENCED IN CODE OR CONFIGURATION, RAN SINCE <time>, BLOCKED BY A DORMANT TASKFLOW, SCRATCH, or SAFE. The reference scan must cover every file type the orchestrators and hosts read (.json, .yaml, .env, cron entries), not only code: a scan of .py and .sh files missed 11 tasks named in an orchestrator's rollback-plan JSON, so 25 'SAFE' candidates were really 13; treat bookkeeping fields such as 'replaces', 'replaced' or 'excluded' lists as non-uses. Objects that belong to another workload sharing the org look SAFE because nothing in your stack calls them: merge the keep lists of every application in the org (one such task was pulled at the last minute). Keep rollback-path objects until the agreed soak date (for example one green week) and delete them in a later wave. Right before each delete re-verify every object: the name still matches the id; no task-level schedule (the v2 list hides `scheduleId`, so GET each task, L-CDI-146); not in any lane or taskflow (taskflow references page at 50); no run since the cutoff, including taskflow sub-entries. Download and open a v3 export package of exactly these objects, then `DELETE /api/v2/mttask/<id>` (200) and read back (403 = gone); delete a now-empty schedule only after confirming that no task or taskflow references it. Afterwards rescan the IICS catalog source so lineage drops the deleted objects (Metadata Change Option = Delete, L-CDGC-028). Undo is a v3 import of the package (new ids, so nothing may call them by id). Delete your own scratch drafts with the same backup step (L-CLEAN-024, L-CLEAN-025).
evidence: Wave 1: a re-inventory cut 25 candidates to 13; 13 tasks and 1 empty schedule deleted, each DELETE 200 and read-back 403, after a 20-entry export package was checked; no lane impact and no overlap with the live plan

title: After an org move, give every source-org object a delete verdict from the id map and the import log before deleting anything
text: Build the source-org decommission list from three inputs (the source inventory, the source-to-target id map and the target import's object log) and give each object one verdict: READY (the import created a twin and its target id is mapped); HOLD-VERIFY (the id map has a twin but the import log says 'Reuse existing object', so the target kept an older same-named object: compare content first); NO-TWIN (not in the target, for example an object the target rejected, such as initial-load tasks failing vendor validation with 403: never delete); test probes (delete any time); dependencies matched by name with no target id (connections, runtime environments, folders: delete last); and shared or vendor content (bundles, other teams' folders, hosted runtimes: never delete). Generate the list with a script so it can be rebuilt whenever the id map changes, and keep deletion a separate, owner-approved step after cutover and smoke tests (L-CLEAN-034).
evidence: 228 source objects classified: 180 READY, 9 HOLD-VERIFY, 7 NO-TWIN (5 rejected initial-load tasks), 3 probes, 13 name-matched dependencies, 16 shared or vendor objects; built read-only from local files

title: After moving to a new org, send one batched vendor case with only what the vendor alone can fix, each item with its evidence
text: Collect the post-cutover gaps that no headless or UI step can close and send them as one case, ordered by urgency: (1) the real monthly job limit when the Licenses page shows no jobs row and every limit reads -1 on a trial edition (an earlier org with the same reading stopped at exactly 10,000 jobs, L-IPU-041), plus a request to raise it or move to a non-trial licence; (2) services that restart-loop for lack of a licence or setup (for example the Data Access Management agent and proxy exiting with code 133 after 'Initializing TMS and CMS configuration services', L-AGENT-091), with the licence-read evidence; (3) CAI assets stuck with duplicate runtime rows ('singleton sequence ... 2 items') or no runtime entry (AvrEntryNotFoundFault) that block deletes (FRS_082, L-CAI-078); (4) reproducible product defects with a minimal repro (for example DBMI CDC shifting fractional-second digits, L-DBMI-024); (5) the engine and selection-list diff against the old org. Leave out tenant issues of other products (BI OAuth policy, SaaS storage), re-check each item the same day and drop those that resolve before sending, and post the case number where the team tracks work.
evidence: One case covered the job limit, the DAM licence, 2 stuck CAI assets, the DBMI defect and the missing services; two earlier items (the data gateway, BigQuery profiling) were removed after they started working

title: Meter allocations and usage behind Administrator > Metering, and why a trial org's '10,000' is compute-unit hours, not the job cap
text: The Metering page reads two services (captured from the page's own requests with the browser session, cookies plus XSRF; the same calls with a REST session header are untested): `GET https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/license-service/api/v1/metering/org/('<orgIdV3>')/instances?aggregatedMeterOnly=true` returns each meter with `strMaxValue` and `strUsed`, and `POST https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/metering-service/api/v1/metering/org/('<orgIdV3>')/queryAggregatedMeterData` with `{"orgId":"<orgIdV3>","meterId":"<meterId>","dataGranularity":["ALL"],"startTime":"<iso>","endTime":"<iso>"}` returns allocation, remaining and daily average. On a trial-edition org the page showed one service, 'Org Consumption', with three meters at max 10,000 and used 0 (Data Integration with Advanced Serverless, Advanced Data Integration, Advanced DI with Advanced Serverless). These are serverless compute-unit hours; Secure Agent jobs do not draw from them, so they say nothing about the monthly job limit (L-IPU-041). `GET .../license-service/api/v1/OrgLicenseAssignment('<orgIdV3>')/Views()` names the base edition (for example 'Intelligent Data Management Cloud Trial'), which identifies a trial org before you plan job volumes, while its `EffectiveLicenses()` limits still read -1 and the Licenses page has no jobs row (L-AUTH-072). No API exposes the jobs cap on such an org: assume the 10,000 jobs a month seen on a sibling org until the vendor confirms otherwise, and budget test rounds in jobs (L-IPU-058).
evidence: Read on one trial org: Licenses page with 3 trial licences and no Jobs row; 32 EffectiveLicenses limits, all -1; the Views() edition name; 3 Org Consumption meters at 10,000 max and 0 used (2026-09-29); job counts from the activity log after the test rounds (2026-10-01/02)

title: Watch for a licence or entitlement change headless: diff the per-org licence record and the agents' engine lists, and alert on content, not updateTime
text: Licence changes that matter (a new package such as the data gateway, a lifted job limit, a new edition) arrive without notice and are partly invisible (limits read -1 and the job cap does not appear), so poll instead of re-checking by hand. Every 10 min: `GET /public/core/v3/license/org/<orgIdV3>` (v3 session; the 22-character id, L-AUTH-073), normalizing `customLicenses[]` to licenseDef|licenseType|startDate|expirationDate and `assignedEditions[]` to edition|startDate|expirationDate and keeping `updateTime` separately; then for each agent `GET /api/v2/agent/details/<agentId>`, mapping `agentEngines[].agentEngineStatus.appname` to `status`. Diff a normalized fingerprint against the stored snapshot, append any change to a log and send one notification per change. `updateTime` changes while every licence and edition stays identical, so alert on content and report an updateTime-only change as information. The decisive signal that an entitlement reached a Secure Agent is a new engine in the agent details (or a looping service leaving RESTARTING), because a licence line alone deploys nothing (L-AGENT-097, L-AGENT-098). Read-only; nothing in IDMC changes.
evidence: Watcher every 10 min from 2026-09-30 with one push per change: it recorded an updateTime-only change with the same 6 licences and 8 editions, and a later data-gateway licence appeared as a new RUNNING engine on every agent within about 10 minutes

title: Under a monthly job cap, budget a test round by write waves, not by stories
text: With event lanes that coalesce (a minimum gap between runs of a lane, L-CDI-128), events that land within one burst share one lane run, so a QA round costs per write wave, not per story. One event-lane run cost about 18 jobs: 129 stories run one by one would have cost about 1,750 jobs, while 42 priority stories grouped into 7 waves cost about 250, and three story rounds still burned about 294 jobs in 1.7 h. Rules: read the job budget before the first wave and after each one (L-IPU-043); leave at least 3 minutes of quiet after a write wave so the lanes drain; put read-only checks in waves of their own (0 jobs); reuse retries of one story to cover double-submit stories instead of creating new identities; set a cap and a hard stop per round (for example 300 / 350); never run the round in a fast mode that removes the lane gap (every event then costs a full lane run, L-IPU-054); probe SaaS storage headroom before the write waves and purge afterwards (L-CONN-088). When several sessions test one stack, give each a fixed write wave inside the hour (L-METHOD-124). Rule-specification previews (for example from CLAIRE rule tests) also appear in the activity log as short `PreviewMapping_RULE_SPECIFICATION` runs (~3 s); whether they count against the cap was not verified.
evidence: Planned and costed against the orchestrator's job ledger: about 18 jobs per lane run, 7 waves of 42 stories about 250 jobs against about 1,750 for 129 stories run singly; three rounds about 294 jobs in 1.7 h; 18 rule-spec preview rows in 24 h of activity log (2026-10-01/02)

title: When the job-cap reset date is unknown, guard on the worst of four windows and fail closed
text: A hidden monthly job cap (L-IPU-041) may reset on any of four windows: the calendar month in UTC, the calendar month in the org's timezone (`timezone` in `GET /api/v2/org`), the licence anniversary day, or a rolling 30 days. A guard that counts only the UTC month can be off by thousands of jobs: in one org the four windows read 2,899, 2,811, 6,774 and 6,774 jobs at the same moment. Take org usage as the maximum over all four. The activity log keeps only about 4 days, so on every run append an hourly-maxima snapshot to your own ledger (L-IPU-043) and merge it, flagging hours nobody observed as estimates, and add the sources the activity log misses: profile run history and catalog jobs filtered by your catalog-source ids (L-IPU-055). Make the pre-run check fail closed: exit non-zero when a read fails, when usage plus the planned jobs would cross a lane's month, day or hour budget or an org-wide pause threshold set below the cap, when a cap-error text ('exceeded your monthly limit') appeared within the block window, or when a login was rejected. At the recent daily pace, project for each window the date it reaches each threshold, and freeze lower-priority tenants of a shared org well before the cap.
evidence: The guard ran live against one org: 3,806 log rows in 4 pages, window totals from 2,899 to 6,774; its check returned ALLOWED at 13 lane jobs and BLOCKED, exit 3, in 5 tests (lane day budget, oversized plan, simulated org total over the pause, simulated lane day total, simulated cap-error text)

title: At the monthly job cap only the first run of a lane carries the error; the rest log as zero-row non-success, and 'last successful run' freshness freezes
text: When the monthly job limit is hit, the run that starts first fails with 'You have exceeded your monthly limit of 10,000 jobs.', and the remaining tasks of each lane are recorded with an empty error, 0 rows and a state outside 1/2/3 (state 4 in a run ledger mirrored from the activity log). In 2 hours that was 8 FAILED runs carrying the message against 121 such zero-row runs across 33 tasks, and event-triggered lanes kept adding about 54 attempts an hour.
