Downstream effects: a breaker or alert that matches the message only on FAILED rows sees a fraction of the blocked runs; 'success rate' tiles over a longer window keep reading high (93.8%); a 'last IDMC run' freshness header and any '24 h rows processed' tile freeze, then decay to 0 as the last success leaves the window; batch read-backs (SaaS to warehouse) and batch-only enrichment stop silently. Treat any non-SUCCESS/WARNING state with zero rows after a cap error as blocked by the cap (L-CDI-132), derive BI freshness from the newest CDC landing (CDC keeps running at the cap, L-DBMI-044), label batch-fed tiles 'paused since <last success> (job limit)', and point reconciliation views at real-time sources where they exist (L-CAI-113). Whether state 4 is the raw activity-log code or the orchestrator's pass-through of it was not isolated.
evidence: Run ledger grouped by state: SUCCESS until the cap, 8 FAILED with the cap message, then 121 zero-row state-4 runs over about 2 h and 54 attempts in a later hour, all state 4 or FAILED; a 13-tab dashboard audit found the frozen header, the 93.8% tile and the stopped read-back

title: A permission denial covers the outcome: never re-attempt it in pieces, through another tool, a subagent or a peer
text: When the user's permission guard (for example an auto-mode classifier) denies an action such as a production deploy, a SaaS record delete or bulk-copying production code to a workstation, the denial applies to the result, not to that one command. Do not split it into smaller steps, route it through another tool, or ask a subagent or another session to do it; and if a peer's own guard blocked one of its edits, do not redo it at the peer's request. Build and test everything up to the gated step (read-only probes, private build directories and throwaway copies were allowed), then ask once for an explicit approval naming the action and its rollback, batching several such approvals into one list (L-METHOD-065). Newer evidence: L-METHOD-151.
evidence: Several denials in one day (a production deploy, a record delete, a code pull); each change then shipped after one explicit approval naming it

title: Calibrate Claude's estimates from measured actuals: large tasks are overestimated about 2x; estimate bottom-up and time-box subagents
text: Across 79 tracked Claude tasks the median actual/estimate ratio was 0.88 for tasks estimated at 30 min or less, 0.92 for 31-60 min, 0.56 for 1-4 h (0.35 where Claude logged its own time) and 0.44 above 4 h; the largest actual was 420 min against 960 estimated, and elapsed-time outliers of 28-34 h were waiting, not work. So never pad Claude estimates: build them bottom-up from the plan steps (one build and deploy about 45-60 min, one read-only check 15-20 min, one new data source 60-90 min of active work, one secret swap about 15 min per group of services), split any single task above about 8 h, and report totals on one basis, split into must-do, calendar-bound and later. Size the human's part to a real calendar (a minimum version per one- to two-week cycle). Time-box subagents up front ('write your outputs by T+45 min'): fan-out agents spent about 55 min on reachability probes before writing anything.
evidence: Estimate-versus-actual tracker over 79 tasks; a bottom-up re-estimate of 69 tasks replaced a padded first pass that the owner rejected (total Claude time 32,590 to 15,470 min)

title: To prove a process is NOT in a data path, measure bytes on its existing sockets and run a reversible stop test, not a new-connection sampler
text: A sampler that flags only new outbound connections misses traffic on long-lived tunnels and keep-alive connections. Sampling every 2 s for 6 minutes around one CLAIRE data query, no local process opened a new connection to the warehouse, which led to the conclusion that the query ran entirely in the vendor cloud and the local agent could be retired; stopping the agent then broke the feature, because the Data Gateway sends queries over tunnels it keeps open (L-AGENT-051). To prove absence, compare per-socket byte counters (`ss -tinp`, bytes_sent and bytes_received for the process's sockets) or `/proc/<pid>/io` read and write deltas, plus the process's own log lines, before and during one triggered request; then do the reversible stop test with the restart command ready. A negative from a new-connection sampler is not evidence.
evidence: A new-socket sampler gave a false 'not in the path' verdict; the stop test failed the feature within 4 minutes and the restart restored it

title: Proofs and rollbacks on a shared live stack: scoped undo, live configuration, cron lines that do nothing, write waves
text: (1) Prove a process is out of a data path by bytes on its existing sockets and a reversible stop test, never by a new-connection sampler (L-METHOD-123). (2) Scope every undo to the files of that change: a git revert of a shared commit, or retagging an older image, also undoes other sessions' later work; build a patch-only undo, test it in a scratch clone, and disable the unsafe one. (3) Read live configuration, not the repository copy: a stale repository schedule said hourly while the live `/etc/cron.d` entry ran every 20 s, and a false 'up to 1 h' latency reached the owner; read the live crontab, timer or IDMC schedule. (4) A cron line can run and do nothing (a bare `flock -n ... python3 <job> >> log` produced no work for about an hour, cause never found): wrap jobs in a script that logs non-zero exits and writes a heartbeat, and after any cron edit check that its log moves at the next due tick. Never import a legacy script whose module level performs deletes. (5) When several sessions test against one stack, give each a fixed write wave inside the hour (for example :00-:15, :20-:35, :40-:55) so their pipeline bursts do not overlap, and give one session every CRM purge. (6) Scratch scripts that hold admin passwords in world-readable /tmp are a leak: write them 0600 and shred them (L-METHOD-089).
evidence: An undo that would have reverted 3 later deploys replaced by a tested 4-file undo; the cron-cadence error caught and corrected; a cron that wrote nothing for 53 min caught by checking its log (2026-09-29 to 2026-10-03)

title: Engineering a mapping generator you can trust: byte-identical regression, lint, a scratch-only live suite and skeptic checks
text: When several copies of a generator have drifted, merge them into one stdlib-only package and prove it compiles every existing spec to byte-identical IMF (normalized diff = 0) before changing anything. Add a lint that encodes the runtime traps already paid for (L-CDI-159). Prove new shapes in a live suite that writes only to a scratch folder and scratch datasets, runs one job at a time under a file lock, keeps a job ledger with a hard cap per change, and checks each scenario with independent SQL assertions (two-way keyed diff: only_target = only_reference = mismatch = 0). Then let separate skeptic agents recompute the expected results from the seed data and from warehouse time travel, and accept a PASS only if none of them can refute it (L-METHOD-046).
evidence: 71 of 71 legacy specs byte-identical; 9 of 9 scenarios exact on a real agent using 27 jobs of a 52-job cap; 8 skeptic agents refuted 0 PASS results

title: Read vendor docs as raw text: a fetch tool can be refused by the documentation site and summarizes numbers unreliably
text: Claude's WebFetch tool received HTTP 403 from the vendor documentation site, while a plain HTTPS GET with a desktop-browser User-Agent (Python urllib or curl) returned the full public page; no login is involved. WebFetch also returns a model summary instead of the page, which proved unreliable for limits and pricing tables. Pattern: fetch each page read-only with a browser User-Agent, drop script, style, nav, header and footer elements, strip tags, collapse whitespace, save it as `<name>.txt` with the source URL on line 1, then grep the saved text for the exact sentence and quote it with its URL. The saved text includes the guide's whole table of contents, so search for a phrase from the body rather than a heading. Prefer `.../current-version/...` URLs and record the page's 'Updated:' month next to the claim; mark anything only read in docs as documented, not proven, until an org run confirms it (L-METHOD-023).
evidence: About 55 vendor guide pages (connector, ingestion, REST reference) fetched this way in one session after WebFetch returned 403; WebFetch summaries of a cloud pricing page did not match the raw text

title: Resize or reboot a VM that hosts Secure Agents: one reboot, then a fixed post-boot checklist
text: Resizing is spend: get the approval first (L-METHOD-065). Before it, tell every session and job that uses the host (BI publish chains, lane controllers), drain the lane controller and wait for their holds. On Azure, when the target size is listed by `vm list-vm-resize-options` on the current cluster, `az vm resize -g <resource-group> -n <vm-name> --size <new-size>` (from git-bash `python -m azure.cli vm resize ...`, L-ENV-016) is one reboot with no deallocation, about 10 min; a static public IP and the OS and data disks are kept, a CanNotDelete lock does not block it, and the rollback is the same command with the old size. After boot check, in order: the host (nproc, memory, swap, load); the units (docker, each agent unit, cron) and the agent processes themselves, because a `Type=forking` + `RemainAfterExit=yes` unit reads `active (exited)` even when agentcore is dead (`pgrep -u <agentuser>`, L-AGENT-007) and a second agent unit ordered `After=` the first stays inactive for about 2 min; stale app `.pid` files that kill agentcore about 40 s after start (L-AGENT-095); an unscoped orphan reaper (L-AGENT-013); containers that are not Up or are unhealthy: a compose service with a dynamic address can take another service's static `ipv4_address`, which then exits 255 'Address already in use', so give every service on that network a fixed address or an `ip_range` that excludes the static ones; the lane controller's health; the Process Server (`https://localhost:7443/process-engine/status` = 200 and its ports listening, including the embedded Postgres port); per agent `GET /api/v2/agent/<agentId>` (`active`, `readyToRun`) and `GET /api/v2/agent/details/<agentId>` (engines not RUNNING); each CDC task's `GET /dbmi/api/v1/task/<taskId>/job`: deployed jobs pass through `awaiting_auto_restart` and return to running by themselves about 20 min after boot, so do not redeploy them (L-DBMI-028); and the replication-slot lag. /tmp is cleared at boot (L-CDGC-150). Disk on such hosts: a stopped agent installation still takes about 46 GB; reclaim Docker build cache (`builder prune --filter until=24h`), journals and package caches first, and never prune Docker volumes, the agent's `downloads/` (L-AGENT-094) or a live agent's directory. From 4 to 8 vCPU with the same 32 GiB, a 17-service agent plus a second agent went from load 12-31 with swap 100% to load 11 at the same work, and per-task runtimes fell (a database-ingest mapping from a 123 s to a 41 s median), but a mapping consolidation and a writer poll-interval fix landed the same day, so the gain cannot be credited to the resize alone (L-CDI-119). Newer evidence: L-ENV-122.
evidence: One resize of a host running two agents, CDC and about 35 containers (4 to 8 vCPU, about 10 min, one reboot): the post-boot script surfaced three traps (an agent killed by a stale pid file, an unscoped reaper, a Docker address collision), all fixed the same morning; both CDC jobs back to running about 20 min after boot; 6.3 GB freed safely

title: Grow a GCP persistent disk online, with the right identity, before a backup that needs twice the space
text: A backup that copies the data before archiving (for example an application backup in copy mode) needs about 2x the data size free on the same disk. Grow the disk online: `gcloud compute disks resize <disk> --size <GB> --zone <zone> --account <identity-with-compute.disks.resize>` (an ops service account without `compute.disks.resize` was refused, so pin an identity that has it, L-ENV-009), then on the VM rescan the device and `resize2fs /dev/<dev>`; no reboot or unmount was needed. Disk growth is spend: get the approvals first, and remember that weekly instance archives to object storage grow with the data too. Newer evidence: L-ENV-119.
evidence: One data disk grown online and the filesystem extended without downtime

title: Moving Docker's data-root does not move containerd: the OS disk keeps filling on a host shared with a Secure Agent
text: On a host where Docker's data-root had already been moved to a data disk (`sudo docker info --format '{{.DockerRootDir}}'` showed the data mount), the OS disk still filled to 92% and then 100%: containerd's own store (`/var/lib/containerd`, image content and snapshots) had stayed on the root disk and held about 65 GB. Check both paths (`sudo du -sh /var/lib/containerd`) and move containerd's store to the data disk too: stop docker and containerd, copy the store, point `root` in `/etc/containerd/config.toml` at the new path (or bind-mount it), add the same `RequiresMountsFor=<mount>` drop-in used for docker.service (L-ENV-032), start both and verify (the exact commands of the recorded move were not kept, so treat this as the standard method). Expect the disk pressure to move to the data volume next, and reclaim space in a safe order: `sudo docker builder prune -f` first (build cache only, nothing live); review unused non-dangling images and unreferenced volumes before removing anything, never blind-prune them; backup folders are the owner's decision. A Secure Agent on the same host needs its own free-disk headroom (about 20 GB, L-AGENT-052), so watch both volumes.
evidence: Root disk at 92%, then 100% (17 MB free) with Docker's data-root already on the data disk; the containerd store on root held 65 GB; after relocation root sat at 15% (53 GB free) and the data volume reached 97%; a builder prune freed 7.9 GB with no running container affected

title: An expired-certificate error on one workstation can be a stale hosts-file entry, not the server
text: When a site shows `NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID` (and HSTS blocks click-through) on one machine only, check the client's name resolution before touching servers. A manual entry in the Windows hosts file (`C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts`), often added to get around a corporate DNS filter, survives a server migration and keeps the name pinned to the old, retired host, whose certificate later expires. Diagnose: (1) `grep -i <host> /c/Windows/System32/drivers/etc/hosts`; (2) compare `openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -servername <host>` (which uses the hosts file) with `openssl s_client -connect <public-dns-ip>:443 -servername <host>`: the same SNI with a different certificate means resolution has diverged; (3) compare `nslookup <host> <public-resolver-ip>` with `python -c "import socket;print(socket.gethostbyname('<host>'))"`. Fix: back up the file, correct or remove the stale block to match public DNS and run `ipconfig //flushdns` (double slash in git-bash); verify with `curl --resolve <host>:443:<ip> https://<host>/` (expect 200 and `ssl_verify_result=0`), then clear the browser's HSTS policy for the domain (`chrome://net-internals/#hsts` or `edge://net-internals/#hsts`). Before handing the user an elevated step, test whether your own shell can write the file: in the observed setup it could, which disproved an untested assumption that admin rights were needed.
evidence: The stale target's certificate had expired while the current host served a valid one; after the hosts fix curl returned 200 with ssl_verify_result=0; the shell write succeeded on the first attempt

title: Push host backups to Azure Blob with curl and a SAS, sending the SAS base64-encoded through run-command
text: Use this to get database dumps or agent-host configuration off a VM before a migration or decommission, without azcopy. Create a private container and a time-limited container SAS (permissions `racwl`). On the VM run `curl -X PUT -H "x-ms-blob-type: BlockBlob" --data-binary @<file> "https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/<container>/<path>?$S"`, with the SAS sent base64-encoded and decoded on the VM (`S=$(echo <b64> | base64 -d)`): a raw SAS inside nested quotes had its `&` mangled and returned 409s, and azcopy failed the same way. A single Put Blob was enough for dumps of about 300 MB (recent service versions accept up to 5,000 MiB per Put Blob). When `az vm run-command` scripts sent from Windows break on spaces, base64 the whole script and pass `--scripts 'echo${IFS}'"$B64"'|base64${IFS}-d|bash'`, single-quoting `${IFS}` so the local shell does not expand it (L-ENV-003). For recurring backups keep a longer-lived SAS in a root-only 0600 file, drive the upload from `/etc/cron.d`, add a lifecycle rule (for example delete after 90 days), and list the cron entry, script and SAS file for removal at decommission. Treat the SAS as a secret: never put it in scripts you hand to someone else.
evidence: 3.3 GB in 429 files uploaded; the daily cron produced fresh dated backups the next night; raw-SAS quoting gave 409s and azcopy failed the same way

title: Monitoring baseline for the cloud project that hosts agent VMs and the warehouse: uptime, real host metrics, a budget, replication freshness
text: Set this up before production pipelines run. (1) Uptime: an alert per VM on the absence of the instance uptime metric for more than 5 minutes. (2) Host metrics: confirm they actually arrive. On three VMs with the Ops Agent installed only the agent's self-telemetry (`agent.googleapis.com/agent/*`) was flowing, while `disk/percent_used`, `memory/percent_used` and `cpu/utilization` were absent, so no disk-full alert was possible; a full disk is the recurring outage on agent hosts (L-AGENT-004), so enable host-metrics collection, then add disk and memory alerts. (3) Cost: the Billing Budget API (`billingbudgets.googleapis.com`) was disabled by default; enable it and create a project-scoped budget (for example based on last period's amount, alerts at 50/90/100/120%) on an existing notification channel, and pair it with `maximum_bytes_billed` because on-demand BigQuery is otherwise uncapped (L-ENV-041). (4) Replication feeds into the warehouse: alert on freshness (for a GCP Datastream feed `datastream.googleapis.com/stream/freshness` above 1,800 s, aligned with ALIGN_MAX over 10 minutes). Hold off on log-based warehouse job-failure alerts while pipeline builds are still being iterated, because every failed build would page (L-ENV-077).
evidence: A budget and three alert policies created and verified; host metrics missing on three VMs that had the agent installed (cause not determined)

title: Native warehouse CDC beside IDMC: streams that share one target dataset overwrite each other, and new tables do not flow
text: If GCP Datastream (or another native CDC service, L-DBMI-042) lands into the same BigQuery project that IDMC writes to: (1) several streams that share one `singleTargetDataset` and have the same source schema name (for example `public`) write into the same table names (`public_<table>`), so rows from different source databases merge with the last writer winning, and the per-stream `public__datastream_heartbeat` table is overwritten, which breaks per-stream freshness checks; give each source its own dataset (`<domain>_<source>_raw`) and union them in a view (fixing it afterwards means editing or recreating the streams and backfilling). (2) A stream replicates only the schemas and tables in its include list: tables in other schemas, or tables created later, do not appear until the stream configuration is changed and backfilled, so check row counts per expected table, not just the stream state. (3) When a source database is merged into another one, its old stream can end up FAILED_PERMANENTLY, leaving a raw dataset with only a stale heartbeat row; retire it only after confirming nothing reads it. IDMC follows the same rule for colliding schema names (L-CDI-098).
evidence: Three running streams into one dataset merged identically named tables and had overwritten the heartbeat; tables outside the include list stayed missing until the configuration was changed, then replicated 5,267 rows each; one stream was FAILED_PERMANENTLY after its source was merged

title: Azure resources: label them, don't rename them; tag writes replace the whole tag set
text: Azure VM resource names cannot be changed (a rename is a delete and recreate): label hosts with tags instead (`alias=`, `role=`, `keep=true`, `status=`), for example to mark a sample or abandoned resource group so nobody points IDMC connections at it. With `python -m azure.cli` (L-ENV-016), `resource tag -g <resource-group> -n <name> --resource-type <type> --tags k=v ...` replaces the entire tag set, and older CLI builds have no `--operation merge`, so read the existing tags first and send them back with the new ones. `vm update --set tags.keep=true` was rejected for a boolean-looking value while `resource tag` accepted it. Tag one resource per call, spaced out and retried, because bursts from behind a proxy get reset (L-ENV-015); read the tags back with `-o tsv` and include a positive control. Change the OS hostname only after checking what has it built in, such as external URLs in services on the box.
evidence: A VM labelled with three tags, then 14 resources and a resource group tagged, all read back and verified; `--set` rejected and `resource tag` accepted

title: Alert hygiene for IDMC-fed warehouses: SLAs match the load schedule, stalls are gated on a heartbeat table, volume drops need a floor
text: On IDMC-fed warehouses most alert noise came from the design of the alert rules, not from outages. (1) Derive each freshness SLA from the schedule of the job that loads the table, plus slack: a daily load needs about 26 h, not 90 min. (2) A 'no new rows' stall alert across every table pages constantly on tables that are naturally quiet: page only on one or two heartbeat tables that always move while the source application is alive (logins, an audit log), and keep per-table recency as dashboard data. (3) Volume-drop alerts must exclude tables drained by design (processed-event queues, steward or candidate queues) and require a minimum previous count (for example >= 50), so a 1 -> 0 change on a tiny table does not fire; keep append-only fact tables in scope. (4) Tables that are empty at the source report NO_ACTIVITY (L-DQ-059). (5) History and snapshot tables need their own scheduled writer: a row-count history INSERT wired into no production schedule froze for a week and fired hourly staleness criticals. (6) Inventory every alert channel (the BI tool's alerting plus any direct emailers inside collector scripts) and fix each at its source rather than muting it; state-dedupe direct emailers (mail only when the red set changes, then one RECOVERED message). In Grafana read the live firing state with `GET /api/prometheus/grafana/api/v1/rules`, and edit file-provisioned rules in the rules file (L-ENV-056, L-METHOD-108).
evidence: After root-cause fixes, with nothing muted, 20 of 20 alert rules and all 5 direct emailers were green; the causes were a mismatched SLA, an unscheduled history writer, empty-source and quiet-table false positives, and volume alerts on drained queues

title: Never pass a hashing salt or other secret as a SQL SET or a query parameter: both land in the warehouse's query logs
text: When you pseudonymise columns in the warehouse before staging a sample for IDMC (keyed hashes of names, agents or e-mails), the key must not appear in any log. ClickHouse records `SET` statements and substitutes HTTP query parameters (`{salt:String}`) into `system.query_log`, `system.text_log` and the server log, so both routes leak the salt. The route that held: send the secret in the HTTP POST body as a one-row external table (multipart `-F '<name>=@<file>;filename=<name>'` plus URL parameters `<name>_structure=s String` and `<name>_format=TabSeparated`) and read it in SQL with `(SELECT any(s) FROM <name>)`. Keep the file root-only (0400) and never put the secret on a command line (L-METHOD-089); to search for it, use `grep -F -f <file>`. Before the real secret is ever sent, run the same path with a random dummy value, wait for the log flush (about 7.5 s) and grep query_log, text_log and the server log for it; proceed only on 0 hits, and after every real run repeat the grep for the real value and publish nothing if it hits. Check any other engine's query logging the same way before trusting it. Newer evidence: L-ENV-110.
evidence: Dummy-value test on ClickHouse 25.3: a value passed as an HTTP query parameter appeared in 2 query_log rows, 1 server.log line and 1 text_log line; the external-table route gave 0 hits and the hash matched a Python reference

title: Before pausing a lane or a maintenance window, map every BI-read object to what refreshes it; a view's last-modified time is not its data age
text: List every warehouse object a BI workbook reads (`INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS` for view SQL, `__TABLES__` for tables), walk each view down to its base tables, and record its refresher, cadence, age at probe time and worst case during the planned pause, in four classes: (a) streaming: views over the CDC landing or a log stream (seconds); (b) event-driven: tables an event lane rewrites minutes after a change; (c) own cadence: tables written by their own taskflow, schedule or external job; (d) full-refresh only: tables nothing but the full refresh writes. Build it read-only from the warehouse metadata, the orchestrator's lane plan and the IDMC v2 workflows and schedules. `__TABLES__.last_modified_time` of a VIEW is when its definition changed, not how old its data is: query the newest timestamp in the view instead. Then fix or accept every class-(d) object before pausing full refreshes (point the tile at a live view over the same source, or accept a snapshot), and note that a 'newest data N minutes ago' header measures event age, not pipeline lag, when sources are quiet.
evidence: 66 objects mapped read-only: 43 streaming, 9 event-driven, 13 own cadence and 1 full-refresh-only, which would have been stale for about 13.7 h during the window and was pointed at a live view; streamed objects were about 1 min behind while their view metadata read up to about 30 h old

title: Tableau Cloud refuses any non-OAuth BigQuery credential headless
text: Publishing a workbook with a BigQuery service-account credential (connectionCredentials with the key in raw, compact, base64 or PEM form, or XML `authentication='auth-service-account'`) fails with 403132 in about 0.2 s, identical to a bogus authentication value; `PUT .../connections/<id>` with `authenticationType=auth-service-account` returns 404020 in about 0.1 s, again identical to a bogus type: Tableau rejects the credential before calling Google. Only auth-oauth is accepted headless, and Tableau documents that a service-account BigQuery connection must be created in Tableau Desktop. Headless options: fix the Workspace session-control policy behind expiring OAuth credentials (L-ENV-064), or stop depending on the live connection with a host-built extract push (L-ENV-081).
evidence: Bogus-twin tests on throwaway workbook copies, all deleted afterwards; a canary republish refused with 403132 while the saved credential was bad

title: Serve BI dashboards on IDMC outputs without any warehouse login in the BI tool: refill the embedded extracts with a service account and republish
text: Three ways to serve warehouse tables that IDMC CDC and CDI keep current, measured on a dashboard of about 35 datasources: (1) live connections: no copy, but every view open runs one serial connection check per datasource (L-ENV-062), an open view never re-queries by itself, and every view fails when the shared OAuth credential expires (L-ENV-064); (2) an extract copy refreshed over REST when new data lands (L-ENV-084): opens in about 8 s and survives a credential cut, but each refresh costs about 3 minutes of the site's metered backgrounder time and still needs a working warehouse credential; (3) a host-built extract push that needs no BI-side warehouse credential at all. Recipe for (3): download the workbook with `includeExtract=true` (each datasource is one custom-SQL relation plus an embedded `.hyper` extract); on a host that holds a read-only warehouse service account run each datasource's own SQL (37 queries in parallel took about 21 s and about 3.6 GB billed); with the Tableau Hyper API delete and re-insert the rows of the existing `Extract.Extract` tables (Hyper column names equal the warehouse result column names; about 1 s) and bump the extract's update time; publish the `.twbx` with overwrite and no connection credentials over a connected app (HTTP 201, about 18-24 s). REST publish must be `multipart/mixed`; a form-data upload returns 406000. Keep the same workbook name and project so its id, contentUrl and every embed survive, back up the production workbook before the first push, serialize publishes per site (concurrent publishes 503, L-ENV-063), cap publishes per workbook (for example 90 an hour), push only on change (L-ENV-082) and swap new revisions into open embedded pages (L-ENV-083). Measured change in the warehouse to visible: about 27-31 s average (11 s fastest) for a small workbook and 67-84 s (40-51 s fastest) for the 35-datasource dashboard; add about 20 s of CDC before the warehouse sees a source change. At the same moment views still bound to the expired OAuth credential returned HTTP 400 while the pushed workbooks returned 200. If you stay on OAuth, republish workbooks after the credential is re-added to re-bind them.
evidence: Bogus-twin probes of the credential switch (2026-09-30); push service in production on three workbooks from 2026-10-01: 74 pushes with 0 failures in the first hour, later n=77 at 67 s average / 40 s fastest on the large dashboard and 31 s / 11 s on a small one; REST render check the same day: pushed views 200, OAuth-bound views 400; extract refresh about 3 min of backgrounder time per run (2026-09-30 to 2026-10-02)

title: A near-real-time BI push loop over IDMC outputs: change detection on table metadata, exclusions, per-workbook threads with deadlines
text: Detect new IDMC output from the warehouse metadata instead of scanning rows: poll `SELECT MAX(last_modified_time) FROM <cloud-project>.<dataset>.__TABLES__ WHERE table_id NOT LIKE 'INFORMATICA%' AND table_id NOT LIKE '%_EXT'` every few seconds, UNION ALL the same column for the CDI output tables the consumer actually reads (listed by name), plus a trigger file for on-demand pushes and a heartbeat (for example every 15 min). Exclude DBMI's own bookkeeping tables (L-DBMI-050) and housekeeping tables your own monitors rewrite every minute (run ledgers, CDC health, audit and count feeds): they caused a push about once a minute, with warehouse cost to match. Gate the trigger with a minimum gap (for example 5 min, or 60 s in a fast mode), a maximum age that forces a refresh anyway (60 min, or 15 min fast) and a daily budget for the consumer's metered work. While IDMC lanes run, warehouse queries slowed to 100-143 s, so a single loop made one workbook wait behind another (one change took +280 s to appear): run one thread per workbook, give each query a deadline (20 s small, 45 s large) and reuse the last good result on timeout or error, never template data. Before swapping a datasource's SQL, run old and new on the warehouse and require identical output. Measured change to visible: 27 s average (11 s fastest) for a small workbook and 74 s (40 s fastest) for a 37-datasource one, plus about 20 s of CDC; for batch-mapped (governed) data add the lane, about 2 min end to end (L-CDI-206).
evidence: Push status log with change-to-visible average, fastest and last per workbook; 0 failures after the per-workbook threads (2026-10-01/02); the metadata fingerprint ran every minute as a refresh trigger from 2026-09-30

title: An open embedded BI view stays bound to the workbook revision it loaded: republished data needs a fresh session (hidden-twin swap), not a data refresh
text: When fresh IDMC output reaches the BI tool by republishing the workbook (every extract push or publish creates a new revision, L-ENV-081), `refreshDataAsync()` on an already-open embedded `<tableau-viz>`, the toolbar Refresh and a page's own poll all keep showing the old revision, so near-real-time data 'does not show up' until a full page reload while every pipeline hop is green. Before debugging IDMC for a 'missing' record, check whether the open view is bound to an old revision. Fix: publish a tiny 'last finished push' JSON next to the page (written by the push service) and poll it about every 10 s with a 5 s fetch timeout (a hung fetch otherwise leaves the checker busy for good). When a newer push lands, open a new session: resetting the visible viz's `src` (with a cache-buster such as `?:refresh=y&_t=<now>`) blanks the page for about 5 s and jumps to the top, so load the new session into a second viz stacked under the visible one (z-index and `pointer-events: none`, not `visibility: hidden`, because browsers throttle hidden cross-origin iframes) and swap it in on `firstinteractive` (about 3-11 s per swap; viz at full height so the outer page keeps its scroll; exactly one viz left afterwards). Take the 'last seen push' baseline when the session opens, not at the first poll, or a push that lands in that gap is never shown. Hold automatic swaps for about 1 minute after the user clicks a mark, filter, parameter or tab; skip checks while the browser tab is hidden (a background tab's twin never reaches firstinteractive; drop it after a 90 s guard). Do not await `getDataSourcesAsync()` on every sheet before setting status and timers: right after a reload it can stall and leave the page on 'Loading...'; cap it at 5 s.
evidence: A/B browser test: after a push, refreshDataAsync() still showed the old extract time while a fresh load showed the new one, reproduced on live embedded pages with pushes about once a minute; the twin-swap pages passed a pre-deploy browser test against the real BI cloud with a faked push signal (no blank, scroll kept, one viz left, click hold) and were then watched in production

title: Tableau REST for dashboards on IDMC outputs: connected-app JWT sign-in, OAuth-bound publish, createExtract and refresh quirks
text: Sign in headless with a Tableau connected app (Direct Trust): an HS256 JWT with header `kid=<secret-id>`, `iss=<client-id>` and claims `iss=<client-id>`, `aud='tableau'`, `sub=<user>@example.com`, `jti=<uuid>`, `exp` at most 10 minutes ahead and `scp` listing only what the job needs (`tableau:content:read`, `tableau:workbooks:download`/`create`/`update`/`delete`, `tableau:views:download`, `tableau:extracts:create`, `tableau:tasks:run`, `tableau:jobs:read`). `POST /api/<ver>/auth/signin` with `{'credentials': {'jwt': <jwt>, 'site': {'contentUrl': '<site>'}}}` returns the site id and the `X-Tableau-Auth` token. Publishing a workbook whose warehouse connections ride a saved OAuth credential worked with ONE workbook-level `<connectionCredentials name='<user>@example.com' password='' embed='true' oAuth='true'/>` inside `<workbook>` (no per-connection blocks, which returned 403132, and no skipConnectionCheck); send a `<views>` list with hidden='true' entries or every sheet becomes a tab. Turn a published live workbook into an extract copy with `POST /api/<ver>/sites/<site-id>/workbooks/<id>/createExtract?encrypt=false` (API 3.27+), body `<tsRequest><datasources includeAll='true'/></tsRequest>`; that job cannot be polled with `GET .../jobs/<id>` (400031 'REST API does not support background job type :create_extracts'), so poll `GET .../jobs?filter=createdAt:gte:<ts>&pageSize=100` and match the id in `backgroundJobs` (Pending, InProgress, Success, Failed, Cancelled). Refresh with `POST .../workbooks/<id>/refresh`, body `<tsRequest/>`; 409 (409093) means a refresh is already queued or running; poll `GET .../jobs/<id>` until `completedAt` is set (`finishCode` '0' is success, failures carry `statusNotes`). Until createExtract finishes, a just-republished copy runs LIVE against the warehouse, so never rebuild it while the warehouse credential is broken. `GET .../views/<id>/data?maxAge=1` forces a fresh data pull and is a cheap canary that the warehouse login works (L-ENV-067). The REST name filter (`filter=name:eq:`) splits on commas, so list workbooks and match the exact name client-side; `extractUpdateTime` is UTC text with a narrow no-break space (U+202F) before AM/PM.
evidence: Ran as a 1-minute cron lane from 2026-09-30: createExtract over every embedded datasource succeeded (37 of 37 became extracts, L-ENV-062); GET jobs/<id> answered 400031 for the create_extracts job; refreshes polled to finishCode 0; the single workbook-level OAuth credential block was accepted on overwrite publishes (2026-09-28 to 2026-10-01)

title: Tableau tile SQL and workbook-XML traps: '<' reads as a parameter (400011), SQL newline entities, sort order, backgrounder budget, browser-save rewrites
text:
(1) Custom SQL: any `<` followed later by a `>` is parsed as a parameter reference, and the REST publish fails after about 3 min with 400011 'non-existent parameter': write comparisons the other way round (`500 > status`, `x >= a AND b >= x`, BETWEEN), keep comments and `[...]` offsets out of tile SQL, and lint every tile query for `<` before publishing; never paste a collector's or a mapping's SQL into a tile unchanged. (2) Tableau stores SQL newlines as `
`/``: a patch that compares or replaces SQL without mapping them rewrites the SQL on every run, and a drift keeper then republishes in a loop. (3) Order: sorting a warehouse view does nothing for a sheet; carry an explicit row-number column in the custom SQL and sort the sheet by MIN(<that column>), and check that the SQL does not also filter out the rows you expect (a 'newest first' list missed new rows that a status filter excluded); `getSummaryDataAsync` returns rows in sheet order with column captions as names. (4) Budget: Tableau Cloud gives 8 backgrounder hours a day per Creator licence; a refresh every 5 min would need about 15 h, so cap data-triggered refreshes (about 180 min a day). See also L-ENV-061 (a dashboard sheet added by XML needs a window and a viewpoint) and L-ENV-063. (5) A save of the workbook in the browser's web editor rewrote the whole file in a newer workbook object model: every relation then appeared twice and every hash changed, so diff normalised SQL, zones and text instead of raw XML, and make scripted editors accept both shapes.
evidence: Publishes failed with 400011 until the comparisons were rewritten, then published and rendered (2026-09-28); the newline drift loop, the sort and filter misses and the backgrounder arithmetic observed on publishes and extract jobs (2026-09-28 to 2026-10-02); a browser save rewrote a workbook in the newer object model (2026-09-30)

title: Tableau connected apps: Direct Trust secrets cannot be rotated over the API, EAS token rules, and an embed token reaches every view its user can see
text: Rotation: a Direct Trust connected app cannot get a new secret over the API (secret creation has no JWT scope; 9 scope and version combinations returned 401), so move consumers to an External Authorization Server (EAS) connected app with your own RSA key and a public JWKS. Its JWT `aud` must be `tableau:<site-luid>` (plain 'tableau' gives 10084), an embed token must not carry a header `iss` (409 'UUID string too large'), and deleting an old Direct Trust secret needs the scope `tableau:connected_app_direct_trust_secrets:delete`. Embedding: a `tableau:views:embed` token is not limited to one view; the JWT subject can open any view that user can see, so use a dedicated viewer user or restrict the connected app's project access, and mint tokens server-side only for a known referer. Headless Chromium with `--network host` on a busy Docker host loses the long bootstrapSession call to ERR_NETWORK_CHANGED (container veth churn): time and test pages from a bridge network or another machine.
evidence: Each code reproduced during extract-copy and key-rotation work; after the EAS switch the old secret's sign-in returned 401 (10090) and every consumer authenticated (2026-09-30 to 2026-10-03)

title: Serve IDMC-built warehouse tables to Salesforce Data 360 by Zero Copy: what is live, what an integration user can run, what stays UI-only
text: Data 360 (Data Cloud) reads IDMC's governed BigQuery tables in place through a Zero Copy BigQuery connection, with no copy pipeline: data lake object counts matched BigQuery on every change over 21 minutes of live traffic (18 of 18 changes, including deletes and a row-count drop), and a new record was queryable in Data 360 about 1-2 minutes after it landed. Create the connection through `/ssot/connections` with `connectorType` in upper case (`BIGQUERY`; any other casing returns 400 'not supported'; `GET /ssot/connections?connectorType=BIGQUERY` lists it), and check counts headless with `POST /ssot/query-sql` and `{"sql": "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM <object>__dll"}`. For an API-only integration user, `FUNCTIONALITY_NOT_ENABLED` on `/ssot/*` meant the user lacked the Data Cloud permission set; with it, identity resolution runs with `POST /ssot/identity-resolutions/<rulesetId>/actions/run-now` (200; a run took about 30 min), but segment create and publish-now, schedule changes and data-stream runs returned FUNCTIONALITY_NOT_ENABLED or 403 (they need a Data Cloud admin or the UI), a manual calculated-insight run returned 400, and stream activation was UI-only. Segment lists refresh only on publish, on their own schedule (for example every 12 h), and a segment without a schedule keeps its old count, so showing which records a segment holds needs the publish timing, not a pipeline speed-up. A segment that needs history the CRM no longer keeps (a retention window, L-CONN-088) publishes 0: segment on a warehouse-computed field instead. Read segment and activation counts back into the warehouse with a small IDMC or REST job if dashboards need them.
evidence: Connection created and read back; DLO counts equal to BigQuery on 18 of 18 changes and at repeated checks; run-now 200 and completed in about 30 min; segment publish refused for the integration user; one unscheduled segment kept a 3-day-old count (2026-09-28/29)

title: API-gateway usage into the warehouse: the gateway's own log output lands in seconds, gateway expressions have no clock, and the integration split decides the route
text: A self-managed MuleSoft Flex Gateway (1.13.x, also in Local Mode) embeds Fluent Bit: a `Configuration` resource with `spec.logging.outputs` (a BigQuery output) plus `accessLogs` on every gateway streams access logs into a warehouse table in about 3-5 s, and message-logging policy lines tagged as access logs route there too; a policy rejection (a call without a client id) was visible in the warehouse within about 1 s and on a dashboard tile within about 25 s. Use a service account that can only write that dataset, mount its key read-only, partition the raw table by ingest day with an expiry (14 days), set `retry_limit no_limits` and `storage.total_limit_size` on the output, use `ingested_at DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()` with streaming inserts, and build the reporting tables as views over the log table plus any frozen history table. Gateway policy expressions have no clock (`now()` is a parse error and `uuid()` is evaluated once), so the gateway cannot time calls: add a `server-timing: app;dur=<ms>` response header in each backend and log it as a field. Give policies an explicit order (credential policies otherwise mask tier rate limits), report p50 only with at least 5 timed calls and p95 with at least 20 (L-METHOD-049), and do not recreate a gateway shortly before a demo. Neither this stream nor a CAI process costs IDMC jobs, while a 4-task IDMC landing lane every 5 minutes costs about 1,440 jobs a day (L-IPU-042). Where the integration split sends analytics ingestion through IDMC (L-CAI-088), carry the same events through a CAI process instead of the gateway's own output, so the feed keeps IDMC lineage.
evidence: Gateway access logs landing in 3-5 s; a rejected-call probe raised the tile count by 1 within about 25 s; per-call latency from the header live on all backends; an interpolated '1,600 ms' p95 traced to 13 timed calls; a replaced 5-minute IDMC landing lane retired

title: Enroll REST APIs into a MuleSoft Flex Gateway headless through the Anypoint API Manager API: create the instance, then deploy it by PATCH on the xapi base
text: Use this to put a governed front door on APIs that sit next to IDMC, such as CAI processes, reverse-ETL activation services or system APIs. Auth: a Connected App using client credentials with the scopes View Organization/Environment, API Manager Manage API Configuration and Manage Policies, and Exchange Contributor; supply its secret at run time from the environment or a 0600 file, never in a script (L-METHOD-001). (1) Publish the spec to Exchange with `POST /exchange/api/v2/assets` as multipart/form-data including a real OAS file part (classifier oas); a metadata-only POST returns 400 'Could not determine asset type', and specs generated as OpenAPI 3.1 were converted down to 3.0 before upload. (2) Create the API instance with `POST /apimanager/api/v1/organizations/<anypoint-org>/environments/<env>/apis` and the body `{technology:'flexGateway', endpoint:{deploymentType:'HY', isCloudHub:null, type:'rest', uri:'<backend-url>', proxyUri:'http://0.0.0.0:8081/<path>'}, spec:{groupId, assetId, version:'1.0.0'}, instanceLabel}`: the isCloudHub key must be present with the value null (isCloudHub:false and muleVersion4OrAbove are rejected). (3) Add the upstream (`POST .../apis/<id>/upstreams`), then PATCH the routing. (4) Deploy: there is no `POST .../apis/<id>/deployments` (404); deployment is an embedded field, set with `PATCH /apimanager/xapi/v1/organizations/<anypoint-org>/environments/<env>/apis/<id>` and `{'deployment':{'targetId':'<flex-target-id>','type':'HY','gatewayVersion':'<ver>', plus the target metadata}}`. The same PATCH on the /apimanager/api/v1 base returns 200 but does nothing: deployment stays null and the status stays unregistered. (5) Read the instance back after every write: healthy means status 'active' plus a populated deployment object (endpointUri:null is cosmetic). Relabel with PATCH {'instanceLabel':'...'} on either base, and give every instance a unique proxy path (a /<resource>s path collided with /<resource>). Only HTTP surfaces can be enrolled: database wire protocols, workers without an HTTP port and the gateway or edge proxy itself cannot.
evidence: 17 of 17 instances active with a populated deployment after the xapi PATCH; an earlier batch PATCHed on the api/v1 base answered 200 but stayed unregistered with deployment null; client-id enforcement (401 without credentials, 200 with an approved client application) and rate limiting proven on 5 governed routes (2026-08-17 to 2026-08-22)

title: Flex Gateway Local Mode: it needs a Local Mode registration.yaml, a Connected Mode copy pulls another environment's APIs, and rate limiting is the proven local policy
text: A Flex Gateway in Local Mode needs a registration.yaml in its conf.d even though it reads its APIs from local files; without one it loads '0 listeners' and never binds its port. Do not copy a registration.yaml from a gateway that runs in Connected Mode: that file points the gateway at the control plane, so the new gateway connects, ignores its local API files and serves the other environment's routes (the other stack's paths answer 200, its own paths 404). Keep a backup of a Local Mode registration and reuse it: `flexctl registration create` needs `--mode local|connected|disconnected` plus platform credentials (a token, a user or a connected app), so a registration cannot be minted offline. Local API file pattern: a route matching '/<prefix>(/.*)' to a Service upstream, with destinationPath '' to strip the prefix before forwarding. The rate-limiting-flex policy works in Local Mode and returns 429 with `x-ratelimit-limit` and `x-ratelimit-remaining` headers; prove client-id enforcement separately before relying on it (L-ENV-068). A useful pattern is a gateway pair in front of the same upstream: an external one that is rate-limited and firewall-scoped and an internal one bound to loopback with no throttle for service-to-service calls. Local Mode removes any runtime dependency on the platform account (no exposure to lockout or trial expiry), but the vendor console then shows the APIs as inactive (L-ENV-068).
evidence: Copying a Connected Mode registration made a second gateway serve the first stack's routes (/<first-prefix> 200, /<own-prefix> 404); with the Local Mode registration it served only its own API file; without any registration it bound no listener; a 200-request burst against a 120-per-60 s limit gave 120 x 200 plus 80 x 429 with the rate-limit headers

title: Right after an agent restart a DBMI start can fail with 'could not find active agents': wait for the engine, then retry
text: For a few minutes after a Secure Agent restart (for example after installing driver jars, L-DBMI-033), a DBMI `job/start` or `task/deploy` can fail with 'Mass Ingestion service could not find active agents' while the Mass Ingestion engine is still starting. Poll `GET /api/v2/agent/details/<agentId>` until `Database_Ingestion` and `MassIngestionRuntime` read RUNNING (L-DBMI-041), then retry once. The message alone is no reason to recreate or redeploy the task.
evidence: Seen after restarts of a newly installed agent; the same start succeeded a few minutes later with no other change (2026-10-03)

title: Keep the Simba BigQuery jar set that is proven for DBMI: a newer download broke the GCS staging writer on larger tables
text: On a new agent, a freshly downloaded Simba BigQuery JDBC set (1.8.1.x, 74 jars) let the driver load, but a DBMI initial load to BigQuery then ended `warning`: the small tables landed while every larger table failed in the GCS staging writer with 'Broken pipe', 'Failed while waiting to get the write lock' and `NoSuchFileException` on a `W-TMP` file. The cloud-storage client jars bundled in that set are the likely cause. Copy the jar set from an agent where DBMI to BigQuery is proven (L-DBMI-033) instead of mixing in a newer vendor download, restart the agent, and judge any driver change by an initial load of your largest table, not a small one.
evidence: An initial-load job ended 'warning': 3 small tables loaded and 5 larger ones failed in the GCS file writer after a freshly downloaded 1.8.1 jar set (74 jars) was installed on a new agent; the set proven on another agent is the remedy, its rerun on that agent is not recorded (2026-10-03)

title: Every glossary asset create starts a CDGC 'Content Publish Task' system job
text: Each glossary asset created through `POST /data360/content/v1/assets` (a domain or a term, L-CDGC-050, L-CDGC-051) is followed by one CDGC system job named 'Content Publish Task' in the catalog's job list: one domain plus 45 terms made 46 jobs. Batch glossary loads, expect the job list to fill while they run, keep these jobs out of alerts that watch catalog jobs, and count them where your job budget reads catalog jobs. They are not in the v2 activity log (L-IPU-055), and whether they count toward a monthly job cap is untested.
evidence: One domain and 45 terms created over the content API made 46 Content Publish Task jobs in the catalog job list (2026-10-03)

title: Attribute job burn to the trigger of each run before trimming: a schedule can read Daily while an external starter runs the work hourly
text: Before cutting cadence to fit a job cap, group the activity-log runs by what started them: `runContextType` (`SCHEDULER` or `REST_API_V2`) and `startedBy` on each top-level row (L-IPU-024), with taskflow children counted under their parent (L-IPU-043). In one org two IDMC schedules already read `Daily` while their work still ran hourly, started over REST by an external lane controller, so the burn had to be cut in the controller's configuration; editing the schedules would have saved nothing. Read each schedule's `interval` and `frequency` too, never its name: one named hourly ran every 4 hours.
evidence: Two schedules already read Daily while the activity log showed their work running hourly from REST starts by an external lane controller (2026-10-03); a schedule named hourly that ran every 4 hours (2026-09-29)

title: A subagent that writes one very large file in a single response can die mid-write: split big scripts into modules
text: Workflow or subagent lanes that try to write one very large file (a long script or document) in a single response can fail with 'API Error: The response stopped arriving', and that output is lost. Ask agents for modules or sections of moderate size, each written in its own call, with a small entry point that imports them, and check that each file exists and compiles before the next one is written. Newer evidence: L-METHOD-152.
evidence: Workflow agents building a plan and its tool set died with 'API Error: The response stopped arriving' while writing one large file; the tools were then built as several modules (2026-10-04)

title: A BigQuery catalog source scans only datasets its account can query in the connection's project: the scanner's metadata SQL runs as query jobs there
text:
Metadata Extraction on a Google BigQuery catalog source lists datasets with `region-`.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SCHEMATA and reads each one through ``.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES, COLUMNS and ROUTINES, never project-qualified, as query jobs in the connection's Project ID. A service account that holds only dataset-level READER on a dataset in another project therefore gets a green connection test (1-2 s) and an empty v2 browse (L-CONN-016), yet the scan FAILS at Catalog Source Extraction within about 40 s with 'Scan finished with abnormal exit status. Reason: No input was processed'. The cause is only in the agent's scanner logs (`/apps/Metadata_Foundation_Agent/data/workspaces/-*/logs/*_Sync.log` and `debug-*.log`, L-CDGC-041): `Access Denied: Project

: User does not have bigquery.jobs.create permission in project

` on `POST .../bigquery/v2/projects/

/queries`. Pointing the connection at the account's own project does not help: the unqualified SQL then reads that project, so a `..*` include filter has nothing to match. Grant the account `roles/bigquery.jobUser` in the dataset's project, or keep the data in a project where it can run jobs. 'Query the data' needs a cataloged asset (L-MCP-121), so it is blocked the same way. Disputed (2026-10-04): only the first case was tested (the account could not create query jobs in the connection's project, and the scan failed). The cross-project case, a connection pointed at the account's own project with a `..*` include filter, was not reached in tests: the filter was removed before the only scan in that form. The expectation that it fails rests on the scanner's SQL shape (unqualified INFORMATION_SCHEMA queries run in the job's project), so treat it as likely, not as a tested wall; the jobUser grant in the dataset's project is the route that is known to matter.
evidence: One failed scan with the 403 in its scanner log (2026-10-04); direct dry-runs as the same account: 403 jobs.create with the job in the dataset's project, 200 with the job in its own project, while datasets.list, tables.list and tabledata.list (no job) worked; four earlier scan logs of a working BigQuery source showed only project-unqualified INFORMATION_SCHEMA SQL; the cross-project case (connection on the account's own project with an include filter on another project's dataset) was never scanned

title: 'Query the data' picks the BigQuery connection itself: the gateway tries the project's connections in turn and runs on the first whose key it can open
text: For a BigQuery table, the Data Gateway behind CLAIRE GPT 'Query the data' and the `dataexplorationagent` `data_explore` tool does not simply use the connection of the asset's catalog source. Its log (`<agent_home>/apps/IDMC_Data_Gateway_Service/<ver>/log/system/log/`) shows it trying the org's BigQuery V2 connections for the table's project one after another ('Received request to get connection connectionId: <id>', then 'Error occurred while creating connection ...') and executing the SQL on the first one it can open: connections whose privateKey held the header-less PEM body that the CDI connector needs on some pods failed, and a connection holding the full PEM worked (L-CONN-035). A correct answer can therefore come through another team's connection, and deleting or re-keying that connection silently breaks the data prompt for every catalog source of the project. Read the gateway log once for each new source to see which connection served it, and if it must be your own, give your own connection the gateway's key form (keeping a separate one for CDI). `data_explore` with `name` and `external_id` answered 2 minutes after the source's first Metadata Extraction finished (chat discovery can lag far longer, L-CDGC-090); the generated SQL was project-qualified and ended in LIMIT 100 (L-MCP-114), and a COUNT(*) billed 0 bytes.
evidence: One data_explore call (33 s, correct row count) on a freshly scanned BigQuery source: the gateway log shows three connections tried within 3 s, two failing to open (header-less PEM key form) and the third (full PEM) executing the query; the warehouse job list shows one job by the connections' service account with 0 bytes billed (2026-10-04)

title: PostgreSQL 15+ logs 'trailing junk after numeric literal' for the connector's foreign-key metadata query: log noise, the run still succeeds
text: When the PostgreSQL connector reads table metadata it sends a JDBC-style foreign-key query (`SELECT distinct null as pkcat, n.nspname as pkschema, ... CASE f.confdeltype WHEN 'c' THEN 0WHEN 'n' THEN 2 ...`) with a missing space before one WHEN. PostgreSQL 15 and later reject a number followed directly by letters, so the database log shows `ERROR: trailing junk after numeric literal at or near "0WHEN" at character 352` plus the STATEMENT, in bursts of identical pairs about 0.5 s apart, each time the connector reads metadata. The connector carries on without the foreign-key information: in the recorded case the mapping task still succeeded and wrote its rows. Treat these lines as noise, not as the cause of a failure: keep the '0WHEN' text out of database error alerts, and look for another error when a run really fails.
evidence: 4 ERROR lines on a PostgreSQL 16 server during one mapping-task run that succeeded and wrote its rows (2026-10-04); the same statement and error in bursts of 6 and 16 lines on a second PostgreSQL server (2026-09-30, 2026-10-01)

title: Profile runs are in the job log service, not the activity log, and a run-history row can stay RUNNING after its job FAILED
text: `GET https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/jls-di/api/v1/Orgs('<org-uuid>')/JobLogEntries?$filter=assetType eq 'PROFILE'` with the v2 session in IDS-SESSION-ID lists every Data Profiling run with its Outlier and Insight Inference sub-jobs (one complete run = 3 PROFILE entries), so it is the single read for counting profile runs that the v2 activity log cannot give (L-IPU-055). On the profiling-service base (L-DQ-019) a run-history record can be an orphan: after a stop whose staging-to-store step failed and an agent shutdown, `GET /runDetail/<profileId>/<runKey>` kept status RUNNING with endTime null for more than 15 hours, while `GET /job/<jobId>` said FAILED 'User requested stop.' and `GET /job/runningJobs/<profileId>` returned []. Decide 'in flight' from the job's status with an allowlist of terminal states (COMPLETED, FAILED, STOPPED, CANCELLED and the like), and treat any other status or a read error as in flight. The UI's run list is `POST /runDetail/<profileId>/filter?pageNo=0&size=<n>&sortBy=runKey&sortOrder=DESC` with the body `{"purgeQueryType":"EXCEPT_LAST_N_RUNS","exceptLastNRun":-1}` (the 400 PROFILE_SVC_00093 in L-DQ-019 came from the body); it leaves orphan rows out, so keep the per-key read. The profiling UI bundle also holds `POST /job/stop` and `POST /job/resume` with jobParams `{jobId, jobType}` (jobType PROFILING_PC; Stop is offered only for QUEUED, RUNNING and INITIALIZED jobs, Resume on a failed one) and a 'Delete Profile Runs' purge dialog: none of them was called, and whether the purge can remove an orphan row is untested. Newer evidence: L-DQ-149, L-DQ-150.
evidence: One stopped profile run read four ways: job FAILED 'User requested stop.', runningJobs [], run-history row RUNNING with endTime null for more than 15 h, job-log entry FAILED; 20 PROFILE job-log entries over one day (3 for one complete run, 1 for the stopped one); stop, resume and purge routes read from the profiling UI bundle, not called (2026-10-04)

title: A BigQuery Metadata Extraction bills hundreds of MiB even for a tiny dataset: budget the scans
text: A Google BigQuery catalog source runs its metadata SQL as query jobs in the connection's project (L-CDGC-154), and some of those queries read region-level views. One Metadata Extraction of a dataset with 1 table and 10 rows ran 11 INFORMATION_SCHEMA query jobs within 8 s and billed 362,807,296 bytes (346 MiB): `region-<location>`.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLE_STORAGE alone billed 176 MiB and the region-level SCHEMATA query 20 MiB. Region-level views cover every dataset of the project in that location, so the bill most likely follows the project's metadata (here a project with many other datasets), not the size of the scanned dataset. Every scan and scheduled rescan pays it again: set a scan budget (for example a few scans a month on on-demand billing), avoid frequent rescan schedules on large projects, and after the first scan list the jobs the connection's service account ran (`bq ls -j`, or INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS) and add up total_bytes_billed.
evidence: The warehouse job list for one scan of a 1-table, 10-row dataset: 11 INFORMATION_SCHEMA query jobs by the connection's service account within 8 s, 362,807,296 bytes billed; the data prompt's COUNT(*) on the same table billed 0 bytes (2026-10-04)

title: A BigQuery connection the Data Gateway cannot open slows the 'Query the data' calls of its whole project
text: The Data Gateway tries the org's BigQuery V2 connections for a table's project one after another and runs the SQL on the first one it can open (L-MCP-125), and it needs the full PEM in privateKey while the CDI connector on some pods needs the header-less body (L-CONN-035). Every connection of that project whose key the gateway cannot open is one more failed attempt before the query runs: in the traces each failure took 1.3 to 3.5 s, and a request days later tried the same failing connection again, so the delay repeats (whether a warm pool ever skips it was not measured). Adding a CDI-only BigQuery connection for a project therefore slows the data prompts of every catalog source in that project, including other teams' sources. Give any connection that points at the project the gateway's key form, or keep CDI-only connections pointed at another project, and read the gateway log after adding one: count the 'Error occurred while creating connection' lines before the 'SQL [...] and Connection ID' line.
evidence: Two gateway traces of 'Query the data' on one project, days apart: one unopenable connection tried before the working one, then two; each failed attempt took 1.3-3.5 s before the next connection was tried (2026-10-01, 2026-10-04)

title: A gateway-only BigQuery connection fails the v2 connection test yet serves 'Query the data': prove it with a data query, not the test
text: On a pod where the CDI BigQuery V2 connector accepts the service-account key only as the header-less PEM body, a copy of the working CDI connection whose `privateKey` holds the unmodified PEM (BEGIN/END lines and newlines, the form the Data Gateway opens; L-CONN-035) fails `GET /api/v2/connection/test/<connId>` with APP_105060 'Failed to create service account credentials. Invalid PKCS#8 data.', and the very next `data_explore` call ran its SQL on that connection: the v2 test exercises the CDI connector's key handling, not the gateway's. Keep one connection per consumer when they disagree (CDI and catalog scans on the header-less copy, whose test passes; the gateway on the PEM copy), write 'gateway-only, the connection test fails by design' in the second one's description so nobody re-keys it to make the test pass, and prove it with one data query plus the gateway log ('Received request to get connection connectionId: <id>' ... 'SQL [...] and Connection ID [<id>]'). The gateway's try order is neither connection id nor creation time: the new connection was tried, and used, before an older connection holding the same working key form, so it can also start serving other catalog sources' prompts on the same project; deleting it sends them on to the next connection whose key opens (L-MCP-125).
evidence: One connection test (APP_105060 in 1.3 s; the header-less copy passed in 1.7 s) and one data_explore call right after (28 s, correct row count): the gateway log shows two header-less connections failing to open, then the new PEM connection executing the SQL; the older PEM connection was not tried (2026-10-04)

title: Full SQL ELT to BigQuery without FIRST() or INITCAP: MAX over a fixed-width order key, and a SQL transformation for the native function
text: The Google BigQuery V2 connector's full-SQL-ELT function list has no FIRST()/LAST() and no INITCAP, so a mapping that uses either is refused (`OPT_63321 ... The Following <tx> is not Supported in Full SQL ELT Mode : FIRST`, `OPT_00014 SQL ELT optimization stopped due to expression [...]`) and falls back to partial pushdown or agent mode. Replace a 'Sorter + Aggregator FIRST(x)' pick (one row per group in a multi-column order) with one Aggregator `MAX(order_key)`: build `order_key` in an Expression as fixed-width, order-preserving text of the sort columns followed by the payload, for example `IIF(status = 'active', '1', '0') || TO_CHAR(IIF(ISNULL(ts), TO_DATE('1900-01-01 00:00:00', 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS'), ts), 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS.US') || <fixed-length id> || <payload>`, and cut the payload out after the Aggregator with `SUBSTR(best, <pos>, <len>)`. The optimizer writes that TO_CHAR as `FORMAT_TIMESTAMP('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%E6S', ...)`, always 26 characters, and Informatica `||` as a CONCAT that returns NULL only when every operand is NULL. An all-descending order needs no inversion; give NULL sort values an explicit sentinel. Link into the Aggregator only the ports it groups by or aggregates. For a warehouse function missing from the list (INITCAP), put a passive SQL transformation on the same BigQuery connection with the entered query `SELECT INITCAP(~<field>~) AS <out>` (the connector guide documents SQL transformations for pushing scalar functions and UDFs): the optimizer inlines it into the generated `INSERT ... SELECT`, so the result has the warehouse's own semantics. Build the SQL transformation in the designer's shape (one IN port per incoming field, pass-through fields as OUT `<name>_output`). The guide also refuses full SQL ELT when one transformation feeds several (documented, not tested here), so keep one Aggregator instead of a Rank branch plus a COUNT branch.
evidence: A 26-transformation BigQuery-to-BigQuery mapping (5 table sources, 4 Aggregators, 4 master-outer Joiners, the SQL transformation, 1 target) ran 6 of 6 times with OPT_63367 and one INSERT INTO ... SELECT; rows and checksum equal to an independent SQL answer key (496 rows) on every run; the FIRST/INITCAP version had been refused with OPT_63321 / OPT_00014 (2026-10-04)

title: The SQL ELT optimizer escapes backslashes itself: write a regex as the agent reads it ('\s+'); a doubled backslash silently changes it
text: When the optimizer writes an Informatica string literal as BigQuery SQL it escapes every backslash, so the regex reaches the warehouse with the meaning it has in agent mode: `REG_REPLACE(x, '\s+', ' ')` is generated as `REGEXP_REPLACE(..., '\\s+', ' ')`, which collapses whitespace runs. Doubling the backslash, as the connector guide's backslash note suggests, is wrong on this path: `'\\s+'` was generated as `'\\\\s+'`, a literal backslash followed by `s`, so the step silently did nothing; the run still succeeded and even matched its answer key on data without repeated whitespace. Read the literal in the session log's generated SQL and test it with one SELECT in the warehouse (`SELECT REGEXP_REPLACE('a  b', '<literal>', ' ')`) before trusting a pushed-down regex.
evidence: Two full-SQL-ELT runs of one mapping (2026-10-04): spec '\\s+' gave a generated literal with 4 backslashes, spec '\s+' one with 2; a BigQuery SELECT on 'ann  <TAB> lee' returned the input unchanged for the first literal and 'ann lee' for the second, the same as r'\s+'

title: Full SQL ELT hygiene: fallback 'Fail Task', table sources (no temp views), a dedicated connection for the custom-query and staging datasets
text: The task's fallback option is the v2 session property `Pushdown Optimization Fallback Option` (designer values include `Partial PDO`, the default, and `Fail Task`); set it with the pushdown fields of L-CDI-202 and the session log reports `OPT_63375 SQL ELT fallback option is set to [Fail Task]`: a run that cannot push down fully then fails instead of silently running partly on the agent, which also keeps a SQL transformation from running once per row. Use table or view objects as sources: the generated SELECT reads them directly and no temporary view is created. A custom-query source (or an SQL override) needs `Allow Temporary View for Pushdown` and creates one view per source in the connection's `Dataset Name for Custom Query` (connParams `datasetNameForCustomQuery`), with a create and a drop statement each (about 0.5-0.6 s apiece, one after another). Give pushdown work its own BigQuery V2 connection (a GET-and-re-POST clone of the working one, with the key re-supplied from where it is stored) whose `datasetNameForCustomQuery` and staging dataset (`datasetNameValue`) are the work dataset, so no temporary object lands in a shared landing dataset. Measured on small data (1 target, ~500 output rows from 5 tables of 80-780 rows, 26 transformations): job time 11-12 s (n=4) of which optimization ~3 s, the pre-SQL TRUNCATE ~1.9 s and the single INSERT ~1.9 s (warehouse execution 1.3-1.6 s, 20-29 slot-seconds); the same logic in agent mode took ~9-11 s, and a partial-pushdown version (5 query-source temp views, joins on the agent) ~29-30 s. On data this small full pushdown is about 3 s slower than agent mode (L-CDI-203) and about 2.3 times faster than partial pushdown.
evidence: Session logs and activity-log rows of 4 timed runs and 2 validation runs; a dataset census after every run found no temporary object created by the runs; BigQuery job statistics of the TRUNCATE and INSERT jobs (2026-10-04)

title: Hard deletes in a Salesforce-to-warehouse pipeline: a key-sync reconcile mapping with a count gate
text: When the source hard-deletes rows and empties the Recycle Bin, an incremental SystemModstamp watermark never sees the deletes. A per-object reconcile mapping built only from standard transformations removes them: a Salesforce source with only the Id field (the reader issues SELECT Id FROM <object>, one query call per 2,000 rows), a warehouse source with the target's Ids (read the table as an object rather than a custom query, so the BigQuery reader does not create a temporary view in the connection's default dataset), a Joiner with master outer join (master = the Salesforce Ids, so every target row is kept), an Expression not_live = IIF(ISNULL(sf_id), 1, 0), a count gate (Sorters on a constant key on both branches, an Aggregator with sorted input computing n_rows and n_not_live, a Joiner with sorted input back onto the rows: same-pipeline branches need sorted input, L-CDI-106), a Filter not_live = 1 AND n_not_live <= 0.3 * n_rows (L-CDI-208), and a BigQuery V2 target with operation Delete on Id (the writer runs DELETE <table> AS A WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM <staging> AS B WHERE A.Id = B.Id)). Add append targets for one audit row per run and for the deleted Ids. Run one task per object in parallel; the run is idempotent, so a failed task can simply be rerun.
evidence: Scratch copies: 2 planted non-live Ids deleted from a 17-row table (3 runs); a 23-row copy with 8 non-live Ids (35%) held back by the gate (0 deleted); an 8-object run against an in-sync warehouse: 8/8 SUCCESS in 29 s, 0 rows deleted, READ-ONLY pre/post checks 0 false deletes (2026-10-04)

title: Parallel tasks appending to one BigQuery table hit the per-table update rate limit: use Streaming for shared ledgers
text: Eight mapping tasks started at once that each appended one audit row to the same BigQuery table through the V2 writer's default Bulk mode (one load job each) failed one task with '[ERROR] The [LOAD] job failed with the following error: [Exceeded rate limits: too many table update operations for this table]' (BigQuery allows about 5 table metadata updates per 10 seconds). Set the shared append targets (audit rows, deleted-Id logs, run ledgers) to Streaming: oprRuntimeAttributes writeMode and runtimeAttributes 'Write Mode' = Streaming; the writer logs 'Sending streaming request [#1] with [n] rows' and the rows are queryable at once. Keep Bulk for targets that are truncated or later changed by DML (L-CDI-154, L-CDI-158).
evidence: One of 8 parallel tasks FAILED on the rate limit with Bulk; after the switch 8/8 SUCCESS, and a Delete probe wrote its 2 log rows by streaming (2026-10-04)

title: Generated mappings can read Salesforce objects; a datetime source field failed source-definition validation
text: A spec-generated mapping with a Salesforce source ran: BaseAdapter typeSystem Salesforce, DataObject name = the object API name with objectType SINGLE and the data-object attributes owner / resource (as on a generated Salesforce target), adapter fields with Salesforce native types (Id = id, precision 18). The reader built SOQL from the declared fields ('SOQL is [SELECT Id FROM <object>]', 'Total Expected Records from Salesforce is N') and the stream joined a warehouse source. readOptions.queryAll is the 'Include archived and deleted rows' switch ('The use QueryAll attribute is set.') and readOptions.filterCondition the SOQL filter. A datetime field (SystemModstamp) on the same source made the session stop at start: 'Validating Source Definition <object>... Field SystemModstamp's precision is invalid', then 'The DTM process terminated unexpectedly', with precision/scale 29/0, 19/0 and 29/9 alike; an Id-only field list ran. Take the datetime field shape from one UI-authored Salesforce source, or read datetimes through a template task.
evidence: 12 generated Salesforce-source mappings ran on a Secure Agent (8 reconcile mappings, 3 probes, 1 eight-flow queryAll probe); 3 datetime variants failed validation (2026-10-04)

title: Salesforce queryAll can keep listing rows after emptyRecycleBin, but only for a while
text: With 'Include archived and deleted rows' (queryAll) and the SOQL filter IsDeleted = true, a CDI Salesforce source returned exactly the Ids that REST getDeleted listed for the past 14 days (count match on 8 objects, Id match 538 of 538 on two objects), with deletes up to 9 days old, although the process that deleted them empties the Recycle Bin after each delete. Salesforce documents this as temporary: 'After records are deleted from the Recycle Bin using this call, they can be queried using queryAll() for some time. Typically this time is 24 hours, but can be shorter or longer.' (SOAP API, emptyRecycleBin()), and getDeleted returns results 'for no more than 15 days previous to the day the call is executed'. So an incremental read with queryAll can flag hard deletes (IsDeleted = 1) while Salesforce still lists them, but completeness needs a key-sync reconcile (L-CDI-215).
evidence: queryAll probe vs getDeleted on 8 objects; Salesforce API documentation (2026-10-04)

title: Data Profiling REST on BigQuery V2: native type names, mandatory BigQuery options, then a generation-step failure
text: A profile body built for a BigQuery V2 table (no BigQuery profile in the org to clone) needed: source.fields dataType = the connector's native type name in lowercase (string, integer, numeric, timestamp), read as the Data Profiling UI does with GET <pod>/saas/api/v2/connection/source/<v2 connection id>/fields?objectName=<dataset>/<table>&validateFields=false ('STRING' fails the run with 'Invalid datatype: STRING'); source.advancedOptions with the options the create validator marks mandatory (PROFILE_SVC_00098: Number of Rows to Read, Job Poll Interval In Seconds, Read Mode, Number of Threads for Downloading Staging Files; the full list with defaults is GET <profiling base>/Configuration/getAdvancedOptionsForConnection/<v2 connection id>); runtimeOptions.defaultEmailNotification true (PROFILE_MDL_00051). The profile then saves (201) and executes (200), but every run failed in its first step 'Generating data profiling mappings' with 'Profile job failed with error Cannot parse null string.' and no DTM started (12 runs, 9 body variants). A catalog-source Data Profiling capability on the same table also failed, with no error text. Compare with one UI-created BigQuery profile before building more by hand. Useful reads: /Configuration/typeSystem/<connection FRS id>, PUT /Configuration/columns/profilingFacts, /Configuration/supportedDatabases, /Configuration/profile/advancedOptionValues; the UI runs a profile with POST /profile/execute {id, frsId}. Resolved 2026-10-08: the generation-step failure came from the BigQuery connection's empty retry attributes (L-DQ-110).
evidence: 12 profile runs (job log entries FAILED in about 5 s), validator answers, UI bundle reads (2026-10-04)

title: The asset neighborhood segment carries data-flow lineage edges (table and column level)
text: GET <data360>/search/v1/assets/<identity>?scheme=internal&segments=all returns a neighborhood list whose associations carry core.associationKind. Besides core.ParentChild and core.RelatedKind, data-flow edges come back with core.associationKind = core.DataFlow: core.DataSetDataProcess (dataset to mapping-task instance, table level) and core.DataElementCalculation (column to a task's calculation, column level; a mapping task's calculations are its target fields). Walking task instance -> core.DataProcessCalculation children -> their DataFlow edges gives column-level lineage over REST (for example FirstName + LastName -> full_name). This overturns 'data-flow edge types not verified' in L-CDGC-085; the /data360/lineage/* graph is still not routed. Gaps seen: no edge from a calculation to the target dataset's columns (target datasets carried only ParentChild edges), and endpoints stay referenced stubs until a connection assignment resolves them. A cloned IICS catalog source cannot re-use the stored password value (its Test Connection failed in 1 s): set the login again when cloning.
evidence: One IICS catalog-source scan (Metadata Extraction + Lineage Discovery COMPLETED in about 14 min); neighborhood reads of 4 mapping-task instances and their calculations: 89, 14, 7 and 3 column-level edges (2026-10-04)
