Watch long runs for a flat row count, not only for a failed state.
evidence: Two OOM stacks in the session logs, then clean runs of the same tasks after the heap change (2026-11-01)

title: Attribute-level survivorship in one sorted Aggregator: FIRST(value, condition) per attribute group
text: Read the observations ordered by master id, newest first (warehouse ORDER BY), set the Aggregator to Sorted Input (`inputSorted=true` + advanced `Sorted Input=true`) grouped by the master id, and give each golden attribute `FIRST(value, NOT ISNULL(value))` (text: `LENGTH(LTRIM(RTRIM(v))) > 0`) = most recent non-null value. Use the same anchor condition for companion fields so they come from one observation (`FIRST(tax_year, NOT ISNULL(assessed_value))`), and `FIRST(record_id, <anchor>)` for per-group field lineage. The Aggregator streams (no group cache): 2.5M masters from 2.5M observations in 13 min including rule specifications and two targets. Non-grouped input ports leave the Aggregator with the last row's value, so name every output port distinctly.
evidence: Golden-record mapping run green on 2,519,596 observations -> 2,516,176 masters; lineage ids checked against source rows

title: ClickHouse through JDBC V2: read DateTime as text, write UInt16 from an integer port and UInt64 from decimal(20,0)
text: A custom-query source column of type DateTime64 failed at the first row: 'Error Occured for Transformation - <source> while writing the data to DTM Buffer - Timestamp format must be yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss[.fffffffff]'. Select `toString(toDateTime(x, 'UTC'))` as a 19-character string and convert with `TO_DATE(s, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS')` in an Expression. On the target side a ClickHouse UInt16 column needs an integer (INT32) port: a bigint port fails 'java.lang.Long cannot be cast to java.lang.Integer'; a UInt64 column takes decimal(20,0) (a bigint port fails 'java.lang.Long cannot be cast to java.math.BigDecimal'), and a non-nullable column rejects NULL ('Cannot set null to non-nullable column'). Float32 takes a double port. Newer evidence: L-CDI-291.
evidence: Each error reproduced on one task, then cleared by the change (2026-11-01)

title: $CurrentTaskId and $CurrentRunId are substituted inside expression literals; an in-out parameter is not
text: `'run/' || '$CurrentTaskId' || '/' || '$CurrentRunId'` in an Expression and the same tokens in a custom query arrive as the v2 task id and the numeric run id, so every row can carry real run lineage without hard-coded ids. An in-out parameter behaves differently: inside a custom query `$$p_state_list` is replaced anywhere (also inside quotes), but in an Expression a quoted `'$$p_state_list'` stays literal text; reference it unquoted (`'...' || $$p_state_list || '...'`). The task exposes each in-out parameter's `currentValue` (v2 GET mttask -> edit `inOutParameters[].currentValue` -> POST), so one mapping serves any scope (one state, a list, ALL) without copies.
evidence: Run lineage read back from target rows; the quoted parameter wrote '$$p_state_list' into a manifest (2026-11-01)

title: Address Verifier result codes for property masters: quality 6 is the delivery point, 4-5 a valid premise without its unit
text: With a USA Batch verifier asset returning ProcessStatus (`Verification_Status_Code`, here one letter V/C/A/I) and `Result_Quality`, single-family houses come back C/6 and multi-unit buildings without a unit come back C/4 (the premise exists, the delivery point needs a unit). For parcel-level property masters treat V/C/A with quality 4-6 as a verified premise and record quality 6 separately as delivery confirmed; a condo unit counts as verified only when quality 6 returns the same sub-building token. The sub-building match and result status outputs can come back empty in Batch mode, so do not require them. One DTM ran Cleanse + Verifier at about 550-580 addresses per second.
evidence: Batch-mode verifier runs over property addresses, with the status and quality codes read per row (2026-11-01)

title: Generate a Verifier (address verification) transformation headless
text: TmplVerifier (advanced `version`=R37) with groups `Input group:` (input, all-fields rule) and `MappletOutputTx_Output` (output); `verifierAssetId` = '@<asset frs id>'; `inputFields` and `outputFields` are VerifierFields lists of TxField named after the asset's ports (Address_Lines_1 128, Postal_Code_1 15, ...); `inputGroups` = one TmplVerifierGroup `Input group:` with fieldMappingMode MANUAL and a FieldMapping of TxFieldMapping {name = incoming field, txField = reference to the input TxField}. Incoming fields pass through to the output group. List the asset in the package as type VERIFIER. Shape harvested from a designer-built mapping; imported valid and ran.
evidence: Generated mapping imported valid=true and ran to completion (2026-11-01)

title: Deterministic property match: never merge on parcel or address alone; sort in the warehouse, assign masters with variable ports
text: Same parcel is not same property (condo units share one parcel; some state feeds reuse parcel numbers across counties) and same address is not same property (house plus vacant lot, units with no unit number). A safe automatic merge key for property records is state + ZIP5 + normalized parcel + normalized address + unit + class; everything else stays its own master. Read the observations ordered by that key in the warehouse (no DTM sorter cache), recompute the key visibly in an Expression, and carry the first id of each key run in variable ports (`v_master = IIF(key changed, id, v_master)`). If the warehouse and the Expression ever normalize differently a group is only split (a missed merge), never merged wrongly. Write one cross-reference row per source observation (confirmed / merged) so survivorship reads only the cross-reference.
evidence: One state (2.5M properties): 36,153 shared-address groups were all distinct parcels, 44,907 shared-parcel groups were condos; the key merged none of them (2026-11-01)

title: JDBC V2 reading ClickHouse fails 'Premature EOF' when back-pressure stalls the reader longer than ClickHouse's 30 s HTTP send timeout
text: A long sorted read (millions of rows) into a mapping whose writer is slower than the reader stalls the JDBC V2 reader once the DTM buffers are full. If a stall lasts longer than ClickHouse's `http_send_timeout` (30 s; it applies only in the server's default profile and needs a server restart to change, so a query SETTINGS clause does not help), ClickHouse aborts the query ('Timeout exceeded while writing to socket (..., 30000 ms)' or 'Broken pipe') and the session fails minutes later with `java.io.IOException: Premature EOF` after processing what was already buffered. Fix: read through a buffering reverse proxy (nginx `proxy_buffering on` with a `proxy_max_temp_file_size` larger than the result, on a big disk) so the database can always send at full speed, or keep the downstream as fast as the read. nginx sizes take only k/m suffixes here: `200g` is rejected and the proxy crash-loops; write `204800m`. Newer evidence: L-DQ-148.
evidence: Two runs died after 1.9M and 9.9M rows with the server-side timeout in system.query_log; the same read passed after the proxy temp limit was raised from 512 MB (2026-11-01)

title: Editing a single-file Docker bind mount with sed -i does not reach the running container
text: `sed -i` writes a new file (new inode); a container that bind-mounts that one file keeps the old inode, so a reload inside the container still reads the old text. Edit in place (`cat new > file`) or restart the container; validate the new config before the restart, because a bad value then puts the container into a restart loop.
evidence: nginx -T inside the container still showed the old value after sed -i + reload; a restart picked up the new file (2026-11-01)

title: ClickHouse MATERIALIZED columns are evaluated without short-circuit on INSERT: if(cond, cheap, heavy) pays for heavy on every row
text: A MATERIALIZED expression `if(record_kind = '<kind>', <empty>, <heavy array/lambda expression>)` still evaluates the heavy branch for every inserted row: the INSERT default-evaluation path does not use lazy (short-circuit) execution, and `short_circuit_function_evaluation = 'force_enable'` at query or session level does not change it (an arrayMap in the skipped branch still raised 'Arrays passed to arrayMap must have equal size'). The same expression in a SELECT is lazy (0.16 s instead of 2.8 s for 40,000 rows). Measured on a JDBC V2 target: four completeness columns built from arrays over ~660 fields took 11.4 s of a 15 s single-threaded insert of 40,000 rows, which made the target's insert CPU the bottleneck of every writer lane. Keep heavy derivations out of MATERIALIZED columns of high-volume tables, or compute them in a SELECT path (for example a materialized view over a Null-engine landing table, inserting with insert_allow_materialized_columns = 1; not yet proven).
evidence: Null-engine benchmark of 40,000 captured rows: 9.3-11 s with the columns, 0.05 s without; per-expression SELECT timings 5.6 / 2.8 / 2.9 / 0.1 s (2026-11-01)

title: A ClickHouse Join-engine table cannot be a source query; read its persisted data file instead
text: `SELECT ... FROM <join table>` on a multi-key ClickHouse Join engine (`Join(ANY, LEFT, k1, k2)`) fails in the mapping's source with 'Code: 121 ... Unsupported JOIN keys of type hashed in StorageJoin (UNSUPPORTED_JOIN_KEYS)', also with an explicit column list. Its rows persist in `<data_path>/<n>.bin` (from system.tables.data_paths) as compressed Native: decompress with `clickhouse compressor --decompress < 1.bin > <name>.native`, place it under user_files and read `file('<dir>/<name>.native', 'Native', '<column structure>')`; the row count equals system.tables.total_rows. Reading through joinGetOrNull over a key source misses keys whose base rows changed after the Join was built.
evidence: file() read returned 109,151 and 29,544 rows = total_rows of both Join tables; joinGetOrNull over the base table returned 109,096 (2026-11-01)

title: formatRowNoNewline('JSONEachRow', *) silently picks up a same-named alias of the same SELECT
text: In ClickHouse a `*` inside an expression expands to the table's columns, but a column whose name equals an alias defined in the same SELECT resolves to that alias. `SELECT lower(hex(SHA256(formatRowNoNewline('JSONEachRow', *)))) AS h, count() AS n FROM t GROUP BY h` on a table with a column `n` hashed count() instead of the column: same row count, different checksum, no error. Build the row JSON in an innermost subquery over the bare table with an alias no table uses (`SELECT ... AS __x_h FROM t`) and aggregate one level up. A same-named alias that the row expression itself depends on fails loudly ('cyclic aliases'), so only the silent case needs this guard.
evidence: Reconciliation of a 587-row table: equal counts, identical hash sets after the fix, checksum 10006624177009380784 vs 5883335861068302957 before it (2026-11-01)

title: A v2 mapping task keeps its own copy of the mapping's fixed target object
text: GET /api/v2/mttask/<id> lists each non-parameterized target in `parameters[]` (type TARGET) with `targetObject` = '<schema>/TABLE/<table>' and its connection id, copied when the task was created. Changing the target object of a mapping that already has run-lane tasks therefore means updating or recreating every dependent task (and an OVERWRITE import may fail while it deploys changes to them). Decide target objects before cloning lanes, or parameterize the target.
evidence: Lane task GET showed targetObject on the TARGET parameter (2026-11-01)

title: One Secure Agent ran 14 mapping-task jobs at once; the next job waited QUEUED
text: With 14 mapping tasks running on one agent (one runtime environment, one Data Integration Server), a 15th POST /api/v2/job returned a run id but the job stayed `executionState: QUEUED` in GET /api/v2/activity/activityMonitor (it is not in activityLog yet) until a running job ended, about 6 minutes later. Runners that keep N lanes busy should leave a slot for control jobs (dictionary loads, reconciliation), or expect those to queue behind the lanes.
evidence: activityMonitor: 14 RUNNING on the runtime environment + 1 QUEUED for 6 min, then RUNNING when a lane finished (2026-11-01)

title: Confirm condo unit -> building hierarchy from postal verification, not from inferred memberships
text: Inferred unit-in-building memberships (same address, review status) do not satisfy a serving gate that needs a confirmed parent. A rule that holds up: when address verification confirms the unit (delivery point quality plus the same sub-building token), the unit belongs to the building at its verified premise; build the building id from the verified premise without the unit plus ZIP5 (for example a hash of it), write one confirmed unit_in_building relationship row per unit from the golden-record mapping (a third Router group), keep the inferred membership as evidence in the row, and hold units without a verified unit (code it, e.g. CONDO_PARENT_UNCONFIRMED). Land parcels need the opposite rule: no deliverable address is expected, so certify them as non-postal with the assessor parcel record and coordinates as existence evidence instead of failing them. Newer evidence: L-MDM-089.
evidence: Applied to one state's inferred memberships and land parcels: the premise rule confirmed the unit memberships it could, and land parcels moved from failed to non-postal certified (2026-11-01)

title: A big sorted ClickHouse read for a sorted-input Aggregator: external sort alone still hits the memory cap; shrink merge blocks and shard by hash
text: A golden-record source that ORDER BYs 6-9M wide rows failed every time with 'Query memory limit exceeded ... While executing MergeSortingTransform' at a 10 GB per-query cap, although max_bytes_before_external_sort (2 GB) was set: the merge of the spilled runs keeps one block per run in memory. `max_block_size = 8192` plus `prefer_external_sort_block_bytes = 4194304` brought a 7.4M-row read to 8.5 GB peak (passes a 12 GB cap); the robust bound is a hash shard parameter on the mapping (`cityHash64(id) % N = k` in every CTE, k/N an in-out parameter) so each run sorts at most about 2-4M rows. Shard on the master id so a master and all its observations land in the same run.
evidence: 8 group runs x 3 tries failed in MergeSortingTransform; the same 7.4M-row read passed at 8.5 GB with the smaller blocks; sharded runs followed (2026-11-01)

title: Classify a dataset before matching it: rows repeated per scope in a registry are the grain, not duplicates
text: A source registry that keeps one row per dataset per state repeats every national dataset once per state, so a same-name or same-domain duplicate check reports most of the table as duplicates. Decide the archetype first (entity master, registry, versioned asset, definition, event) and the grain (one row = dataset x scope). Model registries as provider -> dataset -> per-scope feed, and count only same name + same scope as a duplicate. Placeholder foreign keys such as 'unresolved' on the referencing table are orphans and belong in the registry's acceptance gate.
evidence: 1,790-row registry: 70 same-domain groups (1,459 rows) and 27 same-name groups (841 rows), but only 6 same-name-and-scope groups (12 rows) were real duplicates; 220,827 referencing rows carried the placeholder id (2026-11-02)

title: One asset, many ids: build the alias crosswalk before mastering a versioned registry
text: In a captured model registry the same model showed up under three identities: the registry name (family:scope), the artifact file name (scope.asof-date.ext) and the legacy table that logged its evaluations, and some captured rows used a source table name as the model id with the capture run as the version. Every join between versions, artifacts, evaluations and deployments came back empty. Build the asset alias crosswalk first (pattern rules plus a steward list for the rest), then master family -> asset -> version with one champion per scope, and gate on artifacts and evaluations that map to no version.
evidence: 65 version ids vs 284 artifact ids (258 matching no version) and 40 evaluation ids (none matching); artifacts themselves complete (487/487 chunk sets) (2026-11-02)

title: One golden owner per entity scope: competing golden builds and run ids in the replace key give one entity several golden rows
text: Two pipelines both published golden rows for the same entities in one shared table, so part of one state had two golden records per entity. Inside one publication, re-runs also accumulated (4.70M rows for 2.18M entity ids) because the replacing table's sort key carried the record id and publication id, so a replacing merge never collapsed them. Gate on two things: exactly one publication holding golden rows per scope, and count() = uniqExact(master_id) in the current publication. Make the master id the replace key of the golden table. Retire a superseded build with versioned tombstones, not deletes. Newer evidence: L-MDM-083. Newer evidence: L-ENV-139.
evidence: Shared table: two golden publications in one state, 4.70M rows / 2.18M ids in one of them; the separately built one-row-per-entity table passed (rows = ids) (2026-11-02)

title: Reconcile a data dictionary against the live schema in both directions, and check the change plan before retiring a definition
text: A dictionary audit found 457 definitions for a table that did not exist and 10 for columns missing from the live table. The 457, plus 5 of the 10, belonged to a planned rename and a finished table waiting to be swapped in. Retiring them would have broken the cutover. Only 5 definitions had no live or planned column. Reconcile both ways (live columns without a definition, definitions without a live column), tie every definition for a not-yet-live object to a named change, and close the vocabularies. The same audit found one severity concept spelled five ways (hard, error, soft, info, transform) and 5 rule ids defined more than once.
evidence: Dictionary of 1.50M current entries: 457 + 10 definitions without a live column, of which 462 were planned; 26,858 unresolved source mappings (2026-11-02)

title: A mapping whose Source query does all the work is not mastering: move survivorship, vocabularies and rules into transformations
text: A project with 54 mappings looked complete, but most were one-offs (one copy per state, shard or table, none parameterized), and the mastering logic sat in the Source: a 35,738-character warehouse query doing survivorship, then one Rule Specification, an Expression and the Target. An 'address verification' shard had no Verifier at all. IDMC only moved rows, so the DQ assets did not run, lineage showed query -> table, and each change meant editing every copy. Test: if removing every transformation between Source and Target changes nothing the query does not already do, the mapping masters nothing. Keep the Source to select + scope filter + ORDER BY, and put the work in Cleanse/Verifier, Lookup or Dictionary, Rule Specification, Expression variable ports (match), sorted Aggregator (survivorship) and Router (steward queue). Use one parameterized mapping per table and archetype, plus one gates mapping and one taskflow. Newer evidence: L-CDI-293. Newer evidence: L-MDM-086.
evidence: Read-only export of 5 mappings: 4 had no Aggregator, Router, Sorter or Verifier and carried 2-36K chars of SQL; the golden-record stage mapping built the other way (sorted Aggregator + Rule Specifications + Router), like the Cleanse + Verifier stage before it, applied its rules in IDMC (2026-11-02)

title: A dq_status of 'passed' on every row with an empty dq_score is a stamp, not a DQ result
text: A finished one-row-per-entity table carried dq_status = 'passed' on 100 % of its rows while dq_score was NULL on 100 % of them. The status had been written as a constant by the publish step, so every downstream reader (site, dashboards, a catalog scan) would report a perfect score. Make the score the result of executable checks run on the published rows, and gate on 'passed carries a measured score'. Also gate on 'held rows carry a reason code', and count rows with no hard failure as the headline number. Newer evidence: L-DQ-143.
evidence: 101,369,803 rows: dq_status passed on all, dq_score NULL on all (2026-11-02)

title: Vocabularies and rule catalogs generated from the loaded data overstate DQ: blank values listed as allowed, process notes counted as rules
text: A data dictionary's allowed-value lists were generated from the values observed in the loaded data ('state = '': value observed in the loaded data'), so blank and misspelled codes were documented as valid. Its rule catalog held 830 entries, but 573 were info-level process notes ('validation remains incomplete until ...'). The executable ones were mostly insert constraints, which pass by construction. Also, all 1,031 column definitions carried the same access tier, so nothing was sensitivity-classified, and the IDMC profiles had no rules bound (one read a copy table, one never ran). Write the controlled vocabulary first and test the data against it. Count only testable expressions as rule coverage, and report constraint rejects, not constraint pass rates. A profile without bound rules gives statistics, not a score. Newer evidence: L-DQ-152, L-DQ-153, L-DQ-154.
evidence: Dictionary of 1.50M entries: 830 dq_rule entries (573 info process notes), 1,031 columns all access_tier 'internal'; 3 profiles: 2 completed with 0 rules, 1 never run; 0 of 42 catalog rule occurrences on the 4 tables (2026-11-02)

title: Read Data Profiling rule pass rates headless: the rule output column's ValueFrequencies in the metric store
text: A profile's bound rule specifications are profiled like columns. After a run, the metric store's Profiles('<profileUuid>')/Columns lists one column per binding (columnName 'Output', columnKey from 40000 up, distinctCount 1-2). Profiles('<profileUuid>')/Columns('<columnId>')/ValueFrequencies returns each output value with frequency, percent and totalRows: VALID 113,135 / INVALID 154 of 113,289. Map columnKey back to the binding through the profile GET (MAPPLETFIELD outputFieldMappings.columnKey + inputFieldMappings.dataSourceFieldName + frsId), and page Columns with $top/$skip (20 per page by default). The profile-level form Profiles('<id>')/ValueFrequencies?$filter=... answers 400 METRIC_STORE_00022. This gives a headless pass rate per rule binding, so an app or a trend job no longer needs a parallel warehouse scorecard just to read profile results. Decimal-input rule specifications bound to DOUBLE profile columns ran and scored. Newer evidence: L-DQ-151.
evidence: 4 profiles, 53 bindings, all COMPLETED; pass rates read for every binding; on the 1,790-row source registry the 4 shared checks equalled an independent SQL evaluator to 0.01 % (63.18 / 70.67 / 85.59 / 90.89) (2026-11-02)

title: Fix a replacing-engine table with Array/Map columns through CDI: conform in transformations, write a scalar staging batch, merge with the target's Post SQL
text: A replacing table (ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree by version) needs whole rows on every fix, but six of its columns were Array/Map types that a JDBC V2 writer cannot round-trip, and a partial insert would have reset them to defaults. Pattern that worked: the Source only selects and orders; Expression / Aggregator + sorted Joiner / Rule Specifications / Expression conform the values and add steward reason codes and IDMC lineage; the target writes one scalar row per key to a staging table (version = run start in epoch seconds); the target's Post SQL (writerAttrs rt 'Post SQL' plus the transformation's Post SQL property) runs one INSERT INTO <table> SELECT s.* REPLACE (f.col AS col, ..., f.version AS version) FROM <table> AS s FINAL INNER JOIN (latest staging batch) AS f USING the key WHERE f.version > s.version, so the complex columns never leave the warehouse. The staging table keeps every batch (the IDMC user had SELECT/INSERT but no TRUNCATE), and the merge picks max(version). Take an undo copy first. A same-source self-join needs Sorters on both sides and a sorted Joiner, or the session hangs (L-CDI-106).
evidence: 1,790-row registry: one run, 1,790 rows in/out, 17 s; 221 scopes and 258 statuses conformed, 12 shared names disambiguated, all rows re-stamped with the real mapping/task/run ids; Array/Map columns identical before and after (1,790 / 570 / 570) (2026-11-02)

title: Data profiles do move with FRS MoveEntities; FRS_108 marks profile documents the profiling service does not know
text: FRS MoveEntities moved 15 Data Profiling profiles between folders and projects with FRS_200. GET /profile/<id> then reported the new frsProjectId / frsFolderId, the same fields and the same lastRunKey (run history kept). The 3 that failed with FRS_108 were profile documents that GET /profile?limit=200 did not list (orphan shells left by failed creates), so FRS_108 is a property of the document, not of profiles in general (L-DQ-029). Back profiles up before a move by saving GET /profile/<id> bodies: a v3 export of PROFILE objects failed with MigrationSvc_086 (null data record) for every profile, while the mappings, tasks and verifiers in the same move exported fine.
evidence: 15/18 profiles moved FRS_200 and read back (folder, fields, lastRunKey); 3 orphans FRS_108; v3 export MigrationSvc_086 for all 18 profiles, 72 other objects exported in 5 packages (2026-11-02)

title: Change a folder's description: PATCH /frs/v1/Folders('<folderId>')
text: PATCH https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/frs/v1/Folders('<folderId>') with header IDS-SESSION-ID and body {"description": "..."} answers 204, and GET /frs/v1/Folders('<folderId>') reads the new text back. The v3 form PATCH /saas/public/core/v3/projects/<projectId>/folders/<folderId> answers 404 'No static resource'. Keep folder descriptions as a short map of the live assets they hold and where retired ones went.
evidence: 8 folder descriptions updated and read back; the v3 route 404 (2026-11-02)

title: Choose the address verification path by its data files: the cloud service in Certified mode adds CASS, an on-agent verifier adds the Standard geocode
text: Read ResultInfo.DataFilesUsed in the response to see what was applied. The cloud Address Verification REST service (/dataquality/addressverification/api/v1/process) in Mode Certified used VRF/BIA plus CASS VRF/C02-C07 and ENR/EN1 (country-specific: FIPS, census tract/block/block group, MCD, MSA, CBSA, place; global: time zone), ENR/GRT (rooftop) and ENR/GAP (arrival point). It returned the full CASS block (DPV and footnotes, RDI, LACSLink, SuiteLink, eLOT, barcode, carrier route, congressional district). A requested Standard geocode used no file and returned nothing, with no error. An on-agent Verifier whose reference data held only VRF/BIA and ENR/GST/GRT/GAP/EN1 can return Standard, rooftop and arrival-point geocodes and census data, but no CASS fields. So for the most enrichment, run the cloud service in Certified mode with Enrichments {CountrySpecific, Global, Geocoding {Rooftop, ArrivalPoint}}, keep each output JSON, and fill Standard geocodes from a local GST verifier only where rooftop and arrival point come back NothingFound. Batch mode without CASS returned the same geocodes without the CASS block. Unknown enrichment flags are ignored silently.
evidence: Probe of 2 public addresses x 5 request variants (Certified/Batch, all/Standard-only, unknown flag) read DataFilesUsed; the enrichment fields were then checked across stored Certified responses (2026-11-02)

title: Flat-file target in a generated mapping: name the new file and declare the upstream fields; the run creates it and every run overwrites it
text: A target on a CSVFile flat-file connection needs only `object` = the file name (written in the connection's directory on the Secure Agent) and its fields declared in the spec, the same as the upstream fields. A file that does not exist yet has nothing to browse or describe before the first run, so do not look it up: the first run creates it, with or without `createTarget`. The writer puts a header line first and double-quotes every value; a re-run overwrites the file (one header, no appended rows), unlike a create-new-at-runtime table target in Insert mode (L-CDI-166). The generator writes its generic target adapter (it has a flat-file branch for sources only) and the engine picks the file writer from the connection. A connector the docs describe only as a source is not proof that it cannot be a target: build one small passthrough and run it.
evidence: FF -> FF passthrough 189/189 rows in 8 s, session log 'Writing output to: <dir>/<file>.csv'; re-run: the file still held header + 189 rows; the same mapping without createTarget created its new file, 189/189 (2026-11-03)

title: Create a Local (on-agent) Spark advanced configuration headless: clustermanager validation, then an FRS ATS_CLUSTER document
text: Advanced-mode (Spark) mappings and Spark-only connector formats need an advanced configuration. With the cloud platform 'Local', Spark runs on the Secure Agent host, so no cloud cluster is needed. Validate with `POST https://<pod>-ias.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/clustermanager/api/v1/clusterconfig/validation`, body {"clusterConfig": {"name", "cloud_type": "LOCAL", "stagingLocation": "file:///<dir>", "logLocation": "file:///<dir>", ...}, "rteId": "<runtime FRS id>"}. Save with `POST https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/frs/api/v1/Spaces('SYS')/Documents`, documentType ATS_CLUSTER, with the configuration JSON in nativeData.documentBlob. Prerequisite: the agent's 'Data Integration - Elastic' service (Elastic Server) must be RUNNING. Enable it with the selections PUT (L-CAI-066); it pulls in storage connectors too (L-AGENT-040). The older `/cis/api/v1/*` paths answer CMN_001 and are a dead end. In the UI the form is Administrator > Advanced Clusters (main/advancedCluster), with the cloud platforms AWS, GCP, Azure, Self-Service Cluster and Local. Capture the form's Validate and Save calls once to get the full clusterConfig keys for your release.
evidence: the Administrator form's Validate and Save calls captured, then a configuration validated and saved against a Linux Secure Agent runtime (2026-10-26)

title: SESSSTARTTIME follows the runtime's local clock: US Eastern time on the Hosted Agent, the host zone (here UTC) on a Secure Agent
text: A load timestamp written from SESSSTARTTIME came out in New York local time from a task on the Informatica Cloud Hosted Agent. From a task on a Linux Secure Agent whose host runs in UTC it came out in UTC. Both tasks were in one taskflow. A stamp built this way therefore shifts by several hours when a task moves between runtimes, for example in a failover off the Hosted Agent. Write UTC explicitly (convert in the mapping, or let the target column default to the database's UTC clock), and record in the column description which clock it holds. The Hosted Agent value matches the UTC-4 'local' times of the v2 and activity-log fields (L-AUTH-014, L-AUTH-094), so do not mix either with UTC stamps from a Secure Agent.
evidence: Rows from one taskflow: the Hosted Agent step stamped New York local time, the Secure Agent step UTC (2026-10-26)

title: On-agent address verification lives inside Data_Integration_Server: .MD6 reference files under data/avdata, a licence file fetched at each start, and the engine settings printed in the job log
text: There is no separate address-verification engine in `agentEngines`: CDQ and AV run inside Data_Integration_Server. The USA reference data sits in `<agent_home>/apps/Data_Integration_Server/data/avdata/FileSetA/`: `USA_ADV_VRF_BIA_*` (verification, about 1.66 GB), `USA_ADV_ENR_GRT_*` (rooftop geocoding, about 786 MB), `_GAP_*` (arrival point, about 705 MB), `_GST_*` (standard geocoding, about 540 MB) and `_EN1_*` (enrichment, about 399 MB), about 4.1 GB in all and no CASS files (L-DQ-125). The files end in `.MD6`, so a search for `*.MD` misses them. The licence file `data/avLicenseFile/AV_IDMC_IPU.LIC` is downloaded again at every AddressValidator start (LicenseID AV_IDMC_IPU), so on-agent AV is IPU-metered. The job log prints Engine Version, AV Function Version (6.9.0 seen), NumFunctionServers, MaxMemoryMegabytes and preloading usage; the values seen were 1 function server, 8,192 MB and 0 MB preload, i.e. single-threaded with no preload. `Address verification library error (-12000)` 'Address verification failed due to insufficient memory. Review the preload properties on the runtime configuration ...' means the preload and memory settings ask for more than the DTM or its container can give; -12001 was seen once as a generic library error. Measured throughput per DTM was 160 addresses/s in a pipeline that selected its input with a heavy query and 550-580/s in a key-ordered Cleanse + Verifier mapping (L-DQ-120), so measure your own pipeline and scale out with parallel tasks over disjoint key ranges. Raising NumFunctionServers or preload is the documented lever but was not tested here.
evidence: Reference-data and licence file listings on two agents of one org; verifier job logs; one -12000 failure in the activity log; per-run timings (2026-11-01)

title: A Hosted Agent outage shows as APP_105060 'No running service ... AgentGroup <hosted runtime id>' on every hosted connection, and hosted jobs fail within seconds with 'no active Secure Agent in group Informatica Cloud Hosted Agent'
text: When the Informatica Cloud Hosted Agent has no running service for an org, every connection bound to the hosted runtime fails `GET /api/v2/connection/test/<connId>` (L-CONN-014) with 403 APP_105060 naming the hosted runtime's agent group ('No running service ... AgentGroup <hosted runtime id>'), whatever the connector (warehouse, CRM, lakehouse). Mapping tasks bound to the hosted runtime end FAILED 2-3 s after they start, with 0 rows, and the activity-log errorMsg reads 'no active Secure Agent in group Informatica Cloud Hosted Agent'. The signature that tells it apart from a connection fault (L-CONN-018): ALL hosted connections fail at once with the same agent group, while connections on your Secure Agents still pass. There is nothing to restart on your side, and the outage lasted more than 14 hours with no status notice. Open a support case early, then fail over (see the Hosted Agent outage runbook) instead of waiting.
evidence: 5 of 5 connections bound to the hosted runtime failed their test with APP_105060 naming the hosted agent group; hosted runs failed in 2-3 s with 0 rows (11 failures in about 7 h with the 'no active Secure Agent' message); Secure Agent connections kept passing (2026-11-03)

title: After a failover to a 2-vCPU Secure Agent, a CPU-bound data-quality mapping ran 2-2.5x slower than on the Hosted Agent, while a full-reprocess golden-record mapping kept its time
text: The same mappings, timed from the activity log. A data-quality completeness mapping took 62 s on a 2-vCPU Linux Secure Agent running 4 mapping tasks at once, against a 26 s p50 on the Hosted Agent; it also started late because other jobs held the slots. A golden-record mapping that re-reads and rewrites every record (about 1,000 entities, about 10,000 rows) took 118 s on both runtimes (p50 about 116 s over 7 days): its time goes into reading and writing the full set, not agent CPU. Size a fallback Secure Agent for the CPU-bound share of the workload at the concurrency you run, and start the latency-critical task first in the chain. For full-reprocess mappings the lever is an incremental design, not a bigger runtime. Newer evidence: L-MDM-085.
evidence: per-task durations from the activity log, the 7-day p50 on the Hosted Agent against runs on the Secure Agent during an outage; agent load 1.6-2.9 on 2 vCPU during runs (2026-11-03)

title: Read a Salesforce file's bytes into a CAI process as base64: SOAP retrieve of ContentVersion.VersionData
text: A CAI process cannot use the REST file download: `GET /services/data/v<nn>/sobjects/ContentVersion/<id>/VersionData` returns raw binary, not text. The SOAP API returns the same field as base64 text. Add a service-connector REST action `POST {$instance_url}/services/Soap/u/64.0` with headers `Content-Type: text/xml; charset=UTF-8`, `SOAPAction: ""` and `Accept-Encoding: identity`, and this body: `<soapenv:Envelope xmlns:soapenv="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/" xmlns:urn="urn:partner.soap.sforce.com"><soapenv:Header><urn:SessionHeader><urn:sessionId>{$access_token}</urn:sessionId></urn:SessionHeader></soapenv:Header><soapenv:Body><urn:retrieve><urn:fieldList>VersionData,Checksum,Title,PathOnClient,VersionNumber</urn:fieldList><urn:sObjectType>ContentVersion</urn:sObjectType><urn:ids>{$cv}</urn:ids></urn:retrieve></soapenv:Body></soapenv:Envelope>`. The OAuth access token from a REST client-credentials grant works as the SOAP sessionId. Take each value with `substring-before(substring-after($response, 'VersionData>'), '<')`: the namespace prefix does not matter, and base64 holds no '<'. `Checksum` is the version's MD5, so compare it before you attach a copy again, and a re-run makes no duplicate version. Attaching a new version stays on REST: `POST /services/data/v<nn>/sobjects/ContentVersion` with ContentDocumentId, Title, PathOnClient, ReasonForChange and VersionData (base64) answers 201. Keep files under the Cloud Server's 5 MB payload limit (L-CAI-051).
evidence: A 15-page PDF read by SOAP retrieve on every run and written to two file stores byte-identical (MD5); new versions attached by REST with 201 (2026-10-26)

title: Send a file's raw bytes from a CAI process: createAttachmentFromBase64, then a REST action with an attachment input and an empty body
text: On the Cloud Server a process can PUT binary content with no disk and no agent. Turn the base64 text into an attachment with `sff:createAttachmentFromBase64($temp.file, $temp.b64, 'application/pdf')`, where the temp field is typed attachment. In the service connector, give the action one input of `type="attachment"` and a `restSimpleBinding` with an empty `<body></body>`: the connector then sends the attachment itself as the request body. Proven against Azure Blob Storage Put Blob: `PUT https://{$account}.blob.core.windows.net/{$container}/{$blob}?{$sas}` with headers `x-ms-blob-type: BlockBlob`, `x-ms-version: 2021-08-06`, `Content-Type` and `x-ms-blob-content-type` set to the file's MIME type, and `Accept-Encoding: identity`. It answered 201. Keep the SAS (create and write, container scope) in an encrypted connection attribute set with asset/v1/update (L-CAI-132). URL-encode the blob name, set failOnError false and branch on the status field (L-CAI-129). The same action against a storage account with hierarchical namespace (ADLS Gen2) also answered 201, and the file read back MD5-identical through the DFS endpoint. Microsoft Graph decodes base64 inside a JSON batch (L-CAI-149); Azure Storage has no such route, so use the attachment form there. It should suit any REST API that takes a binary body, but only Azure was tested.
evidence: Put Blob 201 on every button press, the blob MD5-identical to the source file each time; the same Put Blob into a hierarchical-namespace account 201 and its DFS read MD5-identical (2026-10-26)

title: A hand-built CAI package must carry every connection and connector its processes reference: MigrationSvc_031, or 'Internal application provider error' on the process
text: Processes whose connections or service connectors are missing from the package fail the import, with one of two signatures. The first is `MigrationSvc_031` 'Correct the errors in the Select Assets section' with empty details, even with their objectRefs entries removed. The second, seen for a process that calls an existing shared connection, is 'Internal application provider error' on the PROCESS, with nothing more in the import log. A CAI process references its connections inside its own XML (service names and reference GUIDs). So put every referenced AI_CONNECTION and AI_SERVICE_CONNECTOR XML in the package. Then limit the import with `includeObjects` to the objects you mean to change. A shared connector that is in the package but not in includeObjects resolves the reference and is not imported, so the live connection keeps its secrets. To find what breaks an import, bisect with throwaway copies under new names (a subset of the steps, a `zz_` prefix). Then unpublish them and FRS-delete them (L-CLEAN-005). Supersedes L-CAI-136: adds the second signature and the shared-connection pattern.
evidence: Import FAILED without the connections and SUCCESSFUL with them (2026-10-08). A process calling a shared connector failed with 'Internal application provider error' until that connector's XML was in the package outside includeObjects; then import and publish SUCCESS, with the shared connection's secrets unchanged (2026-10-26)

title: A CAI process name whose first imports failed can stay unroutable: 'No plan found for service' after a later successful publish
text: After two failed imports of a new process, an import under the same name succeeded and the publish reported SUCCESS. Even so, `POST https://<pod>-cai.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/active-bpel/rt/<processName>` kept answering 'No plan found for service' on repeated calls. The same process XML imported under a new name answered on its first call. When the first import of a new process fails, use throwaway names while you fix the package, and import the final name only when you expect it to succeed.
evidence: Same XML: the old name stayed unroutable after a SUCCESS publish across repeated invokes; a new name answered on the first invoke (2026-10-26)

title: A Salesforce public link (ContentDistribution) for a server-side copy was refused for the API integration user
text: An alternative to moving file bytes through a CAI process is to make a Salesforce public link and let the storage service copy from that URL (Azure 'Put Blob From URL'). Creating the ContentDistribution was refused for an API-only integration user with INSUFFICIENT_ACCESS_ON_CROSS_REFERENCE_ENTITY. Do not retry it. Moving the bytes through the process (SOAP retrieve, then an attachment, then a PUT) needs no public link and no extra Salesforce permission. A public link would also expose the file to anyone who holds the URL.
evidence: ContentDistribution create refused for the integration user; the SOAP-retrieve-to-PUT route worked with the same user (2026-10-26)

title: The Operational Insights GraphQL export answers 200 with the IDS-SESSION-ID header; the documented Authorization: Bearer <session> gets 401
text: `GET https://<pod>-cai.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/active-bpel/opsanalytics-das/metrics?query={processJobReport(start:"<YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ssZ>",end:"<...Z>"){time processName env status executionCount averageExecutionTime}}` with header `IDS-SESSION-ID: <session id>` returned 200 and `data.processJobReport[]`, one row per day, process, environment and status (env is '<agentId>_<agentName>' for an agent or '_Cloud_' for the cloud runtime). The same request with `Authorization: Bearer <session id>`, the header the guide documents, returned 401 'Unauthorized'. L-CAI-049 had only a 400 on a malformed query and the documented header; use IDS-SESSION-ID. Refines L-CAI-049.
evidence: 200 with 237 daily rows for one month with IDS-SESSION-ID; 401 with Bearer on the same query (2026-11-01)

title: A Tableau catalog scan hangs in Test Connection, with no timeout, when an in-scope workbook reads from a warehouse that is gone: the stitching check opens that connection
text: Two scans of a Tableau catalog source sat with Test Connection RUNNING and extraction SUBMITTED, although the Tableau server answered fine; the first was cancelled after 74 minutes. The scanner writes thread dumps every 10 minutes under `<agent_home>/apps/Metadata_Foundation_Agent/data/workspaces/<source>-*/jobs/<ts>-*/debug/thread_dumps/`. The stuck thread was `ConnectionsChecker.checkConnections -> DatabricksRepository.fetchDatabases -> getCurrentCatalogName -> Databricks JDBC Thrift GetOperationStatus`, waiting on an SSL socket read with no timeout. The source's project filter took in workbooks whose data sources read from a Databricks workspace that had been shut down, and the scanner checks those warehouse connections for lineage stitching. Until it is cancelled (L-CDGC-221), the job blocks the next scan with 406 'Job is in progress'. To find the job id: `GET https://cdgc-api.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/ccgf-orchestration-management-api-server/api/v1/jobs?metadataOnly=false&offset=<n>&limit=60`. The list is oldest first, so start at total-60. Fix: give the Tableau projects you need their own catalog source whose stitching names only live warehouse sources, or drop the dead project from the filter. With Metadata Change Option = Delete, a narrowed filter purges every asset of the dropped project (L-CDGC-028), so set Retain first or use a new source. Then re-run the reference MERGE (L-CDGC-201).
evidence: two hung scans, one cancelled after 74 minutes; the stuck thread found in the 10-minute thread dumps (read-only on the agent); a dedicated Tableau source stitched to one live warehouse source then scanned, and both lineage links passed an automated order check (2026-10-26)

title: Curated lineage edges refuse PDF files, SharePoint document libraries and Blob containers as endpoints (INVALID_RELATIONSHIP_CLASS_TYPE), and a reference MERGE matches by path
text: When publishing core.DataSetDataFlow edges through ccgf-contentv2 (L-CDGC-179), these endpoint classes were accepted: Salesforce Object, relational Table and View, flat file, and a lineage-reference core.DataSet. These were refused with INVALID_RELATIONSHIP_CLASS_TYPE: PDF file assets, a SharePoint DocumentLibrary and an Azure Blob Container (for SharePoint folder and file assets see L-CDGC-214). A connection-assignment MERGE (L-CDGC-159) matches by path, so a mapping's reference to an agent-local folder does not merge onto a storage container root. To show a storage hop in lineage, have the mapping read the object itself through a path that resolves to the storage location, so that the IICS reference is the file and maps onto the cataloged storage file. Or draw the edge to or from a lineage-reference dataset. Note: in this round a core.DataSetDataProcess edge into a mapping task instance was also refused, which contradicts L-CDGC-208 (accepted with 201 on 2026-10-19). Re-probe before relying on either.
evidence: probes on one org: edges with Salesforce, table, view and flat-file endpoints accepted; PDF, document-library and container endpoints refused with INVALID_RELATIONSHIP_CLASS_TYPE; the edge to a reference dataset accepted (201), and the storage hop then showed in the lineage (2026-10-26)

title: Cancel a running or stuck catalog job: POST ccgf-orchestration-management-api-server jobs/<jobId>/operations/cancel, from the UI or a script; timing depends on the running task
text: The Cancel Job button (Metadata Command Center > Monitor > <job>) sends `POST https://cdgc-api.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/ccgf-orchestration-management-api-server/api/v1/jobs/<jobId>/operations/cancel` with an empty body, and it answers 200. The same call from a script, with the session used for other cdgc-api calls, also answered 200. The job shows CANCEL_REQUESTED at once. If the running task was Test Connection, it reached CANCELLED within 1-2 minutes and released the source lock, so the next run was accepted instead of 406 'Job is in progress'. One cancel was sent while Catalog Source Extraction was running; that job stayed CANCEL_REQUESTED for more than 50 minutes, with Bulk Ingestion STARTING, and kept its source locked. Poll for CANCELLED before you start the next job, and cancel before extraction starts when you can. Find the job id with `GET .../data360/observable/api/v1/jobs?limit=N` (L-CDGC-037), or with `GET .../ccgf-orchestration-management-api-server/api/v1/jobs?metadataOnly=false&offset=<total-60>&limit=60` (oldest first). Supersedes L-CDGC-221: the script replay is proven, and the cancel time depends on the running task.
evidence: UI cancel captured: 200, CANCELLED in about 2 min. Script cancels: 200, CANCELLED about 30-60 s after the request (Test Connection running); another 200, still CANCEL_REQUESTED after 2,974 s (Catalog Source Extraction running) (2026-10-26)

title: A SPLIT of a connection reference the catalog assigns by location does not hold: the next scan assigns it again
text: A Tableau catalog source's warehouse connection reference was SPLIT from a dead catalog source, and the SPLIT job COMPLETED. During the next scan of the Tableau source the reference read ASSIGNED again: the catalog resolves references by location (referenceAssignmentStrategy LOCATION). The scanner kept opening the dead connection and the scan hung for its full hour. To keep a connection out of a scan, change what the scanning source covers (for example a new catalog source scoped to the workbooks you need), or retire the target source, instead of relying on SPLIT. Refines L-CDGC-159 and L-CDGC-211: SPLIT undoes an assignment, but automatic assignment can redo it.
evidence: SPLIT job COMPLETED just before a rescan; during the rescan the reference read resolved=ASSIGNED and the job hung 60 min on the same connection; a new scoped source scanned COMPLETED in 819 s (2026-10-26)

title: Stitch a mapping that reads an agent-folder copy of object storage onto the storage catalog source: mirror the account/container path, MERGE onto the StorageAccount root
text: Sometimes a mapping reads files that a copy step (a File Ingestion task or a pre-processing command) puts in a Secure Agent folder. The IICS catalog source then names the flat-file reference after that directory (L-CDGC-160). A MERGE of a reference such as `_home_<user>_inbox` onto the storage source's Container root put the nodes under the storage source at `<storage-account>/<container>/home/<user>/inbox/<file>`. They looked like storage, but no scanned blob sat at that path, so the mapping's input stayed a node with no upstream. Make the paths equal instead. Have the copy step write to a directory named `/<storage-account>/<container>/`, and point the flat-file connection there. The reference is then `_<storage-account>_<container>`, and its file paths `<storage-account>/<container>/<file>` equal the scanned blobs' paths. MERGE it onto the StorageAccount root, as for a flat-file folder onto a File System FileServer: `POST .../ccgf-contentv2/api/v1/assignment/connectionAssignment?operationType=MERGE` with targetRootAsset `{"externalId": "<storageSourceId>://<storage-account>~com.infa.odin.models.file.azureblob.StorageAccount", "origin": "<storageSourceId>", "isCaseSensitive": false, "location": "<storageSourceId>://<storageSourceId>/<storage-account>"}`. The Azure Blob Storage catalog source (connection type Microsoft Azure Blob Storage V3, scanned on a Secure Agent) catalogs StorageAccount > Container > files, with files as class com.infa.odin.models.file.flat.FlatFile. Proven on Azure Blob. Other object stores whose scanner roots at an account or bucket should match paths the same way (untested).
evidence: The MERGE onto the Container left the mapping's input with no upstream. With the mirrored directory and the StorageAccount MERGE, the lineage read Salesforce -> Azure Blob -> mapping -> table -> view -> dashboard and passed an automated order check (2026-10-26)

title: Curated lineage edges are pinned to node identities: rescans orphan them, foreign edges pull in other graphs, and RELATIONSHIP_ALREADY_EXISTS proves nothing about the path
text: A curated edge (L-CDGC-179) joins two asset identities, and later scans do not move it. First, when a mapping's input changed (a new directory gives a new IICS reference and new dataset nodes), the curated Salesforce-to-input edge stayed on the old node. That node no longer had lineage, so the hop disappeared. After every IICS rescan, check the hop and re-publish it to the node the task now reads, with an idempotent 'fix hop' script and a registry with undo. Second, an older curated edge from another pipeline's view into a shared library reference pulled that pipeline's whole graph into this lineage. List the inbound edges of shared reference nodes, and DELETE edges that belong to other pipelines (the same publish body with operation DELETE). Third, RELATIONSHIP_ALREADY_EXISTS (403) on an INSERT says that the pair exists (L-CDGC-208), not that lineage shows it: one such pair was missing from both nodes' lineage segments 30 minutes later. Verify with the asset's lineage segment (L-CDGC-181), not with the publish answer.
evidence: An edge orphaned by a rescan and re-published to the new input node; a foreign curated edge deleted, which removed another pipeline's branch; a 403 ALREADY_EXISTS pair absent from both lineage segments 30 min later; both links then passed the order check (2026-10-26)

title: Design mappings for a clean lineage path: each system once, data quality inside the mapping, no second read of the system of record downstream
text: An automated left-to-right check (source system first, BI asset last) failed a two-mapping design in three ways. A rules mapping that joined the source system's record again (to stamp the file version) drew an edge that skipped the storage stage. A middle table read by a second mapping drew an edge back into the pipeline. A parse mapping without rules showed no data quality step on the path. Rebuilt as one mapping per pipeline (storage read, CLAIRE parse, 3 rule specifications, status, one target table), both lineages passed. Carry metadata from the storage side (file name, modified time, checksum) instead of reading the system of record again. Retire the old mappings and tasks from the IICS source scope, then rescan, or their nodes stay on the graph (L-CDGC-197). The catalog draws neither CAI processes nor the copy into storage, so add that first hop as a curated edge.
evidence: Order check before: 3 FAIL reasons per pipeline (skip, backwards, no rules); after the one-mapping rebuild and rescans: PASS for both pipelines (2026-10-26)

title: Catalog scan times on one 2 vCPU / 16 GB Secure Agent, one job at a time: plan about an hour for a full lineage chain
text: Measured, one job at a time on one 2 vCPU / 16 GB Linux Secure Agent. IICS source (Metadata Extraction + Lineage Discovery, one project): 1,295-1,542 s. Lineage Discovery sits STARTING until Metadata Extraction and its Merge Operation and Connection Assignment tasks finish (about 16-18 min), then takes 3-5 min, including Candidate Selection, Recommendations Generation and Auto Accept. Snowflake Metadata Extraction (one schema filter): 768 s, PARTIAL_COMPLETED (L-CDGC-168). SharePoint Online: 493 s, including File Deprecation Analysis. Azure Blob Storage (one container): about 4-5 min. Tableau (a few workbooks, through a tunnel): 819 s. The catalog Data Quality capability takes about 15 min and locks its source meanwhile. A Tableau scan stuck in Test Connection ran into a 3,600 s client timeout. Rescanning storage, IICS, warehouse and BI in that order took about an hour. Run them in sequence, because overlapping jobs share the agent and catalog locks (L-CDGC-045, L-CDGC-210).
evidence: Job timings from scan logs of 9 catalog jobs across 5 source types (2026-10-26)

title: The BigQuery catalog scanner leaves out view lineage for SQL it cannot parse (UNNEST of inline STRUCT arrays, __TABLES__ metadata): fill the gaps with curated edges built from the view definitions
text: Proven on BigQuery. BI views whose SQL used `UNNEST([STRUCT(...), ...])` over inline arrays of undeclared structs, or read a dataset's `__TABLES__` metadata, were cataloged with no upstream edges from the BigQuery catalog source. An idempotent fix: read each view's SQL from the warehouse catalog (`<dataset>.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS`) and extract the tables it references, skipping metadata tables such as `__TABLES__`. Compare those with the view's inbound lineage (lineage segment, L-CDGC-181), then publish only the missing pairs as core.DataSetDataFlow items in one ccgf-contentv2 publish (L-CDGC-179). A 207 reply carries no from/to per item (L-CDGC-208), so confirm each edge by reading the view's inbound lineage back, and keep a registry for undo (operation DELETE). Do not assume a warehouse scanner parsed every view: count the inbound edges per view after each scan.
evidence: 28 missing view edges published in one call and read back; the upstream lineage check from the BI layer then passed (2026-10-28)

title: Check a lineage link before you share it: walk upstream from the BI asset, require every root to be the system of record and nothing downstream of the BI end, then link the BI asset
text: People judge a lineage page by its two ends, so automate the check. Seed it on the end asset: the BI dashboard, or the gold table if BI is not cataloged yet. Walk inbound with `GET https://idmc-api.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/data360/search/v1/assets/<identity>?scheme=internal&segments=all` (the lineage segment gives distance-1 hops, L-CDGC-181), asset by asset up to a node cap. Map each node to a system by its core.classType; for generic core.DataSet references, use core.location (the catalog source id prefix). FAIL the link if any root (a node with no inbound edge) is not the source system, if nodes from other projects appear, if an expected middle system is missing, or if the end asset is not the BI asset or has outbound edges. Re-run the check on a loop while scans and merges land. Share `https://cdgc.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/asset/<id>?tabId=lineage` seeded on the BI asset, so both ends are on screen. A typical failure: after a fresh Tableau scan, the dashboard's upstream stops at the warehouse view until the Tableau source's warehouse reference is MERGEd (L-CDGC-201).
evidence: two links failed the check (first the end asset was a warehouse view, then the upstream stopped at the view) and passed about 10 minutes after the Tableau reference MERGE on 2026-10-26; three gold and DQ tables passed the same check, with 23-30 nodes and 33-54 edges each (2026-10-29)

title: Put files that were loaded outside IDMC at the far left of lineage: catalog header-only copies with a File System source, then publish one curated file-to-table edge per file
text: When something other than IDMC loads raw files into the warehouse, no mapping reads them, so lineage starts at the raw tables. Stage header-only copies of the files (column names and no rows, so no personal data lands on the agent) in a folder on the scanning Secure Agent's host. Catalog the folder with a File System catalog source on that agent, then publish one curated core.DataSetDataFlow per file -> raw table (L-CDGC-179; flat-file assets are accepted endpoints). An upstream walk from the gold tables then roots at the files: file -> raw -> mapping tasks -> silver -> gold. If IDMC itself reads the files, prefer the reference MERGE onto the File System root (L-CDGC-160) to curated edges. Newer evidence: L-CDGC-236.
evidence: 4 export files cataloged as header-only copies, with 4 curated edges; upstream checks from 3 gold and DQ tables passed, with the files as the only source roots besides reference tables (2026-10-29)

title: The generic JDBC catalog-source type offers no Lineage Discovery capability: lineage for a database reached only through JDBC comes from the IICS source or curated edges
text: `GET https://cdgc-api.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/ccgf-catalog-source-management/api/v1/type/JDBC/capability/<Capability>/configuration` (L-CDGC-016) answered 200 for Metadata Extraction, Data Profiling, Data Quality, Data Classification, Relationship Discovery and Glossary Association, but 404 'capability configuration does not exist' for Lineage Discovery; an invented capability name answers 400 'invalid type or capability', so the 404 means 'not offered'. A database cataloged through a JDBC source therefore gets no view-SQL lineage (native scanners derive it, L-CDGC-087). For such a database, get IDMC lineage from an IICS catalog source scoped to the project plus a connection-assignment MERGE onto the JDBC source (L-CDGC-086, L-CDGC-159), and publish curated table and column edges for logic that runs inside the database (L-CDGC-179). Read the type's capability configurations before promising lineage for any source type.
evidence: Capability configuration reads for the JDBC type: 6 x 200, Lineage Discovery 404, a bogus capability 400 (2026-11-01)

title: Feed a Structure Parser from the document itself instead of a listing file: read the PDF as a header-less flat file, keep one row with a filter (the row limit does not apply to flat-file reads), and pass a fixed path
text: To make the document the lineage source and drop the helper CSV, make the flat-file source object the PDF itself. Give it code page ISO-8859-1 (every byte is a valid character), no header (headerLineNo 0, first data row 1) and `retainMetadata` true, so the run keeps the design-time column instead of re-reading field names from a header-less file. The source's `readOptions.rowLimit` = 1 was IGNORED for the flat-file read. All 1,782 lines of the PDF were read, and each one sent the file through the CLAIRE Structure Parser again, a hang of more than 15 minutes. Keep the one row with a filter instead: advancedFilterCondition `SUBSTR(<column>, 1, 5) = '%PDF-'` (the PDF's first line). Give the Structure Parser a constant file path from an Expression. The mapping's IICS reference is then the PDF, which maps onto the cataloged storage file. Re-import with OVERWRITE to keep the mapping id, so the task and the taskflow stay unchanged.
evidence: with rowLimit 1 a 1,782-line PDF read every line and the parser ran for more than 15 minutes; with the header-line filter it parsed once, and lineage showed the storage file upstream of the mapping (2026-10-26)

title: In an advanced-mode (Spark) mapping, CLAIRE could not read a PDF set up in the designer: the Discover Structure model picker never enables Select
text: Take an advanced-mode mapping whose source is a data-lake connection with the Document or CLAIRE format. The 'Discover Structure' step lists the PDF model, but its Select button never becomes enabled, so the source cannot be finished in the designer. Treat CLAIRE parsing of PDFs in advanced mode as blocked in the UI. The working path is a standard mapping on a Secure Agent, with a Structure Parser over a file on the agent (L-AGENT-104, and the flat-file PDF read). For headless generation: an advanced mapping exports as an AtScaleDTemplate document (documentType AT_SCALE_MAPPING) with the annotation mapping_type = CDIE, and the Document format outputs the ports Text, FilePath, FileType and FileName.
evidence: an empty advanced-mode mapping created and exported to read its markers; its source set up with the Document format, where Discover Structure never enabled Select for the PDF model (2026-10-26)

title: Advanced (Spark) mode for document parsing: the limits the October 2026 documentation sets
text: Check these documented limits before you plan CLAIRE document parsing on an advanced cluster. A local advanced cluster needs at least 8 vCPU, 32 GB memory and a 100 GB root disk (20 GB for /var, 30 GB for /tmp). A resource shortfall fails the advanced job and also the jobs already running on that agent. The 'Document' format returns only the file's text (it is meant for chunking and embeddings) and applies no CLAIRE model. The 'Claire' (Discover Structure) format outputs nested fields, which a Rule Specification does not accept, so a Hierarchy Processor must flatten them first. In advanced mode a Structure Parser cannot give relational output. The catalog extracts advanced mappings only with these transformations: Mapplet, Aggregator, Sorter, Expression, Filter, Joiner, Lookup, Normalizer, Rank, Router, Sequence, Union and AccessPolicy. A Structure Parser or Rule Specification step can therefore drop out of lineage. When lineage must show the parse and the rules, or the agent is small, parse in a standard mapping on a Secure Agent (L-AGENT-104).
evidence: documented: Data Integration Advanced Clusters guide and the connector and lineage guides, October 2026, read while planning an in-place PDF read on a 2 vCPU / 16 GB agent (2026-10-26)

title: Merge two mappings into one by transplanting transformations between exports: re-point every $$class by class name and give fresh $$IDs
text: Every IMF document numbers its classes in its own `metadata.$$classInfo`. So a transformation copied from another mapping's export keeps `$$class` numbers that mean something else in the target document. To transplant: deep-copy the node, map each `$$class` number to its class name in the source document, then to that name's number in the target document, adding a new entry (max index + 1) when the target lacks the class. Then give every object a fresh `$$ID` and update the `##ID` references to match. Rename field references to the new upstream's port names (for example the parser's ports instead of the middle table's columns). Drop the intermediate target and its TmplLink, and link the last kept transformation to the first transplanted one. Then refresh the DTEMPLATE zip: the bin entry's size in `fileRecord.json`, `mappingTemplate.json` (description, and references[] for every model and connection still used, L-MIG-076) and the SHA-256 lines in `exportPackage.chksum`. Import with OVERWRITE under the id of the mapping you keep, so its task and the taskflow step run the merged mapping unchanged. Proven by merging a parse-to-table mapping and a rules mapping (3 rule specifications and a status expression) into one parse, rules and target mapping.
evidence: Two merged mappings imported, validated and ran SUCCESS: 29 rows each run, 95-167 s, with the task and taskflow ids unchanged (2026-10-26)

title: CDQ cleanse, deduplicate and decision transformations do not run on the Informatica Cloud Hosted Agent (EP_13236 libIDQTokenStandardiserZTransform.so / libIDQDecisionZTransform.so); rule specifications do
text: Extends L-CDI-247, which covered deduplicate and decision steps (libIDQDecisionZTransform.so), to cleanse. A mapping task with a CDQ cleanse asset (remove spaces, convert case) failed on the hosted runtime with EP_13236 'Could not open the following dll: [libIDQTokenStandardiserZTransform.so]': the hosted Data Integration Server lacks the Data Quality engine libraries. Rule Specification transformations in the same project ran on the hosted runtime. Keep cleanse, deduplicate and decision steps in their own small mappings, bound to a Secure Agent with the Data Quality service (L-AGENT-103). Leave memory-heavy flows such as big aggregations on the hosted runtime, because a small agent can run out of memory on them (L-CDI-260). Refines L-CDI-247.
evidence: cleanse mappings failed on the hosted runtime with the quoted library and ran on a Linux Secure Agent; 9 rule specifications ran on the hosted runtime (2026-10-28)

title: Mapping-task names refuse parentheses (APP_13500): the mapping imports, then the task create fails
text: A generated mapping whose name contained '(...)' imported without complaint, but creating its mapping task failed with APP_13500, so the deploy script stopped halfway: the mapping existed and the task did not. Each object type has its own name rules: connections refuse parentheses with APP_10500 (L-CONN-124), FRS renames refuse them with FRS_082 (L-MIG-080), and folders refuse a dot (L-MIG-079). Normalise every generated name to letters, digits, spaces and hyphens before the first import, and check that each task exists after a deploy.
evidence: a mapping named with '()' imported, then its task create failed with APP_13500; renamed without parentheses, the task was created and ran (2026-10-28)

title: Large cached lookups on a small Secure Agent fail with 'No space left on device': cut port precisions and filter the lookup query
text: A Secure Agent with only about 6.5 GB of free disk failed mappings with 'No space left on device' while it built lookup caches. A cache is sized from the declared precision of the cached ports times the rows, not the actual data width, so wide string ports multiply the disk a lookup needs. Fix: declare small precisions on the lookup ports, and select only the columns and rows you need in the lookup query (`WHERE <key> IS NOT NULL` also guards against the NULL-key trap, L-CDI-257). Keep the agent's cache directory on a filesystem with headroom (L-AGENT-107).
evidence: lookup-heavy mappings failed with 'No space left on device' on an agent with about 6.5 GB free; with smaller precisions and filtered lookup queries they ran (2026-10-28)

title: An Update through a target object that declares only some of the table's columns leaves the other columns untouched
text: Proven on BigQuery V2. A mapping wrote an Update, keyed on the primary-key column, through a target object that declared only 3 of the table's columns, and the other columns kept their values. Use this to write a few derived fields (an id, a flag) back into a wide table without carrying every column through the mapping. Declare the key as the update key. The task keeps its own copy of the target object (L-CDI-271), so check the task again after you change the target definition. Upsert semantics differ by connector (L-CDI-207), so test on the target you use.
evidence: a 3-column Update target written into a wide table: the other columns kept their values after the run (2026-10-28)

title: Drive a resumable verification or enrichment sweep from 'already has a result for this input', never from a cursor kept in deletable control rows
text: Two scheduled address-verification workflows read their keyset cursor back from the latest committed control (run-manifest) row. When those control rows were deleted, both restarted from the first key and re-verified addresses they had already done (duplicate assessments), repeating metered calls, and their schedules kept firing because nothing else stopped them. Select the next batch by an anti-join to the stored results on an input fingerprint (normalized address hash) plus the reference-data version, and re-verify only when the inputs that matter change (for example the 3-digit ZIP prefix or the house number). Dedupe inputs by fingerprint before calling: repeated inputs are common in address data. Unbind the schedules of a pipeline you retire (L-CDI-075), including ones that live in another project. Newer evidence: L-IPU-064.
evidence: Per-run key ranges before and after the control-row delete; duplicate assessment counts; unique-fingerprint count (2026-11-01)

title: A mapping task's $Source$.customQuery only takes effect when the mapping's source query is a parameter; on a fixed-source mapping the run executes the mapping's own query
text: Editing `$Source$.customQuery` on a v2 mapping task (GET, change, POST /api/v2/mttask/<id>) works for the copy-data template because its source is a parameter (L-CDI-021). On a mapping whose source query is fixed in the mapping, the task's copy can be edited without an error but the run reads the mapping's query, much like the fixed target object a task copies (L-CDI-271). This is how a generated build ended with one mapping per source table (357 mappings for 354 tasks). For one mapping over many sources, make the query an in-out parameter used as the Source query (for example `$$SRC_SQL`) or a parameterized source object, then vary it per run (the task's currentValue, L-CDI-265, or a parameter file for long SQL, next lesson).
evidence: Test runs of one capture task before and after its mapping gained an in-out query parameter; audit of a 357-mapping generated build (2026-11-01)

title: Per-run SQL longer than about 4,000 characters: put it in a per-task parameter file on the agent, not in the in-out parameter default (REPO_19001)
text: An in-out parameter whose default value is a long SQL statement (about 4K characters and up) makes `POST /api/v2/mttask` fail 403 `REPO_19001` 'An error occurred while saving the Mapping task to the repository.' Working pattern: the mapping's Source query is the in-out parameter `$$SRC_SQL`; the task sets `parameterFileName` = '<lane>.param', which the agent resolves in `<agent_home>/apps/Data_Integration_Server/data/userparameters/`; the file holds one line `$$SRC_SQL=<the SQL on one line>`. Before each run, install that run's staged file on the agent host (this needs a shell on the host) and fail the item if the install fails, so a lane never reruns the previous SQL. For N lanes, clone the task N times: GET /api/v2/mttask/<base>, drop id, frsGuid, create/update stamps, lastRunTime, orgId, scheduleId and federatedId, pop `parameters[].id`, set a new name and parameterFileName, POST. Start with POST /api/v2/job {taskId, taskType MTT} and poll the activity log by runId. The agent also writes its own `data/parameters/s_mtt_<taskId>.param`; the session-log warning VAR_27062 'Cannot find section for worklet' about it is harmless. When a mapping that already has tasks gains a new in-out parameter, an OVERWRITE import fails while deploying the change to the dependent tasks: delete the task, import, then recreate it (L-CDI-271).
evidence: Two REPO_19001 task saves; 12 cloned lanes then ran hundreds of capture items, each with its own staged parameter file; task delete-import-recreate after the parameter was added (2026-11-01)

title: Sharding lanes by a hash of the whole row can drop rows silently: ClickHouse's cityHash64(*) is NULL when any column is NULL
text: A lane filter `WHERE cityHash64(*) % N = k` leaves every row that has a NULL in any Nullable column out of all N shards, because the hash of a tuple with a NULL is NULL and `NULL % N = k` is never true. No error is raised and each lane's counts look clean. Shard on a key that is never NULL (the table's sort or primary key, or coalesce each argument), and reconcile the shard totals against the source count before trusting a sharded load. Other engines: check whether the row-hash expression you shard or sample on can return NULL before using it (see L-DQ-099 for a portable sample key).
evidence: Rows missing from hash-sharded capture lanes, found during reconciliation; shards re-keyed on the sort key (2026-11-01)

title: Classify mapping-task failures by errorMsg before retrying: transport and capacity errors retry, data and permission errors do not
text: In about 1,100 retained activity-log entries of one project the most frequent messages were: 'Aborted by agent disconnection.' 134 (all 62 full runs of one workflow design ended this way, and every running workflow failed in the same second when the agent host rebooted); 'The job failed.' 86 (the linear-taskflow wrapper: read its child entries, L-CDI-061); 'java.io.IOException: Premature EOF' 30 (L-CDI-267); 'stopped by user ... using the API' 20; custom-query errors 15; target write errors 13; the database's 'Too many simultaneous queries (max 32)' 10; null into a non-nullable column 9. Single runs also failed with 'JDBC V2 adapter not available', 'job not found on agent' and 'User does not have permission to execute the asset ...'. A lane runner retried up to 3 times only on: Premature EOF, agent disconnection, too many simultaneous queries, timeouts, connection reset or broken pipe, HTTP 502/503/504, 'not available', 'job not found on agent', 'DTM process terminated' and database memory-limit errors. Cast errors, null-into-non-nullable, constraint violations, permission errors and repository save errors are deterministic: fix them, do not retry. Failed-target-row counts that repeat (60, 72, 12) reveal the writer's batch size (L-CDI-262).
evidence: Census of 1,076 activity-log entries of one project; a resumable lane runner's retry outcomes over hundreds of items (2026-11-01)

title: The activity log is not a complete run history: a busy project's log held about 1,000 entries, so counts read from it are lower bounds
text: A full read of `GET /api/v2/activity/activityLog?rowLimit=1000&offset=<n>` returned 1,076 entries reaching back three weeks for a project with 354 tasks that started more than 500 jobs a day, and each v2 task carries `maxLogs: 10` (GET /api/v2/mttask/<id>). Run and row totals taken from the activity log are therefore lower bounds. If you need run history (billing proxies, reconciliation, 'who wrote this row'), write your own ledger at completion: task id, run id, start and end in UTC (the *Utc fields, L-AUTH-014), success and failed rows and error text, and stamp the same run id into the rows written ($CurrentTaskId / $CurrentRunId, L-CDI-265).
evidence: Activity-log census (1,076 entries, oldest three weeks back) against 563 jobs in the last 24 hours; mttask GET showing maxLogs 10 (2026-11-01)

title: Dynamic Mapping Tasks are v3 type BATCH_MAPPING and are read at /batch-mapping/api/v1/dynamictask/<id> on the pod host, without /saas
text: A v3 objects query for type DMAPPINGTASK or DMT returns count 0, exactly like an invented type; the Dynamic Mapping Task type is `BATCH_MAPPING`. `GET https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/batch-mapping/api/v1/dynamictask/<v3 id>` with the session headers returns 200 with name, description, mappingId, mappingDocType MAPPING, runtimeEnvironmentId, scheduleId, state VALID, `groups[]` {groupName, enabled} and `parameters[]` {uniqueName 'Source:p_src_conn', name, txName, type SOURCE_CONNECTION, scope, ...} plus the jobs. The same path under `/saas` answers 404 (HTML), and an unknown id answers 500 CMN_001. Two DMTs in the org had been created headless by importing a v3 package (audit event BATCH_MAPPING.CREATE), each with one group and four jobs, so creation by package works. The documented `POST /batch-mapping/api/v1/dynamictask` and running through the managed MCP server jobmanagement (`run_dynamic_mapping_task`, `get_dynamic_mapping_task_status`) were listed but not exercised. Sub-jobs log as type MAPPING. Whether each DMT job counts separately against a monthly job cap (L-IPU-041) is untested.
evidence: GET 200 on two DMT objects, 404 under /saas, 500 CMN_001 for a bogus id; v3 type census; org audit log entry for the create (2026-11-01)

title: Read the real DTM buffers and the generated JDBC V2 SQL from the session log: TM_6660 for pool and block size, DBG_21699 for back-pressure, JDBC_V2_10000 for the exact SELECT and INSERT
text: The session log of a JDBC V2 mapping task states what actually ran: `TM_6660 Total Buffer Pool size is <n> bytes and Block size is <m> bytes` (left at defaults, one task with wide ports got a 22 MB pool and 1.2 MB blocks; with session properties set, 512 MB / 32 MB and 1 GB / 32 MB), `TM_6966 Reducing estimate of the amount of buffer pool memory required` when the request is trimmed, `TM_6187 Session target-based commit interval is [10000]`, and `JDBC_V2_10000 [INFO]` lines with the connection string and the exact SELECT and INSERT the reader and writer issued. `DBG_21699 Waiting for consumer to free buffer block. Please increase the dtm buffer pool size.` from the READER thread means the downstream is slower than the read; on a long read that back-pressure is what precedes the 'Premature EOF' of L-CDI-267. Use block size / declared row width to predict rows per INSERT (L-CDI-262) before changing batch sizes. The start-of-session warnings 'Invalid value false for attribute Truncate Target / Apply Custom Schema' are harmless defaults.
evidence: Three session logs of JDBC V2 tasks (defaults and two tuned configurations) read side by side (2026-11-01)
