title: ClickHouse through JDBC V2, unsigned integer targets: UInt16 from an integer port, UInt32 from a bigint port, UInt64 from decimal(20,0)
text: Adds UInt32 to L-CDI-264. Writing a ClickHouse UInt32 column from an integer (INT32) port failed with an Integer-to-Long cast error; a bigint port works. Together with L-CDI-264 the rule is: UInt16 <- integer, UInt32 <- bigint, UInt64 <- decimal(20,0), Float32 <- double, DateTime read as text. The driver expects the next wider Java type for each unsigned type (Integer, Long, BigDecimal), and the cast error names the type it wanted. Other JDBC drivers map unsigned types differently: read the cast message and give the port that Java type. Keep the full table in the mapping generator's type map so new mappings do not rediscover it. Refines L-CDI-264.
evidence: UInt32 dictionary columns (ordinal and order numbers) written from bigint ports in a generated mapping after the integer port failed (2026-11-02)

title: Cap memory and threads inside every lane's source query: uncapped parallel JDBC V2 lanes exhausted the database and killed each other's long reads
text: Eleven capture lanes reading one ClickHouse server without per-query limits drove it to its 64 GiB server memory limit: one lane failed MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED and another session's long read died with 'Premature EOF' after 9.7M rows. Address-verification shard runs failed 'memory limit exceeded ... 72 GiB' (Code 241) until `SETTINGS max_threads = 4, max_memory_usage = 6000000000` was added to their source SQL. Rules that held: stream on a live production source (no GROUP BY over wide rows), cap memory and threads in the source query, allow external sort and group-by spill (L-CDI-272), and run at most about 3 heavy lanes at once. The database's own concurrency limit is shared by loads, DQ and AV together: 32 concurrent queries on the target produced 'Too many simultaneous queries (max 32)' failures. The query-level caps here are ClickHouse SETTINGS; on other warehouses use the equivalent statement memory limits, resource groups or workload management. Newer evidence: L-MIG-093.
evidence: Server memory limit hit with 11 lanes; 2 of about 70 shard runs failed Code 241; 10 runs failed on the 32-query concurrency limit (2026-11-01 to 2026-11-03)

title: Connector limits for documents in Azure storage: a Blob Storage V3 catalog source refuses the hosted runtime, and ADLS Gen2 document formats are Spark-only and need a hierarchical-namespace account
text: Microsoft Azure Blob Storage V3 reads Flat (delimited), Avro, Parquet and JSON, and also declares a binary formatter (the companion lesson on binary reads says how to check a connector's formats). Its connection test passes on the Informatica Cloud Hosted Agent, but a catalog source on that connection refuses the hosted runtime (DISPATCH_REJECTED), so scan it on a Secure Agent. In the Microsoft Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 connector metadata (cciMeta), the 'Claire' (intelligent structure, AtlanticParserRead) and 'Document' (DocumentParserRead, input type PDF) formats list supportedEngineTypes = spark only. They need an advanced-mode mapping and an advanced configuration (a Local one runs on the agent). ADLS Gen2 also needs a storage account with hierarchical namespace enabled: on a plain Blob account its connection test returns 403. To parse a PDF from plain Blob storage without Spark, land it on a Secure Agent with a File Ingestion task, then parse it with a Structure Parser in a standard mapping (L-AGENT-104).
evidence: connector metadata read for both connectors; Blob V3 tested 200 on the hosted runtime, but its catalog scan was DISPATCH_REJECTED there; ADLS Gen2 tested 403 on an account without hierarchical namespace (2026-10-26)

title: Azure Blob Storage V3 and ADLS Gen2 both declare a binary read format with no engine restriction; only their Claire and Document formats are Spark-only
text: Read a connector's formats from `GET <serverUrl>/api/v2/connector/metadata?connectorName=<name>` (L-CONN-016): each formatter in `cciMeta` lists its `supportedEngineTypes`. For Microsoft Azure Blob Storage V3, Flat, Avro, Parquet and JSON list cloud_native and spark, and a `binary` formatter lists no engine. Microsoft Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 has the same plus ORC and Delta, a `Binary` formatter (the guide's default 'None' format, which 'reads files in binary format'), and 'Claire' (AtlanticParserRead) and 'Document' (DocumentParserRead), which list spark only. 'Blob V3 reads only flat, Avro, Parquet and JSON' is therefore incomplete when you design a document read. A binary read feeding a Structure Parser in BUFFER mode (L-CDI-244) is the candidate route to parse a document in object storage with no copy step and no Spark. It has not been run yet; the routes that ran used a File Ingestion copy and a flat-file read. Check your own store's connector the same way before you choose.
evidence: Connector metadata read for both connectors; the binary formatters carry an empty supportedEngineTypes; the binary-to-BUFFER probe was planned but not run (2026-10-26)

title: HubSpot from CDI: the native connector takes OAuth only; a REST V3 connection takes a static key as an AuthorizationCode access token, but it runs only in advanced mappings and its adapter was not deployed on the hosted runtime
text: The partner-built CDI 'HubSpot' connector authenticates by OAuth only (clientId, clientSecret and a refreshToken from an app install), so it cannot use a private-app or service key directly. A REST V3 connection has no static-header auth, but it TESTS GREEN on a Secure Agent with authType AuthorizationCode, accessToken = the service key and tokenType Bearer. REST V3 is for advanced (elastic) mappings only: a standard mapping task using it failed with APP_13400 (that code also carries unrelated messages, L-CDI-045, so read the text). On the Informatica Cloud Hosted Agent the REST V3 adapter was not deployed (an APP_105060 adapter message, L-CONN-018), although its selections read enabled. Enabling HubSpot, REST V2 and REST V3 on a Secure Agent runtime with the selections PUT (L-CAI-066) made the adapters live about 4 minutes later. For standard mappings, use the native connector with an OAuth app, bound to that Secure Agent.
evidence: REST V3 connection with a Bearer service key tested 200 on a Secure Agent, APP_105060 on the hosted runtime, and the adapter live about 4 minutes after the selections PUT, all on 2026-10-28; APP_13400 with a standard mapping (2026-10-29)

title: Moving a task off a downed runtime is not enough: a lookup reaches its connection through the connection's own runtime environment, so rebind the connections too
text: During a Hosted Agent outage, a mapping task already bound to a healthy Secure Agent still failed, because its lookup used a connection whose `runtimeEnvironmentId` was the hosted runtime. Tasks on the same Secure Agent without such lookups kept succeeding. The task's runtime does not carry its lookup connections with it: the lookup resolves the connection through that connection's own runtime environment, so a failover must move the connections as well as the tasks. To rebind in place over v2: `GET /api/v2/connection/<id>` and keep a backup without the secret. Drop createTime/updateTime/createdBy/updatedBy/majorUpdateTime. Set the body's `runtimeEnvironmentId` and `connParams.agentGroupId` to the live runtime's v2 id (set `agentId` in the body and in connParams only to pin one agent, and remove it when going back to the hosted runtime). Re-supply every masked secret (L-CONN-007; for a BigQuery key, cycle the formats until the test passes, L-CONN-036). Then `POST /api/v2/connection/<id>` and `GET /api/v2/connection/test/<id>`. Inventory both sides before you need them: tasks per runtime (`GET /api/v2/mttask`, L-CDI-013) and connections per runtime (`GET /api/v2/connection`).
evidence: a golden-record task on the Secure Agent failed during the outage while lookup-free tasks on the same agent succeeded; after the warehouse connection was rebound to the Secure Agent and tested 200, the same task ran with 10,186 rows (2026-11-03)

title: A warehouse daily query quota used up by BI refreshes makes every IDMC task on that warehouse project fail with 'Custom quota exceeded'
text: Proven on BigQuery. The project had a custom daily query-usage quota (per project per day), and dashboard extract refreshes on the same project used it up: BigQuery bills at least 10 MB per table referenced in a query, and each refresh ran about 40 queries. From then on, every IDMC mapping task that queried that project failed with 'Custom quota exceeded', including data-quality checks, a downstream enrichment check and the dashboard rebuild. Nothing was wrong with the IDMC connection, so read the task's error text before debugging IDMC. Fix: raise the cap, or keep pipeline and BI work under separate projects or quotas, and refresh BI less often. Read the cap headless first (L-ENV-041). Usage resets daily (for BigQuery at midnight Pacific time), and a raised cap stays until someone sets it back. Warehouses with account-level spend or credit caps can fail IDMC tasks the same way: when every task on one target fails at once, check the warehouse's own limits. Newer evidence: L-ENV-137, L-ENV-138.
evidence: DQ tasks, an enrichment check and a dashboard rebuild all failed with 'Custom quota exceeded' at a 1 TiB/day cap; after the cap was raised to 2 TiB, the same five DQ tasks ran green and the report republished (2026-11-03)

title: Create and run a File Ingestion (Mass Ingestion Files) task headless: POST /mftsaas/api/v1/mitasks, then POST job
text: All calls go to `https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/mftsaas/api/v1/` with the session header. Create with `POST mitasks`. The body needs: `sourceType` CONNECTION with `sourceConnection {id, type: "Azure Blob"}`; `targetType` LOCAL_FOLDER with `targetConnection {type: "local"}` (case matters); `sourceParameters` as a map of STRINGS {filePatternFilter: "true", filePattern, filePatternType: WILDCARD, blobSourceLocation: "<container name>"} (not "/": with "/" the first run failed at listing, see the companion Blob Storage V3 File Ingestion lesson); `targetParameters` {targetDirectory, fileExistsAction: OVERWRITE}; `agentGroupId` = the runtime; and `location` {projectId, projectName, folderId, folderName}. Set the location at create time, because a later PUT refuses to change it. Run with `POST job` {"taskId": <id>}. The errors name the missing field, so iterate from a partial body (as with connections, L-CONN-002). The runtime needs the Mass Ingestion-Files service and the source connector selected (selections PUT, L-CAI-066). That PUT rolls the agent's services for a few minutes, so start no runs on that agent meanwhile. Use the task as a taskflow step that lands cloud-storage files on the agent before a mapping that needs local files. Proven with a Blob storage source and an agent-folder target.
evidence: a File Ingestion task created headless in its target folder and run as a taskflow step; the storage file mirrored to the agent folder and the next mapping read it (2026-10-26)

title: Poll a File Ingestion run over REST, and drive copy-then-mapping from a CAI process: POST mftsaas/api/v1/job, then GET job/<runId>/status
text: `POST https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/mftsaas/api/v1/job` with `{"taskId": "<File Ingestion task id>"}` and both headers `IDS-SESSION-ID` and `INFA-SESSION-ID` (the v2 session id) starts the task and returns `runId`. `GET .../mftsaas/api/v1/job/<runId>/status` returns `jobStatus` and `successFiles`. While jobStatus is empty, SUBMITTED, QUEUED, STARTING or RUNNING, wait and poll again; a 2-file copy reached SUCCESS in under 20 s. The host is the pod host without `/saas` (the `/saas/mftsaas/api/v1/` form returned the login page, L-AUTH-007). From a CAI service connector, the sequence is: IDMC login action, start, then a Wait + Jump poll loop (8 s, capped at 30 polls). Start the mapping's taskflow only when jobStatus is SUCCESS, so a process copies files with the native connector and then parses them (same pattern as L-CAI-153). A task started this way has no used-by link from the process. A cleanup that moved it to an archive folder as 'unused' broke the live flow. Grep the CAI process XML for task ids before you archive anything (L-CLEAN-025).
evidence: 4 runs started and polled from a CAI process, each SUCCESS with 2 files, each followed by a green taskflow (2026-10-26)

title: File Ingestion from Azure Blob Storage V3: set blobSourceLocation to the container name; '/' fails with 'Listing files failed: Unable to connect'
text: A File Ingestion and Replication task read from an Azure Blob Storage V3 connection that names the container and wrote to a local folder on a Secure Agent. With `sourceParameters.blobSourceLocation` = `/` its first run failed at listing with 'Listing files failed: Unable to connect', although the connection tested fine. With `blobSourceLocation` = the container name, every later run was SUCCESS. The task reads back as JSON: `sourceType` CONNECTION, `sourceConnection` {id, type 'Azure Blob'}, `targetConnection` {type 'local'}, `sourceParameters` (string values) {filePattern such as `*.pdf`, filePatternType WILDCARD, filePatternFilter, includeSubfolder, blobSourceLocation, batchSize, fileStability, checkDuplicate}, `targetParameters` {targetDirectory, fileExistsAction OVERWRITE}, `agentGroupId`, `filePickupOption` PATTERN. The runtime needs the Mass Ingestion Files service and the Blob V3 connector, and a selections PUT rolls the engines for a few minutes (L-AGENT-042). To move the task between folders, FRS MoveEntities works (200).
evidence: Run 1 failed at listing with '/'; runs 2-5 SUCCESS with the container name, 2 files each; the task moved to an archive folder and back with MoveEntities 200 (2026-10-26)

title: A hard stop of the source host leaves CDC jobs FAILED with PWX-36749 'Call to read from a replication slot failed' (Not retriable): unlike after an agent reboot, they stay down until job/resume
text: The cloud provider hard-stopped the VM hosting the PostgreSQL source for about 10 minutes. Two Database Ingestion CDC jobs failed with PWX-36749 'Call to read from a replication slot failed', marked Not retriable. They did NOT come back when the database returned. After an agent-host reboot, by contrast, deployed jobs pass through awaiting_auto_restart and recover by themselves (L-DBMI-028). Here the jobs stayed failed for 3 days, because the alert went to an inbox nobody read. `POST /dbmi/public/api/v2/job/resume` {"jobId": <id>} resumed both from their restart points: 2.68 GB of slot lag drained in about 3 minutes, with no re-baseline (L-DBMI-059). A rule that is safe to automate: auto-resume when the failed job's endTime falls in a window around a source restart (30 minutes before to 15 minutes after the database's start time, or the start of the tunnel the agent reads through), at most 3 times per hour. Decide on the failure time, not on log text: the existing log-based watchdog never fired, because it read task logs from the old agent host after a runtime move (L-DBMI-059). The first apply cycle after the resume took 73 s; steady state then returned to about 21 s. Send CDC alerts to a channel that someone works. Also drop latency samples that span an outage, or a catch-up shows an 'average latency' of tens of thousands of seconds.
evidence: two CDC jobs down from a 10-minute source-host stop until they were resumed 3 days later; 2.68 GB of slot lag drained in about 3 minutes; the restart-window auto-resume passed 5 of 5 simulated cuts; latency 73 s on the first cycle, then 20.6 s (2026-11-02)

title: A mapping valid in the API turns Invalid in the Mapping Designer after an embedded rule specification changes: resynchronize the rule-spec transformation
text: A Rule Specification transformation stores a copy of the rule specification's definition. After the rule specification asset was changed, the Mapping Designer badge showed Invalid, with 'The definition of the referenced asset [<rule spec>] has been changed. Synchronize the asset'. At the same time FRS and the v2 API reported the mapping valid, and runs succeeded. To fix it in the designer: select the transformation (the Validation panel item scrolls to it), open its Rule Specification tab, answer Yes to the resynchronize prompt, check the Field Mapping tab (the input links were kept), then Save and reopen. Headless, regenerate the mapping from the CURRENT rule-spec definitions (a fresh export) whenever a rule changes. Then sweep the designer for Invalid badges, because no API reports this state. Same family as L-DQ-113 (field scale) and L-CDI-226 (Structure Parser model copy).
evidence: 2 rule-spec transformations resynchronized in one mapping; badge Valid after save and reopen; next run SUCCESS (166 s); a sweep of 2 mappings, 2 tasks and 2 taskflows showed all Valid (2026-10-26)

title: What a CDQ Deduplicate transformation outputs: every incoming field passes through, Out_RowId/Out_DriverId come as '1 - <SequenceId>', the pair score is Out_LinkScore, and consolidation adds one survivor row per cluster
text: Deduplicate passes every incoming field through to its output, so the result needs no join back to the input. Out_RowId and Out_DriverId come as the text '1 - <SequenceId>'; strip the prefix before joining on your key. Read the pair score from Out_LinkScore, because Out_DriverScore is 1.0 on every row. With consolidation enabled, the output adds one row per cluster with Out_IsSurvivor = 'Y' next to the original rows ('N'). Filter on 'N' for the member records and on 'Y' for the consolidated record, or counts double. Keep unique ids out of the match fields (L-DQ-101).
evidence: a person-name Deduplicate over about 720,000 contacts fed a review queue of about 3,900 pairs; the output shape was read from the run's target rows (2026-10-28)

title: Data Profiling of ClickHouse through a JDBC V2 connection works headless: clone a working JDBC V2 profile body (TOOLKIT_CCI, '<database>/TABLE', NSTRING and DOUBLE fields) and profile typed sample tables
text: Column profiles on ClickHouse tables read through a JDBC V2 connection were created over REST, executed and COMPLETED, including an ALL_ROWS run over a 101M-row, 89-column table, a 1.68M-row 38-column table and two stratified samples. The working body: `connectionId` = the JDBC V2 connection; `source.sourceType` DATASOURCE; `source.dataSourceType` and `source.properties.dataSourceType` = `TOOLKIT_CCI`; `source.properties.sourcePath` = `<database>/TABLE`; `source.name` = the table; `runtimeOptions.runtimeEnvironmentId` null (the connection's runtime is used); `samplingOptions` {samplingType ALL_ROWS, rows -1}; each `source.fields[]` entry {dataType varchar, pcType NSTRING, precision 4000, scale 0} or {dataType double, pcType DOUBLE, precision 15}; each `profileableFields[]` entry {fieldType DATASOURCEFIELD, appliedBy USER, fieldName, sourceName = table, precision, scale}. To add a profile: GET a working one, drop id, frsId, profileKey, lastRunKey, create/update stamps, version, orgId, `source.id` and `runtimeOptions.id`, rebuild fields and profileableFields from the new table's columns, POST `/profiling-service/api/v1/profile` (if the response carries no id, find it by name in GET /profile?limit=200), then POST `/profile/<id>/execute` and poll `/job/<profileJobId>`. Rule bindings (L-DQ-023) and metric-store reads (L-DQ-123) work on these profiles. This overturns L-DQ-119 (NSTRING refused with PROFILE_MDL_00006, 'string' hangs) and the advice in L-CONN-089 not to plan direct profiling of ClickHouse. What differed from the failed attempts (a body cloned from a profile that had already run, NSTRING paired with dataType varchar, another agent and connection) was not isolated, so start from a profile that has run on the same connection type. Profile typed sample tables rather than raw production tables: cast enum and low-cardinality columns to Nullable String, numbers to Float64 and dates to text (L-CDI-264), and pick a stable hash sample (about 2,000 rows per partition, L-DQ-099). ALL_ROWS was the only sampling used, and a full profile of a 1.3B-row table would have pulled about 282 GB through the agent. Newer evidence: L-CDI-296, L-DQ-155.
evidence: Five JDBC V2 ClickHouse profiles COMPLETED (1,790 / 69,782 / 113,289 / 1,679,611 / 101,369,803 rows), two of them created by a cloned-body REST POST; 53 rule bindings run on four of them (2026-11-02)

title: Certified address verification of raw property addresses: classify the 'failed' rows before fixing them, and count 'premise found, unit unconfirmed' as verified
text: Classify the failed Certified responses by ResultQuality, the HouseNumber element and the Street value, read from the stored response JSON. Five classes recur: premise found but unit not confirmed (these rows still carry rooftop coordinates, census data and DPV confirmation, so they are verified premises mislabelled as failed); street with no house number; house number given but street not found; street found but house number invalid; placeholder or no street (for example 'UNASSIGNED LOCATION'). Status contract: treat ResultQuality >= 4 with DPV confirmation D or S as 'verified, unit unconfirmed' rather than failed; it needs no new calls. This is the Certified-mode counterpart of L-DQ-120 (on-agent Batch codes). Rows with no house number and placeholders do not improve with another paid Certified call: route them to a geocode-by-location path or a steward queue, and cleanse plus re-derive ZIP and city before one re-verify. Verified shares vary widely by region and by source quality, so measure your own, by class, before and after the contract.
evidence: Classes derived from a sample of failed responses read from the stored response JSON (2026-11-02)

title: A Verifier asset returns only the enrichments its own settings request: output ports alone gave no geocodes, even with the geocoding reference files installed
text: Three on-agent verifier assets (Hybrid input, BATCH, CountryMode IDENTIFY, outputs = address lines, ZIP, locality, state, ProcessStatus, ResultQuality) verified a large address set and wrote no geocodes and no DPV values, although the agent held the rooftop, arrival-point, standard-geocode and enrichment reference files. A verifier then cloned through a v3 package (fresh GUID and name, `documentBlob.logicalModel.outputFields` extended with internalName `/Variants/0/Enrichments/Geocodes/Standard/Value`, `/Latitude` and `/Longitude` in groupId Geocoding, SHA-256 re-hash, import REUSE) imported, and its mapping COMPLETED, but every geocode output came back empty with no error. In the compiled mapping the address transformation carried no geocoding option (`geoCoding` appeared only in the serializer's attribute list), so adding output fields does not switch the enrichment on. Configure geocoding and enrichment in the verifier asset's own process settings, prove that one known address returns coordinates before a bulk run, and read `ResultInfo.DataFilesUsed` (L-DQ-125) where the path returns it. How to set the option headless is still open.
evidence: Verified rows with no geocode or DPV values; cloned-verifier runs COMPLETED with empty Standard geocodes; v3 export of the compiled mapping inspected (2026-11-02)

title: The cloud Address Verification service also serves /api/v1/info and an OpenAPI document; the catalog JWT is accepted as its Bearer
text: Besides `POST .../dataquality/addressverification/api/v1/process` (L-DQ-015), the service's OpenAPI lists only `GET /api/v1/info` (service status), `GET /api/v1/welcome` and the process call, with one security scheme, a Bearer JWT. An identity JWT minted for the catalog (client_id cdlg_app, L-AUTH-022) was accepted for both /info and a 2-address Certified /process call, so the same token plumbing as CDGC works. Use /info as a no-address check of the token and the host before a bulk run. Unauthenticated doc requests answer 401 'Authentication token not provided' with a serviceVersion field, and 404 bodies show the internal service path `/cdq-av/...`.
evidence: /info and a Certified /process probe with a catalog-minted JWT; OpenAPI document read (2026-11-02)

title: Call the cloud Address Verification service in Certified mode from a CDI Java transformation: 1,000 inputs per POST, renew the token on 401, fail the run on a count mismatch, keep the full response
text: Mapping shape: Source (one partition and one hash slice per run, already-verified records skipped) -> Rule Specification 'required id' -> Java transformation -> Expression -> append-only target. The Java step buffers 1,000 inputs (the per-call maximum, L-DQ-015) and POSTs `https://idmc-api.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/dataquality/addressverification/api/v1/process` with `{"Request":{"Parameters":{"Mode":"Certified","CountrySets":[{"OutputDetail":{"SubItems":true,"ElementStatus":true,"OutputStatusForEmptyElements":true},"Countries":["USA"],"Process":{"Enrichments":{"CountrySpecific":true,"Global":true,"Geocoding":{"Rooftop":true,"ArrivalPoint":true}}}}]},"IO":{"Inputs":[...]}}}`; one input = `{"SourceID":<id>,"AddressElements":{"Country":"USA","SubBuilding":[{"Value":<unit>}],"Locality":[{"Value":<city>}],"AdministrativeDivision":[{"Value":<state>}],"PostalCode":[{"Value":<zip5>}]},"PreformattedData":{"PostalDeliveryAddressLines":[<street>]}}`. Up to 5 attempts with linear backoff (3 s x attempt); on 401 renew the token and retry; throw if the output count differs from the input count. Parse ResultInfo (ProcessStatus, ProcessModeUsed, DataFilesUsed), Variants[0].StatusValues (ResultQuality, MatchPercentage), the address elements, Enrichments.Certifications.CASS (DPVConfirmation, DPVFootnoteComplete, DPVVacantIndicator, DPVNoStatIndicator, DPVCMRA, RDI, CarrierRoute, DeliveryPoint, BarCode, CongressionalDistrict, ELOTSequence, ...), the rooftop and arrival-point geocodes and the census, FIPS, CBSA and time-zone enrichments. Store the whole response JSON and its SHA-256 on every result row: in one build 17 returned fields (LACS/LACSLink, SuiteLink, DPV footnotes 1-4, DPVNoStatReason, DefaultFlag, Building, DeliveryService, Residue, ...) existed only in the JSON and could be back-filled later without new calls. Security and governance: the Bearer token is short-lived; keep it in a tmpfs file on the agent host (expiry + token) renewed by a helper that keeps at least 300 s of validity, never in the mapping, a parameter or a log. No IDMC connection holds this credential, so the call is invisible to connection governance and to lineage: document it. Scale by cloning the mapping into a few shard tasks over disjoint hash slices (4 ran in parallel), and cap the source query's memory (see the lesson on per-query caps). Newer evidence: L-METHOD-145.
evidence: Four parallel shard tasks, runs of 1-8 min each; full responses stored with none truncated (the largest about 5,600 characters); the only run failures were the database memory limit (2026-11-03)

title: When a scan runs through a temporary tunnel, keep the tunnel separate from the polling loop, or one DNS error tears it down mid-scan
text: A Tableau scan reached its server through a temporary SSH tunnel to the scanning agent (L-CDGC-199). The helper script polled the catalog job and closed the tunnel in its cleanup. A transient DNS failure crashed the poll, the cleanup closed the tunnel, and the running scan lost its server. Run the tunnel as its own process for the whole scan window. Make the poll retry DNS and socket errors (read timeouts included) instead of exiting, and close the tunnel only after the job reaches a final state (COMPLETED, PARTIAL_COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED).
evidence: a scan failed after a DNS error ended the helper and its cleanup closed the tunnel; with the reworked helper the tunnel stayed up through DNS blips and the scan completed (2026-10-26)

title: Hosted Agent outage runbook: confirm, inventory, rebind tasks and connections with full-body backups, leave the exceptions, unblock the chain, undo when the runtime is back
text: 1) Confirm it is the platform runtime: every hosted connection fails its test with APP_105060 on the hosted agent group, and hosted runs fail in seconds with 'no active Secure Agent in group Informatica Cloud Hosted Agent'. Open a support case. 2) Inventory: `GET /api/v2/mttask` and keep the tasks whose `runtimeEnvironmentId` is the hosted runtime. List the connections they use, lookups included. 3) Rebind each task: `GET /api/v2/mttask/<id>`, save the FULL body to an undo file, drop createTime, updateTime, createdBy, updatedBy, lastRunTime and agentId, set `runtimeEnvironmentId` to the Secure Agent's runtime, `POST /api/v2/mttask/<id>` (PUT is 405, L-CDI-046) and read it back. 17 tasks moved in seconds; ids, schedules and taskflows were unchanged. 4) Rebind the connections too, re-supplying their secrets, or lookups keep failing: a lookup resolves its connection through that connection's own runtime. 5) Leave on the hosted runtime what the Secure Agent cannot serve, and accept those tasks as down. That covers Salesforce connections whose user is IP-restricted when the agent's egress IP is not in the org's Network Access (L-CONN-110), and connectors not enabled on the agent (enable them with the selections PUT, L-CAI-066, and allow a few minutes for the adapter to deploy). It also covers work the agent is too small for (memory: L-CDI-260). 6) Unblock the orchestration. A chain that stops at the first failure lets the one step still bound to the dead runtime starve unrelated steps behind it (here, data-quality checks queued behind a CRM sync). Put independent steps before it, or make that step's failure reported but non-fatal until the runtime is back. 7) Re-run the failed tasks (`POST /api/v2/job`) and check the downstream outputs. 8) When the hosted runtime is healthy, undo from the saved bodies, put the connections back and revert step 6. If tasks still fail after the move, read their error text: a warehouse-side quota can fail them too.
evidence: 17 mapping tasks and 1 warehouse connection rebound in about 10 minutes, with backups; 4 CRM-sync tasks went back to the hosted runtime because the CRM org did not trust the agent's egress IP; the re-run chain succeeded and the downstream report refreshed; stop-on-first-failure was relaxed for the CRM sync only (2026-11-03)

title: CLAIRE GPT lineage answers walk job-level and SaaS hops, and curated edges, once the integration lineage is set up
text: Downstream lineage of a warehouse table or view returns the dependent views with a LINEAGE card. Upstream lineage now also walks past the warehouse, once three things exist: a Data Integration (IICS) catalog source scanned with Lineage Discovery, its connection references MERGEd onto the physical sources, and curated edges for the hops no scanner draws. 'Show the upstream lineage of the Snowflake view <view>' answered in 75 s with 4 upstream assets over 4 hops: the table, then the MappingTaskInstance that loads it, then the mapping's input DataSet (a SharePoint library reference), then the Salesforce Object, reached through a curated MANUAL edge. The task read connection objects (a library and a file), not a custom SQL query; with custom-query tasks the same prompts still answered '0 upstream assets' after auto-accepted assignments (L-CDGC-148). Without the setup, job-level, SaaS and source-database lineage answered 'no lineage' or '0 upstream assets'. 'What is the downstream impact if <table> changes' answered 'Lineage is not created' for a table that no current mapping writes (a stale table left in the catalog), so ask impact questions about tables on the live path. Supersedes L-MCP-107: the job and SaaS hops are now proven, including curated edges.
evidence: View-to-view lineage 2 of 2 and a 25-asset upstream lineage (2026-10-01). A 4-hop upstream answer through a mapping task, a library reference and a curated Salesforce edge in 75 s; an impact question on a stale table answered 'Lineage is not created' (2026-10-27)

title: With no column classifications in the catalog, CLAIRE GPT's personal-data answer falls back to column names
text: 'Which columns in the <warehouse> table <table> contain personal data' named the e-mail column only 'based on its column name'. It stated that none of the table's 17 columns had a populated classification or sensitivity level. The same answer also printed 'Looks like CLAIRE GPT encountered an error. Can you try again?' partway through and then completed. A newly provisioned catalog tenant can start without data element classifications (L-CDGC-204). So run data classification on the source, and check that the columns carry classifications, before you show a PII answer. Treat a mid-answer error line as noise when the answer then completes.
evidence: One run on a table with no classified columns: the answer took 75 s, named 1 column by name pattern, and printed an error line before completing (2026-10-27)

title: Prove a table migration inside IDMC: per-dataset units and an order-free checksum on both sides, joined by one reconcile mapping that writes a status row per dataset
text: For each legacy dataset measure, read-only and throttled (2 threads, a memory cap), its rows, distinct units and a checksum = sum(hash(unit key)) mod 2^64, which ignores row order, plus the table's last modification time. Stage these legacy stats as a flat file on the agent. The target-side SQL for the same measures comes from a run parameter file (`$$TGT_SQL`, see the parameter-file lesson) and counts a unit only when all its chunks are present. One mapping joins legacy stats (master outer, so datasets missing on the target still appear) to target stats; an Expression sets reconciled / mismatch / mismatch_source_changed (the legacy table changed after capture) / missing_target and writes one control row per dataset per run with run lineage ($CurrentTaskId / $CurrentRunId) and record_version = run id, so the latest run wins. Exact duplicate rows collapse into one record in a lossless capture keyed by row hash: record count() against the distinct row-hash count on the legacy side so the multiset stays provable. A linear taskflow runs the reconcile and the dictionary refresh together. The first two runs over 116 datasets gave 108 reconciled, 5 changed at the source and 3 real mismatches, which turned 'is everything there?' into a list of three datasets to inspect. Newer evidence: L-MIG-091.
evidence: Two reconcile runs covering 116 legacy datasets: 108 reconciled, 5 mismatch_source_changed, 3 mismatch (2026-11-01)

title: Make view-only walk-through copies of mappings with FRS CopyEntities: name and describe them in the call, omit conflictResolution ('NONE' gives XFER_500), and take the new id from tgtGuid
text: `POST https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/frs/api/v1/CopyEntities` (header `IDS-SESSION-ID`) with {"xferSpec": {"targetLocationId": "<folderId>", "sourceSpecArr": [{"sourceEntityId": "<frsId>", "destName": "<new name>", "destDesc": "<text>", "resetExpiryTime": false, "mergeTags": ""}]}}. It answers XFER_200, with resultValue FRS_2xx and the copy's id in value[].statusArr[].tgtGuid. Adding "conflictResolution": "NONE" fails with XFER_500 'Unknown conflict resolution policy', so leave the key out. To set or fix a description later, `PATCH .../frs/api/v1/Documents('<id>')` {"description"} and read it back (as for rule specifications, L-DQ-094). A copy is only the mapping, with no mapping task, so it adds nothing to lineage: an IICS source harvests a mapping only through an in-scope task (L-CDGC-157). Put walk-through copies in a separate project outside the IICS catalog source's filter, and link the lineage of the live assets. Record each source's updateTime before the copy and compare it after, to prove the originals were not touched. Undo = `DELETE .../BaseEntities('<copyId>')` (L-CLEAN-005).
evidence: 16 mappings copied into a new 4-folder project, each named and described in one call; updateTime unchanged on all 16 originals; the conflictResolution 'NONE' probe failed with XFER_500 (2026-11-02)

title: Sweep the Mapping Designer headless for Invalid badges the API does not report: deep links per object kind, the Validation panel, an exact 'Log In' click
text: Open each object at `https://<pod>.<domain>.informaticacloud.com/diUI/products/integrationDesign/main/<kind>/<frsId>/read`, or `/edit` to change it. The kinds are `mapping`, `mct` (mapping task) and `linearTaskflow`; a folder opens at `.../main/explore/<folderId>`. Use a saved storage state (L-UI-005). Wait 35-45 s for the canvas, then read the Valid or Invalid badge in the page header and the 'Validation (<n>)' panel. Each item's detail arrow shows the full message, for example a rule specification whose definition changed. Log in on the identity-service page by filling `#username` and `#password` and clicking the button named exactly 'Log In' (exact match). A substring match also hits the SSO button. Stop on the first failed login, because every attempt counts toward the user's lockout (L-AUTH-095). A designer-only Invalid state (L-DQ-113, a stale rule-spec copy) is found only this way.
evidence: Sweep of 2 mappings, 2 mapping tasks and 2 linear taskflows read each badge; one Invalid mapping found and fixed; one scripted login per batch (2026-10-26)

title: A source, target or transformation that IDMC supports but the generator has no template for: learn its shape from one exemplar mapping, build from it, then add the template to the package
text: A session that finds no template for a connector tends to stall, guess, or switch the user to a connector it does know; all three are wrong. The way forward is an exemplar: ask the user for a mapping in the org that already reads or writes that connector in the needed role, or ask them to create one once in the Mapping Designer (one source, one target, saved; it does not need to run). Export it read-only with the v3 export API, read it offline with `core/mapgen/exemplar.py <zip>` (connection reference, typeSystem, objectType, object path, read and write options, runtime attributes, connector-specific attribute objects, the fields as spec tuples, and any transformation class the generator does not build yet), build the spec from that shape (profile `typeSystem`, object path, field tuples, `writerAttrs`, `set` / `advanced`, or a `generic` node), prove it with one run, and then enrich the package: the connector's row in the Mapping Fast Path, a placeholder-only example spec in `core/mapgen/examples/connectors/`, and a lesson. Steps in the Mapping Fast Path section 7.0.
evidence: A session asked for a flat-file to new flat-file passthrough found no file-target template and fell back to another connector; built on the user's own file connection, the same pipeline ran natively in IDMC (189/189 rows). A reader of the shared KB confirmed that pointing the session at an existing or newly made mapping with the connector unblocks it for any connector the package has not templated (2026-11-03)

title: A profile's SQL Override is stored in a 4,000-character column: a longer override fails the create with 500 PROFILE_SVC_00004; split the columns across profiles
text: A Data Profiling profile on a relational (JDBC V2) source can read through an SQL Override (source.advancedOptions['SQL Override']), which lets one profile sample a large table in place (a hash or granule filter in the query) without copy tables. The override is saved in the profiling repository's advanced-properties table, whose value column holds at most 4,000 characters. A longer override makes POST /profile (and, by the same storage, a PUT) answer 500 PROFILE_SVC_00004 'Repository action failed ... Data truncation: Data too long for column property_value ... insert into ds_adv_properties'. Nothing is created, so there is no orphan to clean up. Fix: keep each override under 4,000 characters by splitting the column list across several profiles (same FROM / sample clause in each, so every group profiles the same rows); about 60 long column names fit comfortably. Count the characters before the POST; wrapping columns in casts (toString, substring) lengthens the query quickly. Newer evidence: L-DQ-159.
evidence: An override of 4,186 characters (one key + 119 columns) was refused on create; the same columns split into two profiles with overrides of 2,111 and 2,259 characters were created and read back (2026-11-04)

title: A JDBC V2 (ClickHouse) profile only sees its connection's own schema, must name a real table of it with its real column names, and must return recognised types natively
text: Three checks run before a JDBC V2 profile reads a row, and each fails with its own message (the job itself often shows only 'Data too long for column error_msg', because the real error is too long to store: read the agent's Data_Integration_Server tomcat log for CCIMetadataResource.createDataOperation). (1) The source path '<schema>/TABLE' is resolved through the connection, which exposes only the schema set on the connection: any other database answers 'Please provide correct path for the Object. [<db>] was not found'. An SQL override that names another database does not help, so profiling every database of a server needs one connection per database (copy the connection in Administrator and change its Schema; the copy keeps the password). (2) source.name must be a table or view that exists in that schema ('Object(s) [<table>] not found'), and every profiled field must be a real column of it ('Invalid operation field name in CCI Metadata Client'): an anchor table with the SQL override reading a different table does not work. The SQL override may still sample (PREWHERE / LIMIT / SETTINGS) and cast, as long as each output column keeps its column name. (3) The reader takes each field's type from the table's metadata, so a column the driver recognises must come back in that type: a plain ClickHouse DateTime turned into text fails 'String cannot be cast to java.sql.Timestamp', a 64-bit integer turned into text fails 'Data for column [x] of type [bigint] should be a of type [java.lang.Number]', and a bare Date fails 'java.time.LocalDate cannot be cast to java.sql.Timestamp'. What worked: numbers and DateTime / DateTime64 bare (field types double / bigint / timestamp), Date as toDateTime(col), Date32 as toDateTime64(col, 0), String bare, and only complex types (Array, Map, Tuple) as left(toString(col), 1000) with a varchar field. Columns the driver does not recognise (DateTime64 with a time-zone argument on some servers) arrive as text, which is why toString casts can appear to work on one table and fail on another. Newer evidence: L-CONN-136.
evidence: On one ClickHouse server: profiles in two other databases failed on (1), an anchor-table workaround failed on (2), text-cast DateTime / Int64 / Date columns failed on (3); after the fixes, 7 test tables covering String, Float64, Int64, UInt64, DateTime, DateTime64, Date and Date32, and 15 tables of a second database through a connection with that schema, all COMPLETED (2026-11-05)

title: Guard a Secure Agent on a shared database host with a watchdog that kills its cgroup on load or IO thresholds
text: A Secure Agent placed on the production database VM drove load into the same overload class as an earlier incident during its first full DQ run, and a graceful `systemctl stop` hung in 'deactivating' while load kept climbing. Killing the agent's control group outright was safe: agent state lives on disk and IDMC only marks the running job failed. Ship a guard unit with the agent that SIGKILLs and disables it when 60-second IO pressure or load crosses a threshold, run the agent under hard caps (memory, CPU, IO bandwidth), and after any restart watch it idle for about 10 minutes before giving it work. The root cause here was a hyphenated slice that inherited a 4 GB parent cap (L-AGENT-110). Refines L-AGENT-110.
evidence: Load 79.6 -> 125 during the run; stop stuck 'deactivating'; guard thresholds io avg60 > 40% or load > 30; caps 8 GB / 2 CPU / 40 MB/s at first; after the slice fix a full 100M-row run kept load low (monitor sample load 2.9, io60 0.03)

title: Host guards keyed on the old agent's service name or path will stop or confuse a replacement agent: give it a new unit name, user and directory
text: The retired agent on a database VM was kept stopped by a window-enforcer job keyed on its service name, and a port-guard cron referenced its install path. Installing the replacement under the same unit name would have let the enforcer stop it. Read every cron, timer and guard that names the old unit or path, give the new agent a distinct unit name, OS user and install directory (on the data disk if the root disk is nearly full), check that each old guard exits cleanly once the old directory is moved aside, and do heavy steps (install, first full run) outside the host's backup window. Refines L-AGENT-111.
evidence: Old agent window config 0-0 enforced by a guard; root disk 92% full so the install went to the data disk; install waited for the 03:00-07:00 UTC backup window; old 39 GB install moved aside, not deleted

title: Saving agent configuration restarts the Data Integration Server about 1.5 minutes later and kills every job on that agent, including other sessions' jobs
text: An address-verification tuning change (preload settings) had to go through the agent configuration form, whose save restarts DIS about 1.5-2 minutes later. Another session was running mastering jobs on the same agent, so the change was deferred. Before any agent configuration save, list running jobs on that agent across all sessions and lanes (activity monitor), and schedule the save in a drained window or announce it on the tracker. Refines L-AGENT-088.
evidence: AV tuning on a shared DQ agent deferred to avoid killing the parallel session's jobs (2026-11-01)

title: Creating an IDMC org through the Azure Native ISV service first fails on the Entra user profile and on a Marketplace purchase block
text: The create validation rejected the user with 'Business Phone Number is not in the expected format (10-25 characters...). CompanyName is empty. Country is empty', then with 'Marketplace is not enabled for the Azure subscription'. Fill business phone, company and country on the Entra user (Graph), and switch the billing profile's Marketplace purchase policy from NotAllowed to AllAllowed only for the attempt: Sponsorship-type credits do not cover Marketplace, so any other Marketplace purchase made meanwhile bills the card. Confirm the plan is the free one before creating, and block purchases again afterwards (verify 0 Marketplace subscriptions remain).
evidence: Profile fields saved and read back through Graph; plan 'Informatica CDI' isFree true, isPayg false, price $0, no payment method required; Marketplace re-blocked after every attempt (2026-11-10)

title: Azure Native IDMC org create from the CLI: the informatica extension, the free plan's own term id, a managed identity and an Informatica Region
text: Use `python -m azure.cli informatica data-management organization create -g <rg> -n <name> -l <region> --company-details @company.json --user-details @user.json --marketplace-details @mkt.json` (in git-bash call azure.cli through python, L-ENV-016). The marketplace offer is publisher informatica, offer prod-idmc_as_azure_native_isv_service, plan idmc_ans_public ('Informatica CDI'); the term id must be the plan's own (read it from the offer's plan availabilities), a guessed term fails validation. The newer API version also needs a managed identity and an Informatica Region, which no Azure API lists (the portal shows a dropdown); the company 'business' field is the business type, and country takes 'USA'. Register the Microsoft.SaaS and Microsoft.Marketplace resource providers first (free; a documented cause of ISV signup failures).
evidence: Request passed Azure validation and reached provisioning once the term id, identity and region were set (2026-11-10)

title: Azure Native IDMC signup: 'Partner signup failed ... Unexpected error occurred' on every variation from a personal-account Sponsorship tenant
text: Once Azure-side validation passed, every create or link-existing-org attempt failed about 1-4 minutes in, inside Informatica's signup step, with 'Object reference not set to an instance of an object' or 'Partner signup failed ... Unexpected error occurred. Please try again later' and no detail. Varying Azure region, Informatica Region value, email (personal, plus-alias, corporate domain), UPN form, company domain and new-versus-link did not change it; Owner role, complete profile, accepted terms and registered providers were all in place. The likely trigger is the tenant type (a personal Microsoft account in a default directory on a Sponsorship subscription), unconfirmed. Do not keep retrying: send the operation ids to Informatica's Azure Native team, or use a company Entra tenant with a pay-as-you-go or enterprise subscription; existing IDMC orgs remain the free route.
evidence: Failures across 3 Azure regions, 3 Informatica Region values, 3 emails, plain and #EXT# UPN, link to an existing org; 0 charges; all test resources deleted (2026-11-10)

title: An AI-generated IDMC build of 357 one-off mappings put all logic in SQL strings and typed fake lineage ids into the data
text: A project generated by another coding agent contained 357 mappings, 354 tasks and 149 taskflows (104 loose at the project root): one per source table, chunk and pilot, none parameterized, 16 MB of SQL inside source queries (median 15.6 KB, max 679 KB), and 222 mappings with `_mapping_id`, `_task_id` and even `_run_id` literals typed into their SQL, so the 'lineage' columns in the data named runs that never produced those rows. It also wrote 60-82 rows per INSERT. Review a generated IDMC build before running it: count mappings per purpose, check for parameters, measure source-SQL length, and grep for literal ids; replace with a few parameterized mappings whose transformations carry the logic (L-MDM-081) and stamp lineage with `$CurrentTaskId` / `$CurrentRunId` (L-CDI-265). Archive the generated build with its ids kept, because loaded rows reference them. Refines L-MDM-081.
evidence: 357 mappings / 354 tasks / 149 taskflows; 0 gold rows; replaced by 4 MDM mappings plus 1 ingest mapping with 12 lane tasks (2026-11-01)

title: An external REST runner that rewrites each mapping's SQL before every run makes the IDMC export alone unreproducible: keep the runner and its query templates with the assets
text: Run history showed that every address-verification run had been started over REST under a user login by a program outside IDMC. That program also rewrote each mapping task's source query (shard and slice predicates) before submitting it. The program was not on the workstation, and reading the VM's scheduler was blocked. So a v3 export plus the activity log showed what ran, but not how to run it again. If a runner owns parameters or SQL, version it with the IDMC assets, name it in the mapping description, and record its path and schedule in the runbook. Better still, move the per-run values into parameter files or in-out parameters that IDMC itself holds (L-CDI-285). Refines L-CDI-102.
evidence: 4 mapping tasks, every run submitted over REST by an external driver; driver location unknown at handoff time (2026-11-03)

title: Lineage stamps can be checked as data: a rule that rejects anything but a real 20-character IDMC object id found most rows written outside IDMC
text: Rows written by scripts or native SQL steps carried lineage stamps such as `native:<step>` or a `<org>17PENDING00000` placeholder in their mapping-id / task-id columns. A rule specification that answers VALID only for a real 20-character IDMC object id (and blank) and INVALID for `native:...` and PENDING placeholders, bound to those columns in every profile, turned 'is this table really built by IDMC' into a pass rate: 76.9 % of gold rows and 48.5 % of staging rows were not backed by an IDMC object, and 72.1 % of dictionary rows carried the placeholder. Fix by moving those steps into IDMC mappings or recording the real ids; re-run the profile to show movement. Refines L-METHOD-043.
evidence: Lineage rule mean pass 59.4 % across 8 columns; gold task-id check 23.14 % (2026-11-04)

title: Never run a whole-table ALL_ROWS profile or read on a 1.3B-row registry of blob chunks over JDBC: it is about 282 GB
text: A model registry table held 1.31B rows, most of them dataset snapshots and base64 artifact chunks averaging about 25 MB each. An ALL_ROWS profile of it would have pulled about 282 GB through the JDBC V2 reader. Profile model, version and evaluation rows in full and only a fixed fraction of snapshot and chunk rows (here 1/4096), and before moving such a table through IDMC test whether one JDBC V2 string field carries a chunk that size or whether chunks must shrink. Refines L-DQ-128.
evidence: 1,311,035,271 rows; sample 1,482,161 rows profiled; 11.1 GB of base64 over 437 chunks (2026-11-02/11-04)

title: Put the DQ agent next to the data: a cross-cloud agent means opening the production database and paying egress on every full-table run
text: The only healthy agent ran in a different cloud from a 100M-row ClickHouse table. Reaching it would have meant opening the production database to the other cloud and moving the full table out on every DQ run, and the hosted agent was no alternative (no profiling engine, no custom JDBC driver, public exposure). Choose the agent location by where the data is: either an agent inside the data's network under strict caps, or profile a sample copy in a database the existing agent already reaches and apply the accepted rules in the warehouse.
evidence: Agent in cloud A blocked on both public and private addresses of the database in cloud B; 101M rows / 16.6 GiB compressed per run would have left the cloud; database logins accepted only internal networks (2026-10-29)

title: Give an IDMC DQ connection a scoped database login: read the source layer, write only a results database, and inherit the shared query limits
text: For a DQ lane on a production warehouse, create a dedicated login that can read only the layer being scored and write only a separate results database, held to the same per-query memory and thread limits as other shared users, and split it into two connections (read, write). Test it from the agent host the way the agent connects, with the password in a file rather than on the command line, and confirm a wrong password is rejected. The results database then holds append-only scorecards that can be compared run to run. Refines L-CONN-012.
evidence: Login read all 100,983,261 rows and a wrong password was rejected; limits 4 GB / 2 threads; separate read and write connections (2026-10-29)

title: Plan one JDBC connection per database when you provision: adding them later needs the stored password, which REST never returns, so 940 tables waited on a human
text: A JDBC V2 profile only sees its connection's schema (L-DQ-134), so profiling 27 more databases needed 27 more connections. Creating them headless needs the reader's password, because GET returns '***' (L-CONN-007). The session's search for that password in local files and the cloud secret store was rightly denied by the permission classifier as credential exploration, and it stopped there rather than working around it (L-METHOD-121). Two paths remained for the owner: copy the connection in Administrator and change only the Schema (the copy keeps the password), or provide the secret through an approved store. Create the per-database connections, or a vault-backed secret, when the agent and reader user are first set up. Refines L-DQ-134.
evidence: 920 legacy tables in 27 databases plus 4 tables in a second schema blocked; one permission denial ('Credential Exploration'); 2026-11-05

title: Build a fix set FROM the gate's own view, not from a re-derived predicate: the re-derived one selected 2,025,064 rows where the gate flagged 2 groups
text: To clear a failing duplicate gate, a helper predicate rewritten from the rule's description (`HAVING uniqExact(id) > 1 AND uniqExact(source) = 1`) selected 2,025,064 rows in one state, because the gate view already exempts most groups through clauses the rewrite left out; the gate flagged 2 groups there. The correct fix set is `INSERT INTO <fix> SELECT <keys> FROM <gate_view> WHERE state = 'XX'`. A tiny canary state (2 groups) exposed the over-select before any mutation ran. Then update in place, scoped to the fix set (`ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE ... WHERE (k1, k2) IN (SELECT k1, k2 FROM <fix>)`), and assert the total row count and the non-target rows are unchanged.
evidence: Fix applied to 7 states: gate 0, row count unchanged at 108,633,427, 0 open mutations (2026-08-03)

title: DQ gates were measuring the legacy table, not the table customers read: point every gate at served gold and run old and new side by side
text: A deep profile of the warehouse found two property tables that disagreed (15.6M ids only in legacy, 7.4M only in gold; 4.9 % of shared ids differed in city or latitude), while the per-state universe gate, state parity, the DQ checks and the coverage marts all read the legacy table that about 15 crons still wrote and customers never saw. A gate PASS or FAIL therefore said nothing certain about what customers saw, and a city repair regression was caught on legacy rather than gold. Point gates (and IDMC profiles and rule mappings) at the served table, run the old and new gate side by side for three days with a source-table tag, then switch; retire the legacy table once nothing reads it. Newer evidence: L-DQ-163.
evidence: Legacy 109.07M ids vs gold 100.84M; 25 of 26 gold views passed through to legacy tables (2026-10-29)

title: Define 'clean' as a fixed list of pass/fail checks per partition, gate publication on it, and certify only after seven green nights
text: 'Make gold clean' became testable once it was written as 22 checks (structure: no gold view reading legacy, no backup/scratch tables, nightly backup covers every database, weekly restore drill; data: 16 value checks per state; process: two named writer logins, one nightly scorecard under 30 hours old). The baseline passed 1 of 22 and only 2 of 51 states passed every data check. A one-row-per-state scorecard appended nightly drives the publisher, which refuses a state whose latest row fails or is stale; an IDMC rule mapping runs the same checks as rule specifications for the governed view (866 of 867 cells matched SQL). Missing values are tracked, not gated: coverage is source work, not cleanup. Certification = seven consecutive green nights.
evidence: Baseline 1/22 checks, 2/51 states clean, about 697k failing cells (2026-10-29)

title: A key-changing repair caused a duplicate-gate regression that was a flagging gap: re-run dependent flags after the repair instead of reverting it
text: Canonical-duplicate groups jumped from 25 to 33,247 in 20 states the day after a repair that replaced county names used as city names. Joining the new groups to the repair ledger proved every one held a repaired row, and they were sibling parcels (house and vacant lot at one address, one source); they failed only because the shared-address flag that exempts such groups was computed by a job that had last run six weeks earlier and never saw the new keys. Fix = re-run the flagging for the new keys, not revert the cities. After any repair that changes a key or a grouping column, list the derived flags and gates that depend on it and re-run them in the same change; diagnose a regression by joining it to the latest repair's ledger first.
evidence: Dry run 33,245 groups / 131,880 rows matched the gate's 33,247 exactly (2 true repeats left for review) (2026-10-28/29)

title: A case-sensitive key comparison let a duplicate gate pass a state holding about a million duplicates
text: The duplicate gate compared city names case-sensitively, so the same home loaded with upper-case and mixed-case city values counted as two homes and the state read PASS. In the same audit a unit-scaling error (bath counts stored x100) went unnoticed because no range check covered it. Normalise case, whitespace and punctuation before any key comparison in a DQ rule, and add plausibility ranges for every numeric attribute a consumer reads.
evidence: One state PASS while holding 966,502 duplicate homes; 199,984 rows with baths stored x100 (2026-10-29 audit)

title: Missing is not dirty: score completeness separately from validity, and do not promise rules will fill empty attributes
text: In a clean-layer definition, keep fill-rate gaps (no value from any source) apart from validity failures (a wrong value). Rules and cleansing can fix or flag wrong values; empty attributes need a new source or enrichment, and columns that are empty everywhere should be dropped or documented rather than scored as failures. Mixing the two makes a DQ score look hopeless and hides the fixable part.
evidence: Served table: beds filled 39%, baths 40%, sale price 22.5%; 75 of 191 columns completely empty; a later full profile found 84 of 89 columns more than half empty

title: Approximate distinct counts cannot prove a key is unique: use exact counts in key and duplicate checks
text: A warehouse-side profiler first used an approximate distinct function (about 1% error) for sort-key uniqueness, which cannot tell a unique key from one with thousands of duplicates on a large table. Use exact distinct counts (or count minus count-distinct on the key) for uniqueness and duplicate checks, keep approximate functions for cardinality profiling, and bound memory by sampling very large tables.
evidence: Switched uniqCombined (~1%) to uniqExact for key checks; exact counts fit memory up to ~20M rows, larger tables sampled at ~10M (2026-10-29)

title: Profile fill rates before writing rules: a classification column was empty on every row of the target table
text: The newest classification column of a 100M-row served table was empty on all rows; rules bound to it would have failed or passed vacuously. Before building rule specifications or a DQ mapping, run a fill-rate pass over every column the rules read and switch to the populated variant (here the previous taxonomy version that the application still used).
evidence: Classification v3 empty on 100,983,201 of 100,983,201 rows; rules moved to the v2 column (2026-10-29)

title: A DQ status that is PASS on every row is not a gate: silver, gold and a CHECK constraint all produced 100 % 'passed'
text: Three more stamps of the kind in L-DQ-121: all 30.1M silver candidates carried `dq_status = PASS`, so the silver gate held nothing back and every hold happened later at the publisher; a data dictionary's `dq_status = 'passed'` was forced by a CHECK constraint; and assessment mappings hard-coded `dq_status = 'held'`, `serving_eligible = 0` on every row, so nothing could ever be promoted. Before trusting a status column, read its value distribution and the code that writes it; a gate must be able to fail (add a test row that makes it fail) and must be computed from rule results, not written as a constant. Refines L-DQ-121.
evidence: 30.1M of 30.1M silver rows PASS; publisher promoted 77,702 of 22.2M decisions (2026-10-29); all assessment rows held 0/0 (2026-11-01)

title: Address verification aimed at the wrong population: 2.4M 'verified' addresses were reference address points, and 0 of the served properties were verified
text: A generated pipeline reported millions of verified addresses, but they were national address-point reference rows (ids `source-unresolved:*`), not the property situs addresses the product serves; 0 properties of the pilot state had been verified. Before reporting verification coverage, join the verified rows back to the entity table and count per served entity; drive the Verifier from the entity's own address (Cleanse + Verifier in the mastering mapping), and judge 'done' by verified served entities. The rebuilt step verified 2,503,090 situs addresses: 86.5 % verified, 3.3 % unit not confirmed, 9.9 % failed (mostly land parcels with no postal address).
evidence: 2.4M verified reference points vs 0 verified properties before; 86.5 % after (2026-11-01)

title: A standardized-address column that is empty on 34M rows makes 'address present' checks fail wrongly: check presence on the raw column and standardization separately
text: The first DQ/DG evaluator run on a 101M-row mastered table checked `address_canonical` for presence; about 34M rows had a raw address but an empty canonical form, so they counted as 'no address' and the address score was wrong; that run was set aside. Check presence on the raw columns (address or street_address), and score standardization (canonical form filled where a raw address exists) as its own rule; otherwise a standardization gap is reported as missing data. Newer evidence: L-MDM-088.
evidence: About 34M rows with address but empty canonical form; first evaluator run superseded (2026-11-02)

title: A payload fingerprint column filled with the SHA-256 of an empty string looks valid and proves nothing: reject e3b0c442...b855 in the hash rule
text: Every gold row carried `record_payload_sha256` = e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855, the SHA-256 of an empty input, because the publish step hashed a field that was empty at that point; a format-only rule (64 lower-case hex characters) passed it 100 %. Make the fingerprint rule also reject the empty-input hash (and the MD5 d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e if MD5 is used), and hash the record's real content. The same table also carried a constant 'passed' DQ status with no score (L-DQ-121).
evidence: Fingerprint invalid on 100 % of gold rows and 4.1 % of staging rows (2026-11-04)

title: IDMC rule pass rates matched an independent SQL recomputation to 0.01 point on a fixed sample; a moving table drifted 0.2 point between reads
text: On the same hash sample, 10 of 10 gold rule pass rates read from IDMC's metric store equalled an independent ClickHouse SQL recomputation to the hundredth (for example ZIP 75.44, address verified 48.19, lot size 97.85). The staging table, which kept receiving rows between the IDMC run and the SQL read, matched only within 0.2 point. For IDMC-vs-SQL parity, read a sample that cannot change (a frozen sample table or a key-range sample of a quiesced table) and record the read time of each side. Refines L-METHOD-053.
evidence: 10/10 gold checks equal to 0.01; 4 staging checks within 0.2 (2026-11-04/05)

title: A profile reading ClickHouse through an SQL override fails 'java.io.IOException: Premature EOF' when the override's own max_memory_usage cap is too small: ClickHouse killed the query (code 241)
text: A JDBC V2 profile whose SQL Override ends in `SETTINGS max_memory_usage = 4000000000` failed with `[FATAL] java.io.IOException: Premature EOF` about 90 s into the run. The profile job says nothing more. ClickHouse's `system.query_log` (type ExceptionWhileProcessing, exception_code 241) showed the real cause: 'Query memory limit exceeded: would use 3.73 GiB ... maximum: 3.73 GiB', hit while reading a `FINAL` over a ReplacingMergeTree table that a rebuild had just doubled. Fix: back up the profile body, raise the cap inside the override (12 GB worked), PUT the full body, read it back, re-run. So 'Premature EOF' has two causes: the send-timeout stall of L-CDI-267, and a per-query cap that you set yourself and that is too small for the read. Check query_log for code 241 before you tune buffers or proxies. Refines L-CDI-267.
evidence: 5 profile groups over the same 3.19M-row sample: groups 1 and 5 failed Premature EOF with the 4 GB cap; after the PUT (read-back confirmed, bindings kept) the same query peaked at 4.5 GB and all 5 COMPLETED in 5-25 min each (2026-11-04)

title: A profile job can fail in its STAGING_TO_STORE step with 'Health check could not ascertain the status. If possible, may resume automatically.' after the profiling mapping itself COMPLETED; resubmitting worked
text: Execute returns a profileJobId. `GET <profiling-service>/job/<profileJobId>` lists jobSteps of three types: GENERATE_PROFILING_WORKFLOW, PROFILING_MAPPING (the DTM read) and STAGING_TO_STORE (the load into the cloud metric store). One run had a COMPLETED PROFILING_MAPPING (2 min, 'No errors encountered') but a STAGING_TO_STORE that ran 23 minutes and then FAILED with 'Health check could not ascertain the status. If possible, may resume automatically.' The job-level status was FAILED and it did not resume by itself. Read the step list to see which stage failed: a failure in the store step is not a source or SQL problem. Resubmit the same profile unchanged. The second run COMPLETED. Refines L-DQ-106.
evidence: 1.48M-row, 39-column profile: PROFILING_MAPPING 22:57:33-22:59:34Z COMPLETED, STAGING_TO_STORE 22:57:33-23:20:25Z FAILED; the unchanged re-run COMPLETED in about 2.5 min (2026-11-04)

title: A failed profile run does not advance lastRunKey, so the 'latest run' read through runDetail still shows the previous COMPLETED run: track the job id that execute returns
text: After a run failed, `GET /profile/<id>` still had lastRunKey 1, and `GET /runDetail/<id>/1` answered COMPLETED with the previous day's start time and row count. A poller that reads 'the last run' reports a stale green. The reverse also holds: an unchanged run number means no run has completed since then. It does not prove that nobody tried to run it. Keep the profileJobId from `POST /profile/<id>/execute` and decide the outcome from `GET /job/<jobId>` (status plus jobSteps). Before you quote a result, check that the run's startTime is after the change you are measuring. Refines L-DQ-106.
evidence: Job FAILED 2026-11-04 23:20Z; the same profile's lastRunKey stayed 1, and runDetail/1 showed COMPLETED, startTime 2026-11-03 23:29Z, 1,482,161 rows

title: Metric-store column value lists include earlier runs' values: keep only the entries whose totalRows equals the column's current totalRows
text: Reading `Profiles('<id>')/Columns` with their value frequencies after a re-run returned every value twice, once with the previous run's counts and once with this run's (for example 'provisional=803161; provisional=801543'). Summing them double-counts, and a pass rate computed from VALID/INVALID mixes the two runs. Filter each value entry to `totalRows == column.totalRows` (the current run) before computing percentages. If nothing matches, fall back and flag it. Refines L-DQ-123.
evidence: Pairs of near-identical frequencies for every value on re-run profiles; after the filter, 10 of 10 rule pass rates matched an independent SQL recomputation on the same sample to 0.01 % (2026-11-04)

title: Bind independent IDMC rules to the pipeline's own proof columns: a 'passed' DQ stamp with no score, a hash of the empty string and placeholder lineage ids were all fake proofs
text: A golden table carried the pipeline's own evidence columns, and rules run in IDMC showed that none of them measured anything. dq_status was 'passed' on 100 % of rows while dq_score was empty on 100 %. The payload SHA-256 on every row was the hash of an empty string (e3b0c442...b855). The lineage columns named non-IDMC SQL steps ('native:...') on 77 % of rows, and a placeholder mapping id on 72 % of dictionary rows. Add these rules to any table that carries self-reported quality or lineage: a status needs a score; a hash must not equal the empty-input hash and must vary; a lineage id must match a real IDMC object id pattern and resolve to an object. Fix the writer, not the rows. Refines L-DQ-122.
evidence: 100 % / 100 % / 100 % of gold rows on the three proof columns; lineage 76.9 % gold, 48.5 % staging, 72.1 % dictionary rows not backed by IDMC objects; 218 checks over 1,290 columns (2026-11-04)

title: Take closed-list rules from the data dictionary's own enum entries, not from observed values: the dictionary and the pipeline disagreed on half the identity-status values
text: Rules for status and kind columns (record kind, stage, resolution status, model status...) used the dictionary table's enum_value entries as the reference list, the way a reference-data table would be used. That surfaced drift in both directions. The pipeline wrote resolution statuses that the dictionary did not list (failing 50.5 % of gold rows and 37.4 % of staging rows), and dictionary rows themselves used a severity value outside their own list (8.4 %). A list generated from the loaded data would have hidden both (L-DQ-122). Fix by adding the values to the dictionary or mapping them to listed ones, and keep the rule. Refines L-DQ-122.
evidence: 60 rule specifications / 218 checks; resolution status fails 50.5 % gold and 37.4 % staging; dictionary severity outside list 8.4 % (2026-11-04)

title: Rule-spec design that scores raw vs gold fairly: validity rules pass blanks, one 'value present' rule judges emptiness, and the same specs are bound to staging and gold
text: Each rule is an IDMC rule specification with one input and output VALID/INVALID, plus a plain-English description and test data. Format, range and list rules return VALID for an empty value. Emptiness is judged once, by a separate 'required value present' rule on required columns only, so a blank is not counted as both missing and malformed. The same specifications are bound to the raw/staging table and to the golden table, so 'better in gold' is the same check on both. Scores are read from IDMC's metric store (L-DQ-123). SQL is used only to spot-check a sample of pass rates. Refines L-DQ-122.
evidence: 60 rule specifications (40 new) -> 218 checks across 17 profiles and 1,290 columns; 171 checks >= 99 %, 9 at 95-99 %, 38 need a fix; 10/10 SQL spot checks equal to 0.01 % (2026-11-04)

title: The profiling-service list GET /profile ignores offset: page with a large limit and check the count, or a find-by-name after create misses profiles
text: `GET <profiling-service>/api/v1/profile?limit=10&offset=10` returned the same 10 profiles as `?limit=10`, and `?limit=1000` returned all of them. Nothing errors, so a pager that walks offset loops on page one, and a look-up 'by name in GET /profile?limit=200' (the fallback L-DQ-128 gives when the create response has no id) silently misses profiles once the org has more than 200. Use one call with a limit well above the expected count and assert that the returned count is below the limit. Or keep your own name-to-id ledger written at create time. Refines L-DQ-128.
evidence: limit=10 vs limit=10&offset=10: identical first 10; limit=1000 -> 80 profiles (all); the same session later created 300+ profiles (2026-11-05)

title: Define each postal-code column's format before you write its rule: an address-verification output column held ZIP+4 text and failed a 5-digit ZIP rule on half the rows
text: A verifier output column meant to hold the 5-digit ZIP held 'NNNNN-NNNN' on 51.5 % of rows, even though the +4 part was already written to its own column. A 5-digit rule bound to it scored about 48 %, which looked like a verification failure when it was a format choice. Check the profile's pattern list first (9(5) vs 9(5)-9(4)). Record the intended format in the data dictionary. Then either keep 5 digits in the column or define it as ZIP+4 and bind a rule that accepts that format.
evidence: Profile patterns on the column: 9(5)-9(4) 51.49 %, 9(5) 6.4 %; every other verifier output (geocodes, FIPS, census ids, USPS flags) passed 100 % (2026-11-05)

title: Data Profiling stores value frequencies and patterns in the cloud metric store: leave PII columns and raw JSON blobs out of a profile before you create it
text: A profile's results (top values, patterns, min/max) live in Informatica's cloud metric store, not on your agent, so profiling a column copies its values out of your network. When profiling a whole server, build the column list from a PII register plus a name filter (owner, mailing, care-of, grantor/grantee, buyer/seller, taxpayer, first/last/full name, contact, email, phone, SSN, birth, agent/broker, tenant...). Also exclude raw JSON or payload blobs that may embed those fields. Put the count of excluded columns in each profile's description so a reviewer can see the gap. Refines L-DQ-081.
evidence: One server: 10,499 columns planned, 402 excluded (PII register + name filter + payload blobs); a wider plan excluded 1,085 of 32,274 (2026-11-05)

title: Profile a live production ClickHouse without hurting it: a separate agent host, a read-only user, one profile at a time, an off-peak window, a load guard and per-query caps
text: The source served a website at about 30,000 queries an hour, and an earlier full profile run on its own host had overloaded it. What ran clean: the Secure Agent on a different VM, reading over the network with a read-only user. One profile at a time, only inside a fixed window (02:00-13:00Z), pausing whenever the server's load average is above 8. The SQL override ends in `SETTINGS max_threads = 1, max_memory_usage = 2000000000, max_execution_time = 1200, priority = 10`. Each profile reads at most 100,000 rows: all rows for small tables, every Nth granule for large MergeTree tables. The runner keeps a done-ledger so a restart skips finished profiles. Refines L-DQ-098.
evidence: 22 of 315 profiles COMPLETED, 0 failures, about 1.3 min per profile (about 6.5 h for the rest inside the window) before the runner was stopped for an unrelated reason (2026-11-05)

title: Before 'profile everything', inventory the server from its system tables and price the run in profiles and jobs against the org's job cap
text: One read of system.tables/system.columns/system.parts gives databases, engines, row counts and column types. Skip objects a profile cannot or should not read: views, materialized views (and their .inner storage), dictionaries, Join tables, empty tables, external or streaming engines (Kafka, S3, URL, MySQL...) and aggregate-state columns. Plan one profile per table, split by the 4,000-character override limit (L-DQ-133) and about 100 columns. Then multiply out to profiles and jobs and compare with the org's monthly job cap and any other demos that share it before running. Here the full scope was about 1,300 profiles, so the owner chose a 'light' scope: the new server plus one legacy database. Refines L-DQ-133.
evidence: Legacy server: 2,003 objects, 56,672 columns, about 6.1B rows in 29 databases; 1,708 objects not profilable or skipped; 'light' plan 315 profiles for 295 tables; new server 62 objects -> 19 profiles (2026-11-04/05)

title: A data volume mounted with 'nofail' can silently miss the boot: the database then starts on an empty directory and the data looks gone
text: After a power cycle, systemd skipped the data volume's mount because the LVM volume was not active in time ('nofail' turns a failed mount into a silent skip), so the database container's bind mount <mount>/<db-dir> resolved to an empty directory on the root disk. The database came up healthy but with missing databases and empty tables; the real files were intact on the unmounted volume. Diagnose with `findmnt <mount>` (no output = not mounted) and a read-only mount of the device elsewhere to confirm the size; recover by stopping the writers and the database, `mount <mount>` (the empty shadow directory is hidden under the mountpoint, nothing is deleted), then starting the database before the writers.
