Prevent it: replace `nofail` with an ordering dependency (`x-systemd.before=docker.service` plus `RequiresMountsFor=<mount>` on docker.service, L-ENV-032) or a pre-start check that refuses to start the database when the mount is absent. A Secure Agent reading that database through JDBC sees empty tables, not an error. Refines L-ENV-032.
evidence: Database reported 0 rows on a 209,657-row table and missing databases after a power-on; the unmounted volume held about 63 GB; one remount restored every count (2026-08-01)

title: A force-expired OS password blocks every non-interactive key login: 'Password change required but no TTY available'
text: When a provider's password reset (console or API) force-expires root's password, sshd with `UsePAM yes` still accepts the public key but PAM's account phase returns NEW_AUTHTOK_REQD, so every `ssh host 'cmd'`, scp and automation run is refused ('You are required to change your password immediately ... no TTY available'); `ssh -tt` reaches a password-change prompt. Fixes that worked: drive the change once over a PTY (a pexpect script), then `chage -M -1 -m 0 -I -1 -E -1 root` and PASS_MAX_DAYS 99999; because a later provider reset force-expires again regardless of max-days, add a small systemd timer that clears a forced expiry at boot and every 15 minutes on a key-only host. The SFTP subsystem was not blocked by the interactive gate and gave file access meanwhile. This is a different failure from memory pressure (see the sshd OOM candidate): here authentication succeeds and the account phase refuses the session.
evidence: Repeated lockouts of the host running the warehouse and a Secure Agent; after the timer and chage fix, BatchMode key logins exit 0 across three reboots (2026-08-01)

title: Make sshd OOM-immune on a database host that also runs a Secure Agent, or memory pressure locks you out exactly when you need in
text: On an 8 GB host running a warehouse plus a full Secure Agent (about 10 JVMs of 300-550 MB), sshd could not fork at about 2 GB available: logins failed with 'kex_exchange_identification: Connection reset by peer' and the provider's own agent rebooted the box three times in one day. Add a drop-in `/etc/systemd/system/ssh.service.d/10-oom-immune.conf` with `[Service] OOMScoreAdjust=-1000` (auth children inherit it), add swap, cap the database server memory, add a second break-glass key, and create provider monitoring alerts for memory, load and disk (there were none). Do not install fail2ban with defaults on a host whose port 22 is limited to a corporate proxy range: the 'invalid user' log lines came from the operator's own proxy egress, and banning it is the lockout. The durable fix remains moving the agent off the database host (L-AGENT-052).
evidence: 3 reboots in one day, load1 up to 11.7 on 4 vCPU; OOMScoreAdjust -1000 verified on the unit and the live process after a reboot (2026-08-01)

title: A container that runs as a non-root uid can read a root-owned bind-mounted drop folder but not rename files in it, so every file batch errors with 0 records
text: A file-drop ingest container running as uid 1500 read files from a root-owned bind-mounted directory fine, but its consume step (rename to `.done`) failed and errored the whole batch, so nothing landed while HTTP sources kept working. `chown -R <uid>:<gid>` the drop directory (or mount it with the right owner). Separately, the first version moved the file to `.done` BEFORE inserting it, so a failed insert lost the file: always read, insert, verify, then move (and tolerate a file another consumer already moved). The same ordering applies to any file listener or flat-file landing in front of IDMC.
evidence: Batches of 0 records until the chown; one data-loss path removed (2026-07-31/08-01)

title: No backup at all: a ClickHouse FREEZE gives an immediate, near-free guard against a bad write while offsite backup waits for spend approval
text: A 1.6B-row warehouse on one host had no backup of any kind (RPO unbounded) while repairs and loads were running. `ALTER TABLE <db>.<table> FREEZE WITH NAME '<tag>'` on each critical table creates hardlinked immutable parts under the server's `shadow/<tag>/` directory at about zero extra space; it protects against an accidental DROP, a bad backfill or a logical corruption, but not against losing the disk or the host. Use it as the zero-cost first step, then get the offsite backup approved (spend rule) and drill a restore. Remove the frozen parts when the offsite copy is verified, or they pin disk as merges replace parts.
evidence: 14 tables frozen with no measurable disk growth; offsite DR still pending approval at the time (2026-08-02)

title: Rebuild a derived table into a staging table and swap atomically: truncate-then-insert left it empty every night when the insert ran out of memory
text: A nightly step did TRUNCATE and then one INSERT ... SELECT over the whole source with FINAL; the insert exceeded the server memory cap, the truncate had already succeeded, and the derived provenance table sat at 1 row (it should hold about 430M) for days while the job log said 'FAIL' only in a file nobody read. Fix: build per partition (`... FINAL WHERE state = 'XX'` merges one partition at a time) into `<table>_staging`, then `EXCHANGE TABLES <table> AND <table>_staging` only if the row count clears a floor; the live table is never empty. For heavy ad-hoc counts on such tables use `uniq()` (HLL) or per-partition aggregation; a global `uniqExact` over 430M ids exceeded a 1.86 GB per-user limit. The same staging-and-swap rule applies to any IDMC target that is fully rebuilt (write to a staging table, swap with the target's Post SQL).
evidence: Derived table at 1 row after two nights of failures; per-state rebuild about 15 min without hitting the cap; true size about 430M rows (2026-08-02)

title: ReplacingMergeTree only dedups on background merges: a re-ingest doubled a partition and every reader without FINAL served each row twice
text: A ReplacingMergeTree property table that was re-ingested for one state held exactly 2x the true rows until merges ran; the application, its counts, its type-ahead and an ML comparables corpus all read without FINAL and so served or trained on every record twice. Later on another estate the gold table held 141,768 extra row versions and a market table about 7.5 %. Readers (including IDMC source queries and profile SQL overrides) must use FINAL, and pinning one partition with `SETTINGS do_not_merge_across_partitions_select_final = 1` keeps FINAL cheap (a city browse 49 ms / 4.8 MiB); 'cheap dedup' alternatives such as many `uniqExactIf` or `LIMIT 1 BY` over the whole state cost 7-16 s and about 1 GB. Benchmark a fix against the correct alternatives, not against the buggy no-dedup query. `OPTIMIZE ... FINAL` per partition, outside writer runs, removes the versions without changing values.
evidence: Partition held 5,030,606 rows vs 2,515,303 true (exactly 2x); gold 141,768 extra versions (2026-08-04, 2026-10-29)

title: A running app container can hold a live-only code edit (hot-reload bind mount) that exists in no image: rebuild from the running container's source
text: On an application host built in place, an override compose file bind-mounted the backend source with `--reload`, so an emergency fix edited inside the container lived in no image and would vanish on the next recreate. Before rebuilding or redeploying, diff the running container's source against the image (`docker exec <c> md5sum ...`), and build the new image FROM the currently running tag (or from the container's /app/src) so both your fix and any peer's live fix survive; afterwards grep the running container for both markers. Always pass the compose project name explicitly (`docker compose -p <project> ...`): a `current` symlink directory made compose infer a new project and start a duplicate container.
evidence: Live-only guard found in the running backend (container source hash differed from the image); one duplicate container created and removed (2026-08-04/05)

title: ClickHouse memory walls on a small shared host were baseline RSS, not query size: settle merges and purge jemalloc before each heavy mutation, never restart mid-loop
text: A per-state ALTER UPDATE backfill kept failing with code 241 although each mutation was small. Causes, in order: RSS stayed high after each big mutation (merges plus jemalloc retention) and the next one started on top; `memory_worker_correct_memory_tracker` makes the server tracker follow RSS, so `max_server_memory_usage` caps RSS directly; and a restart inflates RSS for 60-90 s of warm-up, so restarting mid-loop and immediately running the next state made it worse. What worked: quiesce the host (stop the Secure Agent and other heavy writers), raise the server cap to about 0.8 of RAM, before each state wait until merges drain and run `SYSTEM JEMALLOC PURGE` until resident memory is below a floor, skip states with nothing to fill (a cheap precheck), and set a per-query `max_memory_usage` on the build and the ALTER. A Secure Agent sharing the host (one Data Gateway process was about 1.16 GB) can push a query over the cap at random; retry when merges are idle.
evidence: Peak RSS held under the 6.2 GB cap on a 7.76 GB host for every state after the change; earlier drivers that restarted per large state kept failing (2026-08-20)

title: ClickHouse also constant-folds an external-table value into expression names, so an error message logs it: keep secrets out of warehouse SQL entirely
text: After moving a hashing salt out of query parameters (which ClickHouse 25.3 writes to query_log, text_log and the server log, L-ENV-078) into an external-table POST body, the salt still leaked: ClickHouse constant-folds the value into the expression's name, so any failing query prints it in the exception text and logs. Hash outside the warehouse (in the exporter) or use a key that is not secret; never put a secret into ClickHouse SQL in any form. Also: a quick 'mask' such as `sed 's/=.*/=<MASK>/'` over a one-value-per-line credential file prints the value lines that have no '=', and one lane leaked a password into its transcript that way; never print any line of a credential file (L-METHOD-087). Refines L-ENV-078.
evidence: Found while building a hash-stratified PII-masked sample; one transcript redaction needed (2026-10-04)

title: A planned teardown never ran because its auto-delete schedule was disabled, and a small budget never fired because budgets alert on recorded spend
text: A trial environment meant to delete itself before the trial ended was still present weeks later: its kill schedule had been found disabled and was never re-enabled, and the small budget meant as a backstop had recorded $0 so it could not trigger. Budgets are alerts on billed spend (which can lag or exclude the meter you care about), not caps. Verify auto-delete schedules are enabled and have actually run, and keep a dated teardown item on the tracker as the real backstop.
evidence: Auto-delete schedule disabled; $10 budget recorded $0; resource groups deleted manually on review (2026-10-27)

title: ClickHouse readonly=1 rejects every SETTINGS clause: read-only diagnostic sessions need readonly=2
text: A laptop read-only query helper ran `clickhouse-client --readonly=1`; any query carrying `SETTINGS max_memory_usage = ...` or `max_threads` (needed to keep reads safe on a live server) failed because readonly=1 also forbids changing settings. `--readonly=2` keeps writes and DDL blocked but allows per-query settings. Do not alias a column `sample` either: it is a keyword in ClickHouse SELECT syntax.
evidence: Shared-address dry runs needed SETTINGS under the read-only login (2026-10-28)

title: A nightly database backup that 'works' covered only 2 of the databases, failed every night on dictionaries, and copied 176 GB of backup tables
text: An inventory of every backup found that the scheduled cloud export named only two databases, so the gold, silver, bronze, site and ML databases had no cloud copy at all; it also exited 1 every night on five dictionary objects (so its alert was permanently red and ignored), re-uploaded about 176 GB of in-database '_bak' tables, and copied unchanged tables server-side each night instead of referencing them (8 sets of about 180 GB = 1.42 TiB). Before trusting a backup, list what it covers against the live database list (`SHOW DATABASES` vs the script's list), exclude backup/scratch tables by pattern, export dictionaries as schema only, make 'unchanged' a reference not a copy, and run a restore drill of one partition of the most important table into scratch with a row-count compare. Until the nightly covers a database, in-database repair copies are its only spare: do not drop them first. Refines L-ENV-038.
evidence: Scope 2 of 6 databases; red 8 nights running; 1.42 TiB of cloud sets; 0 restore drills ever run (measured 2026-10-29)

title: Repair 'backups' kept as tables inside the database pile up: 530 tables, 190 GB, 464 copies of 150 table-state pairs on a 91 % full disk
text: Every data repair lane took its own full copy of the partition it touched (`<table>_<state>_<pass>_bak`, wave snapshots, pre-migration copies), and nobody dropped them, so one state's table had six stacked copies and the database disk reached 91 %. Policy that replaced it: two backups only, both off the server (a nightly set of every kept database, and one frozen baseline = the OLDEST copy of each repaired pair, in cold storage with a 90-day expiry); a repair takes a partition backup only for the minutes of its swap and drops it once verified, keeping a small field-level undo ledger (old value, new value per cell) for 90 days; a janitor drops any unregistered `_bak`/`_snap_`/`__pre_`/scratch table older than 7 days; every drop re-checks the table is unchanged since the inventory, unread for 7 days and referenced by no view. Mutations need free disk, so this matters before any large IDMC write.
evidence: 530 tables / 190.5 GB = 464 copies of 150 pairs; keeping the oldest per pair = 64 GB; disk 534 of 590 GB used (2026-10-29)

title: A shell helper that wraps `docker exec -i` swallows a while-loop's stdin, and a trailing `grep -v` makes a successful DDL look failed
text: Two shell traps from database maintenance scripts: (1) a helper like `chq() { docker exec -i <container> clickhouse-client ...; }` called inside `while read x; do ...; done < list` reads the rest of the list as its own stdin, so the loop runs once; pass `</dev/null` to the helper inside loops. (2) a helper that filters noise with `| grep -v <pattern>` returns exit 1 when the output is empty, so a DDL that worked (and printed nothing) is reported as failed; use `grep -v ... || true` only around the filter, and check the statement's own result. Related: `pkill -f <script path>` over a remote shell kills your own ssh command (L-METHOD-113). Refines L-ENV-036.
evidence: Seen in the storage-consolidation scripts (2026-10-29)

title: ClickHouse query_log tables[] lists the tables a query reads as well as the one it writes: filter on query_kind and the target before calling a login a writer
text: When auditing who writes a table, `system.query_log` rows whose `tables` array contains the table include every SELECT and every INSERT ... SELECT that only reads it, so readers show up as 'writers'. Filter on `query_kind IN ('Insert','Alter','Drop','Create','Rename')` and on the statement's target, and use `initial_user` (not `user`) when a remote() or proxy hop is involved. The same audit, done correctly, showed the gold table was written by the publisher login and by the shared admin login; see the 'one door into gold' candidate.
evidence: Liveness/writer inventory of 2,437 tables (2026-10-29)

title: Restructure a warehouse by moving tables, not renaming databases, when hundreds of code files reference the names
text: A target layout of a few purpose-built databases (raw, cleaned, served, site build, ML, ops) kept the existing names for the six survivors and folded the rest in, because about 800 code files referenced them. The first move turns the legacy tables the served layer still reads through views into real tables in the served database, with undo SQL, rehearsed on a scratch copy.
evidence: 29 databases -> 6; ~800 code files used the names; first move: 17 legacy tables (7.6 GB) read by served views

title: Enforce one writer on the served layer: a named repair login, the shared admin login read-only there, and an alert on any other writer
text: The query log showed writes to the served database from several logins (application, default admin, a test user, an ML user) although only the controlled publisher was meant to write it, and every repair ran as the shared admin login, so repairs could not be traced or limited. Give the publisher and the repair path their own logins, make the others read-only on the served database, and alert nightly on any write by another user.
evidence: 4 unexpected writer logins on the served database in the query log; all repairs used the shared admin login (2026-10-29)

title: An approved infrastructure change can still be impossible: test the identity's permission before promising it, and expect expired human tokens in non-interactive sessions
text: A disk resize the owner had approved could not be done: the automation service account and both VM service accounts lacked the resize permission, and every human cloud login on the workstation had expired, which cannot be refreshed from a non-interactive session. The same expired token later blocked a cost report and a status check. Before committing to an infra change, call the cloud's read-only permission test (GCP testIamPermissions) for the exact permission on the exact resource, name the one human step if no identity has it, and keep a scoped automation identity for routine operations you expect (disk resize, billing read). Refines L-ENV-070.
evidence: compute.disks.resize missing on 3 service accounts; 'Reauthentication failed. cannot prompt during non-interactive execution' on 10-27, 10-29, 11-02 and 11-06; disk resize 600 -> 800 GB stayed blocked

title: ClickHouse JSON output quotes 64-bit integers as strings, and FixedString NUL padding breaks text wrappers
text: Inventory scripts reading ClickHouse `FORMAT JSON` results failed when summing row counts because UInt64/Int64 values are emitted as quoted strings by default (output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1). Cast in the reader, or set the setting to 0 for that query. From the same work: FixedString columns carry NUL padding that breaks grep-based wrappers, so read them through JSON output or trim them in SQL.
evidence: Inventory of 2,494 objects / 100,909 columns failed on the first sum until converted (2026-10-29)

title: A temporary bulk-load tweak (fsync off) stayed in force on the target tables after the load and nobody noticed
text: To speed a bulk load into a new ClickHouse target, a session created a temporary async-insert settings profile for the IDMC writer user and, at the same time, set `fsync_after_insert = 0, fsync_part_directory = 0` on two target tables. The profile was dropped eight minutes later; the table settings were never reverted, so the only copy of the migrated data was being written without fsync. Any performance change made for a load (table settings, profiles, server settings) must be listed with its undo and reverted in the same run; read back `SHOW CREATE TABLE` and `system.settings_profiles` afterwards. An independent read-only critic found it from the DDL history in `system.query_log`.
evidence: Profile created 21:34:26Z and dropped 21:42:25Z; table fsync settings still off the next morning (2026-10-31/11-01)

title: A whole-project failure at one minute was a VM reboot by another session's resize: check the host's boot time before debugging the jobs
text: Every workflow of a project failed within the same minute. The cause was not IDMC: `uptime -s` (and `last reboot`) on the host of the target database and the Secure Agent showed a boot at that minute, which matched another session's VM resize. Before diagnosing a simultaneous failure of many jobs, read the agent host's boot time, the database's uptime and the agent's disconnect events; and before resizing or rebooting a shared host, tell every session and job that uses it and drain them first (L-ENV-069). Refines L-ENV-069.
evidence: All project workflows failed at 20:32Z; host boot time 20:31:58Z; 134 agent disconnects recorded over the migration (2026-10-31)

title: A new database host that holds the only copy of migrated data had no backup timer, one local backup on the same disk, and a backup worker that failed on the new table
text: A read-only critic of a migration found that the new target VM had no backup timer, one 85 GB local backup folder on the same disk as the data (never restore-tested), a backup worker that asserted exactly two tables and so failed once a third table existed, and a backup user without BACKUP grant on that table, while the legacy host was already being prepared for retirement. Rule: a migration target becomes 'safe to be the only copy' only after an off-host backup of every table has run and a restore drill passed; check the worker's own table list and the backup user's grants whenever a table is added.
evidence: 0 backup timers; 85 GB backup on the data disk; worker failing on 3 tables vs an asserted 2 (2026-11-01)

title: Cost run-rate without a billing export: a temporary 32-vCPU scale-up, stopped VMs' disks and an unmanaged backup bucket were the big items
text: Asked what the cloud costs per month, there was no billing export and no API that returns spend without one, so the estimate came from an inventory of resources times the public on-demand rates. The largest items were a 'temporary' scale-up of the migration VM (the biggest line, still in place days later), disks and a machine image of a stopped restore VM, 62 snapshots (5 TB) and a backup bucket with no lifecycle that grew every day. Before scaling back, measure the real need: the database used 69 GB of an 80 GB container cap, so the planned 64 GB machine would not fit and the safe step down was 128 GB. Turn on the billing export to BigQuery on day one, put an end date on every temporary scale-up, and set lifecycle rules on backup buckets.
evidence: Estimated run-rate about $3,050/month (range 2,900-3,200); host CPU averaged 71 % (p90 98 %) during the IDMC national backfill (2026-11-02)

title: Address verification at full scale was unknown spend: an IPU-metered licence with no visible meter, and a throughput that implied 10-42 days
text: A plan to verify about 135M candidate addresses on a Trial-edition org ran into three unknowns: the address verification licence was IPU-metered with no meter visible in the org, the on-agent engine ran one function server with no preload at about 160 addresses/s (about 9.8 days nonstop, about 42 days at the scheduled cadence), and the candidate set itself was still moving. A delete in the target also reset both progress cursors, so pipelines re-verified addresses they had already done. Before a national verification sweep: get the metering answer and the spend approval, tune the engine (preload, function servers), drive the sweep from 'already has a result for this input' (L-CDI-283), and classify failed rows first so the run is not repeated (L-DQ-129).
evidence: 160 addresses/s measured on 11-01; 550-600/s per DTM after tuning on the same agent type the same day (2026-11-01)

title: Mass Ingestion is metered by data moved, so agent tuning cuts its IPUs only by avoiding failed re-runs
text: When a customer's IPU growth comes from Mass Ingestion, Secure Agent tuning (memory, per-job heap, parallel tasks, cores, write batch size, a dedicated host) makes loads faster and more reliable, but consumption is metered per GB moved for loads and per million rows for CDC, not per runtime hour. Savings come mainly from moving less data: CDC after the initial load, only the tables and columns used, schedules matched to freshness needs, no duplicate tasks, and filtering archive rows at source. Ask for the task list with GB or rows per run before sizing an increase. Refines L-IPU-003.
evidence: Customer review framing prepared 2026-11-10; metering per the published consumption table

title: Verify that sources actually conflict before designing an MDM survivorship demo: two stores were a byte-identical mirror, so survivorship had nothing to decide
text: A property MDM plan was built on 'MDM reconciles the warehouse against the document store'. An adversarial check of 800 records x 22 fields found the two stores were a byte-identical mirror of one public source (0 divergence, no parcel with more than one source), so a conflict-survivorship demo would have fired on nothing. Measure overlap and per-field divergence between candidate sources first; if none, design a single-source mechanics track (1:1, fuzzy off) and a separate real two-source track on a small area. The same review removed claims that were not in evidence: a 'percent headless' figure, undocumented record-state tokens, and a per-call address limit that does not exist; pin such terms against a live record read and the product documentation.
evidence: 0 divergence across 800 x 22 fields; plan rebuilt as a 98,115-row single-source track plus a 9,105-row two-source track (2026-08-03)

title: After every golden-table rebuild, compare its row count and identity-status mix with the previous build before you declare it done: one rebuild silently doubled the table with held provisional records
text: An overnight rebuild of a one-row-per-entity golden table wrote 203.9M rows, about twice the 101M of the previous build. 50.5 % of them were provisional identities (provisional address, provisional parcel or source-id-only). The serving gate held: none of the provisional rows were serving or ML eligible. But every mastering rule fell to about 49-52 % (class mastered, identity confirmed, address verified), so the table-level score dropped and looked like a data regression. Add a post-build check: total rows, distinct entity ids and rows by resolution status against the last build, with a tolerance. Score eligible rows and all rows separately. Then decide whether held records belong in the golden table at all. Refines L-MDM-079.
evidence: Golden table 203.9M rows written over about 20 h; 50.5 % provisional (21.9 % address, 21.2 % parcel, 7.3 % source id); confirmed rows 66.9 % serving; gold rule score 90.3 % (2026-11-04)

title: Reconcile predicted against realized counts after every bulk fill: a 2M-row gap exposed a silent TSV NULL-encoding bug
text: A class-recovery backfill predicted about 2M more recovered rows than it realized. The gap traced to a `sed` substitution that never matched real tabs, so `\N` stayed in a non-nullable column, ClickHouse read it as an empty string, and 6,526 keys never joined. When correct, prediction and realization matched within 3 rows. For every bulk fill or IDMC backfill, compute the expected changed-row count first (a dry-run SELECT), compare with the realized count afterwards, and stop on any gap above noise; convert NULL markers with a byte-safe parser (some source text was Windows-1252, so a UTF-8 decode crashed), not with sed.
evidence: Predicted vs realized gap about 2M rows before the fix, 3 rows after (2026-07-31)

title: Six parallel audit subagents declared governance absent because they never found the cron-driven DQ system: inventory schedulers before concluding something is missing
text: A six-subagent audit of a warehouse host reported that DQ governed only about 45 demo rows, DQ was single-state and lineage absent, and recommended 'running the DQ job across all states'. Live recon the same day found a mature nightly per-state gate system under a root home directory and an ingest SQL folder (48 states, 106M rows, 24 PASS / 0 FAIL), and the column the audit read as a DQ output was a vestigial upstream source field: backfilling it would have fabricated flags. Before concluding that a capability is absent, list crontabs, systemd timers, scheduler DAGs and IDMC schedules on every host, and grep the scripts for the table names; give the audit's headline to a refute-only verifier (L-METHOD-046). Refines L-METHOD-046.
evidence: 3 of the audit's 4 headline findings reversed by live recon (2026-08-02)

title: A peer session overwrote the reviewed SQL file between review and run, so the run executed the peer's SQL: hash the artifact right before running it
text: On a shared database host, a reviewed promote script was validated in a scratch clone and run two minutes later, but a peer agent had meanwhile overwritten the files on the host with its own design, so the run executed the peer's SQL against the production table; the peer then ran two more DROP PARTITION + reload cycles. `who` and `last` showed nothing (the peer used its own connection); the tells were file mtimes and `system.query_log`/`system.processes`/`system.mutations`. Rules: compare the hash of your local artifact with the copy that will run immediately before running it; check query_log for writes to the target by others in the last 30 minutes and wait for quiescence; correct a peer's result by an in-place scoped UPDATE, never by re-dropping a partition a peer may be refilling; and prove safety by checking that non-target rows are unchanged. Refines L-METHOD-072.
evidence: Peer ran 2 extra partition reload cycles; correction by in-place UPDATE of 15,852 rows; non-target total unchanged at 108,633,427 (2026-08-03)

title: A request-path scan cached per worker made a dashboard spin forever after each deploy: persist expensive summaries in a snapshot table
text: A coverage page computed a per-partition FINAL scan of 51 partitions in the request (about 60 s cold) and cached it in a per-worker in-process cache for 5 minutes; after every deploy both workers were cold and the page sat on 'Loading'. The 30 s worker timeout did not fire because a sync route runs in a threadpool, so there was no error to see. Fix: persist the result in a snapshot table (one row, JSON payload, computed_at) shared by all workers and restarts, serve it instantly, and refresh it in the background when it is older than a threshold. The same applies to any dashboard over IDMC outputs: precompute in the pipeline, never in the request.
evidence: 60 s cold path; 0.01-0.05 s after the snapshot (2026-08-04)

title: When telling someone where assets are, give the org name and the full pod URL: they looked in another pod's project list and found nothing
text: After a build, the user opened the project explorer from a bookmark on a different pod (a different org) and reported the folder missing; the assets were in another org on another pod. In every hand-off, state the org name, the pod host URL of the exact page and the login host, and offer to rebuild in the other org only if it has an agent that reaches the data.
evidence: User link on one pod, assets on another; explained and resolved without rebuilding (2026-10-29)

title: Stopping another session's jobs does not stop their schedules: two enabled schedules with no owner were set to fire again
text: Three sessions received overlapping directives for one IDMC project. One stopped 12 running jobs and a workflow of an earlier build through the API, while another created new mappings in folders whose numeric prefixes collided with the old ones; the two schedules that drove the stopped workflows stayed enabled, so they would fire again at the next boundary. Before any session writes, settle one owner per folder and object family in a coordination file (owner, folders, mapgen profile, state directory, 'will not touch' list); when stopping jobs, also unbind or disable their schedules (with a backup of the workflow body) and read the schedule back at the next boundary (L-METHOD-040). Refines L-METHOD-060. Newer evidence: L-DQ-162.
evidence: 12 jobs stopped at 06:12Z; 2 schedules still enabled afterwards; ownership file written at 06:35Z (2026-11-01)

title: Never edit a lane runner's manifest or state file while the runner is running: it rewrites the file from memory
text: A resumable lane runner (detached, state in JSON, manifest in JSONL) that drives IDMC capture tasks keeps its state in memory and rewrites the state file on every step, so an edit made to the manifest or state while it runs is silently overwritten. Stop the runner, edit, then restart it; new items also need their staged parameter files on the agent first, or each try fails 'param install failed' and the item is marked failed after three tries.
evidence: Seen on the 12-lane capture runner (2026-11-01)

title: When the user describes a deployment the board and docs don't show, inventory the live estate before asking: the real build lived on a new VM made in one day by sessions that never wrote to the board
text: Asked where a deployment stood, the session searched the task board (every project, closed cards too) and local plan files. It found a month-old README and an unrelated six-database plan, presented that, and asked the user, who had to correct it: 'no, there is a new VM'. The real system had been built in about 24 hours by another coding agent's sessions. They left one untriaged card and no project card, so the board could not have answered. The next look worked: list IDMC projects and folders by updateTime (one project, created that day, held 600+ new objects) and list the cloud VMs. Treat the board and README as possibly stale, check the live sources first, and only then report or ask. Refines L-METHOD-079.
evidence: IDMC project created 00:35Z, last change 23:48Z the same day: 303 mappings + 301 tasks, 104 taskflows, 28 profiles; board: 1 untriaged card (2026-11-01)

title: An agentless runtime binding can be deliberate: 'fixing' it re-armed lanes the owner had retired
text: A session found a dozen capture tasks and a reconcile task bound to a runtime environment with 0 agents and rebound them to a live runtime, thinking they were broken; the binding was a deliberate block placed the day before after the owner retired those lanes. It was reverted ten minutes later before any run. Before 'repairing' a binding, a disabled schedule or a stopped task, read the tracker card and its comments for that object (and the coordination file); treat an agentless runtime as a possible off-switch, and record such blocks in the object's description so the next session sees them.
evidence: 12 tasks rebound at 22:20Z and reverted at 22:30Z with no runs (2026-11-02)

title: Validate your own DQ evaluator before reporting it: an empty canonical column read as 'no address' and a script name was accepted as lineage
text: A home-built DQ/DG evaluator produced a first scorecard whose address checks were wrong (it read an empty, not-yet-filled canonical column as 'no address'), and its lineage check passed rows whose lineage was just a script name. It also flagged 6 'duplicate' groups that were different feeds sharing one name. Seed each check with a known-good and a known-bad row, require real runtime ids for lineage, inspect a sample behind every headline number before sharing it, and set aside (do not quietly overwrite) a run found wrong.
evidence: First run discarded and re-run (~13 min); 'duplicates' renamed, nothing merged; after the fix IDMC's rule score matched the evaluator exactly on one table (2026-11-02)

title: Deferring work for shared load or another session's lease needs a bounded wait and a capped fallback: the user had to push 'make it happen now'
text: A read-only evaluation paused itself for more than 20 minutes while another session loaded the shared VM, and IDMC profile runs were not started because that session held the project lease. The user had to ask for both to happen as soon as possible. When yielding to shared load, state the condition and the maximum wait, then fall back automatically to a capped run (fewer threads, memory limit); read-only job runs in a leased project can usually go ahead with a note on the lease holder's card.
evidence: Paused at load 30-44 on 32 cores; restarted with no waits at 4 threads; profiles completed within ~15 minutes (2026-11-02)

title: A filled-in credential template stayed inside a shareable KB for days because each session only noted it
text: A login template file in the KB was filled with a real username and password. The KB's own share gate flagged it, and at least three sessions over several days reported it as 'not mine, needs your decision' and moved on. A secret in a share-bound artefact is a stop-the-line item: blank the values (keep the template), tell the owner to rotate the password, add the file to the ignore list, and put it as the first line of the report rather than a footnote.
evidence: Flagged 10-29, 11-01 and 11-02; empty template confirmed on 11-10 before publishing

title: A reaped lease left a critical-path step with no owner: when a lease expires, reassign its open steps explicitly
text: In a timed run to 'tables ready', the owning session's lease on the target database and IDMC project was reaped at midnight while one step (Certified address verification of 2.27M properties in 8 states, then re-gating them) was still assigned to it; the timeline then showed that step as 'needs an owner' and ready slipped. A reaper that frees locks must also list the steps the expired lease owned and post them for reassignment (or hand them to the lead), not just release the objects. Refines L-METHOD-062.
evidence: Lease reaped 00:00Z; 2,273,173 properties without the step; readiness 05:15Z without it vs 06:00Z with it (2026-11-03)

title: Customer-facing KB rules: describe how the process works, not internal failure rates; give open guidance, not a push toward one technology
text: Owner corrections while building a shareable IDMC knowledge base: do not disclose failure or pass rates from internal test runs, only the method; do not steer readers to a particular technology or treat every limitation in the KB as forbidden; remove all personal, company and project names. Write lessons as options and conditions ('if X, consider Y'), keep measured numbers for product behaviour, and keep internal outcome metrics out.
evidence: Three corrections during one KB version build (2026-11-03)

title: Publishing scrubbers need a rule for every identifier class: a payment account id passed one, and compiled Python caches carried the author's home path
text: A build script that published a skill from internal lessons scrubbed org names, IPs, emails and paths but had no rule for payment-provider account ids, so one went out in a reference file and was copied to 7 places. Separately, 42 .pyc files in three __pycache__ folders embedded the author's absolute home path. Before publishing: delete __pycache__ and add `__pycache__/` and `*.pyc` to .gitignore, add patterns for every vendor id format you handle (payment, cloud subscription, org ids), scan binaries and Office metadata too, and run the secret scan as the last step before push.
evidence: 1 account id in 7 copies; 42 .pyc files with the user path; a live secret key also found in a plain-text archive file (rotation advised); final scan CLEAN on 643 files (2026-11-03 to 2026-11-10)

title: Answer 'how does our pipeline do X' from the exported live assets and run history, not from docs or memory: the remembered method was the wrong component
text: Asked for a prompt explaining how address verification works, the session first wrote one from docs and memory. The user pushed back twice ('go into IDMC and look at how I've done it'). Exporting the live mapping showed the method was not the remembered Data Quality Verifier transformation. It was a CDI Java transformation calling the cloud Address Verification REST service in Certified mode (L-DQ-132), reading from and writing back to the warehouse. The reliable order: list the folder's assets, read run history for the ones that actually ran, v3-export one and read its transformation code, then write the explanation. Quote dates and say what was not re-checked. Refines L-DQ-132. Newer evidence: L-METHOD-157.
evidence: 4 sharded mappings found by inventory + run history + one v3 export; first draft written from memory had the wrong verification path (2026-11-03)

title: A handoff prompt for someone else's org must match their stack and carry the lessons the task implies: the user corrected one draft three times
text: A how-to prompt for a colleague's Claude session went through three user corrections. (1) 'Don't mention our own app, this is for a new org': all our names, ids, hosts and board keys had to go. (2) 'They don't have a VM or ClickHouse': the steps had to fit their actual source and target (flat file to Oracle) and their toolkit's limits (the generator had no Oracle target template, so: learn it from one exemplar mapping, L-METHOD-129). (3) 'This doesn't include the address lessons': their mapping was named for address verification, so the proven verification lessons had to go in as a gated Part 2. Checklist before sending: generic names only, the recipient's connectors and runtime, the generator's known gaps, and the domain lessons, with a stop point.
evidence: Three rewrites in about 25 minutes; final prompt = Part 1 (trim to Oracle) + Part 2 (address verification, do not build until told) (2026-11-03)

title: Before quoting a DQ score, check that the profile's last completed run is newer than the table's last write: a planned overnight re-run had not happened and the swap had changed the table
text: Asked for the current profile of five tables, the session found the most recent scorecard was 1-2 days old. The 're-run at about 05:15Z' in the plan never took place, and the table had since been swapped and rebuilt, so every quoted score described a different table. One profiled table had never run at all. Rule: put each score next to its run's end time, plus the table's latest write time (max load timestamp, or the newest part's modification time). Mark a score stale when the write is newer. Read the run from the job, not the 'last run' pointer (see the lastRunKey gotcha). Refines L-METHOD-041.
evidence: Last profile runs 13:40-15:55Z on day 1; planned re-run on day 2 missing; 1 of 5 tables never profiled; the gold table was rebuilt later that night (2026-11-03)

title: Claude Code reaps a laptop background shell under memory pressure: run multi-hour IDMC orchestrators on a server, with a done-ledger
text: A 6-hour off-peak profiling runner started as a Claude Code background command on a laptop was stopped after about 2 h, with the message 'stopped because the system is running low on memory'. The harness tells the session not to restart it on its own (the reaper can be turned off with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BG_SHELL_PRESSURE_REAP=1). Nothing broke in IDMC, because the runner submitted one profile at a time and kept a ledger of finished ones. But the work stopped until a human came back, and the laptop also had to stay awake and online for the whole window. Run long orchestrators on the agent VM or another server, detached (setsid/nohup or a scheduler, L-ENV-006), with a resumable ledger. Keep only short polls in the chat session. Refines L-ENV-006.
evidence: Runner killed at 02:21Z after 22 of 315 profiles; 0 IDMC jobs left running; restart resumes from the ledger (2026-11-05)

title: Label where every lesson came from: a slide presented general best practice and another project's fixes as 'your lessons'
text: Asked for a slide of lessons from one deployment, the first draft mixed that deployment's real fixes with fixes from other projects and generic best practice, all labelled as the user's lessons; the user had to ask whether they were real. Tag every claim with its provenance (this project, another project, general guidance) while drafting, say so plainly in the answer, and when the audience is a customer, generalise the wording instead of borrowing specifics.
evidence: v1 -> v2 rebuilt with verified items only -> v3 generalised on request -> v4 rebranded (2026-11-10)

title: Consolidate many warehouse databases into a few without copying data: Atomic RENAME TABLE, pause and repoint the writer, leave a read-only view at the old name
text: To fold 29 databases into six by purpose (bronze, silver, gold, site, ML, ops), count code references first (about 800 files named the existing databases, so the six kept their old names and only tables moved). With Atomic databases a move is metadata only: pause the table's writer (cron, lane, publisher, IDMC task), `RENAME TABLE <old_db>.<t> TO <new_db>.<t>`, change dependent views, repoint the writer (for IDMC: the connection's schema or the task's target), resume, compare row counts, and keep a read-only view at the old name for 14 days, dropping it once `query_log` shows no reader. Generate the move, its undo and the per-table writer list from the live inventory, and rehearse on a scratch copy before the GO. A JDBC V2 profile or mapping only sees its connection's own database (L-DQ-134), so a consolidation also cuts the number of IDMC connections needed.
evidence: Plan for 1,648 kept tables; first phase 17 tables / 7.6 GB generated with undo, not yet run (2026-10-29)

title: A lightweight DELETE in the target hid 49.5M rows that IDMC had loaded: counts looked like missing data, and the rows were recoverable only until merges
text: During a lossless migration through IDMC, a cleanup DELETE (ClickHouse lightweight delete) masked rows that the capture lanes had already loaded, so per-table target counts fell far below what IDMC reported (for example 41.6M source rows loaded, 0 visible). The rows were still physically on disk and readable with `SETTINGS apply_deleted_mask = 0` until background merges purged them, which made recovery time-sensitive. Before reconciling an IDMC load against a target, read `system.mutations` and the DDL history for deletes on the target; compare IDMC's success rows with both visible and masked counts; and never run a delete on a migration target without a copy-out or an approved decision, because it also resets any progress cursor kept in the target.
evidence: 50,056,845 physical vs 507,919 visible bronze rows (49,548,926 masked across 147 source tables); run manifests 873 physical vs 61 visible (2026-11-01)

title: Constraints added to a target in the middle of a load reject rows that loaded fine an hour earlier, and the earlier rows were never checked
text: A session added four CHECK constraints (state, year built, living area, geo shape) to a migration target while IDMC lanes were loading; later batches started failing with code 469 on rows of the same shape that had loaded before, and every row loaded earlier was never checked against the new rules. Freeze the target DDL for the duration of a load; if a rule must be added, add it before the first batch or run it as a DQ check (an IDMC rule specification or a scoring mapping) over the whole table afterwards, not as a constraint mid-load.
evidence: 4 constraints at 23:35Z; one lane failed code 469 on a payload checksum constraint (2026-10-31/11-01)

title: 'Everything is in the new tables' cannot be proven while the scope stops at one database engine and the source keeps changing
text: A completeness critic of a 'move everything into 3 tables' migration found the auditors had inventoried only the warehouse: a 27 GB PostgreSQL property database, 12 MongoDB ML collections, a graph database, model files and cloud archives were never listed, and 155 of 251 model files were missing from the target. The legacy warehouse was still being written by crons, an application and the publisher while counts were taken, so no count stayed true. Before claiming a migration complete: inventory every store the product reads (each engine on the host, file stores, buckets), have the owner include or exclude each explicitly, freeze writers or record a watermark, and reconcile per dataset with an order-free checksum on both sides (L-MIG-086), recorded outside IDMC's 1,000-row activity log. Refines L-MIG-086.
evidence: 807 must-migrate objects / 4.96B rows; about 10.3 % in the target at the time; 5 datasets 'mismatch_source_changed' because the source was written after capture started (2026-11-01)

title: A wide 'one table for everything' target used about 11x the bytes per row of the legacy estate: project the disk before loading billions of rows
text: The migration target (one wide table with JSON payload columns per record) used about 626 bytes per row against about 54 for the legacy estate, so the rows still to load projected to 2.1-2.8 TiB against 2.46 TiB free. Measure bytes per row from the first loaded batches (`system.parts` bytes on disk / rows) per record kind, project the full load including rerun duplicates and masked rows, and resize or redesign before the lanes run for days. At the observed 12.4M rows/hour the remaining 3.27B rows would also have taken about 11 days of failure-free running.
evidence: 256.76 GiB / 440.67M rows = about 626 B/row vs 309.1 GiB / 6.15B rows legacy; 2.46 TiB free of 2.88 TiB (2026-11-01)

title: Reading a live production database for a migration: use a dedicated reader login so one KILL stops every lane, and stream instead of grouping
text: Eleven capture lanes that grouped wide rows on the live source pushed its server memory to the limit and production queries started failing. Because all lanes used one dedicated migration reader login, a single `KILL QUERY WHERE user = '<reader>'` freed the memory in seconds without touching production sessions. Use a separate login per migration so you can kill it as a unit, stream rows (no GROUP BY over wide rows) on a live source, cap memory per query and run at most about 3 heavy lanes. Refines L-CDI-292.
evidence: Source memory 63.7 of 64 GB; 3 production queries hit the memory limit; after the kill memory fell to 2.2 GB (2026-11-01)

title: Audit a previous automated build before extending it: count mappings, read full-run history, check lineage is real, and confirm each stage ran on the intended entity
text: A pipeline built earlier by another coding agent looked busy but delivered little: hundreds of one-per-table mappings with all logic in source SQL, run ids typed into expressions by hand, address verification run against a national address-point table instead of the entity table, no golden records at all, and every full-scale workflow failed while only pilot slices landed. Before adding to an inherited build: inventory objects by pattern, read the full-run history (not the pilot runs), check lineage columns come from runtime variables, and sample the output of each stage against the entity it was meant to process. The audit collapsed the build to about 8 mappings. Refines L-CDI-115.
evidence: 357 mappings / 354 tasks / 149 workflows with 16 MB of task SQL; 222 mappings with hand-typed run ids; 0 entity addresses verified; 431M rows and no golden record; all 62 full archive workflows 'Aborted by agent disconnection'; 6 real patterns -> ~8 mappings and 12.6 KB of SQL; 2 forgotten schedules still burning jobs

title: Probing a Secure Agent host without sudo gives false 'agent down' results: its listeners show as java, and its home is unreadable
text: On a VM where the agent runs as its own user, a non-root check found nothing: `ss -ltnp | grep infaagent` matches nothing because the agent's listeners belong to `java` processes, and the agent home owned by the agent user is unreadable to the login user, so log and app-directory checks fail too. Run host checks with `sudo` (or as the agent user), match processes by install path (`ps -eo pid,user,args | grep <agent_home>`) rather than by name, and confirm with `GET /api/v2/agent/details/<agentId>` engine states. Two audit 'anomalies' reversed once re-run with sudo.
evidence: 2026-09-16: a non-sudo pass suggested the agent was missing; the sudo pass showed agentcore and its services running

title: Catalog scans on the agent that also runs CDC overlapped a CDC job failure: schedule scans outside CDC load and timed test windows
text: On one shared agent VM, 40 minutes of CDGC catalog scans (an Oracle source and an IICS rescan) ran while a load test drove the pipeline; a Database Ingestion CDC job failed mid-window with the host load average near 35 and had to be resumed. Run catalog scans one at a time, outside load tests and demos, and if you can, on an agent that does not also carry the CDC job. After any scan window, check CDC job status before trusting freshness numbers. Refines L-AGENT-109.
evidence: scans 16:11-16:51Z; CDC job FAILED 16:28Z at agent load about 35; resumed 16:55Z (2026-10-08)

title: A legacy STOMP publisher must omit content-length so JMS consumers (Artemis, Qpid JMS, CAI JMS/AMQP listeners) receive a TextMessage
text: When a test harness plays a legacy JMS publisher over STOMP into ActiveMQ Artemis, a frame that carries a content-length header becomes a BytesMessage on the JMS side, while one without it becomes a TextMessage, which is what a text/XML listener and a JMS-to-Kafka bridge process expect. With stomp.py, send with `auto_content_length=False`, persistent, to ANYCAST queues, and carry the business ids as message properties whose names are Java identifiers (L-CAI-123). Refines L-CAI-123.
evidence: harness test proved frames go out without content-length, persistent, ANYCAST, with properties; the CAI JMS-to-Kafka bridge consumed them in the live drills (2026-10-08)

title: Timer-driven CAI processes cost runs even when idle: 1 run a minute is 1,440 a day (about 43,800 a month) per process, 1 every 10 s is 262,800 a month
text: Every start of a process counts as one CAI API call, including timer starts that find nothing to do. A poller or retry sweep started every minute costs about 43,800 runs a month per process, and one started every 10 s about 262,800, before any message flows; 13 such publishers at 10 s would add about 3.4M a month. When a design needs frequent polling, start the process once a minute and loop the poll or sweep inside that run (Wait steps), or use an event source instead of a timer. Show timer runs as a separate fixed line next to the per-message calls (L-CAI-148). Refines L-CAI-148.
evidence: measured day: 48 timer runs beside 1,960 message runs; projection: a retry sweep at 10 s = 262,800 idle runs a month vs about 43,800 at one run a minute with the sweep inside (2026-10-09)

title: Documented CAI limits to check before a design: Kafka on the Cloud Server only on AWS pods, Kafka connection and processes on the same agent, no step retry policy, fault alerts need Suspend on Fault, no cron schedules
text: From the CAI guides (Kafka Connector April 2025, Design and Monitor April 2026): the Kafka connector on the Cloud Server is supported only on AWS-hosted pods, and on a Secure Agent the Kafka connection and the processes that use it must run on the same agent; header values arrive as strings, and offset/commit behavior is set only through extra Camel consumer properties. A Designer step has no retry-count or backoff setting: a retry is a Wait step plus a Jump (BPEL has a Retry-Policy Service). An email or custom service on process fault fires only for processes with Suspend on Fault, and a suspended process resumes from the faulted step. Schedules offer Once, Intraday, Daily, Weekly and Monthly with a time zone and default to 'skip if previous still running'; there are no cron expressions and the scheduler keeps no run history. Documented, not lab-tested, except that L-CAI-142 shows agent schedules not firing. Refines L-CAI-051.
evidence: Kafka guide pp.8, 13, 15-16; Design guide pp.209, 241; Monitor guide pp.34, 59, 61 (docs read 2026-10-12)

title: Anonymous processes published to a Secure Agent answer with no login on the agent's process-engine port: keep that port local and front any screen with an authenticating proxy
text: A process with anonymous access published to an agent can be called by anyone who reaches the agent host's process-engine port (`http://<agent-host>:7080/process-engine/public/rt/<process>`), with no IDMC login. A final security sweep found three such demo processes reachable on the host's internal port. Bind or firewall the port so only local callers reach it. When a static web page must call processes, route it through a reverse proxy on the host that enforces basic auth or SSO and forwards only an allow-listed set of process names (one `POST /cai/<process>` route). Add allowed users or groups to any process that is not meant to be public. Refines L-CAI-038.
evidence: 3 anonymous processes flagged in the hygiene sweep; process engine answered on 7080 and 7443 on the host; proxy route checked with caddy adapt (2026-10-09, 2026-10-12)

title: An Oracle catalog scan fails with ORA-00942 on SYS.DBA_* views until the scan user has SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE
text: The CDGC Oracle scanner reads the database's data-dictionary views (SYS.DBA_*), not only the schema's own tables. With a schema user that owns the tables but has no dictionary access, the first Metadata Extraction failed with ORA-00942 (table or view does not exist) on SYS.DBA_* views. Grant the scan user read-only dictionary access (`GRANT SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE TO <user>`), then rescan; give it no write privileges. Make this grant part of the database user setup, before the catalog source is created.
evidence: first scan FAILED with ORA-00942 on SYS.DBA_*; after GRANT SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE the rescan COMPLETED: 1 PDB, 1 schema, 5 tables (2026-10-08)

title: Put systems the catalog cannot scan (Kafka topics, JMS queues, CAI processes, BI workbooks) into lineage as real artifacts in a File System catalog source, joined by curated edges
text: When the catalog has no scanner for a hop (here Kafka topics, JMS queues, CAI processes and BI workbooks), do not invent nodes. Drop genuine artifacts into a folder cataloged by a File System catalog source: one captured message per topic and queue, the exported XML definitions of the published CAI processes, and the exported workbook definitions. Then publish curated table-level edges (L-CDGC-179) from those files to the ledger, warehouse and target tables the scanners did catalog. A walk over the lineage segments (L-CDGC-181) then runs end to end from the queue files to the database targets and the workbooks. Label these nodes as stand-ins wherever you show them. Refines L-CDGC-233.
evidence: 41 curated edges; graph walk 77 nodes, 120 edges; from the JMS queue files to all 5 database tables and all 3 workbooks; 6 business chains checked hop by hop (2026-10-08)

title: An IICS rescan does not resolve a mapping's reference to a newly cataloged database: merge the connection assignment onto the new source yourself
text: After a new CDI mapping wrote to an Oracle target and a new Oracle catalog source was scanned, the IICS catalog source rescan still left the mapping's Oracle connection reference unresolved: that source's lineage filter and its existing assignments only covered the endpoints known when it was set up (the warehouse and the ledger database). The hop appeared only after a connection-assignment MERGE of the Oracle connection reference onto the new Oracle catalog source. When you add a new endpoint system to an existing lineage story, plan four steps: scan the new source, rescan IICS, assign the connection, then read the lineage segment to prove the hop. Refines L-CDGC-146.
evidence: IICS rescan COMPLETED with the Oracle reference unresolved; connection-assignment merge done 5 minutes later; scanner lineage gold -> mapping task -> 5 Oracle tables (2026-10-08)

title: Tune a CLAIRE intelligent structure model headless: flip the model editor's switches inside the model JSON, then create it
text: The model string the structure-discovery service returns (`aModelString`) is `<header>|<base64 of zlib-compressed JSON>`. Decode it, walk `rmodel.script.statementChildren`, and apply the editor's own switches before saving: (1) for each top-level details group with `projectToSeparateGroup` = "1", set it to "0" so its fields join the document's row (one row per document; repeating tables of type ARRAY keep their own group, one row per line); (2) for each free-text node (`blob*`, statementType STRING), set `isExport` = "1" and `projectToSeparateGroup` = "0" so the text CLAIRE left out reaches an output port and an Expression can parse it. Re-encode (zlib, base64, same header) and continue the normal create flow (L-CDI-223). This recovered fields the default discovery dropped (vendor id, tax id, remit e-mail, account number, auto-renew) without custom code. Refines L-CDI-223.
evidence: 6 models tuned and created; one parsing mapping then structured 27 of 27 documents (PDF, XLSX, CSV) into 124 rows with 0 Unidentified and 0 failed rows, run twice (2026-10-07)

title: A Structure Parser built on a tuned model has record_PK and record_FK ports that are not model nodes: their stored id is the record root's node id
text: When a mapping generator builds a Structure Parser's output groups from the model's nodes, a tuned model's record group also carries `record_PK` (and `record_FK` on child groups), keys CLAIRE adds per record. They have no node of their own in `rmodel.script`, so a generator that looks every port up by node failed with KeyError 'record_PK'. In a designer-built parser these ports map to the record root's `uniqueId` (the first statementChild of the script), string 255. Add them explicitly with that id when you generate the parser, or the package will not match what the designer produces. Refines L-CDI-230.
evidence: KeyError 'record_PK' in the generator; adding both keys with the root's uniqueId produced a package that imported and ran 27 of 27 documents (2026-10-07)

title: SUM(NULL) in an Aggregator fails the run: TE_7002 'constant operand evaluated to NULL not allowed'
text: An Aggregator output written as `SUM(NULL)` (meant as 'no value for this row type') validated but the run failed: `TE_7002 Transformation stopped due to a fatal error in the mapping. The expression [SUM(NULL)] contains the following errors [<<PM Parse Error>> [NULL]: constant operand evaluated to NULL not allowed]`. Aggregate a real port, or emit the null outside the aggregate (for example an Expression after the Aggregator, or `IIF(<cond>, <port>, NULL)` inside SUM over a port).
evidence: Run FAILED with TE_7002; summing the real price port instead ran SUCCESS (2026-10-07)

title: Splitting a pipeline into many small mapping tasks costs about 30 s of start-up per task in a linear taskflow
text: Rebuilding a document pipeline as 8 small mappings (one per stage folder, 3 to 10 transformations each, easy to show in the designer) instead of fewer large ones moved the end-to-end time from about 3.5 to about 4.5-4.75 minutes with the same data: each extra task added roughly 30 s of session start-up regardless of rows. Choose the split deliberately: small mappings for readability, few mappings (or a DAG with concurrency, L-MIG-056) for speed. Refines L-MIG-056.
evidence: Two full runs of the 8-step taskflow: 286 s and 260 s, against about 210 s before the split, same outputs (2026-10-07)

title: Build a headless mapping with an Oracle target when your generator has no Oracle target type: copy the target shape from one UI-authored native Oracle target
text: A mapping generator that only knew warehouse and file targets had no Oracle target shape. Author one throwaway mapping with a native Oracle connector target in the designer, export it, and reshape the generated targets to match its target element and attributes; the import then came back valid and ran. A truncate-and-reload pattern worked: the session log shows `TRUNCATE TABLE <schema>.<table>`, the DataDirect Oracle wire-protocol writer and the Post SQL completing. Stamp every row with a run id, write one run-audit row per run, and verify the load row for row against the source (per key, per item, totals), not by counts alone.
evidence: import valid=true; first run 43,361 rows, 0 failed, 47 s; appended as a taskflow step (the taskflow then costs 4 jobs a run); Oracle matched the warehouse exactly: 111/111 orders, 101/101 items, 25/25 mart rows, 43,359 lines, same money total (2026-10-08)

title: Tableau V3 target: nativeType char_string is accepted but every string column publishes as '0.0'; use text
text: In a generated mapping whose target is the Tableau V3 connector, string ports declared with nativeType `char_string` (Java type String) validated, ran SUCCESS and published the data source, but every value of those columns in the published Hyper extract read '0.0'; numeric (`double`) columns were correct. Declaring the same ports with nativeType `text` published the real strings. A green run is not proof here: read the published extract back (Hyper API or a Tableau query) and compare it with the source before pointing a dashboard at it, because a filter on the broken text column silently matches nothing and an unfiltered sum shows the wrong total. Refines L-CDI-251.
evidence: Runs 8 and 9 SUCCESS with grain/channel = '0.0' on all 3 rows, numbers 52/40/100 correct; redeployed with nativeType text, next run published the real labels and the card check passed (2026-10-19)

title: Tableau V3 target: an invalid targetOperation in the plain attribute is silently ignored, the writer uses Create, and the second run fails 403007
text: Setting `targetOperation` = `Replace` in the writer's operation and runtime attribute sets (without the `targetOperation$` parameter form) raised no error at import or validation; the deployed mapping still showed Replace, but the session ran with Create. The first run published; every later run failed in the 'Tableau Rest Runner' step with Tableau error 403007 because the data source already existed. Putting the same bad value in `targetOperation$` fails fast instead ('Exception occurred while converting [targetOperation$] value [Replace] to [Parameter]'). The adapter only knows create/append/overwrite: use `Overwrite` in both forms, and check the session log line 'Target Operation - ...' (TABLEAUV3_10000) to see what the writer actually used. Refines L-CDI-251.
evidence: Mapping JSON read back with Replace; session log TABLEAUV3_10000 '[FATAL] Utils : Tableau Rest Runner: Error Code: 403007'; adapter class strings list create/append/overwrite; Overwrite runs repeated and overwrote the same data source id (2026-10-19)

title: SharePoint Online CDI source: adding fields the connector's object metadata does not list kills the run with 'DTM process terminated unexpectedly'
text: A SharePoint document-library source exposes a fixed field list in its imported metadata (for files: TimeCreated, UniqueId, Exists, ServerRelativeUrl, TimeLastModified, ItemCount, ProgID, Name, WelcomePage and a few more). Adding other SP.File properties to the source by hand in the IMF (for example Length and UIVersionLabel, hoping the connector maps them by name) imported and validated, but the run failed at once with 0 rows: 'Internal error. The DTM process terminated unexpectedly.' Re-importing the previous export restored the run. Read only the fields the connector lists; get size and version from another path (the connector's downloaded file, Microsoft Graph from a CAI process, or the library's list item fields). This is a second cause of that error besides the login failure in L-CONN-109. Refines L-CONN-109.
evidence: Run with the two extra fields: state 3, 0/0 rows, DTM terminated; rollback import then 33/33 rows SUCCESS (2026-10-07)

title: The SharePoint Online connector's UniqueId is the same GUID SharePoint uses in its own file links
text: The `UniqueId` field the CDI SharePoint Online source returns for a file equals the file GUID inside SharePoint's own document web links. Use it as the stable document key between the connector's rows, links shown in a dashboard, and Microsoft Graph lookups, instead of the path or name, which change on rename or move.
evidence: Connector UNIQUE_ID compared with the GUIDs in the library's web links for the xlsx and csv files: identical (2026-10-07)

title: The native Oracle connector needs no runtime-environment selections change and no engine restart: the planned 'connector enablement' window was not needed
text: The build plan assumed that adding Oracle meant enabling a connector on the shared Secure Agent, which would briefly restart its engines, so the Oracle stage was held back until other lanes finished verifying. In fact the native Oracle connector was already part of the agent's Data Integration service: the connection was created and its test answered success with no selections PUT and no restart. Check the agent's installed connectors, or simply create and test the connection, before you schedule a disruptive enablement window. Third-party JDBC drivers are different (L-CONN-049, L-CONN-051).
evidence: GET /api/v2/connection/test/<id> -> 200 'The test for this connection was successful.' in 1.3 s, no selections PUT, no restart (2026-10-08); the stage had been delayed waiting for an enablement window

title: SharePoint Online document-library write: the connector does not create a missing folder; the upload fails '<path> :Error 404 Not Found'
text: A mapping writing files to a document library (ServerRelativeUrl = target folder, Name = file, bytes from the connection's Attachment_File_Path on the agent, L-CONN-107) staged the files correctly but failed with `[FATAL] /sites/<site>/Shared Documents/<folder>/<subfolder> :Error 404 Not Found` because the sub-folder did not exist. The writer posts to GetFolderByServerRelativeUrl(...)/Files/add and does not create the path. Create every target folder first (SharePoint REST `/_api/web/folders`, Microsoft Graph, or a pre-processing step) and make the folder names deterministic from the data. Refines L-CONN-107.
evidence: Task 1b: files staged on the agent, upload FAILED 404 for a not-yet-created per-solicitation folder (2026-10-13); later runs after the folders existed transferred every version at the Salesforce file sizes

title: After an agent's egress IP changes, add it to Salesforce Network Access through the Metadata API with an admin user; an integration user gets INSUFFICIENT_ACCESS
text: A Salesforce connection or catalog source that logs in with a password (no security token) works only from trusted IP ranges (L-CONN-110), so moving the agent to a new host breaks it until the new egress IP is added. Headless: retrieve the `Security` settings metadata, add one `ipRanges` entry (start = end = the new IP), deploy, and read the setting back; keep the retrieved file as the undo. The Metadata API needs a user with ModifyAllData or ModifyMetadata: the integration user answered `INSUFFICIENT_ACCESS: use of the Metadata API requires a user with the ModifyAllData or ModifyMetadata permissions`. The Salesforce `sf` CLI used for this crashed on Node 20 (a bundled library needs Node 22+): a portable Node 22 next to it fixed that. Prove with one catalog scan or a Salesforce read task from the new agent. Refines L-CONN-110.
evidence: Diff of the deployed setting = exactly one new range, read back with 5 trusted ranges; Test Connection and a Salesforce catalog scan logged in from the new IP (2026-10-19)

title: Unused logical replication slots on a CDC source fill its disk: find which slot the live CDC job uses before dropping the rest
text: On a demo PostgreSQL host that fed Database Ingestion CDC, leftover replication slots from earlier tasks kept retaining WAL: about 700 MB, which pushed the data disk to 92% against an 85% rule. Before dropping anything, map each slot in pg_replication_slots to a running CDC task (a polling job's slot shows active=f between cycles, L-DBMI-016), drop only the orphans, and set max_slot_wal_keep_size so a forgotten slot cannot fill the disk again (L-DBMI-014). Include a slot and disk check in every pre-demo checklist. Refines L-DBMI-014.
evidence: data disk 92% full; about 700 MB held by unused slots; left untouched pending a slot-to-task mapping (2026-10-12)

title: Azure actual cost headless: when the costmanagement CLI extension has no query, POST the Cost Management query API with az rest, once, with no retry loop
text: Some Azure CLI builds' `costmanagement` extension exposes only `export`, so `az costmanagement query` fails. Call the REST API: `az rest --method post --url https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<sub>/providers/Microsoft.CostManagement/query?api-version=2023-11-01 --body @q.json` with `{"type":"ActualCost","timeframe":"MonthToDate","dataset":{"granularity":"Daily","aggregation":{"totalCost":{"name":"PreTaxCost","function":"Sum"}},"grouping":[{"type":"Dimension","name":"ResourceGroupName"}]}}` (or timeframe Custom with timePeriod from/to). It throttles hard with 429: after back-to-back calls every retry of a backoff loop stayed at 429, so make single calls minutes apart and cache the result. Month-to-date cost by resource group still lists groups that were deleted, which shows a teardown and lets you read the forward run-rate from the falling daily total. `az disk list` returned empty without `-g`.
evidence: 2026-09-15: query subcommand absent; a daily query got 429 on every retry; deleted groups still billed month-to-date; the daily total fell from about $39 to about $12 as residuals rolled off

title: Query Azure Log Analytics without the CLI extension: az rest against api.loganalytics.io, naming the real mount points
text: When `az monitor log-analytics query` is unavailable (extension not installed), get the workspace GUID (customerId) through ARM and run `az rest --method post --resource https://api.loganalytics.io --url https://api.loganalytics.io/v1/workspaces/<guid>/query --body @q.json` with `{"query":"Perf | where CounterName=='% Free Space' | where InstanceName in ('/','/data') | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, CounterValue) by InstanceName"}`. Name the mount points explicitly, because an unfiltered disk query is flooded by snap and overlay mounts. Use it to re-check an agent host's data disk before trusting an old 'disk nearly full' note (a remembered 97% was really 77%).
evidence: 2026-09-15: agent-host monitoring data flowing; free space per mount returned; unfiltered output dominated by snap/overlayfs mounts

title: Azure tag writes from git-bash can silently no-op, and az resource tag without -i replaces every tag: address by -g/-n, merge with -i, read back after a few seconds
text: `az tag update --resource-id <long ARM id> --operation Merge` and `az resource tag --ids <long ARM id>` returned no error but did not change a VM's tags under git-bash (the az.cmd wrapper mangles the long `--ids` value and drops large JSON output), and `az vm update --set tags.k=v` did not land either. What worked: `az group update -n <rg> --set tags.k=v` for a resource group, and `az resource tag -g <rg> -n <name> --resource-type Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines -i --tags k=v` for a resource. Without `-i`, `az resource tag` replaces the whole tag set, so pass `-i` or resend the existing tags. Tag reads lag writes by a few seconds: wait about 6 s before the read-back, and capture stdout and stderr through python instead of redirecting az straight to a file. Refines L-ENV-016.
evidence: 2026-09-16: three write forms were silent no-ops with unchanged read-backs; the short -g/-n -i form landed and read back after a 6 s wait

title: Before deleting or keeping a cloud app stack, check what it really runs: a container on the platform's quickstart image is a placeholder, not a deployment
text: A resource group that looked like a full duplicate deployment (web app, container app, Postgres, serverless document DB, key vault, storage) had no IDMC footprint at all, and its container app ran `mcr.microsoft.com/k8se/quickstart:latest`, the platform's hello-world image. Before a keep or delete decision, inspect each compute resource's image or package, its app settings for IDMC connection references, and the resource-group tags (purpose, keep markers), and inventory its data stores first because deletion is irreversible. When ownership is unclear, label both sides with additive tags (legacy/new, which one holds the IDMC connection) instead of deleting.
evidence: 2026-09-16: 8 resource groups, 62 resources, 1 VM; the duplicate stack's container image was the quickstart placeholder

title: Azure CLI behind a TLS-intercepting corporate proxy fails with 'Certificate verification failed': trust the proxy's root CA
text: On a laptop whose HTTPS exits through an inspecting proxy, Azure CLI calls (including the `vm run-command invoke` used to drive an agent VM) can fail mid-session with 'Certificate verification failed. This typically happens when using Azure CLI behind a proxy that intercepts traffic with a self-signed certificate.' Export the proxy's root CA and point `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` at a bundle that contains it (the CLI's Python honours it); do not disable verification. It can appear intermittently when the egress path changes, so make scripts that drive a VM through az surface this error instead of a generic failure.
evidence: 2026-10-03: the error ended a run-command loop mid-task; split egress (proxy and direct paths) observed 2026-09-16. The CA-bundle fix is the CLI's documented remedy, not re-tested in this session

title: A free Oracle database for IDMC and CAI demos: Oracle Database 23ai Free in a container next to the Secure Agent
text: Run the `gvenzl/oracle-free:23-slim` image (Oracle Database 23ai Free) as a compose service on the agent host: bind 127.0.0.1:1521 only so just the local Secure Agent reaches it, set mem_limit about 3 GB and cpus 1.5, rotate its json-file logs, restart unless-stopped, and create the schema in the pluggable database FREEPDB1. The edition is free to license and capped at 2 CPU threads, 2 GB of memory and 12 GB of user data, which suits demos. The same container served CDI loads, a CDGC Oracle catalog source (with SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE, see the ORA-00942 lesson) and PL/SQL APIs exposed through Oracle REST Data Services for CAI (L-CAI-146).
evidence: container healthy; version banner 23.x Free; 5 tables, 43k rows; whole-host memory caps 6.2 GB including Oracle (2026-10-08)

title: A free event stack for CAI listener demos on one VM: single-node KRaft Kafka, ActiveMQ Artemis, PostgreSQL and a Kafka console, all on localhost beside the Secure Agent
text: Compose these on the agent's VM: `apache/kafka-native:4.1.0` (single-node KRaft, no ZooKeeper), `apache/activemq-artemis:2.42.0-alpine` (AMQP 5672 and core 61616 for the JMS/AMQP side), `postgres:16-alpine` for a ledger, and `redpandadata/console` for topics, partitions, consumer-group lag and message headers/key/value. Publish every service on 127.0.0.1 only, so the CAI event sources on the same agent connect locally (the Kafka connection and its processes must run on the same agent), and put any human-facing console behind a reverse proxy with basic auth. Keep data directories on the data disk owned by the container uids (Kafka 1000, Artemis 1001). In customer material, say that one node is a demo shape, not the 3-replica production design.
evidence: stack up in under 1 minute; CAI listeners consumed from it for days; 600/600 delivered through a mid-stream listener restart (2026-10-08)

title: ActiveMQ Artemis crash-loops with 'Initial heap size set to a larger value than the maximum heap size' when you cap only -Xmx
text: The Artemis image starts the JVM with a default -Xms512M. Setting only a lower -Xmx (for example 384M) to fit a shared agent host makes the broker exit at once and the container restart forever with 'Error occurred during initialization of VM: Initial heap size set to a larger value than the maximum heap size'.
